Zachary snapped the bottles back into their loops, took the gauze and tape and the card, and carried them over. "We're rinsing it with water," he announced. "Fresh instructions." He held up the card. "Doctor if it's deep, gaping, or won't stop bleeding. Yours is just a line, so you're probably fine."

Mr. Vogel held out his thumb, and Zachary wrapped the gauze around it, then around again to replicate the first loop exactly, and tore the tape with his teeth.

"That's the neatest bandage I've ever seen on this thumb," Mr. Vogel said. "Ever consider a career in banking?"

Zachary peeled the backing off a butterfly strip, smoothed it down across the cut, and said, "Hold still. I'm not done."

The X-ray tech slid the film onto the light board, and Kate forgot all about her throbbing arm. Her bones glowed white against a gray blur that she guessed was her skin, like a ghost hand drawn in chalk. "Thea's going to think this is so cool," she said. Her mom was filling out forms at the desk, so the only person near the exam room door was Mr. Choi, her neighbor, who had driven them when the coach called from the gym.

"Coach said you supervise the climbers all day, and I still managed to fall off the wall," Kate said, feeling foolish. Mr. Choi waved that away and leaned closer to the light board with her.

"I heard the doctor tell your mom it's a clean break," he said. "You'll get a cast."

Kate stared at the film. She had assumed X-rays worked like photographs, but a photograph showed skin perfectly, and here her skin was barely visible while the bones burned white. She thought about the museum gift shop where she'd once bought a counterfeit fossil, a fake with a plastic skeleton glued inside real rock. You could tell it was fake by shining a strong light through it; the plastic showed up darker than the stone. Her arm was doing the opposite of that. Something in her bones was soaking up the X-rays, the way a wall soaks up a flashlight beam, while her skin let them pass right through. "The calcium," she said slowly. "The calcium in my bones absorbs more of the X-rays than the softer stuff around them. That's why they show up white and my skin barely shows at all."

Mr. Choi smiled, and just then the doctor came in, so Kate decided to test her idea on someone who would actually know. "Can I ask something?" she said. "Is it the calcium? That's why the bones are white?"

The doctor looked at the film, then at her, clearly pleased. "That's exactly right. The calcium in your bones absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them, so the bones come out white."

"Like a laser pointer stopped by a wall but shining straight through a window," Kate said.

"Close enough," the doctor said, and started unwrapping the roll of cast material. "Pick a color."

Kate pointed with her good arm at the bright purple on the shelf. "That one. And can I keep the X-ray? I want to show Thea and Tori what calcium looks like when it wins."

"You'll have to beat them to the signature line," the doctor said, holding out a marker. "Who's first?"

Alyssa sat in the third row of the town hall with her notebook open on her knees. The room smelled like coffee and folding chairs, and the overhead lights gave the wooden stage a strange luminous glow. She had come because her class assignment was to ask a real question about government, and Imane had dared her to actually speak into the microphone instead of just writing the question down.

The panel was talking about a new bike-path bill that had been in the news. Alyssa had read that the House had passed one version and the Senate had passed another, and she could not figure out which one would become the law. She raised her hand, and when the moderator called on her, she stood up so fast her chair squeaked. "There are two versions of the bill," she said. "Which one wins?"

A man in the front row, Mr. Zhang, who ran the garden store near her school, turned around. "Neither one wins yet," he said. "The House version has to pass the Senate too, exactly the same, word for word. A bill has to pass both the House and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president."

Alyssa wrote that down, underlining it twice. So it was not a race between the two versions at all. She had been sorting the bills into a category called "winners" and a category called "losers," but that was the wrong way to think about it. The two versions had to match first, like two copies of the same recipe. She tried to paraphrase it in her own words so she would remember. "So the House bill and the Senate bill have to become one bill, the same in every word, and then it goes to the president to sign."

"Exactly," Mr. Zhang said, and the moderator nodded.

After the meeting, Markus from her class caught her by the door. "Did you actually talk into the microphone?" he asked. "I heard you from the back."

"It wasn't that scary," Alyssa said, which was not quite true. She tore out the notebook page, folded it, and put it in her back pocket. "I'm going to read it to the class tomorrow."

Piper stood in the middle of the guest room with a rolled-up rug in her arms and a question in her head. Grandma arrived in two hours, and Mom had handed her the rug without a word, pointing at the hallway. Piper carried it to the garage, then went back and stared at the pale rectangle it left on the floor. Why that rug? The doormat stayed. The bathroom rug stayed. She walked the whole house, counting: every rug by the stairs, gone; every flat mat in a corner, still there.

She found Mom wrestling the guest room curtain rod. "Grandma can step over a rug," Piper said. "She's not that old." Mom shook her head. "Grandma's sixty-eight, and in the United States, falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged sixty-five and older." Piper repeated the words silently. Not car crashes, not illness. Falls. She had never once thought about a rug as something dangerous.

Outside in the backyard, Leland and Keegan were stringing a banner between the fence posts, and the smell of the hamburgers Dad was grilling drifted across the grass. "We need to check the yard too," Piper told them. "Grandma will want to sit out here." She tested her idea the only way she could think of: she filled a watering can almost full, like a person who couldn't recover balance quickly, and walked every path Grandma might take. The loose flagstone near the tomato pots wobbled under her sneakers. The garden hose, coiled across the walk, caught her toe. "That would do it," she said, and dragged the hose flat against the fence.

Keegan tested the flagstone himself, jumping on it twice. "It rocks like a seesaw," he reported. Piper pried it up and packed sand underneath until it sat solid, then stepped on it, stepped off, stepped on again. Leland held the banner higher so it wouldn't brush anyone's head going through the gate. "You're kind of nurturing this whole yard," he said, and Piper laughed, because that was exactly what it felt like, tending every sharp corner and wobbly stone until the place was safe to land on.

At dinner that first night, Grandma mentioned she'd had a dizzy spell last month. "The doctor said it was an inner ear thing, not anything serious," she added, waving her fork. "A diagnosis, finally. I was starting to worry." Piper set down her water glass and watched Grandma walk to the patio door, step over the threshold, and come back without a single wobble. The path held. It would hold all week.

The last evening, Grandma sat in the lawn chair under the banner, which sagged now in a buoyant, lopsided way that made everyone laugh. She looked around the yard, at the flat hose, the steady flagstone, the clear walk. "How did everything get so tidy?" she asked. Piper shrugged, but she was already wondering whether the flagstone by the school gate rocked too, and whether anyone had ever tested it the way she did. "Grandma," she said, "tomorrow, can we go look at a sidewalk together?"

Amelia stood on Grandma's porch with her phone propped against a flowerpot, waiting for the choir call to start. In two weeks the middle school chorus would sing at the spring concert, and Mr. Rodríguez had split them into two parts. Amelia had the melody, the part that came naturally. Suri had the harmony, the part that wandered off somewhere lower and, in Amelia's opinion, seemed designed to drag her along with it.

The problem had shown up at Thursday's rehearsal. Every time Suri's section slid into their notes, Amelia's voice followed them down like a dog following a scent. Mr. Rodríguez stopped the piano and said, "Amelia, you're merging. Hold your line." She tried again and merged again. That was why she was at Grandma's house on a Saturday, because Grandma had a piano in the front room and nobody to complain about the noise.

Suri arrived on her bike ten minutes later with a folder of sheet music and a granola bar for each of them. They stood at the piano, and Suri sang her part alone while Amelia listened without singing, tapping the beat on the piano lid. Then they tried together. Amelia followed her down within four bars.

"It's like my ears take over," Amelia said. "I hear you and I just go."

"Your ears aren't the problem," Grandma said, coming through with a watering can. She set it down and pointed at her own throat. "It's these two little vocal folds in your larynx, right here. They vibrate when air passes between them. You tighten them, the pitch goes up. You loosen them, it goes down."

Amelia put her fingers on her throat and hummed a low note. She could feel a buzz, faint but real, like a phone set to vibrate. She hummed higher and the buzz seemed to quicken under her fingers. So that was what was happening every time she slid after Suri: her folds were loosening, dropping her pitch, and it all happened out of sight inside her neck. She couldn't watch it, but she could feel it and, more importantly, she could control it.

"Sing your part," she told Suri. "I'm going to hold my fingers here and keep my pitch up no matter what."

Suri sang. Amelia pressed lightly on her throat, kept the folds tightened on her own note, and held. Her ears pulled at her, but her fingers reported the truth: steady buzz, steady pitch. When they finished the phrase, Suri stared at her.

"You stayed," Suri said. "Eight whole bars."

"Mr. Rodríguez will be so pleased he might make an extravagant speech about it," Amelia said, and Grandma laughed from the doorway. They ran it again, and this time Amelia let her hands hang at her sides and held the line anyway.

"Monday," Suri said, snapping her folder shut, "you contribute the melody, I contribute the harmony, and nobody merges with anybody."

Amelia touched her throat one last time and hummed.

Ariana sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her notebook open to a page that read, in careful pencil, "My Family in Mandarin." Tomorrow she had to record herself describing her whole family in full sentences, and every sentence so far sounded like a robot reading a grocery list. Wǒ yǒu yī gè māma. Wǒ yǒu yī gè bàba. She said it out loud and wrinkled her nose. Something was missing, and she couldn't see what.

Then she remembered the confusing part. Her flashcards had two words where English had one. She flipped through the stack until she found them. One card said gēge. The other said dìdi. Why would a language need two words for "brother"? She turned the cards over and over, as if the answer might be hiding on the cardboard itself. She was skeptical of her own guess, because it seemed almost too strange: the words cared about order of birth, not just about having a brother at all.

She needed a test case, so she grabbed her tablet and typed a message to Paxton, who was in her Mandarin class and, more importantly, was a twin.

"Question for science," she wrote. "Was your brother born before you or after you? Exact minutes please."

The reply came fast. "After. Ten minutes after. Why?"

Ariana sat back on her heels. Ten minutes. That was shorter than a TV commercial break, and yet in Mandarin it split the word for brother into two. She typed back, "In Mandarin gēge means older brother and dìdi means younger brother. So what does that make YOU?"

The typing bubble appeared, disappeared, appeared again. "Wait. He's only older than me by TEN MINUTES. How is he my gēge? That's like winning a race by one step."

"But he did win," Ariana wrote. "By ten minutes. The language doesn't care about the margin."

For a long moment nothing came back, and Ariana wondered if she'd pushed too hard. Paxton had complained all year about being the "younger twin," and Ariana could almost feel the old resentment coming through the screen, the kind that builds up over years of being handed the smaller piece of cake. Then the reply arrived.

"Okay. Fine. He's my gēge. I'm not happy about it, but it's true. I'll say it in class tomorrow and everything."

Ariana flopped onto her back and laughed at the ceiling. She tried her sentences again, this time with the new words tucked in like puzzle pieces snapping into place. Wǒ yǒu yī gè mèi mei. Wǒ yǒu yī gēge. The robot voice was gone. She could see it now, the pattern hiding inside the language, and it made her wonder what other secrets were waiting in the rest of the flashcards. She reached for the stack, flipped to the next section, and started to read.

Aurora sat on her front steps with the phone warm in her hands, thumbing through the group chat. Jazlyn had posted a poll about the science fair, and Khadija had already voted for volcanoes twice using two different emoji. Aurora was about to type "volcano, obviously" when the chat buzzed with a new message from Jazlyn: Post a selfie from wherever you are RIGHT NOW. Winner gets bragging rights.

She flipped the camera around. Her hair looked good today, the afternoon light was soft, and the porch swing made a nice background. She took three shots, picked the best one, and her thumb hovered over send. Then she noticed something small in the corner of the photo, pale and square against the door frame. She pinched the screen and zoomed in until it filled half the image. The house number. All four digits, crisp and readable.

Jazlyn sent a photo of her own feet on a bus. Khadija sent one from the library, and behind her shoulder Aurora could just make out the edge of the school logo on a banner. Aurora stared at it while her brain tried to digest what she was seeing. Anybody in the chat could look at Khadija's picture and know which school they went to. Anybody who was not even in the chat, if the photo got shared on, could see it too, because once something was posted it never really went away. And her own picture had the house number in it, which meant anyone could work out exactly where it was taken. Not the town. The house.

She thought about last summer, when she had posted a picture of her new bike leaning against the garage, and a comment had appeared from an account with no profile picture: nice bike. She had deleted it and forgotten it. Now the memory sat uncomfortably, like a stone in a shoe. She couldn't see who had written it. That was the trouble. There was no mechanism for knowing who was watching, or how far a photo travelled, or who saved it to their own phone.

Aurora cropped the picture until only her face and a strip of porch railing remained. "Where's your background?" Khadija typed. "Boring steps," Aurora sent back. Then Jazlyn posted her bus selfie again with a caption, "look closer at the window reflection, you can see my stop." Below it she added, "Uh. Maybe delete that one."

Mr. Menon came up the walk with his dog, raising a hand in greeting. Aurora raised the phone, snapped a picture of just the dog, and sent it with the caption, "safest selfie of the day." The chat filled with laughing emoji as she hit send on the cropped one too.

Muhammad stood on the stage of the community theatre with his note cards sweating in his hand. In three days he had to give a two-minute speech at the youth showcase, and his topic was why people should finish antibiotics they're prescribed instead of stopping when they feel better. He had an opening hook: "Imagine feeling sick and then holding a tiny bottle of medicine in your hand." He had three points, and Ms. Bear had written explicit instructions on the signup sheet: hook, three points, closing. But he had no closing at all.

His friend Jaxon sprawled across a red velvet seat in the front row, scrolling his phone. "Just say 'thank you' at the end," Jaxon offered.

"That's not a closing, that's a fire alarm," Muhammad said. He tried reciting his points, pacing the boards. The speech had a start and a middle and then it just fell off a cliff. He wondered why some speeches felt finished and this one didn't. Was there something invisible, some rule he was missing?

Jaxon held up his phone. "Soraya texted." Muhammad climbed down and read the message: "Stuck on your ending? Look at your first line. When a closing returns to the opening hook at the end, it makes a speech feel complete. My brother calls it a callback. Try it."

Muhammad read the message twice. His hook was about the bottle of medicine. So the ending could come back to it. He walked to centre stage and tried it out loud, recounting his three points, then: "So take the pills until the bottle is empty. Because that tiny bottle isn't holding medicine for today. It's holding medicine for the whole war." He paused, half expecting it to fall flat again, but instead the last line seemed to click into place like a stage flat swinging shut.

"Whoa," said Jaxon. "Do that again."

Muhammad grinned, flipped his cards back to the top, and began, "Imagine feeling sick and then holding a tiny bottle of medicine in your hand."

Matthew sat in the waiting room of Ms. Mercado's studio with his fingertips pressed against the cold metal leg of his chair, because cold felt better than the burning he got whenever he touched his guitar strings. He had been playing for exactly one week, and he was ready to draft his letter of resignation. He'd even worked out the first line: "Dear Guitar, this isn't working out."

"You're quitting?" said Denis, who was waiting for his drum lesson and drumming on the armrest of the couch without using his hands at all, which took real talent. "You practiced like four hours last Saturday."

"That was the problem." Matthew held up his left hand. The tips of his fingers were shiny and red, like little strawberries. "The strings dug grooves in them. I played 'Ode to Joy' nine times and now I can't even feel my locker combination."

The studio door opened and Maisie came out, sliding her own guitar into its case. She was two years ahead of Matthew in lessons and could play a riff that made everyone in the school talent show forget about the magic act. She looked at his hand, and instead of saying something sympathetic, she laughed. Then she held out her own left hand, palm up, and tapped her fingertips.

"Feel those," she said.

They were hard, like the heels of a shoe. "Calluses," she said. "Mine used to hurt too. First month, I almost quit. Then I practiced a little every single day instead of four hours once, and the skin got tough."

"Wait," Matthew said slowly. "So practicing more spread out makes it stop hurting?" He turned this over the way he turned over ideas in class, like the time he'd argued in social studies that a monarchy wasn't automatically obsolete just because it was old, and had actually won the debate. Maybe the same thing applied here. Maybe the problem wasn't the guitar. Maybe the problem was the plan.

That evening he made a chart on graph paper: ten minutes a day, every day, no heroics. By Tuesday his fingers still stung. By Friday they stung less. On Wednesday of the next week, he pressed down a chord and felt the strings push back against something that felt like a thin, hard shield, and he played "Ode to Joy" three times in a row without once wincing.

At his next lesson, he walked into Ms. Mercado's studio, sat down, and laid his left hand on the music stand like evidence.

"Listen to this," he said, and hit a G chord that rang out clean and clear all the way to the sidewalk.

Tristan slumped at the kitchen table with his tablet, watching the group chat scroll. It was called Lunch Crew and it had forty-three people in it, which was already strange, since his grade only had two lunch tables. Last night he had posted a photo of himself in his older brother's dinosaur costume, and he had deleted it after ten minutes because it was dumb and his face looked weird. Now it was fine. Gone. He kept checking his page anyway.

Then Chaya posted a screenshot of the dinosaur photo with the caption "TREX LIVES." The chat erupted. Forty-three people could see his costume, his kitchen counter, and, in the corner, the whiteboard on the fridge with their address written on it for the pizza delivery guy. Tristan's stomach dropped. He typed, "I deleted that." Chaya answered fast: "Deleting just takes it off your page. I saved a copy the second I saw it. So did Ezra, probably."

Ezra sent a message: "Guilty." Then, after a pause: "Also, whoever added all those extra people should know they can see everything, including your address, Tristan."

Tristan thought about that. He couldn't see who had taken copies, or how far the photo had traveled, but the whiteboard was a clue. He tried something. He asked Chaya to crop the address out and post the fixed version, so the newer copy would spread instead of the old one. She did it within a minute, because Chaya wanted to be the person who fixed things, the meticulous keeper of the chat who documented every inside joke in a folder she called The Archive. "Already cropping," she said. "I keep records. Deleting is for amateurs."

By evening the cropped version was the one everyone was replying to. Ezra sent a private message: "Old copies are still out there somewhere. Can't un-save what people saved." Tristan read it twice. He texted back, "I know. But at least the address one is crowded out." Then he got up, walked to the fridge, and erased the whiteboard with his sleeve.

Evelyn had clicked the little green "Ad" tag on the same search result four times before Fatimah leaned over her shoulder in the computer lab. "Why do you keep doing that?" Fatimah whispered. Evelyn explained her experiment: type "pangolin extinction" into the search bar, count the real results, then count the ads at the top. She wanted to prove she could tell them apart, because Mr. Malik had said it was a crucial skill and she planned to confess in front of the whole class that she couldn't. That was the plan, anyway. The problem was that every time she clicked an ad, it took her to a strange page about "wildlife sponsorships," and she clicked back and clicked it again, testing whether the ad would follow her like a shadow.

"Stop," said Violet from the next station, not even looking up. "That ad's going to keep coming back no matter how many times you poke it."

Evelyn froze with her finger over the mouse. On the whiteboard at the front of the lab, Mr. Malik had written "TODAY: SEARCH LIKE A DETECTIVE," and beside the projector sat his laptop, which was open to a video he had queued for the class. Evelyn could read the title from her seat: an interview with the owner of a small online plant shop. When Mr. Malik finally pressed play, the shop owner held up a potted fern and said, "Advertisers bid in an auction for search keywords, and usually they pay only when someone clicks their ad. It's called pay-per-click."

The room went quiet except for the fan humming in the corner. Evelyn's stomach dropped. Every click. She looked down at her own screen, at the sponsorship ad she had poked four times, and did the math fast: someone, somewhere, had just paid for four clicks from a girl who wanted a pangolin. She wasn't testing the ad. She was spending a stranger's money.

She raised her hand. "Mr. Malik, I have to confess something before we start."

He paused the video and raised an eyebrow.

Evelyn dragged her chair aside so the whole class could see her screen. "I found out how ads work. The expensive way."

Paige pushed a piece of broccoli around her plate and pretended to chew. Tomorrow was the semifinal, and she was the backup goalie, which meant she might stand in the net for the whole game or for none of it, and her stomach could not decide which one was worse.

"You're quiet," her mother said, spooning rice into her bowl. "Bad day?"

"Not bad exactly." Paige set down her fork. "Emaan says I'll probably have to face at least one penalty shot. She's the regular keeper, and she told me her secret. Before a penalty shot, she breathes out slowly, longer than she breathes in. She says it settles her body down so the stress doesn't take over." She glanced up. "Is that a real thing or just a goalie thing?"

"It's a real thing," her mother said. "Slow breathing with a long exhale is a coping skill. People use it on purpose, right before a stressful moment, because it calms the body's stress response. I do it before big meetings." She smiled a little. "I used it today before I told my boss I needed better boundaries around weekend emails. That word means lines you set so people know what you'll accept. My hands were shaking and my anxiety was doing cartwheels, but I breathed out slow, and it helped."

Paige looked at her plate. In science class, Ms. He had taught them that you couldn't just believe a claim, you had to replicate it, which meant trying the same thing yourself and seeing if you got the same result. Devyn had replicated the herbivore experiment with two mealworms and a pile of leaves, and it had worked. Maybe a goalie's trick could work the same way. She sat up straight, breathed in through her nose, and let the air out slowly, counting to eight while her mother kept talking about Saturday plans.

The tight feeling in her stomach didn't vanish, but it loosened, like a knot someone had worked a finger into. She tried it again, this time while imagining the ball on the penalty spot, the whole gym silent. In, then out, long and slow. Her shoulders dropped an inch.

"Feeling better?" her mother asked.

"I think I replicated Emaan's experiment," Paige said. She picked up the brittle cracker from the side of her plate, snapped off a corner, and ate it. "And it worked. Tomorrow, before that penalty shot, everybody's going to wonder why the goalie looks like she's just smelling the flowers."

Charlie knocked on Griffin's door three times before anyone answered. Griffin's mom opened it a crack and said he was in his room, but she lowered her voice when she said it, the way people talk about someone sleeping.

Griffin was not sleeping. He sat on his floor with his back against the bed, a half-built robot on his knees. "Hey," he said, and then nothing else. His hands moved the screwdriver in tiny circles without actually turning any screws.

Charlie sat down across from him. She had been building a theory all the way over, because Griffin had skipped lunch twice this week and had not laughed at Heinrich's joke on Friday, which never happened. "Is it the competition?" she asked. Griffin's robotics team had won the regional championship in the fall, a big prestigious tournament, and everyone expected them to go to state. "Everyone keeps asking if we'll win again," Griffin said. "Heinrich keeps grabbing my controller to show me stuff. I keep telling him no and he does it anyway." He set the screwdriver down. "I can't sleep. My stomach hurts before school."

Charlie remembered the poster outside Mr. Ngo's health classroom, the one she had read while waiting for the water fountain in September. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She had stood there thinking it was strange that "social" was on the list, right next to emotional, like friends were part of the same system as feelings. At the time it had seemed like a poster fact. Now it seemed like a clue. If social counted, then Heinrich grabbing the controller was not just annoying. It was part of what was making Griffin sick, the same way lost sleep was.

"I made an assumption," Charlie said. "I thought you were just stressed about winning. But it's more than that." She picked up the robot and turned it over. "Heinrich keeps violating your boundaries. You said no and he does it anyway. That's not a small thing."

Griffin looked at the robot in her hands. "I didn't know you could call it that. I thought it meant I was being dramatic."

"You're not being dramatic. Stress is a real thing, anxiety is a real thing, and there are ways of coping with them, and one way is telling the person causing it to knock it off." Charlie handed the robot back. "Want me to text Heinrich?"

Griffin pulled out his phone himself and typed while Charlie watched. He held the screen up so she could read it: "You keep taking my controller after I say no. Stop. I mean it."

"Send it," Charlie said. He did.

Ethan set the pizza dough bowl on the picnic table and glared at it, because the last two batches had come out of the grill oven dry and cakey, more like biscuits than bread. Markus leaned over the fence from next door, and Ethan felt a stab of envy at the perfect-looking bun Markus was eating. "Your dough still sad?" Markus asked. "It's a paradox," Ethan said. "Follow the recipe exactly, get exactly the wrong thing." Ryder arrived on his bike just then, skidding to a stop on the grass. "You can't follow a recipe exactly," he said. "Nobody can."

That was the problem, Ethan realized. He had been measuring the flour by dipping the cup straight into the bag, the way you'd scoop sand at the beach. His grandma had shown him once, spooning flour gently into the cup and leveling it off with a knife, but he'd thought it was just her being fussy about tidiness. Now he wondered if there was a real difference. So he tried an experiment right there at the picnic table. He scooped a cup of flour straight from the bag, dumped it onto the scale, and wrote the number down. Then he spooned flour into the same cup, leveled it, and weighed that too. The scooped cup was heavier, a lot heavier. Same cup, same flour, two different amounts.

"So the recipe thinks a cup is one thing, and your cup is another," Markus said slowly, watching the numbers. Ethan nodded. "Scooping packs the flour down. Weighing it is more accurate than any cup." He was quiet for a second, then said in his most assertive voice, "New rule. Nobody scoops in this backyard." Ryder raised his hand. "What if it's ice cream?" "Ice cream is exempt."

Ethan weighed out the flour for a fresh batch, kneaded it until it felt like an earlobe, which his grandma said was the goal, and slid the dough into a bowl to rise in the sun. When he punched it down an hour later and it sprang back soft and smooth, he whooped so loudly that Markus dropped his bun over the fence. "Dinner's at six!" Ethan called. "Bring your appetite, not your scooping hand."

Carter stood in the kitchen holding six index cards and a kitchen timer, and he said, for the fourth time, "Today I will talk about bees." His dad looked up from chopping an onion and nodded politely. His little sister kept drawing her dinosaur. Carter stopped. He had a two-minute speech due in Ms. Hoang's class on Friday, and it was supposed to have an opening hook, three points and a closing, and so far every practice run had made his family act like furniture.

He tried again in the living room that evening. "Today I will talk about sharks." His dad flipped a page of his magazine without reading it, Carter was almost sure. That was the strange part. His dad liked sharks. So why did everyone's attention drift away the second Carter began? He sat on the arm of the couch and wondered about it. It was like the audience's focus could fluctuate, rising and falling depending on something Carter couldn't see, some rule hiding underneath the words themselves.

On Saturday his friend Charles-Edouard came over, and they watched old speeches on a tablet. One kid started with "Today I will talk about recycling," and Carter felt his own eyes go fuzzy. The next video opened with "Did you know a single beehive can hold fifty thousand bees?" and Carter sat up without meaning to. He rewound it. He watched three more videos, keeping a tally on a napkin, and a pattern appeared. The speeches that grabbed him began with a question, a surprising fact, or a very short story. The boring ones began with an announcement.

"See, it's the first line," Carter said. "It's called a hook. A question, or a weird fact, or a tiny story."

Charles-Edouard frowned. "So it isn't about the topic at all?"

"It's about the opening." Carter grabbed a fresh card. He wrote three hooks for his bee speech: a question, a fact, and a thirty-second story about the time a bee followed him around the backyard for a whole afternoon like a tiny buzzing protagonist. Then he decided to test it, because a pattern on a napkin wasn't proof. Sunday dinner, his whole family at the table, was his laboratory.

He cleared his throat. "Which is smarter, a bee or a pigeon?" The conversation stopped. His sister put down her fork. "A bee," his dad said, "surely." "Wrong," said Carter, and launched into his first point. His sister interrupted twice to argue, which was rude but also, Carter thought, exactly the point. Nobody picked up a phone. Nobody drifted. He finished with his closing line, checked the timer, and grinned. Monday at recess he found Finlay by the fence.

"Hey, Finlay. Want to hear the smartest insect in the world?"

Mila stood at the front of the drama camp's black-box studio, notes shaking in her hand, and began her two-minute speech about why her school should keep its bee garden. "Um, honeybees visit, um, two million flowers just to make one pound of honey," she said. From the front row, Zayden clicked a tally counter with every "um," and by the end of the first run-through it read thirty-one.

Thirty-one felt terrible, but Mila noticed something while she watched the playback on Ms. Friedman's tablet. When she paused silently before her second point, Zayden leaned forward. When she said "um," he glanced at the ceiling. She wondered if the filler words were the problem rather than the nerves underneath, and she had a way to test it. "Count again," she told Zayden, "but this time clap when I pause instead of counting ums."

The second run had fewer than half the ums, because every time she felt one coming, she shut her mouth and let the quiet sit there. The pauses felt enormous to her, like falling, but Zayden clapped twelve times and only sixteen tally marks appeared. Jared, who was writing the closing line of his own speech, looked up and said, "You sound way more confident when you stop like that. It gives me a second to actually take in the point." That matched what Mila had seen on the playback, and she wrote "PAUSE" in red letters at the top of each of her three points.

The camp showcase came on Friday, with parents folding themselves into the small chairs. Mila's opening hook about the two million flowers landed, and when she reached her second point she paused, one second of silence in a room that had been noisy all morning. Nobody fidgeted. Her closing line, "The bees did the work; the least we can do is keep the garden," got a real laugh and then applause.

Afterward Zayden held up the tally counter, which read four. "Four, and two of those were borderline," he said. Mila grinned and tossed her notes into her bag, because even the protagonist of a bee speech deserves a break, and trivial mistakes were just data now. "Same time tomorrow?" Jared asked, waving his still-unfinished closing line at her. "Bring the counter," Mila said.

Jaxson's whole week had started to revolve around the science project on Ms. Sánchez's back table: a battery, a bulb, a switch, and three wires that were supposed to make light. Yesterday it had worked. The bulb had glowed like a tiny sun every time he flipped the switch, and Tristen had clapped so loudly that a kid two rooms over probably heard it. Today, on demo day, he flipped the switch and nothing happened. The bulb sat there, dark and smug, like it was keeping a secret.

"Maybe the bulb died of boredom," Tristen said, leaning over Jaxson's shoulder. The table smelled like pencil shavings and the orange peel somebody had left there since Monday.

"It worked yesterday," Jaxson said. "That's the part that's making me crazy." He wiggled each wire where it clamped to the battery. He unscrewed the bulb and screwed it back. He clicked the switch up, down, up, down, and even held it halfway, which Finley said was like standing in the median between on and off. Still dark. Finley offered a replacement bulb from her kit, and the whole class watched, because whether Jaxson's project could be fixed had somehow become the most controversial question of the morning, bigger even than whether cafeteria pizza counted as breakfast.

Then Jaxson stopped moving his hands and thought. Something invisible had to be the problem, because everything he could see looked fine. A circuit was a loop, and the loop only lit the bulb if something was flowing through it. What if the thing flowing had stopped, not because of a broken wire, but because the battery itself had run out? Yesterday he had left the switch on by accident, all afternoon and all night. The battery could have been slowly using itself up the whole time. "Tristen," he said slowly, "hand me the battery out of Finley's kit."

He swapped it in, pressed the wires tight, and flipped the switch. The bulb blazed. The class actually cheered, and Ms. Sánchez raised both eyebrows like she'd won something.

"So what happened?" she asked.

"The battery turns its stored chemical energy into electrical energy," Jaxson said, holding the old battery up like evidence in a trial, "and when those chemicals get used up, it goes flat. Mine went flat, because I left my switch on overnight and drained it." He turned the dead battery over in his fingers and grinned. "This little guy worked himself to the bone."

"Rest in peace," Tristen said, saluting the battery.

Jaxson dropped it in the paper cup marked "dead batteries" and flipped his switch off, very, very deliberately.

Addison slid her story across the desk to Kendra, who read fast and then frowned. "You only fixed the spelling. Mr. Virtanen said we have to revise."

"That is revising," Addison said. "New commas and everything."

Kendra, who wanted the reading corner spot by the window and knew Mr. Virtanen gave it to whoever improved the most, shook her head. "No. He told Liana the word revise comes from the Latin revisere, meaning 'to look at again.' Revising means seeing your draft with fresh eyes."

Addison looked at her page again. All she saw was the same page. She tried standing up, walking once around the desks, and coming back. That was no better. Then she had an idea: if her eyes were the problem, maybe her ears were the answer. She read the first paragraph out loud in a low voice.

"Leila walked slowly and quietly through the very dark and spooky old hallway." It sounded flat, like a hallway itself. She crossed out slowly and quietly and wrote crept. She crossed out very dark and spooky old and kept only the shadowed hallway. Then she noticed something else. Every sentence was long. Every single one had two commas in it. She cut one sentence down to four words: "The floor creaked. She froze."

Her pencil wanted to rebel against deleting words she had worked hard on, but she reminded herself she was being frugal, keeping only what the paragraph truly needed. Reading aloud took stamina, because she kept stopping to slash adjectives, but by the end she had crossed out eleven of them.

She read it to Kendra again. "The floor creaked. She froze." Kendra grinned and pointed at the last line.

"Read that part one more time," Kendra said.

The bus was leaving the historic site at two thirty, sharp, and Ms. Ngo had already promised that anyone left behind would become "part of the exhibit." Dylan took this as a personal challenge, not because he wanted to stay, but because the old farmhouse had one thing he could not stop staring at: a writing desk in the corner with a dark, shiny patch worn right into the wood.

He drifted toward it while the guide talked about candle molds. His fingers were halfway to the patch when Jagger grabbed his sleeve like a lifeguard. "Whoa. You can't touch that. Ms. Ngo said. The oils and salts from your skin build up over time and stain the wood, or damage the surface. That's why they put ropes around everything."

Dylan pulled his hand back and stared at the dark patch again. Something clicked. "Wait. If skin oils build up over time and stain the surface, then that patch is like a fingerprint collection. Hundreds of hands. Maybe the family counted their money there, or wrote letters, or did homework, even." Victor wandered over, chewing the strap of his backpack. "That's not a credible theory. It's a desk. Desks get used. Case closed, detective."

"It's not just used," Dylan said. "The stain has a shape. Look, it's not everywhere, it's in one band along the front edge. That's an anomaly, Victor. It means people stood on one side, over and over, for years." Victor squinted at the desk, then at the window beside it. "Okay, or the sun hits it there." Dylan considered that, then shook his head. "Sun fades wood. This is darker. And shinier."

The guide was already moving the group toward the kitchen, and the clock on the mantel said 2:15, which meant fifteen minutes before the bus became a memory and they became history. Dylan raised his hand like he was launching it off his wrist. "Can you cite any record of who used the desk? Like letters or inventories?"

The guide blinked, then smiled. "As a matter of fact, yes. The middle daughter ran the farm's accounts from that desk for forty years. Standing at the front edge, where the light from this window fell on her ledger."

"Ha!" Dylan spun around to Victor and Jagger, pointing at the dark band of forty years of ledger-keeping. "Standing. Front edge. I told you."

"You got lucky," Victor said, but he was grinning.

"Excuse me," the guide added, "I'd ask you not to high-five next to the desk."

Dylan and Jagger froze, palms hovering in the air, and backed away to the sound of the whole class laughing at them.

Lily slid her draft across the library table until it bumped Archie's elbow. "Read this and tell me what's wrong with it."

Archie read. "Nothing's wrong with it. It's good."

"See, that's the problem. You can't see anything in it." She tapped the page. "My whole field trip essay is 'nice' and 'interesting' and 'good.' My grandmother read it last night and asked me what exactly was nice about the trip. I said, you know, nice. She said the word gives my opinion without showing anything, and a concrete detail lets the reader picture it and judge."

"That sounds like something a grandmother would enforce at dinner," Archie said.

"She did. She wouldn't pass the potatoes until I answered."

Lily picked up her pencil and read her opening sentence aloud, quietly, because Mr. Bekele was reshelving books two rows over and his rule about voices was the one rule he actually enforced. "The science museum was very interesting." She crossed out "very interesting." Now she had "The science museum was." She stared at it.

Himmat dropped into the third chair with his backpack, which was, as always, perpendicular to the table instead of under it, so everyone had to step around him. "What are we doing?"

"Concrete details," Lily said. "Apparently 'good' and 'interesting' are words you write when you haven't decided what actually happened."

Himmat looked wounded. "I use those words."

"You do. Your volcano essay said the demonstration generator was 'cool.' Was it loud? Did it spark? Did it smell like burnt toast? Cool tells me nothing except that you liked it."

"It did smell like burnt toast," Himmat admitted. "The whole lab did."

Lily wrote that down. Then she kept going, testing each sentence the way her grandmother had tested her: if the word only gave her opinion, out it came. The giant turbine became a wheel taller than Mr. Bekele. The good exhibit became the one where you cranked a handle and a light bulb glowed faintly, then died, then glowed again. The nice bus ride home became thirty-seven minutes of Archie humming one song without stopping.

"I heard that," Archie said, not looking up.

"You were meant to." She read her new opening under her breath: sentences short, then long, then short again, like her grandmother's own storytelling, which never used the same rhythm twice in a row. She turned the page around and slid it back across the table. "Now tell me what's wrong with it."

Archie read. "Nothing's wrong with it. It's good."

Lily raised her pencil. "Try that again with a detail."

The community hall behind the mosque smelled of cardamom and wet umbrellas, because it had rained all morning and everyone's shoes sat in a dripping pile by the door. Logan stood at the back with his prayer mat rolled under his arm, feeling like a fake. His family had moved here in March, and tomorrow he was supposed to fast for the whole day for the first time, all the way from dawn. Today, though, he had a smaller job: joining the afternoon prayer with the others, which meant he actually had to know how to pray.

Umar was already inside, holding his phone out like a waiter's tray. "Logan, look. There's a compass app." A thin arrow wobbled on the screen, and behind it a green line pointed off toward the corner of the hall. Logan knew what the line was for, in a general way. Muslims pray five times a day, and when they pray, they turn toward the Kaaba, the black cube-shaped building in Mecca. What he didn't know was which direction that was from here, in this hall, on this rainy Tuesday.

"I thought the wall with the designs was the front," Logan said. Mathieu, who had come along because his own family was busy and he wanted to see what a mosque was like, pointed at the geometric tiles. "Then why does your app point at the coat rack?"

Logan walked over to the coat rack, holding Umar's phone out flat, and watched the green line. It stayed steady, pointing a little left of the coats, toward the big windows on the far wall. He turned ninety degrees, and the line swung behind him. He turned back, and it locked onto the windows again. So the tiles were pretty, and the tiles were not the point. The point was Mecca, wherever Mecca happened to be. "The front isn't where the designs are," he said slowly. "The front is toward the Kaaba."

Ms. Grewal, who ran the community lunch and had been stacking paper cups, set the cups down and came to look. "You've got it," she said, and nothing more, which made Logan feel oddly proud, as if he'd solved it himself instead of an app solving it for him. Some of the older men were already laying out mats in long neat rows, angled the same way the green line pointed. Logan unrolled his mat and nudged it until it matched.

He prayed the way his grandfather had shown him over video calls in the spring, standing, bowing, forehead to the mat, and when he rose he was less worried about tomorrow. A whole day without food or water would restrict a lot of things, but the praying part no longer felt impossible. Mathieu sat quietly by the windows until Logan finished. "So," Mathieu said as they rolled up the mat, "does Umar's phone have a monopoly on compasses, or can I try it too?" Logan laughed and held out the phone, the green line still pointing toward the windows, steady as a compass on an exceptional day.

Nolan's map of the world lay flat on the library table, and his finger hovered over a grid of thin lines nobody had ever explained to him. Mr. Ito had promised that whoever could pinpoint a mystery city using only its coordinates would win the last spot on the geography team, and Nour was already halfway done across the room.

"Thirty degrees north, ninety degrees west," Harley read off the card. "That's got to be somewhere in the United States, right?"

Nolan traced the lines with his pencil. Latitude ran sideways, longitude ran up and down, and where they crossed, there was the city. New Orleans. He wrote it down and felt his whole chest lift, until he saw the second question on the card: "If it is 3 p.m. in New Orleans, what time is it in Tokyo, 135 degrees east?"

The room had no clock showing Tokyo. There was only Mr. Ito, restacking map tubes well away from the radiator because old paper was flammable and he treated those maps like treasure. Nolan couldn't ask him. He stared at the numbers instead, and something about them lined up like fence posts. Fifteen degrees, thirty degrees, forty-five. Each jump of fifteen was one hour. Earth turned 15 degrees of longitude every hour, so time zones ran roughly fifteen degrees wide. New Orleans to Tokyo was a hundred and sixty-five degrees, which was eleven chunks of fifteen.

"Eleven hours ahead," he whispered to Harley. "It's two in the morning there."

When the bell rang, Mr. Ito checked the cards. "New Orleans, and Tokyo at 2 a.m.," he said, and wrote Nolan's name at the top of the team list.

Nour leaned over. "How did you get the Tokyo part?"

"I'll confess I guessed the rule first, then tested it on two cities I knew," Nolan said, and slid the map across the table so his friend could see the fence posts too.

The bus to Camp Windrow left at dawn, which meant Owen had to commute across town with his duffel bag banging against his knees the whole ride. He found a seat near the back and read the letter his grandfather had tucked into his pocket two nights before. "Ticks are worse this year than any summer I can remember," it said. "Blacklegged ticks, some people call them deer ticks. They can carry Lyme disease out here, so after you hike, check everywhere. Behind your knees, your hairline, everywhere." Owen folded the letter and watched the lake slide into view, long and gray-green, with the camp dock jutting out like a finger.

That evening, after the whole cabin had tramped through a meadow of tall grass to reach the dock for swim checks, the counselor called for the nightly tick check. "Everyone, line up, shirts up, hair down." A boy named Lev groaned and dropped onto his bunk. "I'm skipping it. We just walked through grass, that's all. Nothing happens from grass."

Owen thought about his grandfather's letter, and about the pattern he had noticed on the bus: three campers scratching their ankles, all of them from the meadow trail, and none of the kids who took the gravel road. He held up the letter. "My grandpa says blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, spread Lyme disease in this part of the country. That's why they do the checks. It's not about the grass, it's about what's hiding in it." Lev squinted at him. "How do you know they're actually there if nobody saw one?"

"Same way you know the wind's blowing," Owen said. "You look at what it moves." He pointed at the scratches. "Gravel-road kids aren't itchy. Meadow kids are." Lev considered this for a moment, then stood up and pulled his collar loose. "Fine. Check my hairline, and I'll check yours." Owen ran his fingers carefully through Lev's dark curls and stopped. There, small as a poppy seed behind Lev's ear, sat a tick. Lev went stiff, and Owen kept his voice steady while the counselor came over with the tweezers and a little plastic case.

Afterward, Lev sat on the dock with Owen, both of them dangling their feet over the water. "You can't even see a microbe with your eyes," Lev said, peering at the case. "Something that small." Owen shrugged and took off his synthetic rain jacket, wadded it into a pillow, and lay back against the warm boards. Lev picked up a flat stone and sent it skipping across the darkening lake. "Four," he counted. "Your turn."

Isla pressed her nose against the kitchen window and counted the snow day's treasures: no spelling test, no bus, and a whole street turned white and quiet. Then she saw him. Mr. Gupta, three doors down, was attacking his driveway with a shovel, scooping huge shovelfuls of the heavy wet stuff and hurling them to the side. He stopped after every few throws and stood with a hand pressed against his coat.

Something twisted nervously in Isla's intestines. She had heard her mother on the phone last winter, telling Aunt Carol that shoveling heavy snow was hard work for the heart, and that doctors advised taking breaks and lifting small loads rather than big shovelfuls. Isla had never thought about it again until now, watching Mr. Gupta pile his shovel high and wobble under the weight.

She pulled on her boots and jogged down the street. "Mr. Gupta! Can I help?" He looked hesitant, like he wanted to say no, but another pause for breath made up his mind for him. "The last two rows," he said, pointing. "Then hot chocolate, deal."

Isla took the shovel and tried an experiment. First she filled it the way he had, a mountain of snow that made her arms shake. Then she tried a half load, and a quarter load, shoving each one quickly to the edge. The small loads were faster, easier, and she wasn't puffing at all. "See?" she said, breathless only from excitement. "Little scoops. And we rest between rows." She made him sit on the porch step while she cleared a whole stripe, then they traded, and he cleared the next one with her small-load method, standing straighter than before.

"Where did you learn that?" he asked.

"Experiment," Isla said proudly. "Science."

Mr. Gupta laughed. "Then here is your reward." He held out a thermocap of cocoa, and Isla adjusted her grip on the shovel to take it, but he pulled it back with a grin. "One condition. You shovel my walk tomorrow too, Doctor Isla." She saluted, cocoa steaming in the cold.

Evelyn sat between her dad and her older brother at the sports bar, but she was not watching the game on the big screen. She was reading the message Cali had sent an hour ago: "Tournament Sunday. We get one pick. Becca or Dara? Both average 12 points. HELP."

The TV showed two basketball players' stats side by side, and a commentator said something that stuck in Evelyn's head. "Same scoring average," he said, "but completely different players." She leaned closer. The screen flashed each player's last five games. One had scored 14, 13, 12, 13, 12. The other had gone 30, 2, 25, 0, 3. Same total. Same average. Totally different story.

"Interesting," her dad said over his nachos. "One guy you can count on, the other is a coin flip."

Evelyn began to hypothesize: if the average was a whole season squashed into one number, then it could hide how the games were spread out. She pulled out her notebook and wrote it down. On Monday she tracked down the rec center's score sheets and found Becca's and Dara's games. Becca had scored 12, 11, 13, 12, 12. Dara had scored 28, 1, 22, 3, 6. Both totaled 60. The average was identical, but Becca never had a terrible game, and Dara swung between great and awful.

On Tuesday, Philip cornered her by the gym doors. "It's settled, right? Twelve is twelve. The pick is trivial."

"It's not trivial," Evelyn said. "The average hides it. Dara might score zero on Sunday." She did not mention that the team's old rivals had folded last month, and their extinction from the league had left this tournament as the only trophy left to win. That was exactly why the pick mattered.

She texted Cali: "Pick Becca. Same average, but steady every game. Dara's either brilliant or invisible, and we can't risk invisible on Sunday."

Cali replied with a thumbs-up and one word: "Proof?"

Evelyn photographed the score sheets, both columns side by side, and hit send.

Eleanor sat at the kitchen computer with her science worksheet beside the keyboard. One question was underlined twice: Is the claim "houseplants improve focus" backed by tested evidence, or is it only a story about one person's experience? She typed the claim into the search box and got a blog post first, written by a woman who said three ferns on her desk had changed her life. The post was funny and easy to read, and Eleanor almost copied the address onto her worksheet.

Then she noticed the second result, an article in something called a journal. It was harder to read, full of words like "participants" and "controlled conditions," and it described an experiment with fifty students, half of them seated near plants and half not. She scrolled down both pages side by side. The blog was one person's bizarre, wonderful luck with ferns. The journal article documented its results in tables, and at the bottom it said the article had been reviewed before publication. Reviewed by whom, Eleanor wondered, and why did that matter?

She called Jordynn, who had finished the worksheet the night before. "Did your article say anything about being checked?" Eleanor asked. "Mine says it was reviewed." There was a rustling on the other end, then Jordynn's voice, pleased with herself. "That's peer review. Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors." Eleanor wrote the words down. "So the blog lady's ferns," she said slowly, "nobody checked those." "Right," said Jordynn. "She's just telling you what happened to her. That's a story about one person's experience, not tested evidence."

Eleanor looked at the two windows on the screen. If she used the blog, her worksheet would take five minutes, but the answer would be wobbly, and the consequence might be a red mark from Mr. Henry, who liked sources. The journal article had taken her twenty minutes to puzzle through, but fifty students beat three ferns, and experts had combed it for mistakes first. She clicked print on the journal page, picked the warm sheets off the printer, and wrote her answer in her best handwriting. Then she set a small pothos cutting beside the monitor, just in case the fern lady had been onto something anyway.

On Saturday mornings Landon worked at Ms. Ross's farm stand, stacking baskets of strawberries and trying not to eat the evidence. He had one job rule taped to the register: if a price looks strange, figure it why before you touch it. Ms. Ross said it was training for what she called "the real world," which apparently included fruit.

At noon the strawberries were four dollars a basket. At five o'clock, right before closing, Ms. Ross marched out and turned the sign to one dollar. Landon stared at it. "That's backwards. Everyone loves strawberries. Shouldn't popular things cost more?"

Sabrina, who was sweeping between the pie table and the cooler, leaned on her broom. "It's supply and demand," she said. "We learned it Tuesday."

"A contradiction, that's what it is," said Landon. "More people wanting them should mean more money, not less. Unless you're hiding something, like a strawberry thief."

"Feel the flat," Ms. Ross said, dumping a crate of unsold baskets into his arms. The cardboard was porous and already going soft where the juice had touched it, and under the green smell of the berries there was a faint edge of something sweeter, something almost wrong.

Landon turned a basket over in his hands and did the math out loud. "These were picked yesterday. They can't just sit around. Fresh strawberries spoil within days of picking, so if you have too many, you can't store them for later. You have to cut the price to sell them now, or they're garbage by Tuesday."

"Garbage by Monday, actually," said Ms. Ross, "but you've got the idea."

"So the price isn't about how much people want them," Landon said slowly. "It's about the clock." He adjusted the sign so the big one-dollar side faced the road, and within ten minutes three cars pulled in.

Sabrina counted the last basket into a woman's bag. "Supply and demand," she said smugly, "and the demand of strawberries to become compost."

Alexandre stood at the shallow end of the school pool, staring down the twenty-five metres of roped-off lane water. Mr. Georgiou had promised that anyone who swam the full length with side breathing would get a sticker shaped like a shark, and Alexandre wanted that shark more than he had wanted anything since the sandwich trade fiasco in grade four, when he had swapped a whole sandwich for one cookie and regretted it for a week. Francesca had already earned hers. Billy was still working on not panicking.

His first try went badly. He pushed off, counted strokes, lifted his head to the right every time, and smacked face-first into the lane rope before he was halfway down the pool. Billy hauled him upright. "You went totally sideways," Billy said. "Like a crab. A very slow crab."

Alexandre sat on the edge and thought about it. He had been breathing to the right on every second stroke, and he always ended up drifting right. That night he drew a picture in his notebook, little stick arms turning over and over, and noticed something odd. If he breathed after three strokes instead of two, the breathing side would switch, because three strokes put the other arm in the recovering position. Three was odd, so it never landed the same way twice in a row. He wrote a note and left it in Francesca's cubby: "Dear Francesca, I have solved why I swim like a drunk seal. Three strokes, not two. If this works I owe you a juice box. If it doesn't, I owe you two juice boxes for witnessing it. Signed, Alexandre."

The next lesson, he pushed off and counted one, two, three, breathe. Left side. One, two, three, breathe. Right side. He felt like a pendulum, swinging even, and the far wall came up straight in front of him instead of sideways. He touched the tiles, gasping, and Billy was shrieking and Francesca was waving the note over her head like a flag. Mr. Georgiou peeled the shark sticker off its sheet and held it out.

"Two juice boxes," Francesca called. "The seal was pretty drunk."

The gymnasium smelled like potting soil and tape, and Kaylee balanced her poster board against the bleachers while she hunted for a free table. She found one near the equipment cage, right beside Jean, whose two bean plants sat in matching pots under a sign that read Does Music Help Plants Grow?

"Mine's about water temperature," Kaylee said, unpacking her watering bottles. "Cold versus room temperature, everything else the same." She held up a small brass valve she'd borrowed from her dad's garage. "This controls the drip so both pots get exactly the same amount. I have to keep it durable enough to survive three kids bumping the table."

Jean wasn't listening. She was staring at her plants, and one was tall and leaning while the other was short and straight. "They were identical," she said. "Same music, same soil, same water. I even measured. But the tall one only got tall this week, and I don't know why."

Kaylee crouched down to look. The tall plant was stretched sideways, reaching, its leaves turned one direction. She turned the pot slowly, then turned back. "Which one sat closer to the window?"

Jean looked up at the tall windows above the bleachers, then at her table. "The leaning one. It's been in that spot since Tuesday. I moved the whole setup to make room for Tyler's volcano."

"So it's not the music," Kaylee said. "In a fair test, every other condition has to stay the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one thing you changed." She said it slowly, checking it against her own experiment as the words came out. "Your one thing was supposed to be music. But sunlight snuck in there too, so now you can't tell what caused what."

Jean groaned and put her head in her arms. "The fair opens in forty minutes."

"Then swap them," Kaylee said. "Put both pots the same distance from the window, equal light on both sides, and start your counts over. Or, wait." Kaylee pointed at the other side of Jean's sign, which had room left. "You could keep the old data and elaborate on it. Write down what went wrong. Judges like it when you show how you caught a mistake."

Jean sat up. "Really? Not just crossed out and redone?"

"Mine almost fell apart twice," Kaylee said. "The valve dripped unevenly for two days before I caught it. I logged that too." She handed Jean a fresh index card and her own marker. "Here. Start with the window."

Tyler wandered over from his volcano, wiping baking soda off his hands, and read Jean's card while Jean wrote. "So the plant wasn't reaching toward the music," he said. "It was reaching toward the light."

"Exactly one variable," Jean said, and underlined the last line of her card.

By the time Mr. Cohen came around with his clipboard, Jean's table held two evenly lit pots, a drip valve borrowed from Kaylee's kit, and a sign that read, in fresh marker: A fair test keeps every other condition the same. The tall plant still leaned toward the window, stubborn and green, like it was pointing at the answer.

The app kept asking for her birthday, which Ivy thought was strange, because a game about matching colored tiles had no reason to care when she was born. She sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with the family tablet, tapping the little calendar again. The kitchen light down the hall made a sparse stripe across the carpet, and she could hear her mom humming while she scrubbed a pot that had been saturate d with burnt rice at dinner. The form wanted a year. Any year. Ivy tried typing the year she was born, and the screen flashed red: "You must be 13 or older to create an account."

Thirteen. She counted on her fingers even though she didn't need to. Two years and four months away. That seemed like a long time to wait for a tile game. But why thirteen? Her dad's chess app had never asked his birthday. Neither had the weather site. It was almost like the matching game was something else, something bigger, hiding behind the tiles.

At school the next morning she slid her notebook across the table to Evelina, who was drawing a cat with a suspicious expression. "Why would a game care how old you are?" Ivy asked. "Does yours ask?" Evelina shook her head. "My sister's app does, but she's fourteen, so she just clicks through." Jax leaned over from the next seat. "It's a law thing. My cousin told me. The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998. Websites need parental consent before they collect personal information from kids under 13. That's why so many sites make you be 13."

"A law," Ivy said slowly, turning her pencil over. So it wasn't the game being picky. The app wanted her name, her birthday, maybe her town. Collecting personal information. The tile game was keeping a file on her, and the law said an adult had to say yes first. She wondered how many kids just typed a different year and walked right past the rule, and whether the app could even tell.

That evening she found her mom drying dishes. "Can I sign up for something if you give permission? There's a law, from 1998, and I'm under thirteen, so you have to consent first." Her mom set the dish down and looked at her for a long moment. "Show me the app," she said. "We'll read what they collect together." Ivy carried the tablet over, screen glowing, and tapped the calendar one more time.

Jack got up before sunrise and ate two pieces of toast, because Ramadan had started and he was fasting for the first time, at least until lunchtime. Then Dad said they were driving to the cemetery to visit Grandpa's grave, and Jack put on his camouflage jacket and carried the folded prayer mat even though the mat had a synthetic surface that scratched his arm.

At the cemetery the artificial grass near the headstones was damp. Jack read the dua Dad had written on a card, and then he began to shiver. By the time they walked back to the car, his teeth were knocking together, and his forehead felt hot when Dad pressed a hand against it. Dad gave him a bottle of water, and Jack drank half of it before he remembered the fast. His stomach dropped.

"I broke it," Jack said. "I ruined my first fast."

Dad felt his forehead again. "You have a fever. Islam excuses people who are sick or travelling from the Ramadan fast, and they make up the missed days later."

Jack sat with that. "So I owe one day? Like homework I have to turn in late?"

"Exactly like that," Dad said.

"But you can't prove I'm sick," Jack said, testing the idea. "You can't see a fever."

Dad held up the thermometer from the first aid kit, and it read thirty-eight point two. "There. Evidence." Then he pointed through the fence at the row of graves. "You know who else never fasted a whole Ramadan in his life? Grandpa. He was diabetic, and he was sick, and every year he made up the days after, in small ones, whenever he could."

Jack looked at the headstone with the wet grass around it. Grandpa, who had taught him chess and never missed a Friday prayer, had spent all those years making up days, quietly, one at a time. Jack drank the rest of the water.

"Tomorrow, when I'm better," he said, "I'm starting over."

The craft fair signup sheet went up on Monday, and Lily was the first to enroll. She wanted a table of her own, mostly because of the wind turbine model she had built in science, a little spinning thing with blades made from plastic spoons. But her friend Alix had different plans. Alix wanted money, real money, for a new skateboard, and she had a shoebox full of woven bracelets to sell.

The fair was loud and crowded. Alix put her price at five dollars a bracelet, which seemed high to Lily, and by lunchtime the shoebox was empty. "Sold out," Alix announced, holding up the empty box like a trophy. Lily looked down the row of tables. Nobody else was selling bracelets at all. There were candles, cookies, painted rocks, but no bracelets. Five dollars, zero sellers besides Alix, and every bracelet gone. Something clicked in Lily's mind, though she couldn't quite say what yet.

Two weeks later the school held a second fair, and Lily decided to be systematic about it. She walked every row with a notebook and wrote down each bracelet seller and each price. This time there were eight bracelet tables. Eight! Yassin had one, two girls from her class had one, even Mr. Tehrani's nephew had one. And the price? Four tables were asking one dollar, three were asking two, and Alix, still trying for her skateboard money, was asking three. Almost nobody bought at three. With bracelets everywhere, buyers could pick the cheapest one, and sellers kept dropping their prices just to make a sale.

Lily found Alix behind her table, chin in her hands. "Nobody wants mine," Alix said. Lily flipped her notebook open. "Watch this," she said. "I'm going to test something." She made a sign for Alix's table that said BRACELETS, $5, and taped it up. Then she waited. Within an hour, two more kids had signed up for the last empty tables, both carrying boxes of string and beads, both having heard that bracelets were going for five dollars.

"Take the sign down," Alix groaned, but Lily was grinning, scribbling in her notebook. "Don't you see? When the price goes up, more sellers show up." At the next table, Yassin was already knotting his next bracelet.

Kate set the mixing bowl on the picnic table in the backyard, where the light was good enough to magnify every lump in her dough. She had promised her family fresh bread by dinner, and she had never made bread before. Last summer, before her grandmother moved away, they had baked a loaf together on the porch, and Kate remembered stirring flour and water and watching her grandmother knead the dough for ten whole minutes while Kate fidgeted. "The kneading matters," her grandmother had said. "You'll see why someday."

Kate had skipped most of the kneading that summer, wandering off to chase dragonflies, and the loaf had come out dense and sad. She still wondered whether that had been her fault. Her premise now was simple: if flour and water made something on their own, and kneading changed it, then a short knead and a long knead should give her two different doughs. So she pulled off a small piece of dough, set it aside, and gave the rest a full ten minutes of pushing and folding on the table, her arms burning by the end.

The neighbor, Mr. Cho, leaned over the fence. "Looks like you're punishing that poor dough."

"I'm strengthening it," Kate said. "Flour has proteins in it, and when they mix with water, something called gluten forms. Kneading makes the gluten stronger and stretchier." She held up both pieces. The short-kneaded bit tore when she stretched it, like wet paper. The ten-minute piece stretched thin without breaking, until she could almost see light through it, a little window in the dough.

She covered the bowl with a towel and left it in the sun. Her grandmother had never gotten to taste the loaf they started together; that choice, to wander off instead of staying, sat with Kate while the dough rose and puffed under the towel. Maybe the old dense loaf had been her fault, maybe not. When she peeled the towel back an hour later, the dough had swelled round and proud, and she carried the bowl inside to the oven, calling over her shoulder, "Mr. Cho, come back at dinner. You get the first slice."

The sign at the gas station read "Water: $4.00" in red marker, and Lucy stared at it with her last five dollars crumpled in her fist. The storm was coming that night, and the shelves that usually held dozens of bottles held exactly seven. Two days ago the same bottles had cost a dollar, and she knew it, because she'd bought one after soccer practice.

"Four dollars for water," Adrian said beside her, holding his own money. He had been planning to buy hot chocolate from the machine, but he'd given that up the moment he saw the emptying shelf. "That's robbery." Two men at the register each took one bottle, looked at the price, and put them back, saying they'd fill jugs at home instead. A woman took two, paid, and hurried out. Lucy counted the shelf again. Six bottles. Five. Nobody was grabbing armfuls the way they'd grabbed cheap batteries last summer when the price had dropped to twenty-five cents and the whole rack emptied in an hour.

"Wait," Lucy said. "When the price was low, everybody bought tons. Now it's high, and people are putting it back." She checked the memory against what she was seeing, and it fit. "Adrian, I think when the price rises, people buy less, and when it falls, they buy more. Like, always, as long as nothing else changes."

"That sounds like a rule," Adrian said. "Rules need a name."

"The jury's still out on the name," Lucy said, and he laughed so hard a man at the coffee station turned around. The cashier leaned toward them. "There's a name," she said. "Law of demand." She tapped the sign. "Consistent as sunrise."

Lucy bought one bottle instead of three, and Adrian, instead of sulking, spent his money on her second-choice, a jug of juice that had stayed cheap because nobody wanted it. At the door she paused. "You intervened in the hot chocolate crisis and saved the day," she said, holding up the juice.

Adrian bowed. "The jury of one finds me heroic."

Jack sat under the oak canopy at Riverside Park, digging the toe of his sneaker into the dirt like he could excavate the whole flowerbed if he tried hard enough. He was waiting for Jayden, who was late, which was new. Jayden was never late. But then, Jayden had spent every afternoon this week at the skate bowls with Aila instead of meeting Jack at the climbing wall, so maybe lateness was just the newest symptom of a bigger problem.

When Jayden finally arrived, he didn't sit down. "You texted me four times," he said. "My mom said you knocked on the door."

"Because you disappeared." Jack stood up. "We had a wall day. Tuesday, Thursday. That was ours."

Jayden shrugged, which stung worse than an argument would have.

Ms. Oyelaran, who was running the park's volunteer crew a few meters away, called out to a kid on her team who kept talking over his partner. "Try active listening," she said. "Rogers and Farson came up with it in 1957. Repeat back what you heard, in your own words." Then she went back to counting shovels, and the kid tried it, and his partner stopped looking like she wanted to leave.

Jack watched the two volunteers, and a small rebellious part of him wanted to say it was corny. But he was the one sulking under a tree, so maybe corny was worth a shot. "So you felt like... I was mad, even though I never said it out loud?" he tried.

Jayden blinked. "You were mad. I could tell."

"That's not what I mean. I mean, say what you heard me say."

Jayden blew out a long breath. "So you felt I picked Aila over you. Like she replaced me."

Something loosened in Jack's shoulders. "Yeah. That." He hadn't known that was the shape of it until Jayden said it out loud.

"Nobody replaced you," Jayden said. "Aila's trying to build a skate video for the park's summer contest, and she needed a cameraman who wouldn't laugh at her falls. She doesn't even know you're jealous, man. She asked if you'd hold the second camera."

Jayden finally sat down on the bench beside him. "Wall day tomorrow? And filming Saturday?"

"Both," Jack said. He pulled out his phone and typed a message to Aila: I'm in for Saturday. Bring the good camera.

Joshua tapped his pencil against the empty poster board and frowned at the glittery letters Mayar had glued down that morning. "Plants like music," they announced, with a vine drawn around the words. It looked fantastic. It also said almost nothing, and the science fair was in four days.

Mr. Aziz wandered past their lab table, humming. He was notorious for stopping at half-finished projects and asking one question that made everything harder. "Charming poster," he said. "Now, how would you test it?"

Joshua glanced at Mayar, who shrugged and kept arranging the vine. "We'd play music for a plant," Joshua said.

"Any plant? Any music? And what would you expect to see?" Mr. Aziz picked up a bean seedling in a paper cup, turned it toward the window, and set it back down. "Try again Thursday." Then he moved on to torment Calvin, whose volcano had sprung a leak.

"Great," Mayar muttered. "Now we need an actual experiment too."

Joshua took the bean seedlings home, along with three more cups from the supply shelf that Mr. Aziz let him borrow. He lined up four seedlings on his windowsill and thought about the question all through dinner. What would count as a plant "liking" something? He couldn't ask it. He couldn't see liking. But he could see height, and new leaves, and how fast each cup's soil dried.

The next morning he wrote his idea on an index card. In class, he slid it across the table to Mayar. "If I play music for two seedlings and keep two seedlings quiet," he read aloud, "then the music seedlings will grow taller by Friday." Mayar leaned in. "That's a hypothesis," she said, pointing at his card. "Mr. Aziz mentioned that word yesterday, remember? It's a guess you can actually test."

So they tested it. Calvin donated his phone as the music source, since his volcano was already ruined anyway. Two cups went behind a cardboard box where the phone played soft piano for an hour each morning. Two cups sat in silence on the other side of the sill. Every day, Joshua measured with a ruler and logged the numbers, and Mayar drew a chart with a line for each plant.

By Friday, the numbers told them something unexpected. The quiet seedlings had grown taller, by half a centimeter, and one music seedling had barely grown at all. "So our hypothesis was wrong," Joshua said slowly, writing the results down anyway.
