"Then the poster's wrong too," Mayar said, peeling off the glittery letters. Calvin grinned. "Can we write 'plants might not like music' in giant letters instead?"

"Hypothesis overturned," Joshua said, and uncapped the marker.

Eva typed number = input("Pick a number: ") and then print('7' * 3), because she wanted to test what a loop's inner line would do before she built the whole thing. On the screen, where she expected 21, appeared 777. Behind her, Kohen laughed so hard he knocked his mouse off the desk. "Your times table thinks seven times three is seven hundred and seventy-seven," he said, and Mika leaned over to see.

Eva stared at the three sevens marching across the monitor. So multiplying text by a whole number repeats the text, she realized, instead of doing any math at all. The quotes were the clue. She had put quotation marks around the seven, so Python thought she was printing a word made of one character, and '7' * 3 gave '777'. Last month she had done the same kind of thing and quit in frustration, deleting a whole project because she assumed the program was broken. That memory sat with her now, the way the computer lab always sat cold in November because its walls had almost no insulation, so everyone coded in jackets. She had regretted deleting that project for weeks. This time she kept going.

She retrieved her draft from the saved file, found the line with the quotes, and took them away. Then she wrote the loop: for i in range(1, 13): print(number, "times", i, "is", number * i). She pressed run and typed 7.

The table marched down the screen, seven times one is 7, seven times two is 14, all the way to seven times twelve is 84. Mika slid her chair over. "Do nine," she said. "Nines are the weird ones."

Eva cleared the input and typed 9, and while the table scrolled she thought again about the project she had thrown away, and whether next time something looked wrong she would stay or leave. The cursor blinked in the empty input box, waiting.

"Try twelve," Kohen said.

Max had one job at the gallery's Saturday drawing table: make a paper sphere look like it was sitting on a paper table instead of floating above it. His pencil sphere had a nice highlight on the top left, where Ms. Gallagher had set a little lamp, and a fat gray shadow underneath, but somehow the ball still looked like it was hovering in midair, ready to drift off past the portraits.

Gwen leaned over from the next easel. "Yours is levitating too? Mine looks like a moon." Naomy held up her sketch, which showed a plum with a dark smudge right at the bottom. "My grandpa taught me this one," she said. "The darkest part of a cast shadow is right where the sphere touches the surface, because almost no light can get into that narrow gap. He called it the anchor spot." Max squinted at her plum. It sat on its table like it weighed something, like a real plum, heavy with nutritious juice, ready to roll.

Max wasn't sure he believed it. What if it just looked messy? He decided to test it. First he drew a new sphere with an even, medium shadow all around, and it floated like a soap bubble. Then he took his pencil and pressed hard in one tiny ring right where his ball met the table line, leaving everything else pale. When he held the paper up, the sphere dropped onto the table so convincingly that he actually glanced down to check it wasn't sitting on the real desk.

"Whoa," Gwen said. "Do mine." Max anchored her moon, and it landed with a soft thump that only existed in their heads. Ms. Gallagher walked past, studied the drawings, and announced that the three of them were hereby founding the gallery's first Anchor Guild, membership requiring one perfectly grounded sphere. "What does the ring symbolize?" Gwen asked, pointing at the dark spot. Naomy grinned. "Gravity," she said, "in pencil form." Max wrote it on his sketch in block letters: GRAVITY, and underlined it twice.

Vincent stared at the caption he had typed for the community centre project board: "This carving was made by an Inuit named Jobie." Something about it itched. He had been sent home from Elianne's kitchen table an hour ago, where the whole project had nearly fallen apart.

Earlier that afternoon, Elianne had spread out her grandmother's photographs, the smell of old paper and dried fish still clinging to them. Ephraim leaned over a soapstone carving of a kayak, turning it so the light caught the grey lines. "You can't write 'an Inuit' for one person," Elianne said, tapping the screen. "My grandmother would calibrate that sentence in about two seconds." Vincent had frowned, because he had written exactly that. He tested a quick idea: if plural words sometimes stayed the same in the singular, like "fish," then maybe not. No, that failed. "So what is one person called?" he asked. Elianne smiled the way she did when she knew the answer and wanted you to earn it. "An Inuk," she said. "One is an Inuk. Inuit means 'the people,' in Inuktitut. So saying 'an Inuit' for my grandmother is like saying 'an the people.'"

Ephraim laughed so hard he knocked over the glue. That was when the printout of Jobie's portrait slid under the radiator, and Vincent spent ten minutes with a butter knife and his arm at a bad angle, fishing it out while the metal ticked with heat against his knuckles. The paper came back warm and curled at one corner, smelling faintly of dust.

Now, back at the table, he deleted the old line and retyped it: "This carving was made by an Inuk named Jobie." He read it aloud twice. The fundamental fix was one letter wide, which struck him as unfair in a way he couldn't quite argue with. It was a small insight, but it belonged to him now, along with the warm paper and the glue Ephraim still hadn't cleaned up. He heard the front door open and Ephraim's voice from the hallway.

"Did you fix it?"

"Fixed it," Vincent called back, and pressed print.

Gabrielle set her phone face down next to her plate, which was a rule at the dinner table, but she couldn't stop thinking about what was on the screen. Tomorrow morning was the deadline for the school newspaper, and she had half an article written about Friday's soccer match against Lakeside. Then Aspen had texted her a screenshot that said Lakeside's coach had been suspended for cheating and the whole team might be disqualified.

"Two more bites of rice and then you can be excused," her dad said, passing her the chicken.

She ate, chewing fast, and turned the screenshot over in her mind. The post came from somebody on the Northview side, the school Lakeside had beaten last week. It was from a friend of a friend, no name, no source. But Northview kids hated Lakeside right now, so of course they'd share it.

"Can I ask something weird?" she said. "If you already think a team is bad, and somebody tells you the team cheated, do you check it?"

Her mom tilted her head. "Usually not. People grab anything that fits what they already believe and doubt anything that doesn't. Your aunt calls that confirmation bias."

Gabrielle rolled the phrase around. It fit what she was watching herself do. She had read the screenshot and instantly believed it, because Lakeside winning had stung, and the story made the sting make sense. If the post had said Lakeside's players volunteered at a shelter all weekend, she would have demanded three sources.

The deadline ticked closer with every minute. She imagined printing the rumor and then watching Lakeside show up Friday, coach and all, to play the game. The whole article would sit on a foundation that wasn't there. Worse, a rumor like that could spread until it sustained itself, passed along by every Northview kid who wanted it to be true, without anyone checking a single fact.

She picked up her phone, opened her messages, and typed to Aspen: Did anyone actually confirm the suspension? Call the athletic office?

Aspen replied with a shrugging emoji, then: my mom works near the district office, I'll ask.

Gabrielle finished her rice while she waited, watching the screen instead of the plate. A message finally buzzed through. "No suspension on record. Coach is running practice right now, Aspen saw the lights from the parking lot."

"Good news or bad news?" her dad asked.

"Good news for my article." She was already deleting the paragraph, fingers moving fast. "I get to write about how a rumor spread through two schools in one afternoon."

Then she typed a new headline: HOW A FAKE STORY RAN FASTER THAN THE TRUTH.

Grandpa's laptop sat open on the kitchen table, next to a plate of biscuit crumbs and a coffee mug shaped like a bee. Christopher had spent two whole days building his game, Catch the Nectar, where a bee zipped around a garden and collected drops from flowers. He had figured out loops, so the bee would flap its wings forever, and if-then blocks, so touching a flower added points to the score. He was ready to recruit his cousin's kid, Mahi, age seven, as his first official player.

"Watch this," Christopher said. Mahi grabbed the mouse and played like a maniac, swooping through flowers, laughing when the bee bonked into a fence. The score climbed to 57. Then Mahi announced she was done and wanted a fresh game.

Christopher clicked the green flag again. The score box cheerfully read 57.

"That's counterfeit!" Mahi shouted, jabbing the screen. "I never earned those! New game means new score!"

"That's not fair," Christopher agreed, though a strange thought was tickling him. The points weren't random. They were exactly the old total, sitting there waiting. He remembered Ms. Brown once saying that a Scratch variable keeps its value between runs. He'd nodded then, half listening, and now the words came back with an ironic little buzz.

So he tested it. He stopped the game, changed nothing except one thing: a block at the very top, before the loop began, that set score to 0. He pressed the flag. The box read 0. He played, got 12, stopped, pressed the flag again. Back to 0. Mahi played again and finished with 34.

"See? Justice," she said, hands on hips like a tiny judge.

"You recruited yourself as quality control, you know," Christopher said. "Every game tester gets one biscuit."

Mahi held out her hand, palm up, and said, "Two. I found the bug."

The snow had come in the night, and by morning school was cancelled, which meant the whole day stretched ahead like the hill behind Eve's house. She pulled on her boots, grabbed the red saucer sled, and met Sydney and Caitlin at the top of the slope, where the pines stood with their branches bowed under the weight of fresh snow.

Eve was halfway through her first run when she noticed something odd. Every time she crashed into the powder at the bottom, the snow flew up in a glittering cloud, and the flakes seemed to hang in the air long enough to be seen. She held out her dark wool mitten, caught one, and looked closely. Six arms, thin as eyelashes, branching out from a tiny center. She caught another. Six arms again. A third flake, lopsided where it had half melted, still showed six.

"Sydney, come look," she called. "I think they all have six."

Sydney tramped over and held out her own mitten, which was navy blue and porous enough that the flakes sank into it and vanished. "Mine keeps eating them," she complained, so she borrowed Eve's. Caitlin nominated herself as record keeper and pulled off a glove to write tallies in the snow with one finger.

They caught flakes for a long while, sledding between rounds, and every single one came out with six. Eve thought about the ones she had seen in picture books and on window screens, and realized she could not remember ever counting one with five, or seven, or eight. "It's like there's a rule," she said. "Snowflakes almost always have six sides or six arms. It must be something about how the water freezes."

"So a five-armed one is impossible?" Caitlin asked, still scratching tallies.

"Almost," said Eve. "That's why I want to keep checking."

Then Sydney shouted so loudly that a crow lifted off the fence post. On her mitten sat a fat, ragged flake that looked like a star that had lost a point. "Seven!" Sydney yelled. "I nominate this one to break the rule!"

Eve leaned in until her breath almost touched it. The flake had two centers, she saw, two little hearts pressed together, with arms overlapping where they had collided on the way down. Each half, when she traced it with her eye, had six arms of its own.

"It's two stuck together," she said. "A snowflake alliance."

Caitlin added two tallies to the snow and looked up, grinning. "Then the rule holds. Now somebody race me to the bottom."

The shovel leaned against the fence post like it had been there all summer, and maybe it had. Andrew picked it up and ran his thumb over the blade, which was the colour of dried blood and flaked when he scratched it. In the shed, the spade hung on its nail, clean and grey and sharp. Same iron, same grandpa, two different endings.

"Grandpa," Andrew called, "why is this one all crumbly?"

His grandpa came out wiping his hands on a rag. "Left that out since June, I expect. Rain and all." He tapped the shed wall, where a small wind turbine spun above the roof, charging the light inside. "The one in here stays dry. That matters, apparently."

Andrew set the rusty shovel beside the spade and crouched down to compare them. He was supposed to be learning this at school, physical changes and chemical changes, and Ms. Szabó had said something about it just last week. Melting was physical; the stuff was still the same stuff, just softer. Burning was chemical. He tried to evaluate which this was. If he scraped the rust off, would the shiny iron come back underneath, the way ice came back when water froze? He scratched. What came off was orange dust, and what was left was thinner than it should have been. The iron hadn't just changed shape. It had turned into something else, and it wasn't turning back.

"I think it's chemical," Andrew said slowly. "Like burning, but slow. The iron with the water and the air, it makes a new thing. It's called iron oxide." He'd found the words in his notebook at the bottom of his backpack, half-copied from the board.

"Is that a fact," said his grandpa, which was not really a question.

Andrew carried the shovel to the fence and laid it flat where he could keep an eye on it. Last summer he remembered leaving his bike out in the rain for two weeks because bringing it in felt like too much trouble, and the chain had squeaked all autumn no matter how much oil he used. He still wasn't sure that had been laziness or just a kid forgetting. He'd been planning to bring it in. Planning, he thought, wasn't the same as doing.

He got the wire brush from the shed and started on the blade, orange dust drifting onto his sneakers. The turbine above the roof spun and stopped and spun again. "Can I keep the good spade in here too?" he asked. "Somewhere dry, where it stays dry?"

His grandpa looked at him for a second, then hung it on a lower nail, within reach.

Luca counted the candles on his grandmother's menorah three times before Cyril arrived, and every time he got nine. That was the problem. Hanukkah lasted eight nights, his grandmother had said so at dinner, and eight nights should mean eight candles. He was still staring at the silver branches when the doorbell rang and Cyril came in, shaking snow off his jacket.

"Whoa," Cyril said. "Why does that thing have nine candles if the holiday is eight nights? That's weird."

"I don't know yet," Luca said, "but I'm going to figure it out before we light it."

He crouched down next to the menorah on the windowsill. One candle stood slightly apart from the others, raised a little higher on its own branch. The eight matched in a neat row, but the odd one sat off to the side like it had a different job. Maybe that was the clue. He took out his phone and snapped a picture, then zoomed in until he could see the branches clearly.

"Look," he said, showing Cyril. "Eight of them are in a line. The ninth one is separate and taller. It's not part of the pattern. It's like the frontier candle, standing outside the group."

Cyril frowned at the screen. "So what does it do?"

Luca's grandmother called from the kitchen that it was time. She handed Luca the matches, and Luca watched her nod toward the tall candle. "You start with the shamash," she said. "The helper."

Luca struck the match and touched it to the shamash, then used that flame to light the first candle in the row. The tall one had to burn first so it could kindle all the others, night after night. That was the whole answer, and he had found the edge of it himself, just from looking.

"So it's nine because one candle is the helper," Cyril said. "Eight for the nights, plus one to light them. Got it."

"Exactly," Luca said, and watched the flame of the shamash consume the wick's edge as the window glowed against the dark.

The group chat had been going all afternoon, mostly about the weekend hike Ms. Lee's class was taking to the plateau above the river. Mia was halfway through packing trail mix when her phone buzzed.

Are you mad at me?

It was Macy, in a private message, not the group chat. Mia blinked at it. She scrolled back up. The last thing she had sent Macy was one word: Okay. Except she had typed it "Okay." with a period, the way her thumb automatically did after every sentence.

"I'm not mad," she said out loud to her empty room, then typed, why would I be mad? and hit send with no period at all. Macy replied with a single thumbs-up, which somehow looked even angrier, and Mia flopped backward onto her bed. Something was going on that she could not see, some invisible rule about the messages themselves, and she meant to find it.

She scrolled through their whole conversation, looking for patterns. Messages that ended in periods: "Fine." "Sure." "Okay." Every one of those had started a small argument. Messages with no punctuation, like "haha okay" or "omg yes," always got a happy reply. She remembered last month, when Macy had sent "See you tomorrow." and Mia had spent an hour wondering what she'd done wrong. It worked both ways, apparently. A period at the end of a short text made it feel like Macy was closing a door.

The next morning, Mia brought it up on the way to class. "Marcus, if I text you 'okay,' is that friendly?"

"Obviously," Marcus said. "If you text me 'okay' with a period, you sound like you're firing me from a job."

"That's a real thing, you know," Macy said, catching up to them in the hallway. "My cousin told me about it. In 2016, researchers at Binghamton University found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one." She shrugged. "So it's not just me being weird."

"You looked it up?" Mia asked.

"Last night, after I thought you were mad. I wanted proof before I apologized for something that wasn't even happening." Macy pulled out her phone and showed them the article, and the three of them stood there in the crowded hallway reading it while somebody's trumpet case bumped past.

Marcus wants the group chat to keep planning the hike, and he wants Mia to accompany him on the steep trail because he's scared of heights and won't admit it. "So we're all good?" he asked.

"We're good," Mia said. Then, feeling resilient after a night of worrying, she typed into the group chat: okay no periods ever again, deal?

Three thumbs-ups came back within ten seconds, and one of them, she noticed, had a period after it.

Oliver knelt in the grass beside the pond at Mr. Ross's farm, pencil in hand, drawing his food chain on the back of a permission slip. He started with the frog, then an arrow to the snake, then an arrow to the hawk, because that was the order he'd thought of first.

"That's arbitrary," said Kallie, looking over his shoulder. "You can't just start anywhere." She held out a note she'd written during the bus ride, a message she'd been saving to tease him with: "Your chain starts with a frog. Frogs don't make food out of nothing. Where does the frog's energy really come from?" Oliver read it twice and frowned. He remembered, suddenly, the pond's green scum from last summer, before the drought. He'd skipped rocks across it while Kallie warned him not to. Now he noticed the same green film edging the shallows, thick along the sunny side and thin in the shade of the willow.

"The sun," he said slowly. He erased the frog, drew a sun instead, and put the arrow from the sun to the algae. "Most food chains start with the sun. Plants and algae, the producers, use sunlight to make their own food by photosynthesis. Then everything that consumes them, the tadpoles, the frogs, the snakes, the hawk, is just passing that energy along." He added the arrows one at a time, sun to algae, algae to tadpole, tadpole to frog.

Chantelle, who had been sampling cheese at the artisan stall near the barn, wandered over with a napkin still in her hand. "So what happens if the algae goes?" she asked. Oliver tested it with his thumb, covering the algae. The chain broke in half. "Everything after it goes hungry. The tadpoles starve, then the frogs, then the hawk. The top predator loses too, even though it never ate algae in its life." He thought about skipping those rocks last summer, how little he'd wondered about any of it. He drew the sun bigger, then wrote his name at the top of the page.

"Alright," said Mr. Ross from the fence, "bring your chains up to the barn."

The note was folded into a square and tucked inside Gavin's lunch bag, in Viviane's round handwriting: "Burned the toast AGAIN this morning. My brother says it's just melted, like ice. Physical change. Is he right? Bring evidence. Viviane." Gavin read it twice, then looked down at his own sandwich and grinned. Today Ms. Clarke-Williams had promised them the lab with the hot plates, and this was his chance to settle it.

"Toast," he announced, dropping his bag on the counter beside Viviane and Betty. "We're testing toast." Betty raised an eyebrow, but she helped him set out two slices of bread, a plate of ice cubes, and a magnifying lens while the hot plate ticked and warmed. The lab smelled like vinegar from the period before, sharp enough to make Gavin's nose wrinkle. He laid an ice cube on a tray and watched it pool into clear water. "Physical change," he said. "It can go back to ice in the freezer."

"But toast can't go back," Viviane said slowly, watching the bread on the hot plate. The edges had turned pale gold, then deeper brown, and a smell like Sunday morning drifted up, warm and almost sweet. Gavin bent close with the lens. The surface wasn't just darker. It was different, rough and blistered where it had been smooth.

"That's it," he said. "I can deduce it from the color. Melting doesn't make new colors, it just changes shape. But this brown stuff is new. It didn't exist in the soft bread." He flipped the toast with tongs, and the underside had gone nearly black at one corner where he'd left it too long against the rim. Betty poked the burnt edge with a pencil. It crumbled.

"So could my brother fix it?" Viviane asked. "If he's right, he just melts it back."

Gavin shook his head. "He can't. It's a chemical change, because heat creates new brown substances and the toast cannot turn back into soft bread. That's the difference. Ice goes back. Toast never does." Viviane wrote it down word for word on the back of her note, as if it were a message from the frontier of science, some place no one had mapped yet.

Ms. Clarke-Williams drifted past their station and sniffed the air. "Bread, Gavin? Interesting choice." He held up the burnt slice and the melted ice cube side by side. "One goes back," he said, "and one never does." She smiled and moved on, and Betty leaned over the counter.

"Text your brother," she told Viviane. "Tell him toast beats ice."

Viviane pulled out her phone, thumbs already flying, and Gavin slid the perfect golden slice onto a napkin and broke it in half, offering the bigger piece to Betty.

Easton tugged the lion head over his shoulders and blinked through the mesh eyes. The gymnasium behind the community temple smelled like incense from the hall next door, and the drums were already thumping in his chest. In two weeks, the temple's New Year gathering would feature the lion dance, and Ms. Leung had chosen him and Hope to perform it. He could not wait.

"Lion dance has two dancers," Hope said from behind him, her hands on his waist. "One in the head, one in the tail. Same costume." That was the rule, and it was the problem too, because every time Easton stepped left, Hope stepped right, and the whole lion collapsed in a tangle of red and gold fur.

They tripped again. Easton sat on the floor, breathing hard, and remembered the video he had watched three nights ago, when the idea first sparked. The lion in that video had moved like a single animal, front legs and back legs flowing together, and at the time he had assumed the dancers were just lucky. Now he suspected something hidden: the two dancers could not see each other at all, so they had to be following the same signal. The drums, the gongs, the cymbals. The music was telling both of them when to move.

"Test it," he said, jumping up. "Don't watch me. Listen. One drumbeat, I step forward. You step forward too. Gong means jump."

They tried it. Drum, drum, both feet landed together. Gong, and the lion leapt, fur rippling, tail snapping behind. It worked so well that Charlize, who had been categorizing the costumes into repair piles by the wall, dropped her clipboard and cheered. "You look like one creature!" she shouted. "Like a real lion!"

Ms. Leung watched from the doorway, then changed her mind about the schedule. "You're ready to perform at the gathering," she announced. "Not just the practice demonstration. The real one."

Later, drying sweat from his neck, Easton overheard a grandparent telling Charlize that many dancers in the temple troupe were descendants of the original founders, and that this gathering was considered the most prestigious one in the neighborhood. Easton grinned so wide his cheeks hurt.

When the drums started again, he lifted the head, felt Hope's hands settle on his waist, and together they sprang forward into the golden light.

At the reunion, the whole back garden smelled of sausages and cut grass, and Zachary stood with his cousins in a line, feet wide, waiting. In two weeks his school group would perform the haka Ka Mate to welcome new families at the community hall, and Uncle Hone had promised to check his form today. Zachary stamped, slapped his thighs, and puffed out his chest, but his feet kept tangling on the third move. The practice video was ambiguous about which foot went first there, and he had assumed it was the left, because most of the dance favoured the left. He had been wrong before with assumptions. Last year he had quit the school kapa haka group after one rehearsal because he felt clumsy, and he still wasn't sure whether that had been sensible or just lazy.

"Hold," said Uncle Hone, tapping his own knee. "Again, from the top. Slow."

Zachary went again, slower. He had a new idea: instead of copying the whole sequence at once, he would break the moves apart the way Ms. Kamau, his science teacher, described a decomposer breaking a fallen log into pieces an ecosystem can use. Third move only, ten times. Then the third and fourth together. It was tedious, but by the seventh repetition his feet stopped arguing with him, and by the tenth the pattern felt like walking.

"Why do we shout the words so loud?" his cousin Alaric asked, wiping his forehead.

"Because of what they're about," Uncle Hone said. "Ka Mate was composed around 1820 by the Ngāti Toa chief Te Rauparaha. He'd been hiding from enemies who were chasing him, and when he came out alive, he made this to celebrate surviving."

So the stomping was not just noise, Zachary thought; it was a man's heartbeat after coming out of hiding. He stamped the third move, hard, both feet planted.

"That one," he said. "Watch this."

Emilie had exactly one hour before her class project was due, and the account with all her slides was locked. She had used her old password, the one from the game site, and it no longer worked because last spring she had let her cousin guess it in about four seconds. She still remembered her cousin's grin, and she still felt annoyed at herself for choosing her cat's name followed by the number one.

The repair shop worker at the computer store near her house leaned over the counter and clicked through the account page. "You can't get your old password back, because the site doesn't have it," he said. "Well-run websites store a hash of each password, a scrambled one-way fingerprint, instead of the password itself." He drew a quick squiggle on a napkin to show how the letters of her password might look after the site scrambled them. "They can check a login without keeping the real password. That's why they can only let you make a new one, never tell you the old one."

Emilie stared at the squiggle. So the site held a fingerprint, not the password itself. That meant nobody at the site could read her password even if they wanted to, which felt strange but also somehow safe, like a translucent window that let light through without showing her face. She thought about the game site where she had reused that same password everywhere. If one site leaked its fingerprints, someone could try her password on other sites too. That was the pattern she had never seen before, and now she couldn't stop seeing it.

She typed a new password, something long and odd, and wrote a hint on a card she kept in her desk drawer at home, under a small hierarchy of papers organized by subject, homework on top. Then she opened her slides and submitted the project with six minutes to spare. Her friend Maeve texted, "Did you make it?" Emilie sent back the napkin squiggle, photographed on the counter. "New password. It's called a hash, sort of. Long story. Ask me at school."

Brayden sat on the spinning stool at ClearVision Optical, twenty minutes before his mom's car had to be back at the garage. The optometrist had already told him his vision was 20/200, which meant the big E at the top of the chart had been a blurry smudge. Now he had to pick frames before the store closed at five, and the clock above the register read 4:41.

He tried on a pair of black wire frames and looked in the mirror. Behind him, Alessio and Felicia sat on the bench by the window, passing a bag of pretzels back and forth.

"You look like Mr. Katz," Alessio said.

"I do not." Brayden squinted at his reflection. He kind of did.

Felicia held up her phone. "My cousin in Australia just texted me. She says she has six-six vision and she's really proud of it. Is that better than Brayden's twenty-something?"

Alessio shrugged. "Six is smaller than twenty, so probably worse?"

Brayden took the phone and read the message himself. His cousin was bragging, the way you brag about good eyes. He thought about the eye chart on the wall, the letters he'd squinted at all morning. The numbers on charts measured the same thing. Six-six had to be their way of writing perfect vision, the same as twenty-twenty, because countries that used metres would measure distance differently. It was like spelling "color" as "colour."

"I think six-six is the same as twenty-twenty," he said. "Australia uses metres, so they write it different. Her eyes are just normal."

The optometrist, passing by with a tray of lenses, nodded. "That's right."

"See, she's not better than anyone," Brayden said, handing the phone back. Some small resentment about the bragging faded, which surprised him.

The wire frames pinched his nose. He swapped them for round tortoiseshell ones and the world in the mirror still looked soft, because the lenses were plain glass until his real prescription arrived. Through the window he could see the lush green of the hedge along the parking lot, one blurry green mass.

"They'll preserve your new lenses if you get the coating," the clerk said. "Scratch guard."

"Get it," Brayden said. His mom was already at the counter, pulling out her card.

He put the glasses back on and looked at the wall of frames, each one suddenly sharp-edged and separate, all the little screws visible. "Whoa," he said. "Those have screws?"

Kaylee sat in the dentist's waiting room, kicking her sneakers against the chair leg and reading the same poster about flossing for the fourth time. Across the room, her classmate Cale was hunched over, gripping the armrests of his chair like it might bolt for the door. He wasn't even here for an appointment; he'd come along with his older sister. "You okay?" Kaylee asked. Cale shook his head. "My chest feels tight and my heart's going crazy. I think something's really wrong with me." His breathing went fast and shallow, and the paper cup of water in his hand crumpled until the water dwindled down to a few drops on the carpet.

Kaylee's first reasoning went like this: tight chest plus racing heart equals call somebody, immediately. She shot up and waved down Ms. Anderson, the dental hygienist, who crouched beside Cale and felt his pulse. While she checked him, something odd happened. Cale's breathing slowed on its own, and the color came back into his face, and after a few minutes he said the squeezing feeling was almost gone. "That was so weird," he mumbled. "It hit me out of nowhere and it was like the worst it could possibly get, and now it's just... leaving."

"It sounds like a panic attack," Ms. Anderson said quietly. "It's a sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes. It can feel like a heart attack even though it isn't one." Kaylee blinked. That was exactly backwards from what she'd assumed, that scary things only get worse until a doctor fixes them. She'd been ready to sprint down the hall screaming for an ambulance, and instead the peak had come and gone like a wave hitting the beach.

"Subjective," Kaylee said slowly, trying out a word from her vocabulary homework. "It felt like a heart attack, but the feeling wasn't the facts." Cale managed a weak grin. "Thanks, walking dictionary." Ms. Anderson said Cale's sister and his parents should hear about it from him today, so a grown-up who knew him could keep an eye out, and Cale nodded and pulled out his phone. Kaylee slid the crumpled cup into the trash and dropped into the chair beside him. "Next time your chest does that," she said, "squeeze my hand instead of the cup. The cups are innocent."

Mathis had to sit with his knees pulled up because his sneakers pressed against the heater vent, and even that didn't help. "Dad, my shoes feel like clown shoes are coming. I mean they don't fit. Again."

"Again?" His dad glanced over from the driver's seat. "We bought those in September."

"That's the bizarre part," Mathis said, wiggling his toes against the toe of the shoe. "September. And look at my jeans." He smoothed his hands down his legs. "Still fine. Not even short."

They pulled into the mall parking lot, and Mathis was already unbuckling. At the shoe store, the cashier measured his foot and raised her eyebrows. "Size up a full size and a half since fall," she said. "That's a big jump."

Mathis stared at the metal measuring thing like it was treasure. A full size and a half, while his jeans still fit. He turned the fact over the whole time his dad paid. His feet were somehow ahead of the rest of him, running a race his legs hadn't started yet. He had assumed growing up would happen all at once, like a plant shooting up evenly, but the evidence said otherwise. Feet first, apparently, then everything else.

He tested his idea on the way to the food court. "Dad, hold on. If feet grow before legs do, then I bet my arms are going to be next. Or my legs. Something's coming." He held up his hands and studied them. "These are, like, the candidates. The scouts. The advance team."

His dad laughed so hard he had to set down the tray. "The advance team. I'd like a report when they arrive."

Monday morning, Mathis found Adelina at her locker before the bell. "Adelina. Scientific question. If your feet get bigger and your jeans still fit, what does that mean?" She squinted at him. "It means you're about to get tall," he said, grinning. "I'm expecting a growth spurt any day now. I'll keep records. Shoe box receipts and everything." He looked down at his brand-new sneakers, still blindingly white, and pointed his toes down the hall.

Anna wanted a new profile picture before Monday, and the mall fountain made a good backdrop, with its polished stone and the big skylight overhead. Malory leaned in on one side and McKayla on the other, and a passing stranger offered to take the shot so all three could be in it. He took two photos on Anna's phone and walked off toward the food court.

"Post the second one," McKayla said. "My hair wasn't ready in the first." Anna sat on the fountain's edge to look through them. She zoomed in on McKayla's hoodie, where the letters of their school, Jefferson Middle, sat right above the crest. Then she zoomed further, past Malory's shoulder, to the mall directory mounted on the pillar behind them. The strip of shops along the bottom was labelled Millbrook Road. She scrolled back out and looked at the whole picture again. Somebody who had never met them could read a school name and a street name off one photo, and the mall had exactly one entrance on Millbrook Road.

She tried an experiment. She asked Malory and McKayla to slide down the bench until the directory was out of the frame, then she swapped positions so the school crest faced away from the camera. "Can you demonstrate the new pose one more time?" she asked, and McKayla flipped her hood inside out and grinned. Anna took the photo herself, zoomed in, and checked every corner. Wall, plants, skylight. Nothing that named a street, a school, or a house number anywhere.

"Since when do you care?" Malory asked.

"Since a guy I've never met just held my phone," Anna said. She posted the clean picture and put her phone in her pocket.

At the science store window, an ear model made of rubbery cartilage stood beside a jar marked with a toxic symbol from some chemistry kit. "We should get that for Ms. Lavoie's room," McKayla said, tapping the glass. Anna pulled her phone back out, framed the two of them with the ear behind them, and said, "Okay, but check the background first."

The word card said "colour," and Florence felt her stomach drop. She was standing at the front of Mr. Chowdhury's classroom, the last three spellers left in the school bee, and the judges had just handed her a word she had argued about only two weeks ago.

"Can I have the language of origin?" she asked.

"English," said Mr. Chowdhury, who was reading from the official list.

Florence's mind went back to the lunch table, where Liam had been waving his phone around. His cousin in Toronto had sent him a photo of her school spelling list, and half the words looked wrong to him. "Colour," he had said. "Honour. They spell it with a u up there. Who's right?"

They had looked it up together in the library instead of going outside. Florence had found the answer in a dusty reference book while Liam leaned over her shoulder so close she had to compress herself into the corner of the chair to keep reading. Before 1828, English spellings were a tangle, and then Noah Webster's American Dictionary of the English Language pushed simpler spellings, like "color" instead of "colour," and those became standard in the United States. Neither spelling was really wrong. They just belonged to different places, like two doors out of the same room.

Katia, sitting in the second row now, mouthed something at her. Florence couldn't read it. The clock on the wall hung slightly off true, tilted a few degrees from perpendicular, and she fixed her eyes on it to steady herself.

Here was the trap. At lunch, Liam had said the school bee would follow American convention, but Florence had never actually checked the rules sheet. She thought about it now, fast. This was a school bee in Ohio. The pronouncer had given every other word in American spelling when he read the vocabulary sentences. If the card said "colour," then the judges wanted the British spelling, and they had written it that way on purpose to see if spellers knew it was a variant, not a mistake. If she spelled it the American way, she might be marked wrong.

"C-o-l-o-u-r," she said. "Colour."

Mr. Chowdhury checked his sheet and nodded. "That is correct."

Liam, eliminated three rounds earlier on "manoeuvre," smacked the desk softly. "You remembered the lunch argument."

After the bee, which Florence won on the word "perpendicular" of all things, she found Liam by the door. He was holding his phone, probably about to text his cousin the news.

"So who won the spelling war?" he asked. "Webster or the Canadians?"

Florence thought about the book in the library, about her own choice to look things up instead of guessing. "Nobody," she said. "They just went through different doors." She tucked her trophy under her arm and pushed open the classroom door.

Ryan sat on the end of his bed with a printed page in his hands, one he had grabbed off Ms. Bighorn's classroom shelf before the bell rang. His left knuckle still stung where he had punched his desk that afternoon, after Rudy had grabbed his sketchbook and held it open above his head for the whole bus line to see. Ryan hadn't planned to hit anything. His hand had simply gone before the rest of him could vote.

The page was from a science magazine. He read the same sentence three times: the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties. He put the page down on his quilt and looked at his hand, then at the wall above his desk, where a dent from a thrown controller still marked the paint from last spring.

He flashed back to that afternoon, seconds before the desk punch. Rudy waving the sketchbook, the crowd laughing, Isra saying "just give it back," and then a kind of white gap where the punch should have been in his memory. It was like trying to remember a hallway with the lights off. He had walked through it, but he couldn't see it.

That was the part that interested him. If the planning part of his brain was still under construction, then maybe the gap wasn't him being a bad person. Maybe it was like trying to drive a car that was still getting its brakes installed. He decided to test it. He took out a notebook and wrote a rule at the top: any time Rudy grabs something, count to five before moving. It was a way of lending the unfinished part of his brain a substitute. He couldn't eliminate the impulse, but he could build a wall around the part where his hand decided things on its own.

At school the next morning, Rudy snatched the notebook itself right off Ryan's desk. Ryan felt the same hot spark go off behind his eyes, and he counted. One, two, three. Isra leaned over from the next seat and said, "That's the prefrontal cortex thing you were reading about, right? The part that plans stuff?" Ryan nodded, still counting. Five. Then he stood up, walked to Ms. Bighorn's desk, and said, "Rudy has my notebook and I'd like it back." Rudy blinked, handed it over without a joke, and the class went back to its worksheet.

At lunch Ryan told them the whole story, including the dent in his wall, as an anecdote about the controller. "It sounded smart at the time," he admitted. "Thinking I'd never get frustrated." "That was a little naive," Isra said, and Rudy laughed so hard milk came out his nose. Ryan laughed too, and slid the notebook, safely, into the bottom of his backpack.

Sarah stood on a kitchen chair in the living room because it felt more like a podium, and held her note cards at an angle nearly perpendicular to the floor, which made them impossible to read. "Two minutes," her mother said from the couch, thumb on the timer. "Opening hook, three points, closing. Go." Sarah opened with a question about school lunches, listed her three points about longer recess, and then mumbled toward the end, "So, yeah. Thanks for listening." The timer read one minute forty. "Your closing just kind of fell off a cliff," her mother said gently. "Want to try Devon's trick? He practiced in front of his dog."

That was the problem. Sarah had a strong hook and three solid points, but the ending slid away from her like the last bit of a smoothie through a straw. She flopped onto the rug and stared at the ceiling, where a water stain looked like a lopsided map. Then she remembered Ms. Côté's class, the day they had listened to a recording of a speech from 1963. Martin Luther King Jr. had said "I have a dream" over and over, and even kids who doodled through everything had sat still for it. When Devon asked afterward why it worked, Ms. Côté had said only, "Repeating the same words at the start of several sentences is called anaphora," and refused to say more, which drove everyone crazy. Sarah sat up so fast her pulse seemed to accelerate.

Maybe the repetition itself was the principle, the thing doing the work, like a drumbeat you could feel in the floor. She grabbed a fresh card and wrote four sentences, each one starting the same way: "Recess gives us time to think. Recess gives us time to move. Recess gives us a reason to love Tuesday afternoons. Recess gives us back our brains." She read them aloud to the ceiling and grinned, because the fourth one made her laugh every time.

She climbed back onto the chair and tapped her cards straight. "Timer," she said. Her mother smiled and held up her thumb. "Two minutes. Go."

The after-school culture club was making a display for the hallway bulletin board, and Kaitlyn wanted her section to be the best one. Every member had drawn a small map with arrows showing where their families had come from. Imane had drawn Morocco and Canada with a bold line between them, and Charly had taped a photo of a grandmother's kitchen in Manila. Kaitlyn's own arrows were easy, from Ireland and from Mexico to here, but the new boy, whose name tag still said hello, I'm Adnan, had drawn nothing at all.

"Where are you from?" she asked him, because that was the whole point of the map.

Adnan turned his pencil over and over in his fingers. "I've lived in Turkey, then Malaysia, then Egypt, and now here," he said. "My parents are from Pakistan. But I was born in Turkey, so I don't really." He stopped and started again. "Every time someone asks, I feel like my answer is too long, and it must sound made up."

Kaitlyn frowned. Everyone else at the table had answered in one word, and his answer needed four countries plus one more. She wondered whether there was a word for a person whose answer was a whole list. While the others worked, she went to the library cart that Mr. Ngo had wheeled in beside the art supplies, the one stacked with books about families and migration. She flipped through one about children who move around the world, and there it was in the second chapter. An American sociologist named Ruth Hill Useem had coined the term "third culture kid" back in the 1950s, for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture. Kaitlyn read the sentence three times to be sure she had it right.

She carried the book back to the table and set it down in front of Adnan. "Third culture kid," she said. "That's an actual term. A sociologist made it up."

Adnan looked at the page, then at her. "That's a legitimate thing? People study it?"

"Look at the author and the date," Kaitlyn said, pointing. "It's real."

Charly leaned over. "So Adnan's map needs five arrows."

"No," said Adnan, and for the first time that afternoon he smiled. "It needs a circle. All the places, and me in the middle." He began to draw, and Imane offered him her good colored pencils, which she never lent to anyone, a small ritual she performed only when something mattered.

Kaitlyn went back to her own arrows and found that they didn't diminish next to his circle. They were just different, side by side on the same board. When Mr. Ngo came by to check the display, he studied Adnan's circle for a long moment, then gave a slow nod and wrote something in his notebook.

At the end of the meeting, Adnan tore a corner off his scrap paper and copied the title of the book. "For my little sister," he said. "She hates that question too."

"Tell her there's a name for it," Kaitlyn said, and slid the colored pencils back across the table to Imane.

Paisley sat in the computer lab during lunch, refreshing the school club page for the third time. The Robotics Club roster was gone, replaced by a plain notice: "Page under repair." She needed the list because she had promised Mr. Demir she would delegate jobs to each member before Friday's build session, and now she couldn't remember who had signed up for the sensor team.

Iris leaned over from the next computer. "It was up yesterday. I read the whole thing, even the part where Yuna wrote her name in all capitals. YUNA. Like she was announcing an emperor."

Paisley laughed, then stopped. Yesterday. Something nagged at her, and it wasn't the roster. Yesterday she had also seen a different page, the one from last month, the one where the club's old president had posted a photo of Paisley mid-sneeze with the caption "Club mascot." She had been so relieved when someone told her the post was deleted. She had even gone back to check, twice, and it was gone. Deleted meant gone, she had decided. Like erasing a whiteboard.

"Can I borrow your screen?" Paisley asked. Iris slid over. Paisley typed the way Mr. Demir had shown the class one afternoon, on a site he called the Wayback Machine. She remembered him saying only one sentence about it, that it had saved more than one trillion web pages. A trillion. She had thought that sounded like a made-up number, like something a kid would invent to win an argument.

She typed the club page's address and clicked the snapshot dated last month. The page rebuilt itself, sneeze photo and all. Paisley stared at her own crumpled face, mouth open, one hand mid-air.

"Whoa," Iris said. "I thought it was deleted."

"It was." Paisley pointed at the address bar. "It's saved here anyway. Deleted from the page, not from everywhere."

"So the roster might be too," Iris said. "From before the repair."

Paisley typed again, found a snapshot from Tuesday, and there it was: seventeen names, sensor team circled in green marker by whoever had scanned the sign-up sheet. She copied the names onto her palm with a pen.

Yuna appeared in the doorway, lunch bag swinging. "You found it? Wait. Is that the sneeze picture?"

Paisley closed the old snapshot slowly, the way you close a door you don't want to hear. "It was only ever supposed to be temporary," she said.

Yuna came over and stood behind them, looking at the blank screen.

Alexis dragged the picnic table into the shade of the fence and set out her sketchbook, two pencils, and a pink eraser worn round at one end. Liv dropped onto the bench across from her and peered at the page, where Alexis had drawn a horizon line with two dots on it.

"Two dots," Liv said. "That's it? That's your room?"

"They're vanishing points." Alexis set a fresh hard pencil against the paper. "Every edge of the room has to point at one of them. Watch, I'll draft the walls first, all light, like scaffolding." She drew a vertical line for the corner of the far wall, then angled lines out from its top and bottom toward each dot. Soon the page held a whole network of faint lines, fanning out in every direction, with a box of a room caught in the middle of it. Was this how real artists saw the world, she wondered, invisible lines streaming out of everything toward the edges of the page?

"Can I try?" Liv grabbed a soft pencil, the dark one, and pressed hard as she drew a line from the corner toward the left dot. The line gouged shiny gray into the paper. Alexis drew the window, darkened the real edges of the room, then reached for her eraser and swept it across the network of guide lines.

Half of them came away. Liv's line did not.

Alexis erased again, harder. The line only turned smudgy, a ghost stamped into the paper. She rubbed until the eraser squeaked, and the line sat there, bold as a fence post, cutting straight through her window.

"Liv. Look." Alexis held the sketchbook up to the light, and the groove Liv had pressed shone back at them. "You carved it in. It won't come out."

Liv winced. "My brother says our stubbornness is hereditary. Maybe my pencil has it too."

From the other side of the fence, Ms. Smith leaned over, watering can still in hand. "What's the disaster over there?"

"Nothing," Alexis called back, though she was already testing an idea. She took the hard pencil and drew one more guide line, barely touching the paper, quick as a whisper. She darkened a shelf edge over it, then erased. The guide line vanished clean, leaving only the shelf. So that was the trick. Light hands for the guides, heavy hands for the real edges, and the room stayed a room.

"New page," she said, and turned it herself. "This time you get the hard pencil. One line, feather light. If you can see yourself pressing, you're pressing."

Liv took the hard pencil and hovered over the paper like it might bite. "Feather light," she repeated, and drew a line so faint they had to tilt the page to find it.

"Perfect," Alexis said, and pinned the corner of the sketchbook down before the breeze could argue.

James counted the money in his pocket for the third time: one five-dollar bill and four quarters. The milk was priced at $4.99 on the shelf, exactly what his mom had written on the note, and he had $6.00. He could do this.

Walking to the corner store alone still felt strange. His mom usually came with him, but she had twisted her ankle watering the plants, and she needed milk for dinner. "You're eleven," she had said, pressing the bill into his hand. "You can be my legs today."

The automatic doors whooshed open, carrying the smell of cardboard and cold air from the freezer case. James found the milk, its plastic jug chilling his palms, and marched to the till. The cashier rang it up and said, "That'll be $5.36."

James blinked. "The shelf said $4.99."

"Plus tax," the cashier said, tapping the register screen.

He winced, but only a little, because $5.36 was still less than $6.00. He handed over the five, then dug out the quarters, and the cashier gave him back a dime and four pennies. Fourteen cents. Outside, he counted it again to be sure, the coins warm from his pocket, and worked out the tax must have been thirty-seven cents. So that was the hidden rule: the shelf price wasn't the whole price. He would need to bring extra next time.

At school the next morning he told Maxine and Francesco about it at lunch. "I had enough, but barely," he said. "The shelf price leaves out sales tax. It gets added at the till."

Francesco shook his head. "Not where my cousins live. In the UK, the price on the shelf already includes VAT, so what you see is what you pay." He spread his hands like he was laying out a map. "Same in most of the EU."

"Wait," Maxine said, spooning her yogurt. "So when my family visits my aunt in London, the price is the whole price?"

"That's what Francesco said," James told her, grinning.

That afternoon, his mom sent him again. This time he brought seven dollars, a whole extra cushion, and he picked out the milk himself. When the total came up, he counted his change out loud at the door, dime and pennies clinking into his fist.

"Fourteen cents again," he said, and pushed the doors open into the warm afternoon.

The August game was only eighty-two degrees, yet by halftime Benjamin felt like he was dragging a sandbag up a hill. His shirt stuck to his back, and sweat rolled down his arms without drying. He remembered the tournament in June, when the thermometer had read ninety-five but the air had been crisp and dusty. That day he'd played three games and still had enough energy to shoot hoops with Kaden afterward. Today, in cooler weather, his legs felt like wet rope.

"Sprint it back," the coach called, and Benjamin tried to comply, but his feet argued with him.

Bailey subbed in for him and sat beside him on the bench with a towel. "It's not even that hot," Bailey said, fanning himself with his hand. "Why is everyone dying?"

Benjamin thought about the puddle of sweat on the floor beneath him. In June, his arms had dried between quarters. Today nothing dried. He looked at the drops sitting on his wrist like beads, and an idea clicked into place, the same way a pass route suddenly makes sense. "In June the sweat dried," he said slowly. "Mr. Ba said sweat cools you when it evaporates. Today it just sits there."

Mr. Ba, watering the sideline plants, called over, "Humid days are like that." That was all he said, but it was enough.

"It's the wet air," Benjamin told Bailey. "The sweat can't dry, so it can't cool us." Bailey had been insisting the problem was the heat, but now he changed his mind. "So the water bottles aren't enough," Bailey said. "We need breaks."

The next timeout, Benjamin asked the coach for a full break in the shade, and the coach agreed, saying it was the most feasible option left in a game they were barely hanging onto. Benjamin felt it as his obligation too, since he'd figured it out. Under the tree, the breeze finally dried a patch of sweat on his neck, and a small coolness spread through him.

In the fourth quarter he stole the ball at half court, and the ball left his fingers in a clean, rising arc toward the hoop.

The new eighth-grade group chat had lasted exactly one day before it became a disaster, and Mr. Ramírez had given Sarah until lunch to propose rules or lose the chat entirely. He had agreed to supervise the project, which mostly meant standing by the whiteboard and looking pessimistic, which he did well.

"We could ban all caps," said Eugenie, who had been shouted at in the chat for spelling Beyoncé wrong. "All caps means yelling, right?"

"That's one rule. We need actual official ones." Sarah was typing. In 1995, she discovered, someone really had written official online manners, a document called RFC 1855, and it was titled "Netiquette Guidelines." Netiquette. She said the word out loud twice and decided she could never say it with a straight face, which was a problem, because she now had to present it.

Baylee had her own agenda. She wanted the rule to be that group members could post fan art of the volleyball team's mascot, the screaming piston, which was a truck engine with a face. "Two of my drawings got buried under forty messages about cafeteria pizza," she said. "Buried. Under pizza."

At lunch, Sarah stood up and reported that rules for online manners actually existed, written in 1995, a document called RFC 1855, and its title was "Netiquette Guidelines." Eugenie laughed so hard she knocked over her milk. Then Mr. Ramírez cleared his throat and admitted that the 1995 guide said nothing about truck engine mascots, because 1995 had never imagined a group chat about cafeteria pizza either.

"So we follow it and add our own," Sarah said, writing RULE 7: NO CAPS, RULE 8: PISTON ART ALLOWED. Baylee held up her drawing as the class voted.

"Motion passes," said Eugenie, raising her milk-less hand.

The ranger station at the park had a small porch, and Jacob sat on its steps on the last morning of the trip, watching steam rise off the distant geyser basin. Their flight home left that evening, straight east, back to their house near the coast. He felt great, and that was the strange part. Six days ago they had flown west to get here, and he had bounced off the plane ready to hike, while his mother wandered the trail like a sleepwalker for two days. He turned that over in his mind. Same length of flight, same number of hours, but going one direction had knocked her flat and going the other had done nothing to him.

Mr. Khoury, the ranger whose residence stood behind the station, came out with two mugs of cocoa and handed one to Jacob's friend Reed, who had traveled out with his own family on the same flight. "You two look like you're solving a puzzle," Mr. Khoury said. "Last day, most kids are just sad."

"Reed's mom was fine when we flew out here," Jacob said, "but my mom wasn't, and now everybody's worried about the flight home. Same trip, backwards." He stirred his cocoa slowly. "Flying east hits people harder than flying west. I don't know why. It's just the pattern."

"Alvin said the same thing after his trip last summer," Reed said. "He got home from Japan and slept through two whole days."

So there was a rule, and it worked on people like weather works on a mountain: invisible itself, but you could see what it did. Jacob decided to test a simple idea. If flying east was the bad direction, then on the day of an eastward flight he should go to bed later and sleep later, not earlier, so his body would already be leaning toward the time waiting at home. Tonight he would refuse the airplane nap, stay awake until midnight in his own bed, and let his mother try it too.

He found her at the cabin, packing, and laid out the plan. She listened, frowned, then nodded. On the flight home Jacob kept his window shade up, refused the meal he didn't want, and stared at the seatback until the cabin dimmed. They landed at one in the morning local time, and his mother was asleep before the wheels stopped.

At breakfast she came down bright-eyed and poured herself coffee. "Radical idea of yours actually worked," she said. "I'm going to nurture it into a family rule."

Jacob spread jam on his toast and grinned. "Rule one," he said. "Eastbound, stay up late."

Eli had eleven signatures and a problem: the delivery trucks behind Mr. Fischer's building idled outside his bedroom window at eleven at night, and he had until Monday's council meeting to do something about it. Monday was three days away, which felt like a lot until his mother reminded him she'd already paid for the meeting slot.

"Twelve signatures," Shea said, reading the clipboard over his shoulder at the kitchen table. "That's not a petition, that's a birthday card." Eli winced and pulled the clipboard away. On the screen in front of him was the city website, which was mostly a camouflage of blue links and helpful-looking buttons that led nowhere. Somewhere in there, he was almost sure, was a rule about trucks at night. He just had to find it.

He did not find it that way. He found it by calling Mr. Fischer, who owned the building and answered his door in a cardigan. "Bylaws," Mr. Fischer said, chewing the word like a peppermint. "Look under noise, or garbage collection. Municipal bylaws cover that sort of thing. Parking, noise, pets, garbage." He said it the way a person lists groceries, then went back inside.

Eli typed the four words into the search box and there it was: a bylaw about collection times, sitting in a PDF with a watermark across every page. So the city had already made a rule; the trucks were just breaking it quietly, every night, to nobody's attention. He tested his theory the way he'd test anything: he walked behind the building at ten thirty and took a photo of the idling truck, its clock glowing in the photo's corner. Then he took three more, on two different nights. Photos were objective. Nobody could argue with a timestamp.

At the kitchen table, Shawn helped him staple the signatures to the printed bylaw and the photos. "You're going to stand up in front of the whole council?" Shawn asked. "In a shirt?" Eli looked down at his hoodie, considered the question seriously, and went upstairs to find one.

"Order of business, item six," the clerk said Monday evening. Eli stood up, photos in hand, and said, "I'd like to talk about garbage collection."

The pool at Riverside was so dilapidated that the diving board had been roped off with caution tape and the tiles near the shallow end had turned the color of old teeth. Charlotte loved it anyway, because for the first time the rec center had a real swim team, and she was on it. The city had promised new revenue from pool passes would pay for repairs, so everyone kept saying, but the first three weeks of practice felt more like a war than a season.

Nayla insisted on doing backstroke starts from the middle lane. Leandro wanted everyone to sprint the warmup, and the boy from the other side of town, whom nobody had named out loud yet, kept drifting to lane six to be alone. They argued about lane order, about turns, about whose fault the dropped relay exchange was. The coach blew the whistle so often that Charlotte stopped flinching.

Sitting in the bleachers one evening, waiting for her ride, she spotted a thin paperback left behind on the bench, a psychology book with a chapter about how groups develop. She read a page while the过滤器 hummed. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages, and one word in the middle of the list made her sit up straight: storming. The stage before it was called forming, and after the storm came norming, and then performing.

At the next practice she cornered Nayla and Leandro by the kickboard bin. "I read that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing," she said. "Storming is a stage. Like, the arguing is part of it, not the end of it."

"So we're supposed to fight?" Leandro said, wringing out his cap.

"We're supposed to get through it." Charlotte pointed at the boy in lane six. "First we integrate him, and I mean actually put him in the relay, not just in the pool."

It did not click that day, or the next. But when Nayla gave up the middle lane for starts, and Leandro slowed his warmup enough for the newest swimmers to keep pace, something shifted, the way current shifts under the surface and you feel it before you see it. By the meet against Fairview, the relay exchange they had dropped eleven times in practice snapped together cleanly, four hands slapping the wet concrete in rhythm.

They took third place out of six teams. Nobody had a trophy to hold up, so Leandro held the ribbon over his head like a banner, and the boy from lane six grinned and bumped his shoulder against Charlotte's.

"Same time Monday?" Nayla called from the ladder, hair dripping.

"Same lane," Charlotte said.

Jaxon lined up the cans from his school food drive on the kitchen table and tapped each one with a spoon, listening. He had agreed to volunteer at the community food bank on Saturday, his first time, and he wanted to bring good food, not trouble. One box smelled faintly like old cardboard, and he had a theory: somewhere in the pile, one can had started to deteriorate, letting dampness in, and that single can was quietly ruining its neighbours. He couldn't see the culprit, so he tested for it. Any can that rattled or gave a dull thud instead of a firm ring went into the suspect pile.

"You're tapping soup," said Frank, who had come over to help carry boxes. "Soup doesn't confess."

"One of them might," Jaxon said. He held up a dented can of pears. "This one sounds wrong."

At the food bank on Saturday, Mr. Oyelaran showed them where to shelve things, and during break Jaxon read the history posted on the break-room wall. "Listen to this," he told Frank. "The first food bank was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, started in 1967 by John van Hengel." He read the name twice because it felt important. "This whole idea, sharing food like a bank shares money, started with one guy."

Then came the twist. When Jaxon pulled out his suspect can of pears and opened it for inspection, Mr. Oyelaran peered inside and laughed. "That's a legitimate can of fruit cocktail," he said. "The rattling is the maraschino cherry." The dull thud had been a cherry the whole time.

Jaxon turned red, then grinned, and Frank laughed so hard he knocked over a box of macaroni. One elbow later they were both on their knees, and in the spilled noodles crawled a single fat larva, the real culprit from the smelly box at home. Jaxon pointed at it. "See? I was right. Just wrong can."

Mr. Oyelaran handed them a broom. "Sweep first," he said. "Gloat after."

Brody set two pitchers on the kitchen counter, one full of strawberry lemonade and one half empty, and stared at the leftover jug from Saturday. He and Emy-Rose had charged three dollars a cup at the end-of-summer stand in his driveway, because fresh strawberries cost a lot at the farm stand and they wanted their money back. By four o'clock, three full jugs sat unsold in the shade, and Andrei had biked home shaking his head. Brody's motive had been simple: cover the cost of the berries. The result had been a row of jugs nobody bought.

He remembered February, when the three of them had tried the same stand in the garage. A flashback surfaced as he rinsed a spoon: Ms. Saleh, their neighbour, trudging through snow to buy two cups at four dollars each, because strawberries in winter came from far away and there were almost none. That day they had sold out in an hour and still had a waiting list. Now, in August, when every garden and farm around overflowed with berries, they had priced high and ended with jugs.

On Sunday evening, Emy-Rose texted him a message, and he read it twice. "My mom says a farmer dumped a whole truck of peaches yesterday because nobody would pay what he asked. The peaches were worth more to him unsold than cheap. Is that going to be us and our jugs?" Brody typed back, "Come over tomorrow. Bring Andrei. And a funnel."

The next morning the kitchen smelled of mint and lemon. Brody laid it out while Emy-Rose stirred. "In winter we charged a lot because strawberries were scarce and people still wanted them. This weekend we charged a lot when they're everywhere. We offered way more lemonade than anybody wanted to buy at that price, and it piled up." He tapped the jug. "Andrei found the word last night. Surplus." Andrei grinned from the doorway, holding his phone. "So tomorrow we drop the price until the cups move."

They transmitted the new plan to the whole street with a hand-lettered sign: one dollar a cup, strawberry lemonade, today only. Ms. Saleh was first in line, and by noon only a sticky ring remained at the bottom of the last jug. Brody poured the final cup and handed it to Andrei. "Two dollars next time," Andrei said, and Brody laughed and shook the empty jug upside down.

The talent show was at seven, and John had signed up to sing. He had been practicing all week behind the canoe shed, and Alicia was his only audience, so she knew exactly how good he sounded. That was why it was so strange when she caught a whiff of something sour while they lugged the sound equipment across the field. John kept talking about his song, oblivious, and Alicia realized he probably could not smell himself at all. Nobody could, she figured, because your own nose got used to you. That was the hidden part.

"You need a shower before seven," she said, and then, because he looked embarrassed, she added, "Everyone does. It's camp." She had learned that the hard way on Tuesday, when Zain had slid a deodorant stick across the picnic table without a word. Alicia had stared at it, mortified, until Zain said, "Puberty. Our sweat glands go into overdrive and the bacteria that accompany the sweat make the smell. Showering washes them off, deodorant keeps them down. Mr. Wardak showed us the handout." Alicia had taken the stick to the bathhouse and noticed, for the first time, that she actually felt cleaner afterward, and that the feeling lasted through capture the flag. It was not permanent, though. By morning the smell crept back, which proved there was a cycle, and a cycle could be beaten every day.

John agreed to shower, and Alicia helped him carry the mic. Then, halfway through his song, his voice cracked so hard on the high note that a little kid in the front row laughed. John's face went red and the note came out as a squeak. Afterward he sat on the dock, and Alicia sat beside him, working it out aloud. "Your voice box is growing," she said. "Zain told me. During puberty the larynx grows and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys. So your voice is changing shape, kind of like the rest of you."

John touched his throat. "So it's not broken?"

"It's the opposite of broken. It's being rebuilt." She felt a stab of empathy for the kid in the front row too, who probably hadn't known better. Then the loudspeaker crackled, announcing the final act, and John stood up, cleared his new, rumbling voice, and said, "Same time tomorrow behind the shed?"

At 7:43 on Tuesday evening, every light in Nevaeh's house died at once, and the fridge stopped its low humming for the first time in her whole life. She heard her mom bump her hip on the coffee table and say a word Mom pretended she never said. Nevaeh found the flashlight in the junk drawer, then felt her way to the freezer and laid both palms against the closed door, as if she could hold the cold in by willpower alone.

"It'll stay frozen for a while if we don't open it," Mom said from the kitchen. "But if this lasts all night, everything in there could thaw, and then we throw it all out."

"All of it?" Nevaeh said. "The chicken, the peas, the ice cream?" The idea of throwing out a full freezer felt arbitrary to her, like deciding to demolish a whole building because one window was cracked. There had to be a line somewhere between safe and not safe, and she wanted to find it. She texted Tala, whose power was still on three streets over: "do you still have internet? IMPORTANT freezer emergency." Then she took the fridge thermometer from the drawer, the one Mom used for hygiene reasons when testing meat, and slid it inside the freezer door's gap, wedging the door barely open. The needle settled at 28 degrees.

Tala texted back a screenshot from a food safety site, and Nevaeh read it aloud to Mom by flashlight: "Thawed freezer food can be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals or is at 40 degrees Fahrenheit, that's 4 degrees Celsius, or below." Mom frowned and said that sounded like something a scientist would say, and Nevaeh said a scientist probably had.

At 9:15 the lights snapped back on and the fridge began to hum like it had never left. That was when Scott, who had come over because his house was "boring and dark," stuck his hand into the freezer and pulled out the bag of peas. "Ice crystals," he announced, holding the bag up to the kitchen light so it glittered like a tiny frosty galaxy. "Still crunchy. We are saved." He looked so pleased with himself that Nevaeh let him have the honor of sliding the bag back onto its shelf.

Mom checked the thermometer, wrote "28 degrees, fine" on a sticky note, and slapped it on the freezer door like a victory flag. "The ice cream?" Scott asked hopefully. Nevaeh opened the carton and found it softened around the edges but still frozen in the middle, ice crystals and all. "Refreezable," she said, "but weird. It'll never be the same." Scott gasped, hand on his chest, as if she had insulted his grandmother. "Give it here," he said, and reached for the spoon drawer.

Piper's new glasses arrived on a Tuesday, in a purple case that snapped shut like a tiny alligator. She had inherited the habit of pushing them up her nose from her mom, who also wore glasses, and by recess she had done it about forty times. The world looked sharp now. The chain-link fence had little diamonds in it. She could see there were actually two separate basketball hoops, not one blurry one that wobbled.

Tony found her by the swings, squinting at the eye chart printout the nurse had given her. "What's that?" he asked. She held it up. "My vision score. Twenty forty." Tony nodded slowly, the way he did when he was about to be wrong on purpose. "That's amazing. Mine's only twenty twenty. You beat me by twenty."

"You don't want the bigger number, doofus," said Lina, dropping onto the swing beside Piper. Lina wanted the glasses, honestly. She thought purple frames were the best thing to happen to fourth grade all year, and she'd already asked Piper twice where she got them. "Smaller is better. Like golf."

Piper wasn't so sure either way, so she decided to test it. At the far end of the blacktop, past the hopscotch squares, the janitor had painted a big white H on the wall for some kind of game. Piper paced it off, heel to toe, counting her steps out loud while Tony and Lina trailed after her. Sixteen steps was roughly ten feet, so she doubled it, planted her sneakers on a crack, and turned around. "Okay. Twenty feet away. Tony, you read the H."

Tony frowned at the wall. "It's an H." He read it easily. Then Piper pulled out the nurse's printout, which had the same letters at the same size, and held it up. At twenty feet, Tony rattled off the twenty twenty line like it was nothing, but at the forty line he had to squint and guess. Piper thought hard, pacing in a small circle. If twenty forty meant she had to stand twenty feet away to read letters that normal eyes could read from forty feet, then Tony, with his twenty twenty, could back up twice as far and still read them. "Lina, take this to the wall and keep walking back until Tony can't read it."

Lina jogged off, holding the paper over her head like a flag, which was not exactly what Piper meant, but it worked anyway. Tony shouted letters all the way back: "E, F, P, T, O, Z!" He only gave up somewhere past the soccer net. Piper did the same test with her glasses on and ran out of blacktop at almost exactly half his distance. She whooped so loudly that Mr. Chan, on yard duty, strolled over to see what was going on.

"Everything all right over here?" he asked, and Piper explained the whole experiment, waving the printout, while Tony rubbed his eyes and complained that Lina had walked faster when it was his turn. "Anyway," Piper finished, "I have to stand twenty feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from forty feet. So there."

"Normal eyesight," Tony muttered. "Rebellious eyesight, more like."

Lina spun the purple glasses case toward herself. "Trade you my seat at lunch tomorrow for one afternoon with them."

"Absolutely not," said Piper, and snapped the little alligator shut.

Mia slumped into the plastic chair beside the cabin's only computer and clicked the green flag for the tenth time. Her cat sprite trotted across the stage, walked straight over the golden coin, and kept going. The score stayed at zero.

"You're still on that?" Jayden asked, leaning over from the next screen. "You've been at it since lunch."

"The coin worked yesterday," Mia said. "I added the score part and now nothing happens. It's like the coin turned invisible." She dragged the cat with her mouse and dropped it right on top of the coin. Still nothing. Jayden shrugged and went back to his racing game.

Elia wandered over after swim period, dripping lake water onto the floor despite Mr. Johansson's rule about towels. "Move over," she said, pulling a chair up. "Show me the script."

Mia opened the coin's code. The blocks sat there in a neat little stack: when the green flag is clicked, if touching cat, change score by one, hide. "See? It says if touching. The cat was touching it. I watched."

Elia squinted at the screen for a long moment. "Where's the loop?"

"The what?"

"Like Jayden's racing game. His car thing. Everything's inside that orange block." Elia scrolled to Jayden's project on her own screen and pointed at a block labeled forever.
