She slid the lamp slowly around the table and watched the terminator crawl across the plaster like something alive, the whole shadow side turning with it, while the dark oval on the cloth, the cast shadow, swung away like a door. She tried it three times to be sure. When Ms. Sok passed by, Lucy spun the sketchbook toward her, finger on the line. "It moves with the light," Lucy said. "Wherever the light goes, that's where the lit side stops."

Ms. Sok gave a nod, the kind Lucy recognized from when someone got it exactly right. "Keep going," she said. "Next week, contemporary portraits, and you'll need this." Lucy bent back over the sphere, compressed the whole night down to one curved pencil line, and beside her Cohen drew a tiny robot, just to be safe.

The bus to the regional bee took forty minutes, and Mr. Silva had brought a box of index cards to fill every one of them. "Practice round," he said, standing at the front while the driver pulled out of the school lot. "Autumn and Wren, you're our two regional spellers. Spell against each other. Loser buys the winner a pretzel at the venue."

Autumn slid into a seat near the middle, and Elisha sat down beside her. Autumn had spent three weeks hoping Wren would catch the flu, or trip over a dictionary, or spell one word wrong. Second place meant you watched someone else hold the trophy. She had decided it would be unbearable.

Wren took the seat across the aisle. "Ready?" he asked.

"Not really," Autumn said, which was true.

Mr. Silva held up the first card. "Sustain. Autumn."

"S-U-S-T-A-I-N. Sustain."

"Correct. Wren, brittle."

"B-R-I-T-T-L-E. Brittle."

"Correct."

They went through twelve words that way, then twenty. Every card, both of them, no mistakes. Elisha kept score on the back of her notebook and after a while stopped writing anything at all, because there was nothing to write. The bus hummed, the cards kept coming, and nobody got a word wrong.

Elisha leaned over the notebook. "You know what happened at the real Nationals? The 2019 Scripps bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. Eight winners. They just ran out of words before anyone missed."

"Eight?" Autumn said.

"Eight. Sharing the title."

Autumn looked at the stack of cards in Mr. Silva's hand. She had been thinking about the bee all wrong, like it was a wall with room for only one person on top. But if eight spellers could each get every word right, then the wall had more room than she had imagined. If she and Wren both spelled perfectly, neither of them had to lose. She turned to the aisle.

"Wren," she said, "what if we both just keep going until the cards run out?"

"Then we both get pretzels," Wren said, "and we each buy our own."

"That works too."

Mr. Silva shuffled the deck once more. "Privilege," he said. "Autumn."

"P-R-I-V-I-L-E-G-E. Privilege."

"Correct. Wren, crescendo."

The choir room at the concert hall smelled like dust and old velvet, and Ryan stood between Shea and Yanis holding his folder like a shield. Mr. Hassan had split them into two groups, and Ryan's group had to sing the lower line while the other group held the higher one. The trouble started the moment both groups sang at once. Ryan kept drifting upward, sliding into the other part like a paper boat pulled along by a current.

"You're doing it again," Shea whispered after the third crash of sound. "You follow whoever is loudest."

Ryan frowned. He wasn't doing it on purpose. It felt almost like gravity. "Why does the high part drag me up like that?" he asked. Yanis shrugged, but Ryan kept turning the question over in his mind while Mr. Hassan played the two lines on the piano, one after the other. Something about them nagged at him. They clashed when they were wrong, but when they were right, the high line sounded strangely familiar, almost like his own line wearing a taller hat.

At break, Ryan dragged Shea to the piano and played the low note, then the note an octave up. "Sing this one," he said, pointing at the low key. Shea sang it. "Now this one." Shea sang the high one. Ryan's eyes went wide. "They're the same note," he said slowly. "It's like the same note, just higher. An octave, Mr. Hassan called it. So when I hear the other part, it sounds so much like mine that my brain grabs it and climbs." He wondered if the note's sound was somehow doubling on its way up, and he tested it in his head, humming the low note and feeling how the high one seemed to fit inside it, a smaller copy of the same thing.

Back in formation, Ryan tried a new trick. Every time the high part floated near, he pictured his own note as the floor and their note as the ceiling directly above it, same shape, different height. When the two groups sang together, his voice stayed put. The low line held steady, warm and solid, and the high line shimmered over top of it. For the first time, the sound wasn't a crash. It was a chord, the kind that made the hair on his arms stand up.

Mr. Hassan lowered his hands and grinned at them. "Whatever you just did," he said, "do it again at the concert."

Ryan felt an idea begin to germinate, a whole plan taking root. "Saturday," he whispered to Shea, "I'm going to write a memoir about this. Chapter one: how I stopped floating."

Shea laughed. "Chapter two: how you started bragging."

Juliette found the ginger tea on the clearance shelf, one box left, an endangered supply if her grandmother had anything to say about it. Grandma was two aisles over comparing cough drops, and Juliette held the box while a woman nearby grabbed three boxes of some purple headache powder and hurried to the register like it was the last lifeboat. At the counter, Mr. Bakker rang her up without a word about miracles. That was the strange part, Juliette thought. If the purple powder worked so well, why was it on clearance?

Grandma had sworn by the tea since Tuesday. Her headache that day had been the worst in months, she said, and by Wednesday morning it was nearly gone. "One cup," she kept repeating as Juliette carried the box toward the front. "That's all it took." Juliette wanted to believe her, but something nagged at her, a small contradiction she couldn't put her finger on. Grandma's headaches came and went anyway, didn't they? Hadn't there been bad ones back in October, before any tea? At the register Juliette set down the box and pulled a receipt from her pocket, blank side up, and began to draft a chart right there, a column for every bad-headache day she could remember and what came after. Mr. Bakker watched her scribble without interrupting.

"You're blocking my register," said a voice behind her. It was Danica from science class, holding cold medicine for her mom. Juliette stepped aside but kept writing. The pattern was there, and it made her stomach tighten. The worst days, the ones Grandma called unbearable, were always followed by ordinary days. Tea or no tea. Even back in October. Even the time in July when Grandma had tried a heating pad instead.

"It's a real thing," Danica said, peering over her shoulder. "Regression to the mean. Worst days drift back toward normal on their own." Juliette stared at her lopsided columns, torn between disappointment and the odd thrill of having caught something invisible in the act.

She bought the tea anyway. "For the taste," she told Grandma, sliding the bag across the seat of the car. "And maybe next bad headache, we time it."

Evan slid his flashcards across the library table and checked the clock above the biography shelves. Twenty minutes until he had to stand up in front of Ms. Li's class and describe his family in Spanish, using full sentences, no single words allowed.

Roger leaned over the cards. "You've got nine sentences. That's plenty."

"It's not the number," Evan said. "Something's wrong with one of them, and I can't find it." He had copied his sentences from his notebook, where his notes had started as a whole page and slowly condensed into neat cards, one per family member. His dog was obstinate, which he'd written as "terco." His mother was a nurse. His grandfather was tall. And his brother was tired, because Hugo had stayed up all night finishing a model bridge.

Kennery dropped into the chair across from them, out of breath. "Ms. Li says start in the corner by the atlas stand," she said. Then she squinted at the cards. "Why does Hugo get two cards?"

He didn't. Evan counted. There was "Mi hermano es alto," from his grandfather's card somehow copied wrong, and "Mi hermano está cansado." He stared at the two little verbs, es and está, which he had been treating as the same word all week. He flipped through his cards and found the same pair again: "Mi madre es enfermera" but "Mi perro está en el sótano." His dog was not permanently in the basement. His dog went outside constantly, tracking mud, chewing the mail. So why would the same English word, is, come out two different ways?

"Roger," Evan said slowly, "say 'my brother is tall' in Spanish."

"Mi hermano es alto. Obviously."

"Now say 'my brother is tired.'"

Roger opened his mouth, then stopped. He looked at the cards, then at Evan, and the room got quiet enough that they could hear the radiator ticking.

Evan tested his idea on the safest card he had, the one about Hugo. If es meant lasting things, like being tall, then saying "Mi hermano es cansado" would mean his brother was tired forever, permanently wiped out, a boy doomed to yawn through every birthday for the rest of his life. And if está was for right now, then his tired-brother card should use está, and it already did. He checked the rest of the stack card by card, pencil hovering.

Kennedy pointed at the grandfather card, the one Evan had botched. "Es alto," she said. "Lasting. That one's safe."

"Ser for what lasts," Roger said, tapping the tall card. "Estar for right now."

Evan scratched out one verb, wrote the other, and squared the cards into a clean stack just as Ms. Li appeared at the end of the aisle.

"Mr. Alvarez," she said. "You're first."

Hunter's grandmother lived three streets from the beach, and the whole family had come down for the long weekend. On Saturday morning his mother slathered sunscreen on his shoulders before he and his cousin Alexia went out to fly kites on the sand. They stayed out until lunch, running back and forth until the kite string hummed.

After sandwiches, Alexia begged to go swimming, and they spent the whole afternoon in the water, diving under waves until their fingers wrinkled. Nobody mentioned sunscreen again. By dinnertime Hunter's back felt tight, and when his grandmother turned him toward the kitchen light, she clicked her tongue. His shoulders were red.

"That's a burn," she said. "You put cream on this morning, didn't you?"

"A whole lot of it," Hunter said. He sat on the counter while she fetched the aloe.

He thought about the timeline while she dabbed it on. He'd been outside for hours, and he'd been in the water for more hours after that. Alexia, sitting on the stairs with her own pink nose, was doing the same math. "Maybe it wears off," she said slowly. "Like, after a while?"

Hunter wanted to test it, but not with another burn. On Sunday he set a timer on his phone before they went out, and when it buzzed at two hours he made everyone stop and put on more cream. They swam after lunch, and the moment they climbed out and toweled off, he called them back to the beach bag for another round. Alexia groaned but held out her arms.

"The things I do for science," she said.

His rebellious little brother tried to run off without any, and Hunter chased him down and got the back of his neck. Their grandmother watched from her chair, saying nothing, just raising her glass of lemonade.

That evening Hunter stood in front of the hallway mirror, twisting to see his shoulders. They were the same color as morning, not a trace of red. He snapped a photo of the timer screen and set a new alarm for tomorrow.

"Ten a.m., beach," he told Alexia. "Bring the bag."

The group chat pinged at 7:14 on a Tuesday evening, while Hannah was watching rain slide down her bedroom window. Abdullah had posted, all capitals: THE SCHOOL IS CLOSING THE WALK TRAIL BEHIND THE FIELD ON MONDAY. Channing answered with three exclamation points. Hannah read the message twice, then a third time, because Monday was the day she and Abdullah walked that trail to the corner store for licorice.

She remembered Ms. Holloway's classroom in September, the tranquil afternoon light on the whiteboard, when a girl named Priya had argued for a crosswalk on Marsh Road. Priya had counted near-misses, actual moments when cars braked hard for kids, and stood at the front saying, "It's my opinion we need a crosswalk, and I counted fourteen near-misses in one week to back it up." Ms. Holloway had written on the board: an opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons. Hannah had copied it into her notebook, and now those words floated back to her like a message in a bottle.

Abdullah's post, she noticed, was only an opinion shaped like a fact. It had no evidence attached at all, no photo, no memo, no reason.

She typed: "Where did you hear that?" Then she set the phone face down on her quilt and made a plan. If the trail were really closing, there would be a sign. Signs had to go up before Monday, because that was how the school did things. She pulled on her rain boots and walked the three blocks through drizzle, past the tranquil pond where the ducks tucked their heads under their wings.

The trail gate stood open, wet and ordinary. No sign. No tape. She took a photo and walked home.

In the chat she posted the picture with the caption "Trail looks fine. Anybody see an actual notice?" Abdullah went quiet for four whole minutes, the little typing bubble appearing and vanishing. Then he wrote: "ok it was just something my cousin said. i thought it sounded true." Channing sent a single laughing face.

Hannah smiled at her screen. "Your cousin can have opinions," she typed. "But next time bring evidence." Then, because a thought was still nagging her, she added one more message: "Also, did anyone check if the store is even open Monday?" Abdullah answered fastest this time: "IT CLOSES AT SIX. MY COUSIN WORKS THERE. I ASKED HIM DIRECTLY."

The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and sweat, and Mr. Ahmadi had looped a thick rope across the center line for the last drill of practice. "Six on each side," he called. "Pull." Alexandre gripped the rope beside Alisa and Abbie and hauled until his shoulders burned, but the rope barely moved, and neither did the other team's. Afterward Mr. Ahmadi shook his head. "Some of you are easing off. I can feel it in the rope."

That evening Alexandre pulled his library book on sports science off the shelf and read until he found it. In 1913, Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller. He read the sentence twice. So it wasn't just his team being lazy, and it wasn't just the coach imagining things. The bigger the group, the less each person pulled on average. He needed to see it for himself.

At the next practice he asked Alisa to help him after the whistle. First she pulled the rope alone, dragging a stack of folded mats, and he marked the distance with tape. Then they pulled together, both hands on the rope, and the mats moved again. Alexandre measured with a tape measure and did the arithmetic on his palm with a pencil stub. Alisa's share was smaller when they pulled together. He ran it again with Abbie added, and it shrank again. "It happens every time," he told them. "More people, smaller pull from each."

Before Friday's meet, Alexandre told Mr. Ahmadi he wanted shorter pulls with fewer players rotating in, so nobody drifted half-hearted on a long rope. Mr. Ahmadi tried it. In the gymnasium the crowd of parents, tenants of the bleachers who paid nothing but cheered loudly, went quiet as the rope crept across the line. The knot, durable and tight, slapped down on their side of the tape.

Abbie pounded his shoulder. "Told you the math kid would figure it out."

Chase spread his poster board across the kitchen table and stared at the empty page. The assignment was due tomorrow: draw a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, and then explain what happens if one link disappears. He had the sun part easy. He even liked drawing the sun, a big blazing circle with arrows shooting out like the whole picture would orbit around it. But after that, his chain wobbled. Grass, then a rabbit, then a fox. Done in three minutes. It felt too short, too simple, and he couldn't figure out what he was missing.

"Where does it all go when things die?" he muttered, chewing his pencil. "Foxes don't live forever."

The doorbell rang. It was Maisie, holding a plastic bag with half a rotten apple in it, because Maisie was like that. "Science emergency too?" she asked. Chase showed her his poster. She frowned at it, then pointed at the apple. "See this gross part? There's fuzz on it. My grandpa calls them decomposers." She peeled the bag open. "Decomposers like fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals. Then the nutrients go back into the soil, and plants use them again."

Chase sat up so fast his chair scraped. That was the missing loop. The grass at the start of his chain wasn't just sitting there; it was pulling nutrients out of soil that dead foxes and rabbits had helped make. "So the chain isn't a straight line," he said slowly, drawing a curved arrow from the fox all the way back around to the grass. "It's a circle. The end feeds the beginning."

"Test it," Maisie said, defiant against his doubt, pointing at his last empty box. "Cross out the decomposers and see what breaks." Chase drew an X through his loop. No nutrients going back to the soil meant weaker grass, fewer rabbits, hungrier foxes. The whole chain went gray. He erased the X, colored the loop in bold green, and added a small note about water rising as vapor into clouds that would rain on the grass again, because the sun really did run everything.

The next morning he carried the poster to school like a shield. Mr. Zhang looked at the curved arrow for a long moment, then pinned the poster to the wall at the very front of the room.

"Class," he said, tapping the loop with one finger. "Start here."

Rosalie stood at Noemie's kitchen counter with a wooden spoon in her hand and a pot of pale, lumpy paste in front of her. The lumps looked like tiny wet dumplings, and every time she stirred, more of them appeared.

"Grandma arrives at six," Noemie said, checking the clock for the third time. "She's French. She'll take one bite and know." Noemie's whole plan for the visit was this dinner, homemade mac and cheese, and now her plan was sitting in the pot looking like a science experiment.

Rosalie frowned at the lumps. They had followed the recipe on Noemie's phone exactly, butter, then flour, then milk, then cheese. So why lumps? She thought about the order of things. The flour had glued itself into little balls the second the milk hit it. Maybe the milk was the problem, not the flour. Maybe it had to go in slowly, so slow the flour didn't have a chance to clump. She scraped the lumpy pot into a bowl and started over.

This time she melted the butter, whisked in the flour, and let it bubble until it smelled like toasted nuts. Then she poured the warm milk in a thin stream with one hand while whisking hard with the other. Her first pour was hesitant, just a dribble, but the sauce stayed smooth, so she poured faster. Within a minute the pot held glossy, velvety sauce. She stirred in the cheese and it melted into a golden ribbon.

Noemie's little brother Eli wandered in and stuck a finger toward the pot. "Your hands are shaking," he said. "It's probably hormones."

"It's probably whisking," Rosalie said, and Noemie laughed so hard she snorted.

From the back fence, Ms. Mercado, the neighbour who traded tomatoes for cookies, called through the window. "That smells like a proper roux. Where did you two learn that?"

"The internet," Rosalie admitted. "But we didn't know it had a name."

"A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel," Ms. Mercado said, "one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking."

Noemie's eyes went wide. "Mother sauces. Grandma is going to be so impressed." Then she paused. "Wait. My birthday is Thursday, and Grandma's visit almost coincides with it, so technically this could count as birthday dinner too."

"That's cheating," said Eli.

"That's efficiency," said Noemie, and she spooned the sauce over the noodles while Rosalie held the pot steady, both of them grinning as the golden sauce ran down in a smooth, unbroken stream.

Violet stood at her grandmother's grave with an empty stomach and a head full of questions. The fast had started at sunset yesterday, and now it was late afternoon, and the horizon was refusing to do anything interesting. She scrutinized the sky above the cemetery fence as if staring could push the sun down faster, which she knew was vain, but she did it anyway.

"Still not eating?" Callum asked. He had biked here to meet her, munching crackers from his pocket, which Violet thought was practically cheating.

"It's not just not eating," she said. "It's a whole day. My mom says it's from sunset yesterday until after nightfall tonight." She counted on her fingers. "That's not twenty-four hours. It's about twenty-five."

"Why the extra hour?"

"I don't know yet. Nobody would just tell me, so I'm figuring it out." She pulled her jacket tighter. The air smelled of cut grass and cold stone, and somewhere a crow argued with itself.

Mr. Vu was there too, watering the mums he planted beside his wife's headstone every September. Last year, on this same day, Violet had been home with a fever, swallowing spoonfuls of the pink antibiotic that sat in the refrigerator door, while her parents came here without her. She had cried about it at the time, sick and left out, and she still wasn't sure whether the crying had been about missing her grandmother or about being left behind. Both, probably.

Tonight she was trying the whole thing for the first time, fast and all, and she had a theory. If it ended only after nightfall, and not just at sunset, then maybe the day wasn't measured by the sun alone. She watched the sky deepen from gold to gray to a blue so dark it was almost black, and when the first stars came out she held up her hand and counted three.

"Okay," she said. "Now."

Her mother unwrapped the apples and honey, and Violet bit down.

Anna typed the loop for the third time and ran it, certain this attempt would work. On the screen, in red letters, appeared the same message as before: NameError: name 'number' is not defined.

"I don't get it," she said, pulling her sleeves down over her hands the way she did when she was thinking hard. "The variable is right there."

Kinsley leaned over from the kitchen chair beside her, chewing the last of an apple. "You named it in the input line, right? Copy it to me."

Anna read aloud, pointing at each word. "Number equals input, times equals int, then for i in range one to thirteen, print Number times i."

Kinsley frowned. "Wait. Say the first part again."

"Number capital N, equals input, 'Which times table?'"

"And in the print?"

Anna looked. "number, small n." Her stomach did a strange little flip, the same feeling as stepping onto the last stair and finding nothing under her foot. Could one letter really break everything?

"Try this," Kinsley said. "Make them match. Capital in both places."

Anna's fingers seemed to contract as she hovered over the keys, then she changed the print line to capital Number and hit run. She held her breath. Instead of red, white text scrolled up the screen: 7, 14, 21, all the way to 84, marching down in a straight column.

"It worked," Anna whispered. She typed 9 in the input box and ran it again, and the nines marched down too. She sat back so fast the chair squeaked. "Number and number are two different variables. Python sees them as two names."

Kinsley dropped her apple core in the bowl. "One capital letter."

"One capital letter," Anna said, and deleted the whole program so she could build it again from scratch, this time watching every n.

Clara had turned her grandpa's garage into a rehearsal studio, with a folding table for a stage and an old paint bucket for a drum. On Saturday Farrah arrived carrying sheet music, and behind her came Jannah, who was skeptical that two people could sing different notes at the same time and not sound like a broken doorbell. "Mr. Weiss says the whole choir has to hold our part while the other part tries to pull us off," Clara said, bouncing on her toes. "If we can do it in here, we can do it anywhere."

They started on the low line, the one Clara had been assigned, and it went fine until Farrah slid up to her high notes. Clara's voice drifted upward after it, like a balloon on a string, and suddenly they were both singing the same wrong note. "It's like my throat follows yours," Clara said. She touched her neck and frowned. Something in there was doing this. She remembered the choir booklet Mr. Weiss had left on the piano bench, and she ran inside to fetch it, skidding back on the concrete in her socks.

The booklet had a diagram. Two vocal folds in the larynx, it said, vibrate as air passes between them, and tightening them raises the pitch. "So when I chase your note, I'm tightening," Clara said, feeling her throat. "The folds squeeze higher. If I keep them loose, I stay low." Jannah looked skeptical, but Farrah grinned. "Test it. Sing your note, and I'll sneak mine in."

Clara held her note like a rope in a tug of war, keeping her throat loose and heavy while Farrah's high part floated above it. For three whole bars they were two notes at once, and it sounded, Farrah shouted, like an actual choir. Then came the twist: the low note wasn't Clara's note at all. When they checked the music, the low line belonged to Jannah, who had been quietly mouthing along. Jannah shrugged. "I didn't want to elaborate on it before, but I've been practicing in my room for weeks." They all shrieked, and Clara dragged the paint bucket over. "Okay, new plan. Jannah low, me high, Farrah in the middle. From the top."

The kitten rode home in a cardboard box with holes punched in the sides, and Avery kept her palm flat against the lid the whole way so it wouldn't slide. His name was Biscuit, and he was hers, which meant she was the one who had to figure out what he needed. The shelter had given her a bag of food, but it was almost empty, and her dad had said, "We'll grab more at the store tomorrow."

At the pet store, Avery's classmate Yassin was there buying dog food for his labrador. He looked at the shelf with her and frowned. "Why do they even make them separate? Food is food, isn't it?" That was exactly what Avery had been wondering, so she turned over a can of dog food and a can of cat food and compared the labels. The lists weren't the same. The cat food had something the dog food didn't. "Taurine," she read aloud, and a cashier nearby said, "You want that in cat food, trust me," and walked off before Avery could ask why.

She wasn't going to guess. Biscuit was too small to be an experiment. At home she looked it up and found something that surprised her: cats can't make enough taurine on their own, and it comes from meat. She read further, and the next part made her sit back. If a cat doesn't get enough, it can end up with heart disease, or even go blind. No wonder the dog food excluded it; dogs didn't need it added the same way. She checked the shelter's bag, and sure enough, taurine was on the label, near the top. She wrote it on the shopping list in capital letters so nobody would come home with the wrong bag.

The next morning Louise came over to meet Biscuit. He had climbed the curtain and gotten stuck halfway up, and he meowed down at them like it was their fault. "He eats better than I do," Louise said, watching Avery measure out his breakfast. Biscuit smelled the bowl, jumped off the curtain rail, and landed with a thump right in the middle of the kibble.

Emily had tried to conceal the problem for weeks, squinting at the board and copying Jorja's notes, but on Friday Mr. Chea caught her guessing at the homework questions written behind him. On Monday she walked into class with a new pair of glasses, purple at the corners, and the board jumped out at her all at once, every letter sharp as a cutout. Jorja leaned over during silent reading. "They look good," she whispered. "Can you see everything now?"

"Even the back wall," Emily whispered back. "The clock says 9:42." She could also see the pamphlet the eye doctor had given her mother, folded into her backpack, and at recess she pulled it out under the old maple at the corner of the yard, where the leaves were still lush and green. One sentence stopped her: studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood. She read it twice. Near sighted. That was her. She thought about her weekends, Saturday and Sunday, screen after screen, curtains shut against the glare.

Aedan kicked a pinecone across the grass. "What are you staring at?"

"This says nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood," Emily said. "All of it. When they were kids." She looked up. "You're outside all the time. Soccer, hiking, everything."

"So?"

"So your eyes had a better chance than mine did. My weekends were all screens." She stood and brushed off her jeans. "I want to test something. This weekend, no screens. Outside, both days, as much as I can stand. I don't think it'll fix my glasses, but I want to see what it's like."

On Saturday morning Emily dragged Aedan and Jorja to the creek trail before anyone could invent an excuse. They caught tadpoles in a jar, lost the jar, found it again downstream, and ate sandwiches on a flat rock that Jorja declared was probably a hundred years old. Emily's legs ached and her socks were soaked, but when the sun slanted low she realized she had not thought about a screen since breakfast. On Sunday they came back, and on Monday Mr. Chea was waiting by the door with a box of seedlings. "Community garden plot," he said. "I'm retiring at the end of the year, and once my pension starts I won't be around to water these, so somebody had better learn."

Emily raised her hand so fast her glasses slid down her nose. She pushed them up and said, "Every day after school. Outside counts."

Megan was lying on her bed with her tablet, half in the science-club group chat and half in a search engine, when she typed her own name just to see what would happen. Up came a comment she'd written two years ago on a fan site for a show she didn't even watch anymore. It had her full name attached, right there, like a fossil nobody had asked to keep.

She screenshotted it and dropped it in the chat. "Um. Why is this here? I posted this forever ago."

Braelynn replied with three surprised emojis. "That's so weird. I thought stuff disappeared when you stopped going on a site."

"It doesn't," Talon typed. "My cousin says search engines have automated programs called crawlers that copy and index public pages. That's how old stuff turns up in search results." His next message appeared before she could answer. "Also, urgent topic: my objective for this weekend is to get everyone to come to the creek cleanup, and I need one more person or Mr. Nikolaidis says the club can't reserve the pavilion."

Megan stared at the screenshot again. "So if my comment is public, a crawler copied it? Like a little robot reading everything and saving it?" She thought of the photo she'd posted last month with the school sign in the background, the one that showed exactly where she'd be every Tuesday after school. Her stomach did a slow flip.

She tried an experiment. She searched Braelynn's username, then her own, then a fake name she made up on the spot. Only the fake name came back empty. "Okay, tested it. Anything public with your real name on it can show up. Anything with a made-up name, nothing."

"That contradicts everything I believed about the delete button," Braelynn wrote.

"Delete is frail," Megan typed. "Public is forever, apparently."

Talon sent a single pleading message: "CREEK. PAVILION. SATURDAY."

"Fine," Megan wrote back, "but I'm deleting my location posts first." She opened her photo settings and got to work.

Rosalie bounced on her toes at the edge of the running track, her shoelaces double-knotted and her hair pinned back for speed. Tryouts for the school relay team started in ten minutes, and she wanted one of those four spots more than she wanted her birthday. Loic was already jogging the curved path by the bleachers, swinging his arms in wide, easy circles, and Daniel was doing walking lunges that made him look like a giant, cheerful insect.

"Come watch with me," said a girl from her class, perched on the lowest bleacher step. "I don't want to waste energy before we run. I'm too nervous anyway." Rosalie almost sat down. Then she noticed something: every kid who had jogged even one slow lap was breathing faster, cheeks pink, and when they stretched they kept moving, never holding still. Mr. Sultani strolled past the bleachers, humming, and called out, "Keep those knees warm, people, be kind to your cartilage," without stopping.

Rosalie thought about her legs like an engine. A slow jog and moving stretches get your heart pumping faster and your muscles warmer, and warm muscles work better when you ask them for something hard. That was what her legs felt like on cold mornings: stiff and slow until she'd run around the yard once. So she tested it. "Race you one easy lap," she said to Loic, and they jogged it together, then did Daniel's funny lunges plus high knees. Her heart was beating quicker now, her legs loose and ready, and she hadn't spent anything she needed.

The whistle blew. The girl on the bleacher, who had only watched, shot off the line fast, then faltered halfway down the backstretch, her steps turning heavy. Rosalie passed her, arms pumping, and crossed the line second behind Daniel, whooping. Loic raised both fists. Later, when the coach posted the relay list, Rosalie's name sat in the third slot, and she ran to show Loic, waving the paper over her head like a flag.

Clara stood in the pharmacy aisle staring at two boxes of anti-itch cream, because her little brother's mosquito bites had turned him into a human scratch machine and their mom would be back from the register in fifteen minutes. The first box showed a lush green meadow and a woman smiling, with a quote that read, "It worked for me in one day!" The second box was plain, with small print that said 300 people had tested it in a lab.

Dorian leaned over her shoulder. "Get the meadow one. My cousin used it and her bites cleared right up."

"That's one cousin," Clara said. She flipped the plain box over and read further. "This one had three hundred people try it." Rowan, who had tagged along to buy bandages for his skateboard elbows, shook his head.

"Three hundred strangers versus a cousin you actually know," he said. "I trust the cousin."

Clara thought about the class survey last week, when Mr. Do had asked three kids if they loved the cafeteria's fish sticks and all three said yes, and then the whole school voted and only forty kids out of two hundred did. She had laughed about it with Mr. Do at the time, and now something clicked. "Three people can all love something by accident," she said slowly. "Two hundred people can't all be that weird."

"So bigger groups are more reliable," Rowan said.

"Because the weird ones even out," Clara said. "Dorian's cousin might just have tough skin."

Dorian frowned. "Then why do companies print the cousin-style quotes at all?"

"Because they're cheap to get, I bet." Clara put the plain box in the basket, then hesitated. "But my brother has sensitive skin. The small print warns it might irritate some people." She carried both boxes to the counter, where Mr. Do was waiting behind the register, and slid them toward him.

"Which one would you trust for a kid with sensitive skin?" she asked. "The one with the smiling lady, or the one with the three hundred testers?"

Mr. Do tapped the plain box twice. "That one."

Clara put the meadow box back on the shelf herself.

Lucas slid into the last seat on the bus and realized Dania was already there, hood up, staring at the window. They had not really talked since October, when he joined the soccer team and she joined debate, and the space between them had grown like something with its own schedule.

"Mr. Pham made us read a study today," Lucas said, because silence was worse than awkwardness. "From 2015. It followed 573 friendships that started in seventh grade." Dania's hood tilted a fraction, which he took as a signal to keep going. "Friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end." He had copied it onto his palm during class, as if he might need proof later, and now he did. "So I guess that's us. You do debate, I do soccer. Less alike every week."

"We were alike in sixth grade," Dania said quietly. "We built that whole volcano. You extracted the baking soda from the cupboard yourself because I was too short to reach."

Lucas almost smiled, then caught something odd in her voice. "Wait. Why do you sound like it already ended?"

She pulled a folded paper from her backpack. It was a withdrawal form, signed by a parent, dated that morning. "It's voluntary. I don't have to stay in debate. But you joined soccer without asking me, so I figured the study was right, and I should just stop pretending." She held the paper out like evidence at a trial. "I was going to hand it in at practice today."

The bus lurched around the corner by the rec center. Lucas looked at the form, then at the soccer field sliding past the window, then at her. "Don't hand it in on my account. Hand it in if you actually hate debate. Do you?"

"No," Dania admitted. "I love it. I just hated losing you."

"Then keep it, and keep me too." He took the form from her hands, folded it into a paper airplane, and launched it toward the front of the bus. "New rule. We test the study. Every Friday, this seat, one thing we both still care about."

Dania caught the airplane as it boomeranged off the window. "Fine. First topic, volcanoes."

Alyssa slid the five-dollar bill across the counter, and the coins came back warm from the register. "Check your receipt before you go," the cashier said, tapping the slip of paper. She said it the same way she said everything, quick and bored, but Alyssa stood still and read it anyway. The paper smelled faintly of the milk crates stacked behind the till. There, in small gray print, the milk appeared twice, and the amount paid was higher than the price of one carton. The scanner had charged her for two.

She counted her change in her palm. Too little left over, and now she knew why. Ms. Martínez had given her exactly enough for one carton and nothing more, so the mistake mattered. "It scanned the milk twice," Alyssa said, holding out the receipt and pointing at the doubled line. The cashier squinted, then hit a button, and the difference came back in coins that clattered into the tray. Alyssa picked them up one by one and counted again, lips moving, until the numbers matched what she had worked out in her head.

Emiliano was waiting by the door, bouncing on his heels. He had wanted to come inside, but Alyssa had said no, this was her solo errand, the one Ms. Martínez had assigned her for the class breakfast. "Did you get extra for the brittle star cookies?" he asked hopefully. He had been talking about those cookies all morning, the ones with the thin sugar shells that cracked like ice when you bit them. Alyssa looked at the coins left in her hand and counted them against the cookie price taped to the window. Not enough for cookies and bus fare never mind that, not enough for cookies at all.

"Maybe tomorrow," she said, and Emiliano's shoulders dropped, just a little. On the walk back she passed the science room window, where someone had left a glass vessel, a big measuring jug, drying upside down on a rack. She thought of the receipt folded in her pocket, every item and every amount printed in order, like the lines on that jug marking exactly how much it held. That afternoon she watched Emiliano dismantle his sandwich at lunch, piece by piece, saving the cookie-shaped crackers for last, and she slid two quarters across the table to him. "For after school," she said. "Bring me the receipt."

Violet sat at the kitchen table trying to open a jar of pickles with one hand, which was impossible, and thinking about the word the doctor had used yesterday. "The break missed the growth plate," he had told her mother, and her mother had looked relieved, but nobody had explained why.

Francesco arrived after school with Dawson, who was carrying a stack of comics. They had declared a truce over the argument about whose fault the treehouse fall had been, since Violet had been the one who hit the ground, arm bending the wrong way under her.

"Did you ask him what a growth plate is?" Francesco asked, poking the edge of her cast with one finger.

"Sort of. He said near the ends of long bones there's cartilage, and that's where bones lengthen while you're a kid." Violet flexed her good hand. "So my arm is still going to grow the same as the other one."

Dawson frowned. "How do you know the break missed it, though? It's inside the bone. You can't see it."

That was exactly the problem Violet had been chewing on all morning. The doctor had looked at an X-ray, but she hadn't seen the picture herself, and she hadn't thought to ask. Something hidden inside her arm was deciding whether her right arm would match her left one for the rest of her life, and she had just accepted "good news" without checking. It reminded her of the time she'd blamed Dawson's wobbly plank without ever climbing up to test it herself. She'd been wrong then, too, probably. She still hadn't eliminated that possibility, and the truce didn't cover it.

"Your mom put the X-ray disc in the drawer," Francesco said. "The one by the fridge."

Violet stood so fast the pickle jar rolled off the table and Dawson caught it. She dug through the drawer, past a toxic-looking bottle of old glue and a tangle of batteries, until her fingers found the paper sleeve. She slid the film out and held it up to the window light, a pale ghost of her own bones, the crack thin as a hair.

"Get me the ruler," she said. "We're measuring where the break ends."

The letter from the city lay open on Grandma's kitchen table, and Emma read it twice before she dared say anything out loud. The community garden behind the library would be paved over for a parking lot unless someone convinced a councillor to change the bylaw before the vote on Friday. Grandma grew her tomatoes there, and so did half the seniors on her street. "Grandma," Emma said slowly, "who's our councillor?" Grandma peered at the letter. "It doesn't say. It just says contact your local representative." That was the problem, and it itched at Emma all afternoon.

She remembered the spring, when the beehives at school had died off and no one knew why. Finlay had insisted it was vandals, but Emma had tracked the blooming bushes along the fence and realized the bees had simply lost their source of nectar when the groundskeeper cut everything down. Things fail for hidden reasons, she had learned, and you have to look for the cause underneath. Maybe politics worked the same way. If every councillor governed a different slice of the city, then emailing the wrong one would be like writing to a beekeeper about a bush two towns over.

She found the city website on Grandma's old laptop and clicked through maps, but the lines wiggled everywhere and the names meant nothing to her. Sophia texted back "just email the mayor" when Emma asked, which felt too easy. Emma sat very still, staring at the address bar, and then it struck her: she could type Grandma's street address into the ward finder. The cursor blinked. She pressed enter, and the screen hung there, white and blank, for what felt like a full minute.

Then the map bloomed with colour. A shape wrapped around Grandma's neighbourhood, labeled Ward 4. Emma turned to Grandma, hardly believing it. "This is a ward," she said. "In lots of cities, each councillor is elected to represent one area, and that area is called a ward." Grandma leaned in, squinting. "So there's one councillor just for us?" Emma nodded and copied the name and the email address onto a pad of paper.

They drafted the message together at the kitchen table. Emma wrote that the garden was fundamental to the street, that seniors depended on it, and that the bylaw should be changed to protect it. She kept it short and polite, the way Mr. Shapiro had taught them for persuasive writing back in September. Then she read it aloud, one last time, her finger under each line. Grandma reached over her shoulder and clicked Send.

Isla sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field with her X-ray printout balanced on her good knee. Her left arm, wrapped in a bright green cast, rested in her lap, and every few minutes the coach blew the whistle and she had to remind herself she wasn't supposed to run out there. Evelyne plopped down beside her, dusty from drills, and leaned over the film.

"Why do your bones look like glowing white sticks?" Evelyne asked. "Your arm and everything else is just a gray smudge."

Isla held the film up against the sky. The two bones of her forearm stood out sharp and pale, and the break near her wrist made a crooked line she couldn't stop staring at. "The doctor said something about it," she said slowly. "Something in the bones. I think it's the calcium. The calcium absorbs more of the X-rays than the softer stuff around it, so the bones show up white and everything else barely shows at all." She turned the film over, as if the answer might be printed on the back.

"Calcium, like in milk," Evelyne said.

"Like in milk." Isla looked down at her cast, and an idea clicked into place. When they'd taken the X-ray, the thick part of the cast had shown up faintly on the image too, a hazy white shadow behind the bone. Old plaster casts had calcium in them. That was why the technician had angled the machine around it. Her idea wasn't just a guess; the same stuff, the same white glow. "I'm going to ask Martha," she said. "She broke her wrist last year. If her old X-ray shows the cast shadow too, then I'm right."

They found Martha by the goal net, breathing hard while Ms. Sato called out instructions to regulate the pace of the scrimmage. Ms. Sato saw Isla's awkward one-armed attempt to carry her water bottle and jogged over to open it for her, then stayed to fan Martha with a clipboard until she caught her breath. Martha dug out her phone, scrolled through photos, and held up her own X-ray. There it was: the bone, brilliant white, and behind it the ghostly outline of her old cast.

"So the calcium drinks up the X-rays," Martha said, "and whatever drinks up the most shows up brightest."

"The tendon doesn't, though," Isla said, pointing at the thin gray thread of tissue near Martha's wrist. "That's why you can barely see it." She flexed the fingers of her casted hand, the last voluntary movement the doctor had allowed her, and grinned. "Three more weeks, and I'm back on that field."

Ms. Sato handed her the whistle. "You can officiate until then," she said. "First call of the scrimmage, right there."

Jonathan had one goal for the season: beat Connor at everything. Connor was the fastest kid on the team, and he knew it, which made beating him even more satisfying in theory. In practice, Jonathan kept coming in second, which was getting old.

Then something strange happened at Tuesday practice. Mr. Sow set up sprint drills, and Jonathan beat Connor. Twice. Connor bent over, hands on his knees, and stared at the grass like it had insulted him. "I've been training every single day since March," he said. "Morning jog, afternoon sprints, evening juggling. I'm the most diligent soccer player in this county." He said it like a badge, but he looked like a melted snowman.

On Thursday, Jonathan beat him again, and this time Atlas noticed too. "You're getting slower," Atlas told Connor, with the kindness of a friend and the delivery of a game show host. "Like, measurably." After practice, Jonathan rode his bike home puzzling over it. Training every day should make you faster, shouldn't it? Unless the getting stronger part happened somewhere he couldn't see, some hidden step between the workout and the speed. His own week suddenly looked interesting: Monday sprints, Wednesday practice, and in between, honestly, a lot of video games and a heroic amount of cheese crackers. He had been resting. A lot. And he had been getting faster.

Friday, he tried an actual test, in the scientific tradition of making stuff up. "Connor," he said, dropping a soccer ball on the bleachers next to him, "take two days off. No jogging, no sprints. Total sloth mode." Connor looked personally wounded. "My legs will forget how to be legs." "Two days," Jonathan emphasized, holding up two fingers. "Then we race Saturday." Connor grumbled, but he agreed, mostly because losing to Jonathan had made him agree to anything.

Saturday morning, the field was still damp and the nets sagged like tired hammocks. Atlas stood at the sideline with a stopwatch he had borrowed from Mr. Sow, who watched from the parking lot with his coffee and one raised eyebrow. They raced sideline to sideline, three times. Connor won the first by a full stride. He won the second by two. On the third, he crossed the line, spun around, and pointed at Jonathan. "You knew! Rest days are part of getting better, you sneaky little scientist!" Jonathan raised both arms like he'd won the World Cup. "Race you to the water bottles," said Connor.

Chase sat on the living room rug with his notebook open, because on Monday he and Yuna had to perform a two-minute improv scene in drama class, and so far every practice had collapsed. Yuna knelt across from him, drumming her fingers on the coffee table.

"Okay," she said. "I'm the captain of a boat."

"There's no boat," Chase said. "We're in a supermarket."

Yuna slumped. "Right. Again."

Chase frowned at his notebook. He thought about Tuesday, when Brent had gone up in front of the class and pretended to toss a ball to a kid, saying, "Fetch, boy!" The kid had answered, "No, that's not my dog," and the whole room went quiet, like someone had pulled a plug. Brent had stood there holding an invisible leash until Mr. Warsame called time. At the time Chase had laughed, but now he wondered whether the same thing was happening to him and Yuna. It was like there was a hidden rule, something you couldn't see, deciding which scenes lived and which ones died. Both times, somebody had refused what the other person offered, and the scene just stopped.

"Let's simulate it," Chase said. "You say the boat thing again, and instead of fighting it, I'll say yes and add something."

Yuna straightened up. "I'm the captain of a boat."

"Yes, and the hull is porous," Chase said, patting the rug, "so we're bailing water with these buckets."

Yuna's eyes lit up. "Yes, and there's a tsunami coming, so we'd better bail faster."

"Yes, and I see an island to the north."

They went back and forth, trading offers, and the scene rolled along like a wheel downhill. A pirate appeared, then a talking seagull, then the seagull turned out to be the coast guard. Chase realized he'd been wrong earlier. He'd thought a good scene meant winning, keeping his own idea on top, but it worked the opposite way. The scene got better when he let go of his plan and built on hers.

"Wait," Yuna said, grabbing his arm. "I get it. When you said 'there's no boat,' that was blocking." She said the word carefully, the way Mr. Warsame had said it once in passing. "Blocking. That's what it's called."

"Then no more blocking," Chase said. He flipped his notebook to a fresh page and wrote the words YES, AND across the top in big letters, underlined twice, then tore it out and taped it to the coffee table where they couldn't miss it.

Yuna picked up her invisible bucket and grinned. "Bail faster, sailor. That wave's getting closer."

Beatrice set the microscope case on the flat rock beside the creek and knelt to open it, because Mr. Gauthier had said the seventh-grade trail lab counted the same as a classroom lab, and her grade in science needed the help. Her job was to peel a paper-thin layer from an onion, mount it on a slide, and label three parts: the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. The wall she could see already, brick-shaped boxes in neat rows. The nucleus showed up as a dark dot once she added the stain. The membrane was the problem. It lay so flat against the wall that it might as well have been invisible, and her diagram, worth half the marks, had an empty arrow pointing at nothing.

Aveer crouched beside her with the field kit, holding a dropper bottle of plain creek water and, in his other hand, a second bottle he had filled from his own lunch, the salty water left over from his pretzels. "You could just evaluate what you've got," he said, squinting through the eyepiece. "Draw the wall, draw the nucleus, and take the partial marks."

"I need the whole diagram," Beatrice said. She thought about it while a jay screeched somewhere up the slope. She had a hypothetical idea, the kind Mr. Gauthier liked: if the membrane was pressed flat against the wall like a wet shirt on a window, maybe it would show if something pulled it loose. She didn't know what could pull it, but she knew she could test the idea fast. "Give me your pretzel water."

"You want my spit-water on your slide?"

"It's just salt water. Hand it over." He did, and she laid one careful drop at the edge of the coverslip and watched it seep under. For a moment nothing changed, and she held her breath, afraid she had flooded the whole slide and ruined everything. Then, slowly, row by row, each cell seemed to shrink from the inside. Something thin and clear peeled away from every brick-shaped wall and crumpled toward the center, like a balloon letting go of the inside of a box. The arrow on her diagram finally had something to point at.

Agam came over from the tree station to see why she was grinning. "What happened to them?"

"Salt water pulls the water out of the cells, so the membrane shrinks away from the wall," Beatrice said, already sketching. "Aveer says it's called plasmolysis."

"It's on the poster in the classroom," Aveer admitted. "I read it this morning."

Beatrice laughed and wrote the word across the top of her page, then bent back to the eyepiece to catch the last row before the light shifted. "Draw fast," she said, holding out a pencil to Agam.

Vincent stared at the whiteboard in Ms. Ito's room like it had personally insulted him. The problem was 2x + 3x = 15, and beside him Charlize was already flipping her paper over to start the next one.

"Five x equals fifteen," Vincent said. "So x is three. Done."

Amine leaned over. "Show your work, or Ms. Ito will call it reckless guessing again."

"It's not guessing, it's confidence." Vincent wrote 2x + 3x = 5x anyway, because Amine had a smug face when he was right.

Then the next problem appeared: 2x + 3 = 11. Vincent wrote 5x = 11 without slowing down, and his hand hovered there while something in the back of his brain raised a small polite objection. He frowned at his paper. In the first problem, two x's and three x's were both x's, so they went together fine. But the three in this new problem was just a three. There was no x attached to it. He tried imagining x as a box of pencils. Two boxes plus three boxes made five boxes, sure. Two boxes plus three loose pencils made two boxes and three pencils, and that was that.

"You look like you bit a lemon," Charlize said.

"I wrote something weird." He showed her the 5x = 11. "Is that legal?"

Charlize tapped the 3. "What's the x attached to there?"

"Nothing. It's just three." Vincent erased the 5x and wrote 2x + 3 = 11 again, untouched, feeling a bit foolish and a bit brilliant at the same time. So you couldn't smash them together. Two x plus three stayed two x plus three, and you had to deal with it some other way. He thought about the balance scale Ms. Ito kept on her desk, the one she'd used to argue that whatever you did to one side you owed the other side. Subtract three from both sides. That left 2x = 8, and then x = 4. He checked it: two times four plus three did make eleven. He did a tiny drumroll with his pencil, which flew out of his hand and rolled under Amine's chair.

"Nice hygiene," Amine said, picking it off the floor and wiping it on his sleeve before handing it back.

"That's not what hygiene means."

"Whose pencil landed on the floor?"

Ms. Ito walked past and glanced at Vincent's paper. "I see you and the three are no longer on speaking terms."

"We oppose each other," Vincent said. "It has no x, and I stand for x rights."

She smiled and moved on, and Vincent started the next problem, writing slowly this time, checking every term for hidden x's like a detective. "Four x plus one x plus seven," he muttered. "Five x, plus seven, and the seven just gets to sit there being seven."

The dining hall smelled like bacon and pine floor wax, and Charlotte held her tray at the edge of the room, unsure where to sit. It was her first day at Camp Whippoorwill, her first time away from home for more than a weekend. A girl with a sunburned nose waved her over. "You're in Cabin Four, right? I'm Emmie. Sit here."

At the gate that morning, Charlotte had noticed a wooden sign by the office: Accredited by the American Camp Association. She'd asked the counselor driving the van what it meant, and he'd answered while shifting gears. "American Camp Association. It was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps." Charlotte had filed that away. Standards meant rules, and rules meant things got counted and checked, which struck her as useful information about any place she was going to live in for two weeks.

The problem appeared at lunch on Wednesday. Every table got chocolate chip cookies, and the counselor at the serving window called out that each table's share was proportional to its head count, two cookies per camper. Cabin Four had ten campers. They got sixteen cookies. Charlotte counted twice, sliding the plate away from the girl who was already reaching. On Thursday, the same thing: ten campers, seventeen cookies. On Friday, fifteen.

"You're going to perceive a pattern here or you're not," Emmie said, watching Charlotte line up the numbers in ketchup on her tray. Charlotte had a theory. Nobody was miscounting, because the count happened in one place, the window, and the shortage happened after, at the table. She thought it through: if cookies vanished between the window and the table, the cause had to be somewhere along that short trip. So she tested it. She volunteered to carry the plate on Saturday.

She walked slowly and watched. At the far end of the third bench, Anson from Cabin Six slid his hand out and lifted two cookies with the ease of a small-time entrepreneur who had been running this scheme all week. He'd figured out that new campers were too busy being nervous to count anything, and that everyone blamed the kitchen.

Charlotte set the plate down, leaned over, and said, "You owe Cabin Four eleven cookies."

Anson turned pink. The camp director, Ms. Patel, was wiping down the next table, and she looked up at the word "owe." When Charlotte explained, counting on her fingers, Ms. Patel nodded toward the window. "The kitchen counts every batch," she said. "Ask them. It'll match." It did: twenty cookies baked for that table, fifteen on the plate.

At dinner, a plate of eleven cookies arrived at Cabin Four's table, carried by Anson himself, handed over without a word. Emmie took the first one and broke it in half.

Joseph flopped onto the couch in the living room and adjusted the pillow behind his back just as the commercial started. A famous streamer he recognized, DexRaven, held up a glowing headset and said, "I never game without ThunderPulse. It's legendary." Then the screen filled with a huge crowd of people, all wearing the same headset, while a voice boomed, "Join the millions who already switched to ThunderPulse. Don't get left behind with extinct, outdated gear."

"That's the one," Maxim said from the armchair, leaning forward. "Everybody at school is getting them before the tournament. If we don't switch too, we're basically playing in the Stone Age." Joseph looked at the price in the corner of the screen and felt his stomach drop. It cost more than he had saved in four months of mowing lawns.

He muted the TV and stared at it, chewing his thumbnail. "Wait. What does it actually do better?" Maxim shrugged. "It's just... better. DexRaven uses it." Joseph grabbed the remote and rewound the ad, watching it again with the sound low. "Notice how it never says one thing the headset does? It says millions switched, and it calls our old stuff extinct and outdated, and it shows famous people. Those are all about making us feel like losers if we don't buy it. None of it is a reason."

Ms. Hoang, their neighbour, had let herself in through the back door to return a casserole dish, and she paused in the doorway, listening. "Sounds like the bandwagon technique," she said mildly, setting the dish on the coffee table. "Urging you to do something because everyone else supposedly is, so you'll want to belong." She waved and headed back out before Joseph could ask her anything else.

"That," Joseph said, pointing at the door. "That's the name for it. Bandwagon." He pulled out his phone and looked up the headset's actual specs, then looked up his own. Same driver size. Same frequency response. Almost the same weight. The only real difference was the coloured lights on the earcups. "So my inference is the ad costs more than the extra tech does," he said slowly. "They spent all that money on a streamer and a crowd shot instead of making it better."

Maxim slumped back, disappointed. "So everybody's buying lights." Joseph unmuted the TV, where a new ad was already promising that everyone was switching to a different brand of energy drink. He tilted the remote toward it. "Look at this one and tell me what it says the drink actually does." Maxim leaned in and squinted at the screen.

Zoe typed `h1 { text-align: center; }` at the top of her style sheet, saved the file, and hit refresh. The big blue heading that said ZOE'S GUIDE TO ORCA WHALES stayed stuck against the left edge of the page like it hadn't heard her at all.

"That's the third time," Barrett said from the next laptop. "Maybe center just doesn't work on headings."

"It works on yours." Zoe pointed at his screen, where GLIDERS OF WORLD WAR II floated neatly in the middle of his page. Hers was the only one clinging to the margin, and she felt a flicker of resentment toward the whole language of CSS. She hadn't even wanted the fancy gradient background that Cedrick kept bragging about; she only wanted one heading, centred, like everybody else's.

Cedrick leaned over, chewing his pencil. "Maybe it's haunted."

"Maybe you're haunted." Zoe scrolled through her file anyway. The heading rule was at the top, plain as anything. Below it were rules for the background, the paragraphs, the images, and at the very bottom, way down where she'd been experimenting an hour ago, sat a line she'd forgotten: `h1 { text-align: left; }`. She stared at it. Both rules said something about the same heading, and hers was first, which should mean it counted first, shouldn't it?

She decided to hypothesize, out loud, because that was what Ms. Dlamini kept telling them to do. "What if the last one wins? What if CSS reads top to bottom and whatever comes later is what sticks?" It sounded backwards, like the last person in line getting the prize, but it was easy to test. She deleted the bottom line, saved, and refreshed. The heading slid to the center of the page so smoothly it was almost smug.

"Whoa," Cedrick said. "It was hiding down there the whole time."

"I read about that somewhere," Barrett said. "It's called the cascade. Later rules beat earlier ones."

Ms. Dlamini wandered past their row and glanced at Zoe's screen, at the blue heading sitting dead center. "Nice work. What did you change?"

"Order," Zoe said. "The last rule was winning the whole time." She put the deleted line back on purpose, refreshed, and watched the heading jump left again. Then she deleted it once more and it hopped back to center. Proof, twice.

By the end of club, she had added a centered subtitle, a centered caption under her orca photo, and, at the very bottom of her style sheet, in a comment she wrote for her future self: nothing about text-align after this line, Zoe, nothing.

Maya's grandfather kept his old guitar in the hallway closet, and by Sunday afternoon she had claimed it. The recital at the community hall started at seven, which gave her three hours to learn something she had promised the music teacher she could do: improvise a blues solo. Her friend Ross was already set up at the upright piano in the living room, where the afternoon light made everything look tranquil except the two of them.

"Key of A," Ross said, playing a low A to lock it in. "So what are the chords?"

Maya stared at the frets. At home she had practiced with a backing track, and it always worked, but the track had chosen the chords for her. She plucked an A and it sounded right, deep and satisfied, but when Ross tried a minor chord under it, the whole room soured. "No," she said. "Try that one but with the seventh on top." She hummed the note she meant, and Ross found it. The chord suddenly slouched, like it had somewhere better to be.

"That's it," Maya said. "A7. Blues chords want that sound." They hunted for the other two the same way, Ross sliding his hands around the keyboard while she tested notes on the guitar. D7 came next, then E7, and when Ross played all three in a loop, twelve bars at a time, it sounded like actual blues, the kind her grandfather put on the record player while he cooked.

The problem was the solo itself. Every time the E7 came around, Maya froze and played nothing, because at home the track had hidden which chord was which. Here she could see Ross's hands, so she made a deal with herself: watch the hands, and when they jumped to the chord built on E, play fewer notes, save the big bend for right there. She tested it once through and missed, tested again and landed it, and the miss itself told her something. The chords weren't decoration under the melody. They were the ground the melody walked on, invisible unless you looked sideways.

Ross's little brother wandered in, turned the thermostat down to sixty, and wandered out, which meant the piano room would soon be freezing, since Grandpa's furnace took its time. "Fifteen minutes, then we pack up," Ross said, shaking feeling back into his fingers.

On the last run-through, Maya closed her eyes over the E7 and the bend came out clean, hanging in the cold air like it might never evaporate. At the hall that evening, her grandfather sat in the front row. Afterward he said only, "A7, D7, and E7. You found them yourself?"

"With some help," Maya said, and Ross bowed from the piano bench.

The lights went out just as Michael was reaching for the freezer door, and his hand froze in the dark. "Mom, the power's out," he called. She came down the hall with her phone flashlight, and they stood together in the kitchen, listening to the fridge's hum die away into silence.

"The food," his mom said. "That freezer is full of everything for the week." Michael closed the door without opening it, then stopped himself. He had opened it, just once, just a crack, to peek. He told himself a crack didn't count, but the thought kept nagging him.

He went to the window. Across the courtyard, the whole apartment building across the street was dark too, and the streetlights were off, so it wasn't just their building. He knocked on the wall the usual way, and a minute later Daisy knocked back from next door. On the third floor he could see a candle in Nour's window, wobbling.

"Half an hour before you opened that door," his mom said, sitting on the couch with a blanket. "You have to stop opening it." Michael got his notebook and, by phone light, wrote down what he knew: a full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, but a half-full one only lasts about 24 hours, if the door stays closed. He'd read that in the booklet that came with the freezer, back when it was delivered, and had thought it was boring then. Now it mattered. The problem was, their freezer was half full at best. His mom had been planning a big grocery run for Saturday, and today was only Thursday. Twenty-four hours, then, if nobody opened the door again.

He thought about that crack he'd made. It was too late to undo, but he could make the rest of the time count. "Daisy," he said through the wall, "do you have ice?" She laughed. "Our freezer's dead too, genius." But then she said she'd ask her mother about the ice trays, and Nour shouted down the stairwell that her family had two bags of ice from a party. Michael counted on his fingers. If they packed the empty top half of the freezer with Nour's ice, the space wouldn't be half empty anymore. It wasn't quite full, but it was closer.

The stairwell was pitch black. He climbed by feel, one hand on the cold railing, keeping his spine straight against the wall so he wouldn't miss a step. Nour met him at her door with both bags, and Daisy came up behind him carrying her ice trays wrapped in a dish towel. Back in his kitchen, they compressed the ice into every gap around the frozen peas and the bread and the endangered chicken that was supposed to be Sunday dinner. Michael shut the door firmly and taped a note on it: DO NOT OPEN UNTIL POWER IS BACK.

Saturday morning the lights came on with a click, and the fridge started humming again. Michael peeled off the note, opened the freezer, and the cold air rolled out over his face. "Still frozen," he reported. "Every bit of it." Daisy leaned in and poked a bag of peas. "Okay," she said, "I take back what I said about your boring freezer booklet."

Cooper had four index cards, one encyclopedia open to the letter V, and no idea how to start his presentation. The assignment was on the screen of the library computer in green letters: explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War. He knew the treaty had punished Germany after the First World War, but "helped lead to" was the part Mr. Fortin would actually grade.

Sarah-Maude slid into the chair across from him with her own stack of books. "I'm doing the same topic," she said. "Jeanne found a whole chapter in this one. Want to split it?"

"Only if you explain the middle part," Cooper said. "I can get from the treaty to Germany being angry. I can't get from angry to war."

Jeanne arrived carrying a photocopy. "Listen to this," she said, and read aloud in a low voice because they were in the library. "In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles, and Britain and France did not use force to stop him."

"That's it?" Cooper said. "That's the middle?"

"That's a piece of it," Jeanne said. "I don't know what it means either."

While they argued, a boy from their class, the one who always sat near the window, opened a bag of chips behind the reference shelf. Food in the library was against the rules. Mr. Fortin was checking books at the desk ten feet away, and he looked up, and he looked back down at his scanner. Nothing happened.

Cooper watched the boy eat the whole bag without hiding it. Then the boy got up, wandered to the display of new paperbacks marked DO NOT REMOVE UNTIL FRIDAY, and put three of them in his backpack.

"Mr. Fortin," Cooper said, before he decided to say it. "He's taking the new books."

Mr. Fortin went over, had a quiet conversation, and got the paperbacks back. The boy got a warning and a call home. Cooper sat down again, and something clicked into place. "That's the Rhineland," he said.

Sarah-Maude frowned. "The what?"

"The chips," Cooper said. "The rule got broken once and nothing happened. So he tried a bigger one. Britain and France let the first break go in 1936, when it was just troops going into the Rhineland. After that, why would he stop?" He pulled a blank card toward him and wrote rapidly. "It's not that the treaty made the war happen by itself. It's that every time somebody broke it and nobody stopped them, the rules kind of eroded. Wore down. Like a path."

Jeanne turned the photocopy around. "It says here the treaty also made German civilians pay reparations, money taken from ordinary people, not just the government. So they were angry and humiliated."

"So you get anger, then a test, then no pushback," Cooper said, arranging his cards in a line across the table. "Anger, test, nothing. Then more."

Sarah-Maude laughed. "It's ironic. The treaty was supposed to prevent another war by keeping Germany weak, and it basically handed Hitler his script."

Cooper stood and asked Mr. Fortin if he could sign out the projector cart for fifth period on Thursday. Mr. Fortin wrote his name on the clipboard. "What's your topic?" he asked.

"How the Treaty of Versailles helped cause the Second World War," Cooper said. "And how you have to stop the first broken rule, or you'll be stopping the second one a lot harder."

On his way back to the table, he passed the window seats. The boy from class was there, and he looked at Cooper for a long second, then zipped his backpack shut and left it on the floor, empty, next to his chair.

Luke had agreed to watch the neighbor's baby for one hour, and for the first forty minutes it had gone fine, mostly because the baby slept in the stroller while Luke sat on a bench near the duck pond. Then the baby woke up and started to cry, and kept crying, and Luke's careful bouncing and patting did nothing at all.

Josie and Channing showed up right about then, which was lucky and unlucky at the same time. Channing had his tablet out because he was filming a video of the ducks for the park's summer contest, and he wanted to win more than anything. "Only one entry gets shown at the nature center," he said, crouching in the invasive vines by the fence to get a low angle. "Mine has to be the one." Josie, who had three younger cousins, took one look at the baby and said, "Have you tried the soother?" Luke found it in the stroller pocket, but it had rolled under the wheel, right through a patch of goose droppings, and there was no way he was putting something like that in the baby's mouth. Every microbe in that park was probably on it now. He envied Josie for how calm she looked, like crying babies were just weather to her.

The crying got louder. Luke's arms ached, and a hot, frustrated feeling rose up in him, and he caught himself jiggling the baby harder than he meant to, a sharp frustrated shake. Right then a Canada goose stalked over and snatched Channing's sandwich out of his open backpack, and in the chaos of Channing yelling "Not the cheddar!" Luke noticed the flyer taped to the bench arm. It was about crying infants. He read it while the baby howled: never shake a baby, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury.

His stomach went cold. He stopped the jiggling instantly, laid the baby flat and buckled safely into the stroller, and stepped three paces away to breathe, exactly like the flyer said to do if you felt overwhelmed. Josie stood beside him. "You okay?" "Yeah," Luke said. "Just need a second." Behind them, Channing was still chasing the goose, which was not going to give back the sandwich.

And then, in the sudden quiet, the baby stopped crying. Not because of anything Luke did. The goose had come back to strut past the stroller, and the baby stared at it, fascinated, and made a small huffing sound like a laugh. Channing froze, tablet still running, and the contest footage caught the whole thing: his goose, mid-heist, and a laughing baby. "That's the shot," Channing whispered. "That is absolutely the shot."

The wind turbine beyond the far curve of the track turned in slow, lazy circles, and Charles watched it while he waited for his heat to be called. He had signed up for the eight hundred metres because Mr. Pereira had put a blank line on the sign-up sheet and dared anyone to try something new. Nikola, the fastest sprinter in grade seven, had written his name underneath. So had Meera, who won every long-distance race the school had ever held. Charles had written his name last, mostly so the sheet would not look lonely.

In the first time trial, Nikola exploded off the line as if the gun owed him money. He led the whole first lap, arms pumping, and then, halfway down the back straight of the second lap, he simply folded. He slowed to a jog, then a walk, and finished with his hands on his knees. "It's like my legs turned to sand," he told Charles afterward. "The first lap felt easy. Easy!" Meera ran her trial the opposite way, drifting along at the back so gently that she looked bored, and when she finally kicked on the last lap she had nothing left either. She was caught at the line and finished fourth, and her look at the finish clock was nearly venomous.

Charles could not stop thinking about it on the walk home. Both of them had run one good lap and one bad one, in opposite directions. That was a pattern, and patterns had causes, even when you could not see them. He remembered a poster in the science wing about two ways the body makes energy. One kind, called aerobic, uses oxygen and lasts a long time. The other kind, called anaerobic, works without oxygen but runs out quickly. The eight hundred needed both at once, which was why Nikola had burned through his fast fuel in one lap and Meera had saved so much she never spent it.

On Saturday he tested it. He asked a parent to stand at the two-hundred mark with a watch, then ran the first lap deliberately controlled, not sprinting and not strolling, like a turbine turning at a steady speed instead of a gust. He wanted to calibrate the pace by feel, so that the first lap used the oxygen kind of energy and saved the quick kind. On the second lap his legs ached, but there was still something left in them, and he finished faster than his first trial by four seconds.

Monday at practice he found Nikola and Meera at the long-jump pit. "It's like a sprint and a distance race at once," Charles said. "You have to feed both engines. Spend the fast stuff only at the end." Meera squinted at him, then at the track, then went to find her shoes. Nikola jogged to the start line and stood there, tapping his toes against the rubber, waiting for them.

Evelyn had decided that the eye gleam was the soul of a portrait, the tiny white spark that made a painted face look back at you. She was seven washes into her watercolour of Kadence, who sat across the art room table posing like a very patient queen, when she noticed the disaster.
