Her sixth wash, a pale shadow of violet meant for the eyelid, had crept sideways and swallowed the little spot of white paper she'd been guarding for the gleam.

"That's the third time you've sighed like a dying dragon," Kadence said. "What happened?"

"I flooded the light. The eye's gone dark all the way through." Evelyn held the paper up to the window. The spot where the gleam should be was a soft grey, like a window with the curtain drawn. "I can't wash it out. Watercolour doesn't lift that clean once it's soaked in."

Brody leaned over from the next table, where he was painting what he claimed was a dragon but looked like an angry avocado. "Just put white paint on it. I have white. Take my white."

Evelyn squeezed a dab onto her palette and tried it on the corner of a scrap first, which was the kind of thing Ms. Santos-Reyes was always suggesting. She painted a shadow, dabbed white over it, and frowned. The white sat on top like chalk, dull and flat, nothing like the shining paper around it. She tried a second dab, thicker. Worse. It looked like a smudge of toothpaste. "White paint isn't the same," she said slowly. "It's cloudy. The real shine on the rest of the paper is just... paper."

She turned the scrap over and over, testing the idea from every angle like a detective. If the brightest white came from untouched paper, then she could deduce something important: highlights had to be planned before the first brushstroke, not rescued afterward. They weren't something you added. They were something you protected, right from the start. Which meant her portrait of Kadence had a villain after all, and the villain was her own impatient brush, sweeping through territories it had promised to spare. Every painting, she thought, hid its antagonist inside the painter's wrist.

"So is it fixable?" Kadence asked. "Or is my face doomed to look like a haunted doll?"

"Starting over is one option," Evelyn said. "Doing surgery with white paint is another, and we've seen how that ends." She considered whether it was feasible to carve the spot back to bare paper with a tiny bit of sandpaper, but she could already picture the scuffed fuzz it would leave, and a fuzzy eye was sadder than a dark one. She pulled a fresh sheet from the pile. "New plan. I draw your eyes first, and before any wash touches this paper, I paint a ring of masking fluid around the gleams. Like a fence. Like a fortress around the light."

Ms. Santos-Reyes drifted past and looked at the ruined portrait, then at the new sheet with its two small amber circles drying over each pupil. "Saving the paper's own shine," she said. "Smart."

The fortress held. Wash by wash, violet and rose and deep brown climbing from light to dark, the amber dots shed paint like tiny umbrellas, and when Evelyn peeled them off with her fingertip at last, two clean white sparks sat in Kadence's eyes, gleaming exactly where they had always meant to.

"It's like you're watching me," Kadence said. "It's like you're actually in there."

Evelyn propped the portrait against the paint rack and stood back, and the painted Kadence stared back at her, alive with light she'd never once had to invent. "The paper was on my side the whole time," she said. "I just had to get out of its way."

The last slice of pecan pie vanished from the kitchen counter sometime between the touch football game and the fireworks Louis's uncle was illegally setting up in the driveway. Louis had been counting on that slice all afternoon, and he took the loss personally.

He began his investigation at the scene. The counter held a fork in the sink, a smear of filling on the edge, and a pie plate wiped cleaner than anything else in his grandmother's house, which was saying something. His cousin Meliane, who wanted to be a lawyer, insisted Kendrick had done it because Kendrick had been in the kitchen right before everyone noticed. Kendrick, who wanted to be left alone, said Meliane had gone in for ice, and that in fact she had been in there twice.

"You were in the kitchen," Meliane said.

"So were you," said Kendrick.

Louis wrote both statements in his notebook, which he had brought for a history assignment. That was the problem with the assignment, actually. Ms. Janssen had given the history club two eyewitness accounts of the morning at Lexington in April 1775, and the two accounts flatly disagreed. The British witnesses said the colonists fired first. The colonial witnesses said the British fired first. Both sides had been standing on the same green watching the same morning, and after all this time, historians still did not know who fired the first shot. Louis had stared at the papers for an hour, waiting for one of them to blink.

He tried an experiment now. He brought Meliane and Kendrick into the kitchen, both of them complaining, and reenacted the afternoon as best he could. Kendrick demonstrated where he had stood getting his soda, on the far side of the refrigerator, with his back half turned. From there the counter was blocked by the plumbing of the hanging pot rack, a thick tangle of hooks and copper bottoms. Meliane's path from the ice machine, though, had a clear view, and she had been carrying a dish towel, and there was a smudge of pecan filling on the dish towel, which was currently folded over a chair like evidence hiding in plain sight.

"Meliane," Louis said.

"I was going to bring it out for everyone," she said, which was not a denial. Her audience dwindled to zero as Kendrick drifted toward the door, uninterested in justice now that it wasn't aimed at him. Louis looked at his notebook, then at the towel, then at the empty plate, and thought about how two witnesses on one green could swear opposite things and both believe themselves completely. He underlined the towel in his notes.

"Deal," Meliane said suddenly. "Half my Easter candy for the last slice next time."

Louis shook her hand.

The cookies came out flat as coasters, and Abigail needed to know why. She slid the tray onto the counter and stared at the sad, crispy circles. Her little brother had made a batch yesterday from the same recipe, and his had been puffy and golden.

"Maybe the oven hates me," her brother said, grabbing a flat cookie anyway.

"The oven doesn't hate you. Something made them collapse, and I'm going to find out." Abigail flipped through her notebook until she found a blank page. "In science you start with a hypothesis. It's a testable guess. You don't just say 'cookies fail.' You say why you think they failed, then you test it."

He rolled his eyes. "Like evolution? That's just a theory, so it's just a guess."

"That's not what theory means." She tapped her pencil on the counter. "A theory is an explanation that's been tested over and over, and every test so far has backed it up. Evolution is that kind. A hypothesis is an idea still being tested, like mine about these cookies. Huge difference."

"Fine, detective. What's your hypothesis?"

Abigail looked at the two mixing bowls sitting in the sink, hers and his. Both had sticky residue, but hers had a translucent film smeared across the rim, glossy and faintly cloudy, like fogged glass. Butter. She remembered scooping hers soft and melty from a bowl that had sat near the stove while the oven preheated. Warm butter, she guessed, had wrecked the structure before the cookies even hit the pan.

"My hypothesis: if the butter is too soft, the cookies go flat. If I use cold butter, everything else the same, they should puff up." She wrote it down, underlined it twice, and texted Diego, because experiments were better with witnesses.

Diego arrived in eleven minutes flat, still holding his bike helmet. "I brought the notebook for official observations," he announced, and Abigail pointed him to a stool.

They made one small batch with butter straight from the fridge, firm enough that the spoon left clean marks in it. As the cookies baked, a thin vapor rose from the oven vent and the whole kitchen smelled like Saturday morning. Abigail crouched at the oven door, watching the dough through the glass. The edges went translucent, then golden, and the centers puffed into soft domes.

"They're rising! Diego, they're rising!" She flung the oven open at the timer's buzz and slid the tray out. Twelve rounded, puffy cookies, warm and tall.

Her brother bit into one and chewed slowly. "Okay, so cold butter. Your guess was right."

"My hypothesis was supported," Abigail corrected, grinning. She wrote the result in her notebook, then paused, pencil hovering. "But one batch isn't tested over and over. So what does that make it?"

Diego leaned over her shoulder. "Still a hypothesis?"

Abigail smiled and started measuring flour for round two. "Exactly. Science needs seconds."

The clock on the dashboard read 4:41, and Victoria's dad kept saying "We'll make it, we'll make it" like a chant that could change traffic. The optical shop closed at five, and if they missed tonight, her new glasses would sit in a drawer all weekend, and she would spend two more days squinting at the whiteboard while Miriam whispered what Mr. Haile had written. Victoria stared out the window, where the street signs were soft gray blobs with fuzzy edges, and tried to guess what they said anyway. The one with two round shapes was probably the school crossing. The tall skinny one might be a speed limit. It was like a puzzle where half the pieces were melted.

"I still can't believe you found out you needed glasses from a poster," Miriam said from the back seat.

Yesterday, Mr. Haile had taped a chart of letters on the classroom wall and asked everyone to read the bottom row for a health unit. Victoria had gotten stuck after the first two letters, and Mr. Haile had tilted his head and said, "Hmm." That single "Hmm" had started everything: the eye doctor, the letter E that looked like a smudge, the words nearsighted and minus two. Now the glasses were ready, waiting in a little case at the shop, and the clock said 4:47.

"I've been wondering something," Victoria said as they turned onto Main Street. "If people have always had bad eyes like me, how did anyone read before glasses were invented? Did they just... not read?" Miriam said she had no idea. Victoria had looked it up the night before, while waiting for her dad to finish filling out forms, and she wanted to test whether she remembered it right. "I think I read that the earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290. So before that, everyone was basically me." She thought about monks copying books letter by letter with eyes like hers, holding pages at arm's length. "That's like seven hundred years of glasses. But everything before 1290, nothing."

"It's like the dinosaurs," Miriam said. "Complete extinction of tiny letters."

Victoria laughed. "Tiny tropical fish in textbooks. Extinct."

Her dad swung into the parking lot at 4:56, and Victoria was out of the car before he had fully stopped. Inside, the optician found her case, and Victoria lifted the glasses out slowly, like they might dissolve. She slid them on.

The world snapped into focus. Price tags, crisp and mean. A tropical fish poster by the register, every scale sharp. Miriam's face, with actual eyelashes.

"Okay," Victoria said, reading the smallest line on the wall chart across the room. "Now somebody delegate me a book with tiny print."

Christopher knocked twice on Drew's front door, then remembered his own mother's rule about knocking hard, and knocked softer the second time. Drew's house always smelled like lemon polish, and today the kitchen table was covered with newspaper, a roll of wrapping paper, and a small brass wall clock in a box.

"Nice, right?" Drew said, turning the box so the clock face caught the light. "It's for the Chens. They moved in next door Friday, and Mom said we should bring a housewarming gift when we visit tomorrow. The clock was on sale." He began cutting the paper in lush green sheets with snowflakes on them, humming like a job half done.

Christopher didn't hum. He was thinking about the word the clock made in his head. Last month his cousin had married into a Chinese family, and at the wedding Christopher had watched his uncle put a clock back on the shelf at the store, fast, like it was hot. When Christopher asked why, his cousin had leaned close and said the one thing he remembered now: "In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because giving a clock sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death." Christopher had thought it was strange then. He thought it was very useful now.

"Wait," he said. "Before you wrap that. What if it's the wrong thing, like, exactly the wrong thing, for this family?" He laid out his reasoning like steps: the Chens were a Chinese family, the clock was a gift, and if the sound of "giving a clock" landed badly, then the Chens would open the box tomorrow and hear something awful inside a kind present. It was a hidden rule, the kind you couldn't see on the object itself. Drew frowned at the clock, then at the snowflake paper. "So we test it," Christopher said. "Call Ms. Malik. She grew up across the street from the Chens' cousin." He said it as a question, not a lesson, and Drew was already dialing.

Ms. Malik answered on the second ring, and Drew held the phone flat between them. "A clock?" she said. "Oh no, my mother would have fainted. Pick something else, boys." When they hung up, Drew sat still for a moment. "That would have been terrible," he said. "The irony is I picked it because it was the nicest thing I could afford." Christopher shrugged. "You picked it because you wanted their new place to feel like home. That part's still good. We just need a different homey thing."

They pooled their money, biked to the corner store, and came back with a heavy ceramic bowl painted with fish. The next evening, when Mrs. Chen opened her door, she took the bowl with both hands, the way you take something that matters, and Drew bowed a little, copying her. She laughed, called something over her shoulder, and held the door wide. "Come in, come in, we'll eat."

Arianna leaned over the crickets in the glass terrarium at the back of Ms. Anderson's science room and counted them twice. Fourteen yesterday, twelve today. Two crickets did not just vanish, she thought, so where did they go? Bo crouched beside her, chin on his fists.

"Maybe they escaped," Bo said. "That's my opinion, anyway."

"It can't be an opinion," Arianna said slowly. "It's a claim. We could check it. There'd be crickets on the floor or holes in the lid." She tapped the mesh. No holes. No dried little bodies behind the water dish either.

Oaklyn drifted over from the rock display, holding her notebook. "You two are weirdly excited about missing crickets." She peeked into the tank. "Oh, I bet something ate them. That's just my opinion, so you can't say I'm wrong."

Arianna remembered last month, when Oaklyn had insisted the Eiffel Tower was in Berlin and ended the argument with those same words: it's just my opinion. Ms. Anderson had overheard and frowned, and after class Arianna had looked it up on the classroom computer until the fact finally clicked in her head. The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin was a checkable claim, and it was false, plain and simple. An opinion was more like crickets are gross, which nobody could prove right or wrong. Bo hadn't been there for that, so she turned to him now. "A false claim isn't an opinion. It's just a wrong claim. The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion."

"So my escape theory could be wrong," Bo admitted. He checked the lid again anyway, thorough as a detective.

Arianna prioritized the possibilities: escape, or something inside the tank eating them. She studied the terrarium. One of the "decorative" rocks she'd borrowed from the display had come from the pond behind the school, and yesterday she'd noticed a small bulge tucked in a hollow of it. Now she wondered. "Oaklyn, get the magnifier." Oaklyn flipped a rock over and the bulgle uncurled, a beetle the size of her thumbnail, jaws like tiny hooks. "Predatory," Oaklyn whispered, delighted and horrified at once. "That thing is absolutely predatory."

They reported everything to Ms. Anderson, who raised an eyebrow at the pond rock. "Well," she said, "you've turned a mystery into an experiment. What's your next step?"

"We keep the beetle in a separate container with one cricket," Arianna said, already reaching for a jar, "and watch what happens." Behind them, Oaklyn sneezed twice and wiped her eyes. "Great," she muttered. "I have an allergy to your new class pet."

Lea sat on her bedroom floor with her phone face down beside her, like it might explode. Chiara had not answered three texts, and at school she had walked right past Lea's locker with her eyes fixed on the hallway clock, which was strange because Chiara never looked at clocks, she looked at people. Something had gone wrong, and Lea could not see what it was, which was the worst part. If she could see the crack, she thought, she could at least figure out where to press.

She replayed Thursday in her head. There had been the group project meeting in the library, where Mr. Dang had asked Lea to be the team's ambassador to the other seventh-grade class. Lea had said yes, and Chiara had gone quiet, and after that they had not really talked. But quiet was not the same as angry, and Lea kept circling the afternoon like a detective with no fingerprints. She even made a list on the back of her science notes: things I did, things I said, things I did not notice. The third column was the longest, which did not help.

On Saturday morning she wandered into the living room, where her mom had left a stack of library books on the coffee table. One was thick and pale blue, about listening, of all things. Lea flipped it open mostly out of boredom, and a line stopped her: the term "active listening" was introduced by the psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957. It meant trying to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words. Lea read it twice. She had been composing apologies all morning, long speeches about how sorry she was, and none of them had room in them for Chiara's side of anything.

She tested the idea out loud, alone in the living room, which felt ridiculous. "So you felt like I got picked and you got skipped," she said to the empty couch. Then she tried it another way, trying to guess what the moment must have looked like from Chiara's chair in the library: her best friend saying yes to a solo job, fast, without a glance sideways. Lea picked up her phone and typed, can you come over. Then she added, I won't do a big speech, I promise.

Chiara came at two, standing on the porch with her jacket zipped to her chin even though it was warm. They sat on the living room floor where the books still lay, and Lea's prepared apology started to rise in her throat and she pushed it down. Instead she said, "I read this thing this morning. It's called active listening. You basically say back what the other person means."

"Sounds like something a teacher would make up," Chiara said, but she unzipped her jacket.

"So," Lea said, and made herself keep going, even though her face felt hot. "When Mr. Dang picked me, you felt like I got chosen over you. Like I would rather prioritize some ambassador job than be on your team."

Chiara stared at her for a second, and then her whole posture loosened, shoulders dropping like a cut string. "That's exactly it," she said. "You didn't even look at me first."

"I didn't know," Lea said. "But I should have."

"I didn't want to be jealous about it," Chiara said. "That's why I didn't say anything. It felt babyish."

"It doesn't sound babyish," Lea said. "It sounds like you wanted your best friend, and I was busy being pleased with myself." She nudged the blue book with her toe. "This says Rogers and Farson came up with it in 1957, and they were grown men with degrees, so wanting to be understood is officially not babyish."

Chiara laughed, a short buoyant sound that popped the last of the tension. "Okay. Next time Mr. Dang picks you for something, you look at me first."

"Deal," Lea said. "And next time you go quiet, I'm going to say back what I think you mean, even if I get it wrong."

"Even if you get it really wrong," Chiara said, and leaned over to steal the blue book and flip through it herself. "Page sixty-three. Show me the part you read."

Victoria sat in the back row of the temple with her grandmother's blue scarf wound twice around her wrist, and she kept her eyes on the candle at the front because looking at the photo beside it made her throat close. The whole hall smelled of marigolds. James slid into the seat next to her and whispered, "You okay?" She nodded, which was not exactly true, and he seemed to know that, because he just stayed there.

After the service, everyone filed out into the courtyard, where Mrs. Okafor had set out tea and little sandwiches nobody was eating. Victoria stayed in her seat. She had been turning one question over all week, the way you turn a stone over to see what's underneath: was wearing the scarf a good thing, or was it a way of hiding from the fact that Grandma was gone? Her counselor at school had said the words "moving on" twice, and now Victoria wondered if the scarf meant she was failing at it.

Mr. Abdi, who taught science at her school and had come to the temple that morning, was stacking chairs near the front. Victoria watched him straighten one chair, then another, like a man solving a slow puzzle. She went over. "Can I ask you something weird?" she said. "If I keep wearing my grandmother's scarf, does that mean I'm not... moving on?"

Mr. Abdi rested a chair on its legs. "Moving on from what, exactly?" he asked. "Grief isn't a train you catch or miss." Then he told her about a book he'd read after his own father died, from 1996, called "Continuing Bonds." He said it had argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects, or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving. He said it in almost exactly those words, the way people repeat something that changed their mind once. Victoria held on to the sentence like a rope.

That afternoon she decided to test the idea, because that was what you did with ideas. She unwound the scarf and laid it on her bed for one hour, and she felt worse, not better, like a bear yanked out of hibernation in the middle of January. Then she put it back on and helped her father cook Grandma's rice and peas for the neighbors, following the recipe written in Grandma's cramped handwriting, and she felt something loosen in her chest instead of tighten. So the scarf was a bridge, not a cage. That was her data.

The next week she brought the rice and peas to school in a container, and James and Meadow ate it on the bleachers and said it was better than the cafeteria's gray propaganda about healthy eating, which made Victoria laugh for the first time in days. Meadow asked about the scarf, and Victoria said, "It's a continuing bond," and left it there, because some sentences you don't explain, you just wear them.

The twist came on Sunday, when she finally opened the scarf's folds all the way and something small dropped out and skittered under the pew: a folded paper, hidden in the hem where Grandma must have sewn it. Victoria knelt and pried it loose. In cramped handwriting it read, "For V, when she needs to find something I left her. Look where the poorest place in the house is richest." Victoria read it twice. Grandma had always called her little window garden "my impoverished kingdom," because it got only an hour of sun.

She ran the whole way home, scarf streaming behind her, and knelt at the window box with her fingers in the dirt. Somewhere below the marigold roots, her thumbnail hit something hard.

Paige had been stuck on the same sixteen bars of "Moonlight Fog" for two weeks, and now she was stuck on them at Madeleine's house too, where the piano sat in a sunny room that smelled of lemon polish. The sheet music said lento at the top, then a sudden allegro halfway through, and Paige's hands refused to believe the two sections belonged to the same piece. "You're rushing the slow part," said Ivana, who had brought her practice pad and sat cross-legged on the rug with her sticks. "It's like you're scared of it."

"I'm not scared," Paige said, though her fingers were tight and she knew it. She played the opening again, and again it crept faster, the way a slippery hill creeps steeper the longer you look down it. Repeating the same sixteen bars was getting tedious, and worse, it wasn't working. Madeleine's little brother stood in the doorway radiating impatience, bouncing a tennis ball until Madeleine pointed him away with a look.

Ivana set down her sticks and squinted at the metronome marking under the word lento. "It says sixty. Do you know what that actually means?" Paige admitted she didn't, not really. Ivana tapped the wall clock above the piano. "Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so a marking of sixty means one beat each second." She pointed at the red second hand. "Watch it. Tap every time it jumps."

They all watched the clock, and Paige tapped her knee each time the hand clicked forward. One. Two. Three. It felt impossibly slow, like watching paint decide whether to dry. When she tried to play the opening at that speed, the melody changed under her hands. The chords that had sounded plain now sounded heavy and deliberate, like footsteps in fog. "That's it," Madeleine whispered from the window seat, and even the tennis ball in the hallway went quiet.

The allegro section was easier once the lento felt right, because the contrast did the work. Paige practiced the jump four times, and on the fifth try she played it straight through, slow into fast, soft into loud, without dropping a note. Ivana grabbed her sticks and played along on the practice pad, keeping the slow beat against the ticking clock until the change, when she doubled her speed and the room seemed to lift.

"Play it once more," Madeleine said, "all the way from the top, dynamics and everything." Paige flexed her fingers, glanced once at the second hand ticking its steady sixty, and began. Ivana came in beside her, and Madeleine leaned against the piano with her eyes closed, conducting the air with a pencil she'd picked up off the music stand.

At the cemetery gate Anais stopped, because for the third morning in a row the world felt foggy and her stomach turned at the thought of breakfast. She had barely slept since Grandma Rhea died, and now she was worried she was catching something on top of everything else. "You okay?" August asked, holding the folded program for the service. "I don't know," Anais said. "I haven't slept all week and I can't eat. I think I'm getting sick." The funeral started in twenty minutes, and she still had to read the poem Grandma had loved.

They walked between the headstones, cut grass sticking to her shoes, the air smelling of damp earth and lilies from the wreaths. August pointed at a flock of geese arrowing south overhead. "Your grandma was the one who knew all the birds, right?" Anais nodded. Grandma Rhea had called herself a student of migratory birds, and every October they used to sit on her porch with cocoa, counting Canada geese until their necks ached. "Migratory birds leave and come back," Anais remembered her saying, "but grandmas don't. Deal with it, girl." That had made Anais laugh, which was Grandma's whole plan.

Last night, though, there had been no laughing. She had stared at the ceiling until two, then picked at a piece of toast at seven and given up after two bites. On the walk over she had tested an idea: maybe she wasn't sick at all. Maybe this was what losing someone did to a body. She'd heard Liam mention, after his grandfather's funeral, that he couldn't eat for days and slept terribly, and then it just faded. Two examples wasn't much, but it was a pattern, and a pattern was a rule you could lean on.

"Try a few crackers," August said, digging into a jacket pocket. "Small bites. Not a whole breakfast, just fuel." Anais ate three, slowly. Her stomach accepted them. When her legs wobbled going up the little hill to the graveside, she sat for a minute on the cold bench and let the tiredness be there instead of fighting it, the way Grandma used to say you let a snowy day happen instead of battling it. "Grief is a strange adversary," Anais said. "It makes your body tired and your stomach shut down like it wants to hibernate, even though it's not even cold out."

"So you're not sick?" August asked.

"I don't think so. I think this is just what it does." She stood, the poem folded in her hand, paper soft as feathers. Mr. Tan nodded to her from the front row. Anais walked to the small podium, took a breath that smelled of lilies and rain, and began, "Because I could not stop for Death, he kindly stopped for me."

James counted his money at the pickle stand twice, because $1,000 in twenties felt like it should weigh more than it did. He had earned it over three summers of hauling bins at the farmers' market, and now his grandmother had written him a letter, which lay folded in his back pocket like a secret.

"Read it again," said Antony, who was supposed to be stacking cucumbers for Ms. Toussaint but had drifted over. James unfolded the paper. "Dear James," he read out, "if you leave your thousand dollars with me for five years, I will pay you 5 percent simple interest. That means fifty dollars a year, so at the end you will have one thousand two hundred fifty dollars. Love, Gran." He had read it four times since breakfast, and the numbers still refused to sit still in his head.

"Fifty a year," Katarina said, arriving with a bag of peaches. "That's the same fifty every year? That's it?" James frowned at the letter. His bank had shown him a pamphlet about compound interest, where the interest earned its own interest, and Katarina had spent all of Tuesday explaining it to him while they were supposed to be pricing tomatoes. He worked it out on the back of a paper bag with Ms. Toussaint's pencil: fifty, one hundred, one hundred fifty, two hundred. "So after five years, Gran's deal gives me twelve fifty, total," he said slowly. "The bank thing would give more." Katarina shrugged. "Maybe. But your grandmother won't charge you fees, and the bank pamphlet had a picture of a sailboat on it, which I personally found suspicious. Like a counterfeit promise. All shiny, no pickle stand."

"That's a weird perspective," Antony said, "but I'm citing it forever." He stole a cucumber and pretended to study it. James looked down the row of stalls, at Ms. Toussaint arguing cheerfully with a man over the price of okra, at his grandmother's handwriting on the page. Last summer he had spent his earnings on a drone that now sat broken in his closet, and he still wasn't sure whether he regretted the buying or the crashing. Maybe giving the money to Gran for five years was just a way of locking the drone mistakes in a drawer. Or maybe it was a bad deal dressed up as a family favor.

He thought about it through the whole morning, weighing fifty a year against the bank's pamphlet and the sailboat that never sailed anywhere. At noon he texted Gran from his mother's phone: "Deal. But can we write compound into the contract for next time?" He slid the pencil back across the pickle stand to Ms. Toussaint. "You owe me one tomato," he said. "Rent for the pencil."

Mackenzie had put on sunscreen at nine that morning, before anyone else was even awake, and by four in the afternoon her shoulders were the color of the camp stove. The family had been at the lake all day. She had swum in the morning, dried off, eaten a sandwich, swum again, played catch with Calvin from the campsite next door, and never once thought about the orange bottle sitting in the tent.

Demi crouched beside her on the picnic table bench and studied her shoulders like a detective. "You put sunscreen on this morning, right? I watched you do it."

"I did," Mackenzie said. "That's the weird part."

Demi pulled out her phone, tapped at it, and read aloud, her voice flat with disbelief. "Reapply every two hours outdoors. And immediately after swimming or sweating." She looked up. "Immediately. You swam twice."

Mackenzie tried to count backward through the day. Nine o'clock, the lotion. Ten thirty, the first swim. If the rule was every two hours, she had needed more by eleven, and the swim before that meant she'd needed it even sooner. Then lunch, then the second swim, then two hours of throwing a frisbee with Calvin in the sun. It wasn't one mistake. It was the same mistake repeated all day long, invisible until now, like a pattern you couldn't see until you stepped back from it.

"My aunt did this last summer," Demi said, peeling the label off the bottle she'd fetched from her own tent. "She said swimming washes it off, but I thought she was just being dramatic." She squirted a white ribbon into her palm. "Arms out. You're not doing this again tomorrow."

While Demi rubbed it in, Mackenzie thought about her grandmother's house, the one her parents were going to renovate next month, and how her grandmother had once told her that some things you couldn't see the damage of until later. Mackenzie had assumed she meant the pipes. Now she wondered if it was a lesson with a wider use, one she could have learned a day earlier and a lot less painfully.

Ms. Swampy, the woman who ran the camp store, walked past with a wheelbarrow of firewood and paused. "Someone spent too long in the sun?"

"Twelve hours too long," Demi said. "Roughly."

Ms. Swampy laughed and kept walking. Calvin jogged over from the water spigot holding a dripping towel and draped it, cold and heavy, across Mackenzie's shoulders without a word.

"Tomorrow," he said, "I'm setting an alarm."

Taylor had typed THE END, printed three copies, and carried them to the school library, where Jaycee and Willyam were already waiting at the corner table. The assignment from Ms. He was due Friday: a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax. Taylor's story was about a girl who rescued a lost dog from a storm drain, and the rescue was the big scene, all shouting and mud and the dog's wet head popping out of the pipe.

Jaycee read fast, the way she always did, and put the pages down. "The storm drain part is great. But what happened to the dog after?"

"After what?"

"After the rescue. The story just stops. Did the girl keep him? Did someone come looking for him? You said he had a collar with a tag."

Taylor had not thought about the tag since chapter one. She took the pages back and read the ending again. Two paragraphs, then THE END, and the dog was still standing in the rain. Willyam leaned over. "It's like the last piece of a puzzle is missing, and the puzzle is on the floor and nobody picks it up."

Ms. He walked past with a cart of returns and stopped when she heard the word climax. "That's the word for your loudest moment, your turning point. Your rescue scene." She shelved two books and moved on.

Taylor looked at her ending and tried a test. She wrote one new paragraph: the girl calls the number on the tag, the owner drives over in a truck with a camper shell, and the dog rides home with his head out the window. Then she wrote a second paragraph where the girl's mother says she can walk him on Saturdays. She printed the new pages and handed them to Jaycee without saying anything.

Jaycee read to the bottom. "That's better. The truck answers the tag, the Saturdays answer the girl wanting a dog. Everything gets tied up." She tapped the last line of dialogue. "Also you forgot the comma before the closing quotation mark right here."

Taylor fixed the comma. Willyam said the storm drain part still made his hands sweat, which he claimed was the highest compliment available in the library. Ms. He, passing again, glanced at the new ending and gave a small nod before pushing her cart toward biography.

Taylor saved the file twice. On Friday she got her paper back with one note in the margin: falling action and resolution do real work. She folded the paper and put it in her binder, behind the history quiz she had nearly failed, where it could insulate that particular humiliation from anyone flipping through. Then she started a new story, this time about a negligent crossing guard, and she knew exactly where the loose ends would go.

The gym had been transformed, more or less. Crepe paper hung from the basketball hoop like a droopy canopy, and the DJ booth sat directly under it, speakers stacked on folding chairs. Livia stood near the door with Kareem and Ireland, all three of them pretending they came to dances all the time. Then the bass dropped, and conversation became impossible. They ended up right beside the speakers because Kareem said the best spot was close to the music, and nobody argued.

At eleven that night, Livia lay in bed hearing a thin, high whine that was not coming from anywhere. She picked up her phone and typed into the family group chat: "Is the wifi doing something weird? I keep hearing a squeal." Her mom replied with a picture of a shrugging emoji. Her older brother, who had gone to concerts all last year, answered differently: "That's tinnitus. Ringing in your ears after loud music. It means the noise was loud enough to actually damage your hearing. It's a warning sign." Livia stared at the message, then pressed her palms over her ears. Still squealing.

She thought back to the fall, when her cousin's wedding had been held outside under a tent so arid and dusty that the DJ had cranked everything to maximum, and she had heard that same faint whine on the drive home. She had blamed the car. It had never once occurred to her that her own ears were the source, and that the ringing was trying to tell her something. Now the pattern seemed obvious: loud music, then the whine. The whine showed up only after loud music. She wanted to verify it before she believed a group chat at midnight.

On Monday she found Kareem at his locker. "Did your ears ring Saturday?" she asked. He nodded, and then said the thing that made her stomach drop. "They're still ringing. Right now. Like a TV that won't turn off." Ireland came over and admitted hers had rung until Sunday morning. Livia pulled out her phone and showed Kareem her brother's message, and he read it twice without speaking.

"So the speakers," Kareem said slowly. "We were basically leaning on them." He looked down the hall toward the gym doors, as if the speakers might still be lurking there. "There's another dance in March," he said. "I'm standing by the water fountain next time. That's like forty feet away." Ireland said she would join him, and Livia said she would too, but first she was going to ask her brother one more question in the group chat. She typed: "Does it go away?" and watched the screen while the typing dots appeared.

The war memorial sat on a low hill at the edge of town, a granite soldier staring east over the river, and Jordan's social studies class stood around it in the wind while Ms. Farah-Ali held up a cardboard box. "The historical society lent us this," she said. "Diaries, letters, a land paper. Find a primary source and use it to explain why people moved west." Jordan had wanted the letters, because letters were short. Colton grabbed those first, grinning, so Jordan took the leather diary with the cracked spine and sat on the memorial's bottom step to read.

The handwriting belonged to a man named Amos Reed, who in 1863 wrote that he had nothing in Ohio but debts, and that "the Homestead Act of 1862 offers 160 acres of public land to any settler who will live on it and farm it for five years." Five years, Jordan thought. That was longer than he'd been at his middle school. He read on. Amos had a wife who didn't want to leave her sister, and a boy Jordan's age, and the diary kept returning to that argument the way a tongue returns to a sore tooth.

"Conductor on the train said the plains are turbulent country," Amos wrote in April. "Wind like a living thing. But land is land." Jordan looked up. Brynlee was photographing the engraved names on the memorial, names of men who'd left farms like the one Amos wanted. He thought of his grandfather, who still farms the acres his great-great-grandmother homesteaded. There was a flashback Jordan couldn't shake: last summer, Grandpa had tried to confide something about the farm, said it hadn't come to the family the way everyone believed, then changed the subject and shelled peas instead.

Jordan had assumed, when he chose the diary, that the answer would be simple: people moved west because land was free. That was the sentence he'd planned for his report. But Amos's wife wrote two pages herself near the end, in smaller, steadier letters, and she didn't mention land at all. She mentioned the boy, and the river in Ohio that had flooded their crop twice, and the fact that staying meant owing money to her brother-in-law forever. Free land was the door, Jordan realized, but people walked through it for different reasons, some of which they barely said out loud.

Then Colton leaned over his shoulder. "Reed. That's my mom's maiden name. That's my family." Jordan read the last line again, the one where Amos Reed wrote that his wife had finally said yes, and he hadn't asked twice. "So your family got 160 acres," Jordan said slowly, "for five years of farming." Colton sat down hard on the step beside him. "My grandpa sold it in 1970. Everybody thinks we still have it." Behind them the granite soldier went on staring east, toward everything that had been given up, or taken, or lost. "You should call your mom," Jordan said, and held out the diary.

Alexia spread her notebook across the library table and stared at the assignment sheet for the fourth time. Write a short story with dialogue, a clear climax, and a final draft due Friday. She did not dread writing itself; she dreaded the red pen Mr. Rossi would use on her dialogue, because last time he had circled half her punctuation and written "See me" in the margin.

Julianna dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of graphic novels and her own notebook. "I want mine to be about a soccer tournament," she said. "The championship goal has to be the climax. Obviously."

"Obviously," Alexia agreed, though she wasn't sure what her own climax would be. She had decided on a story about two friends caught in a flood at a summer camp, because at least flood water rising was a problem that got worse on its own.

Haroun arrived last, carrying his laptop and a printout so meticulous it looked like a book page, margins ruled in pencil. "I'm doing a story about an outbreak," he said. "A scientist has to get the vaccine to a town before the sickness spreads. But I need someone to test-read it, because I can't tell anymore if it makes sense."

"I'll read it," Julianna said, always first to volunteer.

Alexia watched her friend's eyes move down the first page. Julianna's reading slowed at the third paragraph. Her lips moved. Then she frowned and slid the paper back across the table.

"Who's talking here?" Julianna asked, tapping the page. "The scientist and the mayor both have lines in this one paragraph, and I got lost. I thought the mayor was the scientist for like four sentences. Is he mad at himself?"

Haroun leaned over and squinted at his own words. "They're all talking in the same place. That's how paragraphs work, right? One topic, one paragraph?"

Alexia pulled the page closer. In her own notebook, she had been copying dialogue out of a library book, a mystery where two detectives argued on a rooftop. She flipped back a page and looked again. Every single time a new person started talking, the book had started a new paragraph. One speaker, one paragraph. Another speaker, another paragraph. It was a pattern, and she could test it.

She grabbed three books off the returns cart, all with dialogue, and dropped them next to Haroun's story. "Look," she said, opening the first one. "Every time a different character starts to talk, a new paragraph starts. Every time. That's how the reader knows who's saying what without you having to write 'the mayor said' every single line."

Julianna picked up the second book and checked. Then the third. "It's true. Every single one."

Haroun was already retyping, his fingers flying. He hit a key, and the scientist's line dropped down into its own paragraph, alone. He read it aloud to himself in a low voice, and this time the argument between the scientist and the mayor sounded like two people instead of one confused person arguing with himself.

"Now I just need my climax," Alexia said, and she wrote at the top of a fresh page: the moment the rescue boat appears, everyone speaks, one at a time.

Julianna pointed at Haroun's screen. "Read me the outbreak scene again."

He started over, and when he reached the scientist's line about the vaccine, he stood up and acted it, holding the printout like a syringe.

The cardboard box on the passenger seat had two air holes poked in the top, and inside it a puppy the size of a loaf of bread trembled every time the bus braked. Matteo held the box on his lap and whispered through the holes. "Almost home," he said, which was true in a way, because the shelter had called the little dog a refugee that morning, a stray from a flooded farm outside town, and today it would have a home for the first time.

Mr. Saleh was watering his roses when Matteo climbed the front steps, and he peered into the box and grinned. "What's his name?" Matteo hadn't decided, and he said so, feeling like a bad owner already. "Then decide fast," Mr. Saleh said. "A dog with no name never learns to come when you call." He offered to dog-sit for an hour while Matteo ran to the store for puppy food, and Matteo agreed, because Mr. Saleh ran the animal rescue booth at the spring fair and seemed competent with animals, the way some adults just were.

At the store Matteo bought the food, a collar, and, at the last minute, ingredients for brownies, because his mother had asked and because the cashier said the baking chocolate was on sale. He carried everything home in one heavy bag, set it on the kitchen counter, and ran out back to show Mr. Saleh the puppy could almost climb the porch step.

When he came back inside, the bag was on the floor, torn open, the bag of baking chocolate shredded and licked clean.

Matteo stood very still. He had heard somewhere that chocolate was bad for dogs, but he tried to remember whether that was everything or whether there was more to it, some rule he was missing. He grabbed his phone and called Wade, who read everything about animals and had once given a presentation on poisonous plants.

"It's not all the same," Wade said immediately. "There's a thing in chocolate called theobromine, and dogs break it down really slowly. Dark chocolate and baking chocolate are way worse for them than milk chocolate. It matters how much and what kind." Matteo looked at the shredded wrapper, at the word BAKING in block letters, and his stomach dropped. It was the worst kind, and the puppy weighed almost nothing.

"How long do I have?" he asked.

"Hours, not days," Wade said. "Call the vet now."

Matteo dialed, holding the puppy, whose tail still wagged as if nothing had happened. The vet asked the puppy's weight, the type of chocolate, and how much was gone, then told him to come in right away, before symptoms started, that the treatment worked best early. Matteo yelled for Mr. Saleh, who drove them both, taking the corners carefully while the puppy slept in a towel on Matteo's lap.

They waited in a bright room that smelled like disinfectant. The vet came out wiping her hands and said the puppy would be fine, that they had caught it in time. Matteo exhaled so hard his whole body sagged. On the drive home the puppy climbed out of the towel and pressed its nose to Matteo's neck, and Matteo looked at Mr. Saleh and said, "His name is Kicker." Mr. Saleh laughed, and asked why, and Matteo said, "Because he kicked his way out of that box twice, and he's going to thrive here."

Max sat on the bench outside the rink with his skates half-laced, staring at his phone. The tournament roster was due to Ms. Halvorsen by five o'clock, and he had one spot left. His problem was that two goalies, Hana and Lili-Rose, both had save averages of exactly ninety percent over the last ten games. The list on his screen just showed one number next to each name, as if that settled everything.

"Five o'clock," said Ms. Halvorsen, sticking her head out the rink door. "Clock's running, Max."

"Working on it," he called back. He texted his dad: stuck between Hana and Lili-Rose, same average, what do I do? His dad replied with a message that made Max stop and read it twice. Forget the average. Get the game-by-game numbers. An average squashes ten games into one number. Two kids can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, because the average hides how spread out the results are. Ask yourself which one you want when it matters.

Max looked at the rink doors. He began to hypothesize. If the average hid how the games were spread out, then maybe Hana and Lili-Rose had arrived at ninety percent in completely different ways. It was like a formula where you could see the answer but not what went into it. He needed the inputs.

He found the game sheets in the binder by the skate rental desk and flipped back through the season, copying the numbers for each goalie onto a napkin. Hana's line read like a heartbeat: 90, 89, 91, 90, 90, 92, 88, 90, 91, 89. Lili-Rose's looked like a mountain range: 100, 100, 60, 100, 100, 55, 100, 100, 100, 55. Max read them again. Steady versus volatile. One goalie you could count on every single night. The other could be unbeatable or terrible, and you never knew which one would show up.

He ran the numbers twice to be sure, and both columns climbed to ninety. Same average, opposite seasons. So which did he pick for a tournament where one bad period meant going home? Max thought about the semifinal last year, when they had lost in a shootout and he had promised himself he would build a team that never depended on luck.

At four fifty-two he walked to the office. "Hana," he told Ms. Halvorsen, sliding the roster across the desk. "Same average as Lili-Rose, but I'll take the goalie who's the same every night." Ms. Halvorsen glanced at the napkin of numbers Max had paper-clipped to the sheet, then at the clock, and stamped it.

"Roster's in," she said. "Better go tell her before practice starts."

Alexis had exactly one hour before her grandmother arrived for dinner, and she had promised homemade pasta sauce, not the stuff from a jar. She had never made sauce from scratch, and she had certainly never chopped an onion, which is why Blair had come over to supervise.

"Curled fingers, like a claw," Blair said, demonstrating in the air. "Knuckles forward, fingertips tucked. The knife rides against your knuckles and can't get to your fingertips."

Alexis curled her hand into a claw and set the peeled onion half flat side down on the cutting board. She pressed down with the knife, and the board shot sideways across the counter like a hockey puck. The onion half rolled, and she lunged to catch it before it hit the floor.

"Every single time," she groaned. "The board skids when I press down. It did that at your house too, remember? When we made that salsa?"

Blair nodded. "My mom just chases the board around the counter. She says it's part of the workout."

Alexis was not going to chase a cutting board around for an hour. She stood still, thinking. The board skidded when she pressed down. It skidded at Blair's house too, on their smooth counter. But it had never skidded at her grandmother's house, and her grandmother's counter was just as smooth. What was different there? She pictured her grandmother's kitchen: the old dishcloth, always slightly damp, always folded under the board. Alexis had assumed it was there to catch drips. But maybe that wasn't its job at all.

"Wait here," she said, and ran to the sink. She soaked a paper towel, wrung it out so it was damp but not dripping, and laid it flat on the counter. Then she set the board on top and pressed down hard on the onion with the knife. The board did not move at all. She pressed again, harder. Nothing. It sat there like it was glued down.

"You found grandma magic," Blair said, peering at the towel as if it might conceal some secret mechanism.

"It's not magic, it's just a damp towel under the board," Alexis said. "That's why hers never skids. I thought the towel was for mess. It's actually the grip."

From there everything went fast and, for once, consistent. Board steady, claw grip steady, and the onion fell into small, even pieces, though not before the onion made both of them cry so hard that Blair claimed she was weeping over a sad movie she'd never seen. Alexis swept the onion into the pot with the canned tomatoes, a pinch of sugar, salt, and a basil leaf she'd been hiding from her mom's sandwich plans like it was valuable currency. "That leaf," Blair said solemnly, "is worth at least two chocolate bars."

The sauce bubbled, and Alexis stirred it just as the doorbell rang, ten minutes early. She wiped her eyes one last time and went to let her grandmother in.

"Something smells like a real kitchen," her grandmother said, sniffing the air. "And why have you been crying?"

"Onion," Alexis said. "Purely professional onion."

Alexandre had twenty-three dollars in his pocket, saved over five weeks of walking dogs, and he meant to spend it on a basketball jersey at the mall. Ziad and Maxime trailed behind him through the food court, where the smell of sizzling onions mixed with cinnamon from the pastry stand. A giant screen above them showed a famous point guard spinning a ball on one finger. "You gotta try FuelSnax," the player said, winking. "They power my game." Maxime stopped dead. "If he eats them, they work," Maxime said, already digging for his wallet.

At the sports store, a display caught Alexandre's eye before the jerseys did. A banner read "Everyone's Already Switching!" above a rack of socks, with a counter supposedly showing thousands sold today. Ziad squinted at it. "That number just repeats the same digits over and over. I watched it for a whole minute and it never changed." Alexandre felt the pull of the banner anyway, the feeling that everyone else knew something he didn't.

He found his jersey, but beside the register sat boxes of protein cereal with the words "All-Natural Goodness" in golden letters. Natural. Goodness. They sounded strong and safe, and they made him want the box even though he wasn't hungry. He picked it up and turned it over. The ingredient list ran eleven lines long and included things he couldn't pronounce, plus three kinds of sugar. "All-natural," he muttered. "It doesn't even say what's natural about it."

"Ms. Baptiste calls those glittering generalities," Maxime said, peering over his shoulder. Alexandre blinked. "She does?" "Last week. Vague, nice words that make you feel good without saying anything you can actually check." Alexandre looked from the cereal box to the sock banner to the looping basketball video on the food court screen. The sock number was fake, the celebrity was paid, and "goodness" meant nothing he could test. It was like every ad in the mall was using the same three tricks in rotation, consistent as a drumbeat.

He set the cereal down, and on his way past the pastry stand he stopped instead. The woman there was giving Ziad, who had spent all his money on FuelSnax, a free sample of warm bread. "It preserves best if you eat it today," she said with a smile, "but it's real food, from a cuisine my grandmother taught me, not a slogan." Ziad grinned around the mouthful.

Alexandre paid for his jersey, folded it carefully into his backpack, and steered his friends toward the exit. "Next Saturday," he said, "we try every free sample in that food court and rate them for real." Maxime slapped the door handle. "Deal. But Ziad rates nothing until he shares those snacks."

Mr. Sandhu's health class had moved to the unit on growing up, and Gabriella sat in the back trying to make herself smaller. He had just said that puberty meant their bodies would start doing new things, like sweating more, and when he mentioned that everyone would need to figure out their own routines, a few kids laughed. Gabriella didn't laugh, because two days ago, in the middle of a presentation, she had noticed a damp patch spreading under her arm and spent the rest of class holding her binder like a shield. Nobody had said anything about it. Maybe nobody had seen. But how could she know?

She cornered Ariah by the lockers after the bell. "Do you use, like, the white stick or the gel or what?" Ariah shrugged and said her mom bought whatever was on sale, and Tatiana claimed she used nothing at all, which Gabriella was skeptical about, since Tatiana was the fastest runner in gym class and gym was right before lunch. That afternoon, Gabriella got permission to walk to the drugstore two blocks from school, forty minutes of freedom and one specific mission.

The deodorant aisle had an entire wall of options, which should have helped but mostly made things worse. She picked up two sticks and read the labels like they were clues. One said deodorant, and the other said antiperspirant deodorant, which was confusing, because weren't they the same thing? She flipped them over. The plain deodorant never mentioned sweat at all, only odor. The antiperspirant said it reduced wetness. So one of them stopped the smell and one of them stopped the sweat? She turned a third box over, and a fourth, checking whether the pattern held, and it did, every time. "Antiperspirants plug the sweat ducts," she muttered, reading the tiny words on the back. "Deodorants don't stop the sweat." A woman reaching past her for shampoo smiled like she'd heard something funny. Gabriella bought the antiperspirant with her allowance.

The next week, she ran an experiment, though she never called it that out loud. Monday and Wednesday she used nothing, and by gym class her shirt told the story she already knew. Tuesday and Thursday she used the new stick, and the damp patch that usually appeared stayed away, though by Thursday afternoon, when she leaned close to sniff her sleeve, she noticed things starting to deteriorate on the smell front. Interesting. So the wetness and the smell were separate problems, and the stick she'd bought solved only one of them.

Friday morning she set the antiperspirant on the bathroom shelf next to her dad's old deodorant, the green one that smelled like pine. Two different tools, sitting side by side, each doing its own job, like the pipes and the air freshener were separate parts of the same plumbing. She wondered what else about growing up worked like that, one thing that looked like another but wasn't. She rolled the stick on, grabbed the deodorant too, and stuffed both in her backpack, because Monday had a presentation, and she intended to stand in front of the class with both arms moving freely.

Raphael had signed up to cook Friday dinner for his family ever since his mother enrolled him in the community kitchen's six-week course. Tonight was the last class, and everyone had to send a full meal home: roast chicken, rice, and a salad. The instructor, Ms. Sok, had said the meals had to be packed and out the door by six o'clock, because the kitchen closed at six thirty sharp.

He got the chicken into the oven by four forty-five, which left him time for the rice and the salad. He was proud of the chicken. He had dried the skin, rubbed it with salt and oil, and it was already smelling better than anything he made at home. Zia, chopping carrots two stations over, leaned toward his tray and said it looked exceptional, and she did not hand out compliments often.

At five thirty he washed the plastic cutting board he had used to trim the raw chicken, wiped it with a towel, and set the head of lettuce on top of it. His hand was already reaching for the knife when Avianna, who had finished her salad ten minutes earlier, stopped him.

"You used that board for the raw chicken," she said.

"I washed it," Raphael said. "It's clean."

"It's still how you get cross-contamination," Avianna said. "Bacteria from one food spreading to another. Raw meat on a board, then salad on the same board, and the salad goes straight to the table without any cooking to fix it." She pointed to the stack of boards by the sink. "That's why there's a pile of them."

Raphael stood there with the knife in his hand. He thought about the order of things. The chicken would go into a hot oven and stay there for over an hour, and whatever was on it would be dealt with by the heat. The lettuce would go into mouths exactly as he cut it. It was not a complicated equation: cooked food could take the risk, and ready-to-eat food could not.

He put the board back in the sink, took a fresh one from the stack, and chopped the lettuce on that. Then he thought about the towel he had used on the first board, and he threw it in the laundry bin instead of hanging it back up. He wiped the counter with a clean cloth, found a clean bowl, and finished the salad with cucumber and a squeeze of lemon.

At six ten, Ms. Sok checked each station. When she reached Raphael's, she lifted the lid on the chicken, looked at the salad, and marked something on her clipboard. "Board rotation," she said. "Good." Raphael packed the meal into the insulated bag his father would pick up, snapped the containers shut, and carried it to the door just as his father's car pulled up to the curb.

Jonathan had nineteen tomato seedlings on his windowsill and a plan that could not wait. "We're planting Saturday," he announced at school. "Ms. MacLeod gave me the corner plot at the community garden, and tomatoes take forever, so the sooner they go in, the sooner we eat salsa."

Marc-Antoine and Phoenix met him at the garden gate on Saturday morning with a wagonload of seedlings, including peppers and one ambitious little squash. Ms. MacLeod was watering the rhubarb nearby. "Keen," she said, squinting at the sky. "You know your frost dates?" Jonathan did not want to know his frost dates. He wanted to plant. "The sun's out," he said, and marched to his plot.

They dug fast. Rain from the night before had saturated the soil, so every shovel of dirt came up heavy and shining, and Phoenix kept flicking worms at Marc-Antoine, who shrieked like a kettle each time. By lunch they had planted everything, watered it, and named the squash Gerald. "This alliance," Jonathan declared, standing proudly over the rows, "will produce salsa by July."

That evening the sky turned the color of a bruise, and the radio said the temperature would drop below freezing overnight. Jonathan sat straight up in bed. Freezing. His grandmother had lost her whole garden one year to a late frost. He ran downstairs in his pajamas, grabbed every pot, bucket and recycling bin he could carry, and called Phoenix from the front step. "Cold night. Frost kills tomatoes and peppers and squash. They can't take freezing. Come on!"

Phoenix arrived with a duvet. Marc-Antoine arrived with a colander strapped to his head like a helmet, for reasons he refused to explain. They covered every seedling, tucking the duvet around Gerald like a baby. "My shovel is obsolete," Marc-Antoine said sadly. "We're farmers of buckets now."

In the morning, Ms. MacLeod walked over and tapped a pot. "So you learned about last frost the hard way, or almost." Jonathan admitted he'd been in a hurry. "Next year I wait," he said. "Even if the sun looks perfect. Frost-tender stuff goes outside only after the last spring frost, not one day before."

"That's the most sensible thing you've ever said," said Phoenix, lifting a bucket. Underneath, the tomato seedling stood small and green and entirely alive. Jonathan whooped so loudly that a crow flew off the fence.

Marc-Antoine raised the colander in salute. "To Gerald," he said, "and to salsa in July."

Audrey carried the rabbit carrier through the gate and set it on the picnic table while her father unlatched the door. Inside the shelter, a rabbit had been waiting three weeks with no name, only a tag that said "found, Front Street." The shelter worker had seemed surprised when Audrey picked her.

"Nobody wants a found rabbit," Ann had said on the walk over. "You don't know where she came from."

"That's the point of finding out," Audrey had said, though she wasn't sure how anyone could. The rabbit had no collar and no tag. She hopped out onto the grass and flattened herself under the picnic table, ears down.

Audrey sat on the steps and made a critique of the facts she had. Rabbits couldn't tell anyone their address. A lost dog at the shelter had gone home in minutes, because the worker had waved a small box over its shoulder and a number had come up. Audrey had asked what the box was for, and the worker had answered with one sentence: "A microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and it holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details." Audrey tried to paraphrase it to Ann later. "Tiny thing under the skin, scanner reads it, owner shows up." Ann had shrugged. But that was for dogs. The rabbit had been scanned too, the worker said, and nothing had come up. Nothing, or something the worker hadn't said out loud?

Audrey's idea was simple. She called the shelter and asked whether the scan on the rabbit had shown any number at all, even an old one. The woman at the desk put her on hold. When she came back she said the scanner had shown a number after the second pass, but the registry page wouldn't load that day, so it had never been entered. She read the number out loud, and Audrey wrote it on her arm with a pen.

At the kitchen table she typed the number into the registry website. A name came up: Biscuit. An address two streets over, a phone number, and a note that said, "Please call any time."

She called from the backyard with the rabbit on her lap. A woman answered, and after a silence she said, "We buried Biscuit's hutch mate in April and she dug under the fence the same week. We thought a fox got her." Then she asked if she could come by with some of Biscuit's old hay, because the rabbit liked to eat only the authentic kind from the farm, not the store kind.

The rabbit's ears went up when the car pulled in beside the gate. A girl got out holding a bag of hay and stopped at the sight of the picnic table. "Biscuit," she said, and knelt down in the grass.

The bus smelled like sunscreen and old bananas, which Kate decided was just what a field trip to a historic farm should smell like. Ms. Pelletier had handed out worksheets at the gate, but Kate had folded hers into a paper airplane before they reached the barn, because she had a better plan: she wanted to solve the mystery of the sleepy cow. All morning the big brown cow in the corner paddock had been chewing, chewing, chewing, slow as a metronome, even though there was no hay anywhere near her mouth.

"Maybe she's chewing gum," said Alfred, watching through the fence.

"She's not even eating anything," Kate said. "Look. No grass, no bucket. Just chewing." Daisy suggested the cow was bored, which Kate dismissed with a skepticism so strong that Daisy laughed. Something was going on inside that cow, Kate decided, something she couldn't see, and unseen things were her favorite kind of problem. She had heard a rumor from her cousin that cows were basically walking compost heaps, but her cousin also claimed to have caught a lake monster, so the source was questionable.

Kate tested a simple idea. If the cow was chewing something she had already swallowed, then the chewing should slow down the longer it went, the way gum loses its flavor, or it should stop when the cow got fresh food to start over. She leaned on the rail and counted chews under her breath. Fifty-two, fifty-three. Then Daisy offered the cow a handful of clover through the fence, which Ms. Pelletier said was voluntary on the cow's part and perfectly allowed. The cow swallowed, grazed for a minute, and went right back to chewing at the exact same slow pace.

The farm interpreter, a wiry man in suspenders, strolled over. "You've been watching her a while," he said.

"She's chewing nothing," Kate told him. "I counted."

"That's cud," he said. Then he tipped his hat and told them the rest, plainly, like he was reading a grocery list. A cow's stomach had four compartments, and the first one was called the rumen. The rumen held microbes, tiny living things that helped break down tough grass. The cow brought that partly broken-down grass back up and chewed it again. That was what they were watching. That was the cud.

"Microbes," Alfred said slowly. "So her stomach is basically colonized by little helpers."

"Four stomachs' worth of them," Daisy said, and Kate, who had been picturing one sad empty mouth all morning, felt the whole mystery click shut. The cow went on chewing, serene as a queen, and Kate counted one more round for the road: forty-eight, forty-nine, fifty. "She's not slow," Kate murmured. "She's thorough." The cow blinked at her, jaw working, and swallowed.

Ryan had claimed the scruffy corner of Mr. Aydın's farm as his own vegetable kingdom, and he ruled it like a monarchy where the king also did all the digging. "Tomatoes in the middle, beans along the fence, corn in the back," he announced to Delaney, who had come to accompany him on planting day mostly because her mom said screen time was over.

"Your kingdom is a mud puddle," Delaney said, pointing at the low spot where rain collected. "The corn is going to drown."

Ryan refused to remain neutral about that. He built a small dirt wall, planted anyway, and by June he had a problem. The tomatoes in the rich dark soil near the fence were knee-high and cocky. The tomatoes in the tired, pale soil by the gate were yellowing and sulking. Same seeds, same water, same sunlight. Something invisible was different about the soil, and invisible things annoyed him.

Then Mr. Aydynn came by with a wheelbarrow and stopped at the fence row, where the beans grew thick and green. "These look happy," he said. He pulled one bean plant, shook off the dirt, and held up the roots. Tiny lumps clustered along them like beads on a string. "Nodules," he said, and moved on before Ryan could ask a single question, which Ryan considered deeply rude.

Ryan squatted over the roots, thinking. Bumps. On the roots of the plant growing like a champion in the corner where the tomatoes also grew well. He remembered a line from the seed packet, small print he'd skipped: beans and peas host bacteria in those little lumps, bacteria that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use. So the beans weren't just growing there. They were changing the soil itself, quietly, underground, and the tall tomatoes near the fence were living next door to it.

He had to test it. He dug up the sick gate-side tomatoes, mixed a double handful of bean-cradle soil into each hole, and replanted them. "What if I'm just giving them mud therapy?" Delaney asked. "Then they'll feel spa-refreshed and stay yellow," Ryan said. They marked the row with a popsicle stick that said SCIENCE and waited.

Two weeks later the gate-side tomatoes stood greener, new leaves pushing out, leaning toward the fence like they'd heard the gossip. Ares came by, poked the marker, and read it aloud. "Science?" he said. "It looks like tomatoes." Ryan held up the bean roots he'd saved in a jar, lumps and all, and tapped the glass.

"Those bumps," he said, "are running the whole kingdom."

The pimple arrived on a Tuesday, right in the middle of Mr. Zhao's health class, and by lunch it had a classmate: a second one on Amelia's chin. "This is new," she whispered to Ayan, angling her phone camera at her jaw. "Eleven years of nothing, and now two in one day. Something changed." Ayan leaned over and squinted. "Maybe it's the chocolate from the fundraiser?" Amelia shook her head. She'd eaten fundraiser chocolate every fall since fourth grade and her face had always stayed clear. Whatever the hidden cause was, it wasn't chocolate.

Mr. Zhao had just written PUBERTY on the board in big blue letters. Amelia sat up straighter. He talked about growth spurts and voice changes, and then, almost in passing, said that hormones during puberty make the oil glands in the skin produce more oil. He moved on to sleep, but Amelia didn't. She copied the sentence into her notebook and underlined it twice. If hormones were flooding through everybody in this room, then the pimples weren't random. They were a pattern, and patterns could be tested.

She spent the walk to the pharmacy after school building her case. "My inference," she announced to Ayan, holding the classroom door, "is that the extra oil is clogging my pores. So logically, I should strip the oil off. Problem solved." Ayan grinned. "Science fair champion Amelia returns." The plan felt inevitable and satisfying, like solving an equation.

At the pharmacy Amelia stood in front of the face wash shelf and read labels. She grabbed the strongest one, the one that promised to remove every trace of oil, and showed it to Ayan. But the label said something that stopped her: salicylic acid, for skin that is oily and prone to breakouts. The words prone to breakouts nagged at her. A stronger wash meant harsher scrubbing, and harsher scrubbing meant more irritation. What if attacking the oil too hard made things worse? "New plan," she said slowly. "Gentle wash, twice a day, no matter what. Same time, every time. If my hypothesis is right, the gentle one beats the nuclear one." Ayan grabbed a basket. "Then we need a control group. Loik still has that pizza-face situation from the assembly." They texted him immediately. Loik wrote back a single word: "Deal."

The twist came four days later in health class. Loik triumphantly displayed his chin, nearly clear, while Amelia's face had calmed down but not vanished. "Mine's better," Loik bragged. "Because my sister told me the oil even has a name. It's called sebum." He said it like a magic spell. Amelia laughed and pulled out her notebook, already writing the next experiment at the top of a fresh page. "Fine, Loik. But Monday we're testing whether washing three times a day helps or hurts." Loik snatched his bag. "Race you to the water fountain."

The birthday party had spilled from the kitchen into the backyard, where someone's uncle was grilling hamburgers fast enough for the kids to consume two each. Hudson was halfway through his second bun when he noticed the corner by the fence. Three boys from another school circled a kid named Theo, who was holding his slice of cake and pretending not to hear them.

"Nice jacket," one of them said. "Did your mom pick it out?" The others laughed. Theo's shoulders climbed toward his ears, and he set the cake down on the grass like he'd lost his appetite for it.

Hudson's first instinct was to barge over and shout, which would make him the adversary of three bigger boys at once. His second instinct was to do nothing, because what could one person even change? He'd stood by before, at school, and the memory sat badly with him. Was there something in between? He watched the boys and noticed a pattern: they worked off each other's laughter. When one of them paused, the teasing sagged, like a fire losing air. Maybe it didn't need a bucket of water. Maybe it just needed someone to break the circle.

He crossed the lawn, picked up Theo's plate, and held it out. "Hey, they're doing the piñata," he said, as if he'd arrived for no other reason. "You're missing it. Sasha's about to take a blindfolded swing at a crowd of innocent people." He kept his voice easy, not defiant, not scared. The boys blinked. The loudest one glanced at the others, waiting for a cue that didn't come, because the circle had a gap in it now.

"Piñata?" Theo said. He took the plate back and stood up straighter. "Whose dumb idea was candy in the yard?" He walked with Hudson, and the three boys drifted off toward the trampoline like a breeze that had changed direction.

Later, sitting on the porch steps with Sasha, Hudson asked the question that had been circling his head all afternoon. "Does that actually work? Stepping in like that? Or did we just get lucky?" Sasha, who had read every pamphlet in the counselor's office out of pure boredom, nodded. "There was a study of school playgrounds in 2001. When a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases." Hudson turned that over, wondering how many times he'd watched teasing end on its own, and whether it had actually ended because someone quietly stepped in and he'd never noticed.

"More than half," he said. "So you don't even have to win. You just have to walk over there." He looked across the yard, where Theo was now telling the three boys, in detail, exactly why their trampoline technique was wrong. Sasha raised her plastic cup. "To the gap in the circle," she said. Hudson tapped his cup against it.

Mathis slid the battered copy of A Midsummer Night's Dream across the library table and stared at the page like it had insulted him personally. "Puck, round about, go and watch," he read aloud, then stopped. Ms. Le had said their homework was to paraphrase the scene, to turn each speech into plain modern English, and so far his notebook held exactly one line: "The fairy says something about the earth."

Nimrit dropped into the chair beside him and peered at the page. "You've been on that scene for twenty minutes."

"It's tedious," Mathis said. "Half the words look like typos." He tapped the paper. "And look here. Every so often the script says exit, which is fine, that's obviously the guy leaving. But then it says this other word, exeunt, and it's not even a name. Who is Exeunt? Why does he keep showing up?" He flipped pages, and the word kept appearing, always at the end of the busiest moments, when three or four fairies were crowding the stage.

Nimrit frowned and counted characters on her fingers. "Wait. Look at that part. Puck exits alone, and it says exit. Then Oberon and Titania both leave together, and it says exeunt. Try the crowded one, the scene where all four of them have been arguing." They found it: four speeches in a row, then the word exeunt, and nobody left on stage.

Mathis sat back so fast his chair squeaked. "It's not a person. Exit is Latin for he or she goes out," he said slowly, testing it. "Exeunt is Latin for they go out. It's used when two or more characters leave." He checked it against every scene ending in the book, and it held every single time. "So it's like a stage traffic signal."

"Okay, so now you can actually see who's on stage," Nimrit said. "Can you paraphrase the speeches now?"

Mathis looked at Puck's long speech again. Some of it was still fog, but now he could see the shape of it, who was speaking to whom, who was staying, who was going. He wrote, "The fairy says the earth is so full of vapor from the oceans that clouds form," and crossed out the fog. It wasn't perfect, but it was real English, his English. He turned the page and kept going.
