"Two papers, one poll," he said when she arrived. "This one says the team's free throws went from 40 percent to 50 percent, a rise of 10 points. This one says the same thing, same numbers, but it calls it a 25 percent increase. Ten and twenty-five. Somebody's lying."

Ms. Oliveira read both clippings, then handed them back. "That's a real puzzle, Jackson. But I don't think either reporter made it up. You're welcome to figure it out."

He tried the obvious explanation first: maybe the poll was different, or one paper made a rounding error. He checked the dates, the team name, and every number he could find. Both stories matched exactly. If neither story was wrong, he thought, then both numbers had to be true at once, which felt impossible, like two answers orbiting the same question.

At lunch he dragged his clippings to the corner table where Christine was stacking her tray. "Read these. Tell me I'm not crazy."

She read them twice. "They're both saying the same thing."

"But ten isn't twenty-five," Jackson said. He grabbed a napkin and wrote it out. "Forty to fifty." Christine frowned at the napkin like it might be hiding something.

That afternoon in the gym, the coach had them shoot twenty free throws each, and Jackson counted his makes on his fingers like money. When he missed his last five, Allison laughed from the foul line. "You're plague-level bad today."

"Say that again," Jackson said slowly, an idea turning over in his mind. He walked to the bench and did the arithmetic twice, then a third time, because the first two times it seemed too strange to trust. Then he ran back across the gym floor.

"Ten points and twenty-five percent," he told Christine after practice, holding up his wrinkled napkin. "Same change. Forty to fifty. Two ways of saying it. It sounds like a lie, but it's true." He smoothed the napkin on the bleachers between them.

Christine looked at it, then at him. "So both reporters were right?"

"Both right," Jackson said, and folded the napkin into his pocket like a ticket he'd won.

The fire station smelled like rubber boots and old coffee, and Penelope had exactly forty minutes before the bus left, because Mr. Gill had promised the driver they would be gone by noon. Mr. Gill's worksheet was due on the bus, all five questions filled in, and question four was the one she could not answer: "What does this station preserve from its past, and how?" The tour had rushed past the modern trucks and stopped in the back room, where the guide had waved at a scarred wooden desk and a brass pole before hurrying off to answer someone's question about dalmatians.

Hayden reached out to run his hand along the desk's edge, the way you test a railing. "Don't," Nevaeh said, grabbing his sleeve. "Museums ask people not to touch stuff like this. Oils and salts from your skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces." Hayden pulled his hand back and wiped it on his jeans as if his fingers had already done something wrong. "It's just a desk," he muttered, but he kept his hands in his pockets after that.

Penelope looked at the desk more closely. One end of it was pale and dry, the way old untreated wood looks, but the other end, the end nearest the brass pole, had a dark, shiny patch the shape of a handprint, almost like it had been soaked. She thought about that. If oils and salts from skin built up over time, then the dark patch could be decades of firefighters grabbing that same corner while sliding down the pole, each hand leaving a little behind. It was like a pattern you could read backwards: the stain was the effect, and the hands were the hidden cause.

She decided to test it. The desk was off limits now that she knew the rule, but her own sunglasses in her pocket had a smudge she'd been wiping with her thumb all week. She breathed on the lens and looked at the light: a cloudy print exactly where her thumb always landed, faint but there, building. She had never once seen the oils leave her skin, yet there was proof on the glass. "Okay," she whispered, and Hayden asked what she was doing with her sunglasses in a dark fire station. "Proving something," she said.

She wrote her answer for question four: the station preserves the old desk and pole by keeping hands off them, because skin oils and salts build up over time and stain the surfaces, which is why the shiny patch near the pole looks the way it does. When Mr. Gill collected the worksheets on the bus, he read hers twice. "I've taken three classes here," he said, "and nobody ever noticed the handprint before." Nevaeh leaned over the seat. "Show me," she said, and Penelope turned around as the bus pulled out, pointing back toward the station doors.

Andrew spread the poster paper across Colton's kitchen table and weighted the corners with mugs from the cupboard. The sign-language club needed a banner for its booth at the school fair, and Colton had volunteered him because, as he put it, "You have neat handwriting and no other plans on a Saturday."

The design was easy: two hands, blue and gold, and the words JOIN THE SIGN LANGUAGE CLUB in big letters across the top. Andrew had gotten that far when Colton tapped the paper and pointed at the smaller line underneath, the one that read "Open to deaf students and everyone else." Colton wrote something in his notebook and turned it around: Should that d be capital?

Andrew stared at the word. Lowercase seemed right for an adjective, the way you'd write "tall students" or "new students." But Colton's question had a look behind it, like there was a trapdoor under the word and Colton knew exactly where it was. "Does it matter?" Andrew asked, and Colton grinned in a way that meant it absolutely mattered.

They raided Colton's bookshelf, which was stacked with books about sign language and Deaf history, and Andrew found a chapter that mentioned James Woodward. In 1972, Woodward had proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself. Andrew read it twice. So the little d described ears, and the big D described people who belonged to something, a whole culture built around a language, with its own schools and jokes and stories that Colton's family told at dinner with everyone laughing in signs.

Andrew tested his idea out loud. "So if the poster says the club is open to anyone, lowercase deaf covers the condition, but anyone who feels part of the culture can claim the big D." Colton thought about it, then nodded slowly, then shook his head and wrote: Make it capital. The club is about the culture, not about ears. Andrew got it. He had been thinking of deaf as a fact about a person's body, when Colton's club was really about a people.

Mr. Demir, the club's advisor, stopped by to drop off markers, and Andrew showed him the finished banner. "JOIN THE SIGN LANGUAGE CLUB," it read, "everyone welcome, Deaf and hearing." Mr. Demir, who never prescribed rules he could let students discover for themselves, only raised an eyebrow at the capital D and asked, "Whose motivation was that, capitalizing it?" Andrew pointed at Colton, and Colton pointed back at him. "Both of us," Andrew said. Mr. Demir smiled and said the change might be gradual for some people, but the poster looked ready to change a few minds in one afternoon. Andrew rolled up the banner, tucked it under his arm, and carried it out the door.

The waiting room of the eyeglasses store had a chart on the wall with rows of letters that shrank as they went down, and Sofia sat across from it while the optician flipped lenses in a frame that clamped onto her head like a bug. Her friend Lucille had sent her a text that morning: "Good luck. Also, did you finish the science homework? I only wrote two sentences about the extinction of the dinosaurs and Mr. Nwosu will notice." Sofia had typed back that she had written a whole paragraph and left out the part where she had copied half of it.

"Read the smallest line you can," the optician said.

"F, P, T, O, and then it gets fuzzy," Sofia said.

"Right eye, that's 20/40," the woman said, and wrote it on a card.

Sofia stared at the numbers. Lucille had told her once that her own vision was 20/20, and Sofia had assumed bigger numbers were better, the way a score of 40 beats a score of 20. Now she was not so sure, because nobody in the store looked impressed. She decided to test it. The chart hung on the wall and there were floor tiles, so she counted tiles to what she guessed was about 20 feet and stood there. At that distance the F and the P were clear, but when she walked forward to half that distance, they were just as clear and the next line down started to come into focus too. The letter she had been unable to read from across the room was easy up close. So the second number had something to do with how far away the letters were.

She walked back to the chair and asked the optician, "Does 20/40 mean I have to stand 20 feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from 40 feet?"

"That's exactly what it means," the woman said.

So the bigger number was worse, not better. Sofia paraphrased it in her head to make sure she had it: normal eyes read the line at double her distance, which meant her eyes were weaker, not stronger. She felt her ears go warm, because she had told Lucille last week that her eyes were probably better than everyone's. She pulled out her phone and texted: "Correction. 20/40 is not a good score. My eyes are the opposite of good. Also I will help you with the dinosaur thing."

The frame choices were on a spinning rack near the window. Sofia tried on a pair of black rectangles, then a pair of round wire ones that made her look like a substitute teacher. In the mirror, the price tags hung down over her cheeks, and each pair gave her a distinct reflection of the same face, one slightly squashed, one slightly wide. She picked the black rectangles because they stayed put when she shook her head.

The glasses would be ready in an hour, so she and her mother walked to the sandwich place next door. Through the window Sofia noticed that the sign across the street had words on it, actual words, not a gray smear with colored edges. She had been reading that street for years without knowing it was saying anything.

When she picked up the glasses and stepped outside, she stopped on the sidewalk and read the sign out loud. "Lucille," she said to her mother, pointing, "there's a Lucille in that sign. Lucille's Bakery. It's been there the whole time."

The score was tied in the fifth inning when Aubrey spotted Coach holding up three fingers toward the dugout, and she knew exactly what that meant. Kyan, their best pitcher, had only three pitches left. She bounced on the bench, cleats scraping the dirt, because if Kyan could hold the Pirates scoreless here at Riverside Park, the Rockets would take first place for the first time all season.

Kyan threw two fastballs and got two outs, then walked a batter on his last pitch. When he jogged to the bench, Coach met him with a hand on his shoulder. "That's your limit for today, and for the week. Sit down."

Kyan yanked off his cap. "I feel fine! My arm's not even sore." Aubrey watched Coach shake his head and walk away, and something about it bothered her. Kyan had only thrown, what, sixty pitches? She pulled out the scorebook and counted the tallies. Sixty-one. Last week he'd thrown fifty-eight, and the week before that, fifty-five. There was a pattern, and she wanted to know the rule behind it.

She remembered the fourth game of the season, back in April, when the Rockets had been getting crushed and Coach had refused to send Kyan back out for a second inning of relief. Leonardo had joked that a swarm of bees had somehow thwarted the plan, but Aubrey had noticed that Mr. Pérez, their neighbor, was at that game too, and he'd nodded like Coach had done the right thing. Mr. Pérez knew everything about baseball. He'd grown up playing near the old settlement fields on the other side of the creek, and he refereed adult leagues on weekends.

After the game, which the Rockets won 4-3 on a wild pitch, Aubrey found Mr. Pérez stacking coolers by the settlement trail. "Why does Kyan have a pitch count?" she asked. "He's not tired."

Mr. Pérez laughed. "It's not about being tired. Kids his age still have growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of the bones, and that cartilage is weaker than the bone around it. That's why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress. Throw too much, and the weakest part gives out."

"So the rule isn't about the arm being sore at all," Aubrey said slowly. "It's about a part nobody can see."

"That's it exactly," Mr. Pérez said.

On Saturday, Aubrey tested the idea. She brought the scorebook to practice and asked Kyan to help her chart every pitcher on the team, not just the totals but the days between outings. Leonardo joined in, waving an aerosol can of sunscreen over the charts and reading the label out loud. "Caution, flammable, keep away from open flame," he announced. "Which means don't set these on fire, in case anyone was planning to." He set it down and drew a smiley face next to Kyan's name.

By the end of practice the chart showed something real: the two players who pitched two games in a row had been rested for four days after, every time, without anyone saying why out loud. Coach saw the chart draped over the fence, and he tapped the paper with one finger.

"You figured out my rotation," he said.

"Growth plates," Aubrey said.

He grinned and pulled a whistle from his pocket. "Then you're my new scorekeeper. First job: tell Leonardo the sunflower seeds by the concession stand are for eating, not for juggling."

Leonardo caught the bag one-handed and held it up like a trophy. "Too late. Already juggling."

Harrison locked the bathroom door, set his cue cards on the edge of the sink, and faced the mirror. "When nicotine gets into the brain," he told his reflection, "it hijacks the reward pathway, the system that normally responds to food and other good things." His voice cracked on "pathway," so he tried again, slower. Ms. Tremblay had picked him to explain it to the class on Friday, and he was his own tutor until then, drilling in the one room where nobody would interrupt.

Except somebody was interrupting the whole house. His dad had quit smoking on Monday, and by Wednesday he was snapping at everything. That morning he had grumbled at the toaster, lost his keys twice, and snapped at Harrison's little sister for humming. He couldn't seem to focus on the grocery list. Harrison kept wondering: was that just a bad week, or was it connected to the quitting? He had a suspicion, but a suspicion wasn't proof. He needed to test it.

He spread his cue cards on the bathroom floor and made a list on the back of the "Withdrawal" card: grumpy, jumpy, forgetful, dying for a cigarette. Then he copied the same words onto a second card and carried it downstairs at dinner. He watched, not staring, just noticing. Dad fidgeted with his fork, forgot he'd already passed the peas, and got short with Mom about nothing. Every item, checked off, one by one. Harrison chewed a mouthful of rice slowly, letting it all digest while he watched.

He called Sidney after dinner. "You know how my dad's been grumpy all week? I think it's withdrawal. When a dependent person stops using nicotine, they can get irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating, and strong cravings." "Wait," Sidney said, "you mean he's not just in a mood?" "That's what I thought at first," Harrison said. "But it matches, all four things, and it started the day he quit." Archie, on three-way, chimed in. "So it's kind of voluntary, him quitting, but then the withdrawal isn't something he chooses?" "Exactly," Harrison said, surprised Archie had gotten there first.

On Friday, Harrison stood at the front of the class and explained the reward pathway, how nicotine trains the brain to demand more. Then he added, "And here's the part nobody tells you. My dad quit five days ago, and he's had irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating, and serious cravings all week. So if someone you know gets grumpy after quitting, it might not be about you." Ms. Tremblay raised her eyebrows and wrote something on her clipboard.

That afternoon, Harrison found his dad pacing the kitchen with unopened gum in his fist. "Ms. Tremblay says it gets easier after the first couple of weeks," Harrison said carefully. Dad looked at him for a long moment, then laughed, a real laugh, the first one all week. "You did a report on me?" "Sort of," Harrison said, and slid the gum across the counter toward him.

Jaxson slid his ruler across the paper and drew another line toward the dot in the middle of the page. That dot was the vanishing point, and every sidewalk edge, every roofline that ran away from him, had to aim straight at it. Ms. Bekele had promised that by the end of class everyone would have a street that looked like it went somewhere, and Jaxson wanted his to go somewhere amazing.

"I finished!" Alexa announced two desks over, holding up her drawing like a trophy. Then her face fell. "Wait. Why do my buildings look like they're falling over?"

Jaxson leaned over. Her street had shops, awnings, a mailbox, all slanting toward the dot. Every single line was tilted, even the fronts of the buildings that faced her squarely. The window tops pointed downhill. The doorframes leaned sideways. The whole block looked like it was sliding off the page.

He stared at it, and something clicked open in his memory. Last summer, before the perspective unit, he had tried to draw his grandmother's house from across the street. He'd slanted the porch roof, slanted the window frames, everything, and the house had come out wobbly too. He'd thrown that drawing away thinking he just had bad hands. Now he formulated a quick idea to test: maybe the fronts of buildings, the parts facing you directly, were different from the parts running away from you. He grabbed a scrap paper and drew a simple box front-on. The edges going back in depth slanted toward a dot. The edges across the front of the box? He kept those perfectly horizontal and vertical. The box sat solid on the page. He drew another, then a whole row, and none of them fell over.

"Try this," he said, spinning the scrap toward Alexa. "The lines on the front of the shop, the window tops and doorframes, keep them horizontal or vertical. Only the lines running away from you go to the dot."

Alexa erased her tilting fronts, redrew them straight across and straight up and down, and gasped. "It's a real street! Jaxson, it's a real street!"

"Trade secrets," Hendrik said gravely from the next row, "will cost you a seat at lunch."

"You can have two seats," Alexa said, already darkening her doorframe with a fresh ruler line, "if you tell nobody my first draft ever existed."

"First drafts like that are basically extinct," Jaxson said, "the moment the good one appears." He went back to his own street and drew his storefronts front-on, ruled them straight, and added a bicycle leaning against a doorframe that stood, at last, exactly upright.

Lincoln sat at the kitchen table wrapped in his grandmother's quilt, staring at the same glass of orange juice he had ignored for an hour. His throat felt like sandpaper, his nose was a faucet, and worst of all, tomorrow was the regional chess tournament, the one he had earned a spot in by beating Nikola twice in the qualifiers. His mom set a bowl of soup in front of him and felt his forehead with the back of her hand.

"Maybe Dr. Patel can call in antibiotics," Lincoln said, spooning steam toward his face. "Nikola got antibiotics last year when he was sick, and he was back at school in two days. If I got some today, I could still play tomorrow."

His mom tilted her head. "You want me to call and ask?"

"Please." He sneezed into a tissue, then added, "It's the tournament. Coach says it's a privilege to be seeded this high, and I don't want to waste it."

While his mom made the call in the hallway, Lincoln heard a knock. Nikola stood at the door holding a thermos and a paper bag, and behind him was Trystan, balancing a chessboard under one arm. They came in and crowded the kitchen, Nikola pouring hot lemon tea that smelled sharp and sweet.

"Nikola," Lincoln said, "when you took antibiotics, what did you actually have?"

"A strep throat," Nikola said. "Mr. Shin explained it to the whole science class afterward, actually. But wait, I thought you missed that day."

Lincoln's brain, foggy as it was, lurched into gear. Strep. He pulled his laptop across the table and typed, sniffling. Trystan leaned over his shoulder. The screen filled with the answer, and Lincoln read it out loud, his voice cracking. "Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they don't help cure a cold or the flu." He sat back. "Strep is bacteria. That's why Nikola got better fast. But this," he pointed at his own red nose, "is a virus. Antibiotics would do nothing. I could take the whole bottle and I'd still be sneezing through the tournament."

His mom came back in, phone in hand. "Dr. Patel said the same thing, honey. Rest and fluids."

Lincoln pushed the soup closer and took a spoonful. It burned pleasantly going down. He tested one small idea out loud, ticking it off. "So if it's a virus, my immune system does the work, and sleeping is basically my move. If I sleep all afternoon and all tonight, maybe I'm functional by nine a.m."

"Functional enough to lose to me in round two," Trystan said, setting up the board. "I registered as an alternate."

"You're infectious, you know," Nikola said, backing up a step and grinning.

Lincoln laughed, which turned into a cough, which turned into Nikola patting his back and sliding the tea closer. "Okay, board away, germ boy. We'll set up a video call tomorrow so you can watch us play."

"Round two," Trystan said, snapping a pawn onto the table, "is mine."

"We'll see," Lincoln croaked, and raised his spoon like a sword.

Peyton loved Saturdays at Grandma's house, mostly because nobody woke her up. She slept until noon, ate cold pizza on the porch, and texted Giselle about nothing in particular. But on Monday mornings back home, her body felt like a phone at two percent battery. Her stomach knotted up before she even got on the bus, and last week she'd nearly cried over a missing math worksheet. She couldn't see what was causing it, which was the part that bugged her most.

"I think you just hate Mondays," Giselle said when Peyton described it at lunch. "Everyone does. It's basically a law."

Peyton didn't dismiss the idea out loud, but she didn't buy it either. Jasleen was fine on Mondays, and Peyton hadn't hated Mondays back in September, when soccer practice had forced her to bed early every night. Something had changed since then. She started keeping a note in her phone: bedtime, wake time, and how her stomach felt before school. By Thursday she had a suspicion, but she needed more data.

That weekend she was back at Grandma's, who was sorting seed catalogs at the kitchen table. "Still planning your vegetable garden?" Peyton asked, picking up a catalog with a cover full of tomato photographs. Grandma nodded and said agriculture had been her whole childhood, waking before dawn to help on the farm, every day, no exceptions. "Even Sundays?" Peyton asked. Grandma laughed. "Especially Sundays. The cows didn't know what a weekend was."

That night Peyton lay in the guest room bed scrolling on her phone, and her stomach was already doing its tight little Monday rehearsal, even though Monday was two days away. She mentioned it to Jasleen on a video call, and Jasleen read something off a health website: keeping the same sleep and wake times every day, weekends included, kept the body steady. "It's called your circadian rhythm," Jasleen said, pronouncing it carefully. Peyton sat straight up. Same time every day. Like the cows. Like soccer season, when she'd gone to bed at ten and gotten up at seven, even after Saturday games, because her dad drove her to early practice. The knot in her stomach had never shown up back then.

So she ran a test on herself. Friday night at Grandma's, she set an alarm for 7:30, turned her phone face down at ten, and did the slow breathing thing Ms. Quinn had shown the whole class after the fire drill: in for four counts, out for six. When the tight feeling crept in, she breathed through it instead of scrolling past it. Saturday morning she woke up tired but not wrecked. Sunday she did it again, even though Grandma offered pancakes at nine and Peyton had already been awake for ninety minutes.

Monday morning, on the bus, Peyton filled in her phone note: stomach, calm; brain, awake. It might be temporary, she knew, one good day out of many bad ones. But she'd already decided. Next Saturday at Grandma's, the alarm was staying on.

"Seven-thirty again?" Giselle texted her that afternoon.

Peyton typed back, "Same time every day. Even weekends."

Brody set his toast crust on the counter on purpose, the way he had every morning that week, and then walked to the doorway and counted to sixty. When he came back, the crust was gone. He had done this four times now, and every time the crust disappeared.

His hypothesis, which he had written on a napkin and taped inside the cupboard door, was that the dog ate it. The problem was that he could not actually see the dog do it. The dog, a small brown mutt named Patches, was shut in the laundry room every morning until Brody's mother left for work, and the crust vanished anyway. So the dog was out. That was the only thing he knew for sure.

He texted his friend Xavier about it after school.

Xavier wrote back: "this is like the swan thing mr joshi put on the board. No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false."

Brody read the message twice, then typed: "so if i watch the crust a hundred times and don't see who takes it, that proves nothing. but if i catch the thief once, i know for sure it wasn't the dog."

"exactly," Xavier wrote. "also you should get a sophisticated trap. flour everywhere. my brother did that for the cookie thief. it was me. i have the face of a criminal on camera."

Brody skipped the flour. Instead, the next morning he set out the crust and stood very still at the far end of the kitchen, next to the fridge, where the counter met the wall in a shadow. He held his phone up like he was checking the time. He waited. Four minutes. Five.

The cupboard under the sink, the one with the gap where the pipe went through the wall, made a small scratching sound. Then a gray mouse came out, walked along the baseboard, stood up on its hind legs at the corner of the counter, and dragged the crust down off the edge. It disappeared behind the toaster with the whole thing.

Brody lowered the phone. He crossed "dog" off the napkin and wrote "mouse" above it. Then he thought about Xavier's message again. He went back and added, at the bottom, "one crust still there would prove dog wrong. one mouse proves dog wrong. a hundred missing crusts prove nothing."

At dinner he told his mother the verdict, and she said they would get traps. Patches, let out of the laundry room, came over and put his chin on Brody's knee.

"Sorry, buddy," Brody said. "Not you this time." He slipped him a piece of crust anyway.

Piper laid her supplies across the kitchen table: a roll of paper towels, a box of baking soda, a bottle of vinegar, a carton of milk, and two small stacks of paper strips she had cut herself, red and blue. Ms. Gagnon had assigned the whole class a pH project for the science fair, and Piper had volunteered to build the booth because she wanted the blue ribbon more than she had wanted anything all year.

Then she found the note tucked inside the box of baking soda. It was from her friend Izabella, who had taken the supplies home the night before to help cut the strips. "Piper," it read, "my little brother got into the kitchen while I was working. I think he mixed up the strips. Some of the red ones and blue ones might have switched stacks. Sorry! Also my family is helping our new neighbours, who are refugees from Syria, so I might be late tomorrow." Piper stared at the two stacks. If the strips were mixed up, her whole demonstration would be wrong in front of everyone.

She sat down and thought. She could not see any difference between the strips just by looking, but there had to be a way to find out what each one was. Then she remembered the one thing she knew for certain: everyone in the class had been unanimous about vinegar during practice. It was an acid. If she dipped a strip in vinegar and it turned red, that strip was the blue kind, because that was the test: blue litmus paper turns red when dipped in an acid, and red litmus paper turns blue when dipped in a base.

She grabbed a strip from the "blue" stack and dunked it in a saucer of vinegar. Nothing happened. It stayed red. So that strip was actually a red one, mixed into the wrong pile. She tested another, and it turned red the moment it touched the liquid, which meant it was truly blue. Strip by strip, she sorted them, dipping and checking, building two honest stacks. Then she tried baking soda mixed with water, and a true red strip turned blue right before her eyes.

When Izabella arrived the next morning, Piper emphasized the pile of tested strips with both hands. "Every single one is sorted," she said. "Your brother actually helped. I understand the whole thing now, and I couldn't say that yesterday." Izabella laughed and hugged her.

At the science fair, a judge stopped at Piper's booth and dipped the blue strip into the vinegar herself. It turned red, clean and bright as a tiny flag.

Julia slid the giant paper periodic table across the lab table and pinned the corner with her elbow before it could curl up again. Mr. Bui had promised that anyone who could correctly find the number of protons in five elements of his choosing would get to run the demo at the front of the room on Friday, and Julia wanted that more than she had wanted anything that week. The rule seemed simple: the atomic number up top of each box told you the protons. Sodium, eleven. Oxygen, eight. She felt almost smug.

Then Mr. Bui's scavenger hunt sheet said "iron," and Julia's whole plan fell apart. She ran her finger down the columns looking for an I. There was iodine, already claiming the symbol I, and there was iridium, smugly wearing Ir, but no iron anywhere. Ember leaned over from the next table, holding her own sheet. "I'm stuck on iron too," she said. "And if I don't finish this, I can't be your partner for the demo, and I already told my little brother I'd bring home the vinegar-and-baking-soda volcano trick." That was Ember's want, and Julia took it as seriously as her own. "Then we collaborate," Julia said. "You take the left side of the table, I take the right, and we look for anything that could mean iron."

Ananya, organizing the beakers at the supply shelf, called over without turning around. "Are you two hunting for iron? Because I found something last night that will make you feel like a peasant who just discovered electricity." She walked over waving a folded note she had written to herself in the margin of her notebook, and Julia read it aloud: "Dear future Ananya, iron is Fe. Not I. It comes from the Latin word ferrum. Signed, present Ananya, who was also confused." Julia laughed and went back to the table.

She found the box labeled Fe, and there it was, atomic number 26. Twenty-six protons, hidden inside every atom of a metal she could see in the door hinge, the chair legs, the fence outside. She tested her idea on another row to make sure the pattern held: gold, Au, also Latin, 79. Silver, Ag, 47. Copper, Cu, 29. Each symbol sat in its box like a nickname with a story behind it, and the number above it kept its promise every time.

By Friday Julia and Ember stood at the front table, filling a bottle while the class counted down. "Twenty-six protons," Ember announced, holding up the steel wool, "in every single strand of this." Julia struck the match, and the wool bloomed into a small, bright, coherent glow that made the whole second row lean forward in their seats.

The trail climbed through pines until Ms. Whitehead called a rest stop at a granite outcrop, and Layla dropped her pack with a thud. Inside it, rolled tight, were two graphs she'd printed at the library: one for the Sahara, one for the Amazon. Her project was due Monday, and she still couldn't answer the question Ms. Whitehead had written at the top of the assignment sheet. Compare the climates. Explain what makes them different, and why.

The graphs themselves were easy. The desert's rainfall bars were stubs, barely visible except one slightly taller bar in a single month. The rainforest's bars climbed like a wall. The temperature lines told the other half: the desert line zigzagged between scorching days and cold nights, while the rainforest line ran flat and warm, month after month. Layla knew all that. What she didn't know was why. Rainforests huddled near the equator, sure. But deserts weren't at the equator, and they weren't scattered randomly either. She'd noticed something on the classroom globe last week, and she kept turning it over in her mind.

She had stayed late on Tuesday, spinning the globe slowly with one finger while the janitor worked down the hall. The Sahara. Then, below the equator, the Kalahari and the Australian deserts. Then Arabia, and the Atacama on the west coast of South America. She'd grabbed a sticky note and marked them, then stood back. The marks made two belts, one north of the equator and one south, and both belts sat at about the same distance from the middle of the globe. She'd folded the sticky note into her pocket without telling anyone, in case she was wrong.

"Earth to Layla," Conor said, sitting down beside her. He had his binoculars around his neck, the way he'd had them all morning, because he wanted a photo of a pileated woodpecker before lunch. He'd been planning this hike for two weeks and had told her twice that it was not a trivial goal, it was the whole point of walking six kilometres. "You're staring at paper like it owes you money."

"Look at this globe app," she said, pulling out her phone. She opened the map and traced the big deserts with her fingertip. "Tell me what you see."

Conor squinted. "Sand. Lots of sand."

"No, look at where they are. All of them." She waited, letting him find it the way she had, and for a moment nobody spoke. Somewhere downslope, water dripped off a ledge, steady as rain.

"They line up," Conor said slowly. "In two bands."

Layla checked the map's latitude scale with her thumb, the way she'd checked the globe. "About thirty degrees north, and thirty degrees south. That's where they sit." She thought of the graph in her pack, the stubby rainfall bars. It fit, and fitting it made the back of her neck prickle. "Ms. Whitehead said one thing I wrote down. Where air sinks in those belts, it warms up and dries out. So the rain never comes." She said it out loud for the first time, testing it, and it held.

Ms. Whitehead, who had been inspecting the trail register by the old lodge, called back to them that the park service planned to renovate the building next summer, and then asked what they were studying so intently. "Whether that dry-belt thing is a real phenomenon or a coincidence," Layla said. "I'm going to test it tonight. I'll pick three deserts I didn't mark before and check their latitudes on the map."

"If they're all near thirty," Conor said, standing up, binoculars rising, "you've got your answer."

Behind him, a red-crested bird hammered at a dead pine, and Conor spun toward it so fast he nearly fell off the outcrop.

Gabriel stood in front of the washing machine with his mother's laundry basket and a feeling that this should be simpler than it looked. His mom had left for a work trip, and he had promised to handle his own clothes for the week. The basket held a tangle of jeans, socks, towels and one striped shirt that had gone grey in a way he hated.

He dumped everything on the laundry room floor and began making piles, darks in one heap, whites and lights in another, towels in a third, because towels shed fuzz onto everything and he was tired of fuzzy shirts. Sydney, who lived two houses down, had wandered over and sat on the dryer eating an apple. "You're doing it wrong," Sydney said, which was not helpful.

"Then show me right," Gabriel said. Sydney only shrugged and kept chewing.

The problem was the striped shirt. It was mostly white, so it belonged with the lights, but the stripes had faded and the whole thing looked dingy. Gabriel remembered the jug of bleach under the sink, the one his mom used on the white towels. He reached for it, then paused. Last summer a red sock had turned the whole load pink, and that disaster had been only temporary compared to what bleach might do. He turned the shirt inside out and hunted along the seam until he found the care label.

There were little symbols on it. A tub of water, a square with a circle, and two triangles. On his grey sweatpants the label showed an empty triangle. On the striped shirt, the triangle had a bold cross through it, like a tiny no-entry sign.

"That one's crossed out," Sydney said, leaning over his shoulder. "That means no bleach."

"So the empty one means bleach is okay?" Gabriel asked. He checked the white towel's label. Empty triangle. He checked the sweatpants again. Empty triangle. Every single thing that had ever gone in the bleach load had the plain triangle, and the striped shirt had the crossed one. That was a pattern, and patterns meant something.

He set the striped shirt aside, washed the towels with bleach, and ran the lights in plain detergent. When the loads finished, he folded everything into squares that were only slightly crooked, and hung the striped shirt in the sun by the window because the internet said sunlight brightens whites. By afternoon the stripes looked whiter, though the shirt still carried a faint smell like a damp fungus from the basement, so he washed it a second time.

When his mother called that night, Gabriel held up the phone to show her the folded stacks. "Look," he said. "The striped one's clean and the towels are bright. And I learned the triangle code."

Natalie pushed the cart of canned beans down the basement hallway of the public library, where the food bank had its shelves. She had volunteered once a week for a whole month now, and she had learned the system: pasta on the left, soup in the middle, cereal up top. Ms. Sharma, the librarian who ran the whole thing, had one rule that seemed completely arbitrary to Natalie, that every last can of soup had to face label-forward, even the dented ones. "It makes the shelves look full," Ms. Sharma had said. "People deserve full."

The problem started on a Tuesday, when Natalie counted the oatmeal canisters and came up three short. She had counted them herself on Saturday. Nobody had signed out any boxes since then. On Thursday, four more canisters were gone, and a bag of rice too, and still the sign-out sheet stayed blank. She told Ariella, who shelved books upstairs between visits. "That's weird," Ariella said. "But my mom says when stuff disappears at the pool, it's usually the staff, not the swimmers."

Natalie didn't want to believe that. It would imply that Ms. Sharma, who arranged story hour and taped up posters about kindness, was walking food out the side door. But the pattern pointed somewhere. The missing food was always the same kind: quick, kid-friendly stuff, oatmeal and rice and macaroni. Nobody steals randomly like that, Natalie thought. Random would be soup and beans too. Someone was choosing.

On Saturday she came early, before the library opened, and sat on the stairs with a granola bar, watching the side door through the railings. The basement was dim. Somewhere a heater ticked. She waited so long her legs went numb, and she was about to give up when the door opened and Ms. Sharma came through it, carrying two canvas bags, heavy ones, handles stretched tight. Natalie's stomach dropped. She followed, quietly, up the ramp and past the returns desk, and out into the morning.

Ms. Sharma didn't get in a car. She walked three blocks to a house with a folded wheelchair ramp and knocked, and a boy from Natalie's grade, the one who had been out sick for weeks, opened the door. His arm was in a cast from a bad cut that had gotten infected, and his mother was working doubles. Ms. Sharma handed over the bags and said, "I didn't put it on the sheet because it's nobody's business."

Back in the break room later, Natalie stared at the poster on the wall while she ate her lunch. She had read it a hundred times but never really looked: the first food bank was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, started in 1967 by a man named John van Hengel. One person, one city, and now there were shelves of food in a library basement in a town he'd never seen.

She got up, found Ms. Sharma, and said, "The oatmeal. I know. I won't write it down either." Ms. Sharma looked at her for a long moment. "Then grab a cart," she said, "because we're three blocks short on Tuesday."

The bakery smelled like warm butter, and Zoey stood at the counter trying to remember every French word her family had crammed on the plane. Her mother wanted a baguette, her father wanted coffee, and Zoey wanted to order by herself, in French, without her voice going all volatile and squeaky the way it did when she was nervous.

The baker asked her something that ended in "âge?" and Zoey understood enough to know he was asking how old she was. She had prepared for this. Sort of. "Je suis douze ans," she said, proud of herself, because je suis meant I am and douze meant twelve. The baker shook his head, so she tried again, louder, as if volume were the problem. Behind her in the line, a boy about her age cleared his throat.

"J'ai douze ans," he said. His name turned out to be Gregoire, and his English was better than her French by roughly the ratio of a lake to a puddle. "In French, you say I have twelve years. J'ai, not je suis."

"But in English it's I am twelve," Zoey said, and then she stopped, because she could feel the shape of a rule hiding underneath the difference, something she couldn't see directly but could test. "So what about my family? I have a sister. J'ai une soeur?" Gregoire nodded. "And I have a dog. J'ai un chien?" He nodded again, and Zoey grinned so wide the baker laughed. "So you use avoir for everything you have, and that includes your years. Your age is a thing you own."

They moved to a small table by the window while the coffee brewed. Gregoire pointed at a family photo on the wall, three generations of bakers, and Zoey tried to depict them in full sentences: "Il a soixante ans. Elle a un chien blanc. Ils ont quatre enfants." Each one came out a little smoother than the last. When she stumbled, she wrote the phrase in her notebook, the one her teacher Mr. Qureshi had told her to carry everywhere, and when her parents finally claimed their coffee, her page was nearly full.

"Il a un chat," Gregoire said suddenly, pointing at the doorway, where an orange cat had wandered in and settled on a flour sack like it paid rent.

Zoey laughed. "Il a neuf ans," she said, "et il a beaucoup de pain." The cat blinked at her, completely unbothered, and the baker slid a free croissant across the counter.

Jacob stood in the wings of the community theatre, holding a rubber chicken like it was a gold trophy. Mr. Popal's improv workshop had seemed easy when Jacob signed up with Callan and John, but now the stage looked enormous under the lights.

"All you do," Mr. Popal announced, "is take the stage with a partner and build a scene. Ready? Jacob and Callan, you're up."

Callan began brilliantly. He gripped an invisible wheel and shouted, "Look out, Captain, a storm's coming and the cargo's sliding!"

Jacob's mind went white. "What cargo? We're not on a boat," he said. "We're in the kitchen."

The audience went quiet. Callan's hands dropped from the wheel, and he stood there with nothing to say, because there was no wheel and no storm and no kitchen either, really. After five endless seconds, Mr. Popal called time. Jacob jogged offstage feeling like he'd knocked over a birthday cake.

"That was blocking," Callan said as they sat on the steps by the prop table. "You said no to the boat."

"I panicked," Jacob admitted. But his brain was already turning. So the scene had died because he'd rejected Callan's offer. If he'd said yes instead, and added something, the scene would have kept rolling. It was like a rule hiding under the game, invisible until you broke it. He turned the idea over, testing it against what he'd watched. When John and a girl had done a bit about selling a haunted toaster, they'd both said yes to everything, even the ghost, and the audience had laughed until the girl snorted. Nobody had gone quiet then.

"I want to try again," Jacob told Mr. Popal at the break. "With John."

Mr. Popal raised an eyebrow. "Bold. Fine."

This time John started. "Sir, I regret to inform you that you have not paid your mortgage, and the bank is sending me, a bank wizard, to collect."

Jacob almost laughed. His whole body wanted to say, that's ridiculous, there's no such thing as a bank wizard. Instead he grabbed an imaginary letter from John's outstretched hand. "I see. Then I shall pay you in enchanted coins, each one worth a thousand mortgages." He elaborated on the spot, stacking invisible coin after coin into John's arms until John staggered under the pretend weight.

"The coins are floating!" John cried. "The bank wizard's spell has gone wrong!"

"Then we're both rich and falling upward," Jacob declared, and the audience roared.

When they came offstage, Callan punched his shoulder. "See? Yes, and."

Jacob grinned and looked back at the lit stage, where Mr. Popal was already waving them over. "That," Jacob said, "was ironic. The best scene of my life was about a mortgage."

Declan's mother had one rule for bring-your-kid-to-work day: stay out of the way. He was doing fine at that until the office printer jammed, and then, while he waited for the repairman, he noticed her screen.

She had a spreadsheet full of numbers, a column of sales for every week of the quarter, and she was adding them by hand. On a calculator. He watched her type a number, press plus, type another, press plus again, all the way down column B, and his fingers itched.

"You know the computer can do that," he said.

"It can?"

"Vihaan showed me once. There's a formula." He leaned over her keyboard, typed =SUM(B2:B10) into the empty cell under her numbers, and pressed Enter. The total appeared instantly, and his mother laughed out loud. "Declan, do you know how many hours I've spent on that calculator?"

He felt tall as anything. Then she ruined it by pointing at the next column over. "Can you do that one too?"

Column C. Then column D. Then E, F and G, all the way across the quarter. Eleven more columns, and he only knew one formula. He remembered Vihaan saying something once about the formula knowing where it was, but he couldn't recall the details, and the repairman was still wrestling with the printer behind them, so Vihaan couldn't be messaged quietly. He tried typing =SUM(B2:B10) into the cell under column C and the total was wrong. Too small. The spreadsheet was totaling column B again, sitting under column C like a liar.

That's when he thought of the copy command. Vihaan had said the formula shifts when it moves. Declan didn't trust it, though. A formula was invisible; you couldn't watch it change the way you could watch a printer repairman yank a crumpled page free. So he decided to test it in a place where it couldn't hurt anything. He copied the cell from under column B, clicked the empty cell under column C, pasted, and clicked into the cell to look.

The formula had changed by itself. It read =SUM(C2:C10). He checked the total against the column above it and it matched. He pasted the same copied cell across the whole row, under every column, and one by one, every week's total appeared, correct, like the spreadsheet was reading his mind.

Later, when the repairman left and Mr. De Vries from the next desk came over to see what the commotion was, Declan showed him the whole trick, the formula, the copy, the chart he'd built from the totals with blue bars for every week. Mr. De Vries was quiet for a moment.

"Could you do that to my numbers?" he asked, pulling out his chair. "They're in a monstrous file. It might compress my week from two days to about ten minutes."

Declan rolled Mr. De Vries's chair over, sat down, and typed.

John flattened the wrinkled poster against the gymnasium table and weighed its corners down with beakers he wasn't supposed to touch. The periodic table printed across it had smudged in his backpack, and three atomic numbers had turned into gray blobs. His whole project, the one that was supposed to save him from a failing grade in science, depended on those numbers.

"You're still fixing that?" Cleo whispered from the next table, where her volcano sat polished and perfect. She wanted the blue ribbon so badly she had practiced her speech on the bus twice that morning. "Judging starts in ten minutes, John."

"I know," he said. He had written quiz questions for the judges, and the third one was ruined. The question asked how many neutrons a certain atom had, and the answer had to come from the poster, but the atomic number had vanished into a smudge. He stared at the grid of squares. He knew the mass number for his element, carbon, sat at the top of the box, a twelve. He had copied that part down last night at his grandmother's kitchen table, along with something she had read aloud from her old textbook: the atomic number counts protons.

A judge in a gray sweater was already drifting toward Cleo's table. Ms. Tran, his science teacher, stood near the door, watching him the way she did when she expected him to quit. John wiped his palms on his jeans. His practice sheet from last night was folded in his pocket, and he pulled it out, hoping the missing number was somewhere in his own handwriting. It wasn't. There was only the twelve, and next to it, the number of protons he'd worked out then, six, because the atomic number was six.

He stopped. Six protons, twelve for the mass number. He mouthed the math. Twelve take away six. If the mass number counted protons plus neutrons, then whatever was left over had to be the neutrons. His pencil hovered. Six. He tested the idea on another element from memory, oxygen, mass number sixteen, atomic number eight, and again the leftover made sense: eight neutrons. It wasn't random guessing; it worked twice, the same rule both times, like a pattern hiding behind the numbers.

"Next table," the judge called, and suddenly he was standing in front of John.

John pointed at the smudged square. "Carbon has six protons," he said, "and its mass number is twelve, so subtracting the atomic number from the mass number gives six neutrons." The judge raised an eyebrow, wrote something on her clipboard, and slid the sheet aside. "Show me on another element," she said.

John's finger moved down the poster and stopped on nitrogen. "Fifteen minus seven."

Grandpa's dining room table had become a science lab, and Austin was the scientist who had no idea what he was doing. Spread in front of him were two printed graphs for Ms. Gill's assignment: one showing monthly rainfall and temperature for the Sonoran Desert, the other for a rainforest in Brazil. His job was to compare the two climates, and his pencil hovered over the paper without writing anything.

"I need this to be interesting," Austin muttered, "because right now it's just squiggles."

His cousin Adele slid into the chair across from him, balancing a bowl of popcorn. Adele wanted one thing from the afternoon: to be entertained. "Then make it interesting," she said. "What do the squiggles say?"

"The desert gets almost no rain, and the rainforest gets tons of it. That part's easy." Austin tapped the temperature lines. "But here's the weird part. The desert graph swings from blazing hot months to freezing cold months. The rainforest graph barely moves. Warmest month, coolest month, it's all about the same."

"Sounds boring," Adele said, tossing a kernel at him. "Same temperature forever."

"It's not boring, it's..." Austin stopped. He leaned closer to the rainforest graph. Grandpa, drying dishes at the sink behind them, glanced over but said nothing. Austin flipped through his library book on rainforests and found a chart of hourly temperatures at a weather station. His eyes went down the column, and then he sat back like he'd been poked.

"Adele. Look at this. The days get hot and the nights get cool, right there in the numbers." He grabbed his pencil and circled the day's high and the night's low. Then he circled the warmest month and the coolest month on the other graph and compared the gaps. "The swing between day and night is bigger than the swing between the warmest and coolest months. Way bigger."

"So?" Adele said, stealing her own popcorn back.

"So if somebody was packing for the rainforest, they'd think, it's hot every month, I only need shorts. But the nights are cool. They'd need a sweater. In a rainforest." He laughed. "Ms. Gill is going to think I made this up."

"It does sound made up," Adele admitted. "Show me again."

Austin walked her through it line by line, testing his idea against both graphs to be sure he wasn't fooling himself. It seemed logical, but he'd been wrong before, like the time he'd sworn hail was frozen rain and Ms. Gill had gently proved otherwise in front of the whole class. He checked the book a second time, then a third. The numbers held.

"Fine," Adele said, pointing at his blank worksheet, where despair had been about to set in five minutes ago. "Write it down before you forget it. And draw a little person in a sweater."

"That's not scientific."

"I'll mediate," Grandpa said from the sink, without turning around. "One small sweater person, in the name of science."

Austin grinned and picked up his pencil.

Declan had planned to finish his climate project at home, in a house with air conditioning and a printer. Instead his grandfather had collected him from the airport and driven him to a place where the mailbox leaned like it was tired, and now the project had to happen here, in a kitchen in the Arizona desert, over a laptop that connected to the internet when it felt like it.

The assignment asked him to compare a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs. His friend Emy-Rose had the easy half. Her grandmother lived in Hilo, Hawaii, and Emy-Rose had already texted him a photo of her rain gauge with water in it, plus the smug caption "day one." Declan's grandfather owned no rain gauge. What he owned was a cactus, a watering can, and a patio that looked like the surface of a planet that had given up.

Declan started with the graphs. He printed them at the library in town: monthly rainfall bars for a hot desert and for a rainforest, and two temperature lines that both ran high. He laid them side by side on the kitchen table and tried to evaluate what he was seeing. The rainforest bars towered over the desert bars, which was almost embarrassing, since some of the desert bars were so short he had to squint to confirm they existed. He found the median monthly rainfall for each place, and the rainforest number was so much larger that he checked it twice, in case the library printer had made a typo.

The temperature lines were the part that bugged him. Both places were hot. If heat meant dryness, the rainforest should have been dry too, and it plainly was not, judging by Emy-Rose's photo of a puddle in her grandmother's driveway that had lasted three days. He needed a way to test the difference, and the laptop kept buffering, so the internet was not going to be influential in his thinking today. He went outside with a measuring cup and poured exactly one cup of water onto the flat concrete beside the patio, marking the puddle's edge with two pebbles.

Then he did what any scientist stuck in a desert does. He sat in a lawn chair and watched water do nothing. By ten o'clock the puddle had shrunk to a dark ring. By eleven the ring was gone, and the concrete was the same pale gray as everywhere else, and the sun was still climbing. He poured a second cup in the shade of the barbecue, out of some sense of fairness. That puddle lasted longer, but even it surrendered before lunch.

He called Emy-Rose that afternoon. "Question," he said. "The sun and dry air at my grandpa's could evaporate way more water in a year than falls as rain here. Like, a puddle I made this morning was gone before lunch. Is your puddle still there?"

"It's been there since Tuesday," Emy-Rose said. "Grandma says it's practically a pond now."

"So that's the whole difference," Declan said. "It's not just how much rain falls. It's how much the sky takes back." He wrote it at the top of his poster in marker, then drew the desert puddle as a ghost with an exit arrow.

That evening his grandfather came out with two glasses of lemonade, looked at the poster, and looked at the dry patio.

"Learn something today?" his grandfather asked.

"Learned you can't keep a puddle in this yard," Declan said, and taped the last graph down before the wind could evaluate it for him.

Alice sat down at Ryerson's piano with the sheet music for "Moonlight Jig" in front of her. She had been practicing the piece for two weeks, and today was the last rehearsal before the school talent show. A stuffed koala grinned at her from the top of the piano, and she gave its grey marsupial face a pat for luck. "Ready?" she asked. Ryerson nodded and lifted the lid of the percussion box he kept beside the bench.

The first half went well. Alice's fingers found the bouncy opening, and Ryerson tapped the tambourine right on the beat, his wrist flicking in time with hers. Then they reached the middle, where the marking "rit." appeared above the staff. Alice slowed down, letting each note stretch out like taffy, and Ryerson followed her. It sounded beautiful, she thought, dreamy and strange. But when the next section began, something felt wrong. Ryerson's tambourine had gone quiet, and when she glanced over, his hand was hovering in midair, waiting.

"You're still slow," he said. "The whole last page is dragging." Alice frowned at the music. She played the passage again and listened hard. He was right. The slow feeling from the rit. had followed her all the way to the end, like mud stuck to her shoes. She bent closer to the page, wondering if there was a clue she had missed. There, printed small above the bar where the dreamy part ended, were two words: "a tempo." She traced them with her finger. "Rit." had told her to slow down. Did "a tempo" tell her something about speed too?

She tested a simple idea. "Play the opening speed," she said to Ryerson, "just the counting, nothing else." He clapped the original beat, quick and bright, and she matched her hands to his claps. Then she played from the "a tempo" marking forward while he kept time, and the melody sprang back to life, bouncing the way it had at the start. "That's it," she said. "A tempo means go back to the original speed after you've slowed down." Ryerson grinned and shook the koala at her like a maraca.

They ran the whole piece once more, and this time when the rit. came, Alice let the notes wander slow and soft, then snapped the speed back exactly where the marking told her to. The change matched the feel of the music, the way a heartbeat corresponds to what a body is doing, fast when it runs and calm when it rests. Ryerson's tambourine came in clean and sure, and by the final chord they were both laughing. Ms. Ramírez, who had come to pick up her nephew next door, stopped on the porch and applauded through the window. "Again," Ryerson said, tapping the tambourine against his palm. "From the top."

Julia crouched at the end of the hallway with a stopwatch in one hand and a marble in the other. Behind her, her dad held one end of a wooden board propped on a stack of dictionaries, making a steep little hill. The plan was simple: roll the marble down, time it, measure how far it went, and turn the numbers into a distance-time graph for Monday's lab report. Her teacher, Ms. Owusu, had been strict about enforcing the rule that every graph needed real measurements, not guesses, and Julia intended to follow it.

"Ready," she called. Her dad let go, the marble flashed down the board and shot across the floor, and Julia stabbed the button far too late. "Zero point two seconds? That can't be right." They tried again, and again, and every time the marble reached the wall before her thumb could catch up. On the fourth attempt she didn't even press the button. She sat back on her heels and groaned.

Amina's face appeared on the tablet screen, propped against the baseboard. She was supposed to be doing the same experiment in her own kitchen, and she wanted their graphs to match so their group could have the best data in the class. "Same problem here," Amina said. "My ball is faster than my thumb. Maybe we should just make up numbers that look nice."

"We can't," Julia said. "Ms. Owusu wants an objective measurement, something that doesn't depend on us deciding what it should be." She picked up the marble and turned it over in her fingers, thinking. Fast was the enemy. If the ball moved slower, she could actually time it. But how did you slow down a rolling ball without touching it? She looked at the board. The steeper the hill, the faster the marble flew. So a gentler slope might mean a gentler speed. "Dad, take away half the dictionaries."

He raised an eyebrow but lifted the stack down until the board lay at a low slant, more of a whisper than a hill. Julia marked the floor with masking tape every thirty centimeters, the way Ms. Owusu had shown them, and set the marble at the top. When her dad released it, the marble crept down the ramp and rolled along the tiles at a pace she could actually watch. She clicked the stopwatch at each strip of tape, calling out, "One! Two! Three!" while Amina scribbled the times on her own sheet of paper, miles away but shouting them back anyway.

They ran it three times to be sure, and the numbers came out almost the same every trial. Julia plotted them on graph paper, distance going up one side, time going along the bottom, and the dots fell into a nearly straight line climbing from the corner. She stared at it. She had expected a wobbly scatter, but the points behaved like they were following a rule she couldn't see, some hidden law of rolling things that only showed up on paper.

Then her dad leaned over her shoulder. "You know, you're not the first person to try this trick. Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, because the ramps slowed the motion enough for him to time it." Julia sat back, amazed that a scientist from centuries ago had faced the exact same problem in the exact same way, without stopwatches or masking tape or a video call.

"Then we did it right," Amina said through the speaker. "Send me a picture of that graph before my dad confiscates my tablet for the night. He claims my science homework is bad for his beauty sleep, which is basically a crime against commerce, since I'm his daughter and he should be investing in me."

Julia laughed and photographed the graph, the line of dots marching upward like a staircase. "Best data in the class," she said, and taped the graph to the refrigerator door, right at eye level, where nobody walking past could miss it.

Cooper leaned over the counter at the pet store while the cashier lifted a wriggling beagle puppy into his arms. "His name's yours to pick," she said. Cooper had already decided on Biscuit, because the puppy was the exact color of one. Moses and Philemon crowded in beside him, arguing about whether Biscuit would sleep in a crate or a dog bed, and Mr. Traoré, who had driven them all here, checked his watch for the third time.

At home, Cooper set up the water bowl, the food dish, and the puppy's bed in the corner of his room. Biscuit explored everything, sneezed at the cedar shavings, and then disappeared under the desk. Cooper got down on his knees to look. Curious thing: the puppy wasn't just wandering. He kept returning to sniff one spot, Cooper's backpack, which lay on the floor with its flap partway open.

"Hey," Cooper said to himself. What was in there that smelled so interesting? He emptied the backpack onto his bed. Pencils, a crumpled worksheet, three gum wrappers, and a strip of sugar-free gum, still in its foil, half pushed out of the pack. Cooper picked it up and turned it toward the window, squinting at the tiny ingredients like he was looking through a magnifying lens. He saw the word xylitol, printed small. He'd read the label at the store out of boredom while his mom paid, and something about it had stuck: xylitol, a sweetener in some sugar-free gum and candy, makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar.

He wondered whether one strip could really matter. He couldn't see inside Biscuit's body, couldn't watch insulin or blood sugar doing anything, so how would he even know? Maybe the puppy seemed fine now, but maybe the trouble came later. Cooper decided not to guess. First he would verify that Biscuit hadn't already eaten any. He checked the wrappers: all three were old ones from his own pocket, dry and flattened, no tooth marks. The foil strip was whole and sealed. Then, to be sure, he counted the pieces left in the pack and counted them again an hour later. Same number.

"I'm not taking chances anyway," he told Moses on the phone that night. "Xylitol," Moses repeated, like the word tasted strange. "That stuff is in candy too, not just gum. My aunt says her dog isn't immune to any of it, even the tiny amounts." Cooper carried the gum downstairs and handed it to his dad, who dropped it in the outside trash can and clamped the lid down.

Biscuit slept in a heap on the new bed after all, one ear flopped over his nose. Cooper knelt beside him and watched the puppy's ribs rise and fall, slow and steady, and he made a mental list of everything else he'd check tomorrow: the candy dish on the coffee table, the granola bars in his lunchbox, the pockets of his jacket. Biscuit's tail thumped once against the cushion, even in his sleep.

The health elective at Camp Windrow ended with each camper teaching a five-minute lesson on the stage, and Ava had drawn the hardest topic in the jar: how nicotine hooks the brain. She understood the reward pathway well enough to draw it, dopamine sliding into receptors like a key into a lock. What she could not figure out was why her uncle kept saying his vaping habit used to be one pod a week and was now three. If nicotine worked the same way every time, the amount should stay the same.

She spread her poster on the picnic table while Cedar painted arrows and Nahla arranged red buttons for the dopamine. "The brain adapts," Nahla read off Ava's messy notes from the pharmacy trip last weekend, when they had walked to town for sunscreen. "That's what the pharmacist told you?" Ava nodded. She had asked about her uncle, and the pharmacist had said that with regular use, the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect. Then Ava had asked what that was called, and the pharmacist had smiled and said one word: "Tolerance." That word had been sitting in her pocket all week like a stone.

"But how do I show it?" Ava said, tapping the poster. "Nobody can see a brain adapting." Cedar suggested drawing a brain wearing tiny sunglasses. Nahla suggested a rap. Ava stared at the red buttons instead, and an idea arrived, not slowly but all at once, the way spontaneous ideas do. She scooped the buttons into a cup. "Okay, you're the brain," she told Cedar. "Every time I dump five buttons, that's a puff. You inhale, dopamine floods in, you feel great. Show me great." Cedar spread his arms wide and grinned like a cartoon.

Ava dumped five buttons, and Cedar grinned. She dumped five again, and he grinned smaller. On the fifth dump, Cedar barely smiled. "What if," Ava said slowly, "the brain gets used to it, so the same amount stops working?" She tried dumping eight buttons, and Cedar's grin came back full force. Then ten, then twelve, his grin snapping to full brightness only as the numbers climbed. Nahla scribbled the counts on the poster's edge. By the end of the row, the cup was almost empty and Cedar was grinning at fourteen.

"You realize," Cedar said, still grinning, "you just used up all my buttons being addicted." "That's the whole point," Ava said. "It never gets easier, only bigger." Nahla looked at the scribbled numbers, twelve, fourteen, climbing in a ragged line, and said quietly that her cousin had said almost exactly that in April, laughing like it was nothing.

On the last morning, Ava stood on the stage with her cup and her poster. She pointed at the climbing numbers, said the word tolerance out loud once, and then dumped buttons over Cedar's head while he grinned bigger and bigger and bigger, until the cup was empty and his hands were held out for more.

The school bus rattled over the pothole by the gym, and Mackenzie's word list jumped in her hands. She was down to the last page before the county spelling bee, and the words were betraying her. "Bite," she muttered. "B-I-T-E. Why is that e even there? It doesn't make a sound. It's just sitting there like camouflage, pretending to be useful."

Ali leaned over from the seat across the aisle. "You're the one who signed up for this."

"And I can spell everything except the words with sneaky letters." She tapped the paper. "Bite, bone, home. Then bite's weird cousin, bit. One letter changes the whole sound and I can't see why."

Henley, two rows back, poked her head over the seat. "Maybe the letters used to make those sounds and then stopped. Like, the e used to say something."

Mackenzie stared at her. That was actually a thought. If the e had once been pronounced, the spellings wouldn't be strange at all. They'd be records of something that changed. She flipped her list over and wrote out loud sounds with her pencil, mouthing "bee-nay" for bone just to test it, and Ali burst out laughing so hard the eighth graders turned around.

Mr. Adebayo, riding up front with the team, held up a battered paperback. "You'll want this," he said, and passed it back along the seats. Mackenzie found the page he'd marked. Her eyes went wide. "Listen to this. Between about 1400 and 1700, the long vowel sounds all shifted. It's called the Great Vowel Shift." She read faster. "And here's the twist. Printing had already locked the spellings in, so the letters stayed put while the sounds walked off without them."

"So the e isn't camouflage," Henley said. "It's a fossil."

"A fossil that bites," Ali said, and Mackenzie's grin was infectious; even the eighth graders were smiling now.

The bee that afternoon went three rounds before the announcer said "knife." Mackenzie pictured the word's history like a map, the k that had once been spoken, the strange old spellings that no longer matched the sounds. "K-N-I-F-E," she said. The judge nodded, and in the fourth round, when the word was "mimic," she was so relaxed she almost laughed. "M-I-M-I-C. Mimic."

Afterward Ali pretended to be the announcer, mimicking his deep voice. "Our next word is" and she held up a silent, invisible letter e, floating in the air like a tiny trophy.

Avery had counted the hours until lights-out, and now that it was here, she wished she hadn't. The bunk above her creaked whenever Hugo moved, which was often. Somewhere across the cabin, Cassius was pretending to be asleep, but his breathing was too even, too perfect, like a kid performing sleep for an audience. Avery stared at the underside of Hugo's mattress and thought about her kitchen, where the light above the stove was probably on right now. Was she the only one doing this? It felt like a thing no one would admit out loud, which meant there was no way to know for sure. Unless there was.

The next morning she borrowed a marker from the craft bin and taped a scrap of paper to the inside of the bathroom door, where every girl in the cabin would see it and no counselor would. It said: if you miss home, draw one tally mark. She told herself she was being objective about it, like a scientist counting results instead of guessing. By dinner there were eleven tallies. Eleven, out of twelve girls.

That should have made her feel better, but it didn't, quite. She was the one who had put up the paper, so she knew about all eleven. Everyone else still thought they were alone. That was the problem with hidden things. A feeling nobody shows can't be discovered by accident; something has to happen out in the open.

She found her chance at the campfire. Mr. Desir had just finished a story about an enormous fish and gone off to talk to the lifeguard, and the coals were settling into that stage where you could actually hear yourself think. Hugo was hunched over his marshmallow stick, uncharacteristically quiet, and Avery wondered if he was homesick and if his joking usually hid it. She decided to test the idea out loud.

"I miss my dog," she said, to nobody in particular. "Like, a lot. I keep thinking he's waiting by the door."

Hugo looked up so fast his marshmallow slid into the fire. "You do? I miss my mom's cooking so bad I dreamed about scrambled eggs." Cassius leaned over from the next log. "I wrote my little brother a letter and I'm not even sure he can read."

Then came the twist. Mr. Desir, settling back onto his log, said, "Every summer, kids think they're the only one. But research on overnight camps found most campers feel at least some homesickness, and for most of them it stays mild." He said it like he was remarking on the weather, then asked who wanted seconds on marshmallows, and half the circle raised their hands.

"Wait," Hugo said. "Most? Like, most of everybody?"

"Most," said Cassius slowly, like he was working a math problem. "So it's basically normal. We've all just been hiding it in a way that, like, hindered us from finding each other."

"That's the weirdest use of hinder I've ever heard," Avery said, and the whole log of boys cracked up.

Later, at lights-out, Avery pulled her flashlight out from under her pillow. She didn't need it to find the bathroom paper; she knew the number by heart. But she clicked it on anyway and swept it once around the cabin, a slow circle over eleven sleeping shapes. In the beam each face looked the same: ordinary, breathing, here. Somewhere in her head a thought drifted past, that in a hundred years everyone in this cabin would be gone, a kind of extinction that even tallies and flashlights couldn't reach, and that this was somehow exactly why the tallies mattered now. She clicked the light off.

"Avery?" Hugo's voice came down through the mattress springs. "You still awake?"

"Yeah."

"Tomorrow can we put the tally paper somewhere the boys can use it too?"

Avery smiled into the dark. "Bring a marker," she said.

Aria had saved her allowance for two months to buy four tickets in the upper deck, and now she sat between her dad and her cousin Sofia, who had arrived from England three days earlier. Kaelyn and Myla were one row down, sharing a bag of popcorn and arguing about which team would score first. Below them the field gleamed under the lights, and the players were still warming up.

When Sofia found their seats, Aria had promised her a proper stadium experience, and part of that, in Aria's opinion, was the wave. Around the sixth inning, a section near third base started it. Thousands of people stood, threw their arms up, and sat down again, and the standing moved around the bowl like water sloshing in a giant cup. Aria jumped up with the rest of her section, yelling, then plopped back down, grinning.

"What is this called?" Sofia asked, pointing as the wave came around again.

"The wave," Aria said. "You know, the wave."

"We call it the Mexican wave," Sofia said.

Aria frowned. That didn't make sense. There was nothing Mexican about a baseball stadium in their own city. Maybe Sofia had made a mistake, or maybe she was teasing, the way she had teased Aria about the word "biscuit" at dinner. But Sofia was already standing with the next pass of the wave, so Aria filed the question away and jumped up with her.

She tested the idea the way she tested things, by asking around. "Excuse me," she said to the man with the foam finger at the end of the row. "Do you know why some people call the wave the Mexican wave?" The man shrugged. Myla said she'd heard her grandmother in Colombia say it that way too, though Myla wasn't sure why. Kaelyn was pessimistic about the whole project. "Nobody knows," she said. "You'll just embarrass yourself asking strangers." Aria kept asking anyway.

In the eighth inning, a fan a few seats over, an older woman wearing a scarf from a club team, overheard the girls talking and leaned in. "It got famous at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico," she said. "That's why, in a lot of English-speaking places outside North America, it's the Mexican wave." Aria turned to Sofia. "So it's the same thing, just a different name." Sofia nodded, looking a little smug, in Aria's opinion.

On the walk to the exit after the final out, Aria made a quiet amendment to her mental list of things Sofia knew more about than she did: biscuits, football versus soccer, and now this. Myla was still grumbling that her question had been better. "You didn't even have a question," Kaelyn said. "Yes I did," Myla said. "I asked why the hot dogs cost eight dollars." Sofia laughed so hard she had to stop walking. "Now that," she said, "nobody in the world can explain."

Antoine crouched at the end of the gym hallway with a tennis ball, a meter stick, and a stopwatch he had borrowed from Ms. Mercer, who had one rule that afternoon: no running in the hallways, which prohibited anything but rolling. His problem was simple and stubborn. He wanted to know how fast his ball actually went, and eyeballing it told him nothing. Speed was invisible. You could not watch it, only chase it with numbers.

He had written a note to himself that morning, folded into his pocket like a tiny letter to his future self, and now he smoothed it out on the floor. Measure distance. Measure time. Divide. Annie, who was working beside him with a golf ball, leaned over to read it. "You wrote yourself instructions?" she said. "Last month I did the lab without a plan and got everything backwards," Antoine said. "This time I have a technique. Mark every meter, start the watch at zero distance, record where the ball is at each second." Annie tapped the paper. "Then we'll see if my ball beats yours."

Beatrix stood at the two-meter mark with her own stopwatch, calling out the seconds. At one second, Antoine's tennis ball had gone one meter. At two seconds, two meters. At three, three. Annie's golf ball was slower: one meter at one second, one and a half at two, two at three. Antoine wrote each number down, then drew two axes on graph paper and plotted the points, one line for each ball.
