"Thirty minutes. Then straight to bed."

She looked at the thermometer on the counter, then at him. "If you have no fever at seven a.m.," she said, "we'll talk about the party."

Jordan was already writing seven a.m. at the bottom of the page.

Vincent had read the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms twice on the bus to city hall, and both times the words had slid off him like water off a raincoat. Ms. Park's assignment was on the notice board by the council chamber doors: each student had to read one right listed in the constitution and explain it in their own words, out loud, in front of everyone at the mock council session. Vincent's turn was in forty minutes, and he still had nothing.

He found Amina on the bench outside the chamber, holding her own crumpled printout. "What did you pick?" he asked.

"Mobility rights. Easy. You can live and work anywhere in Canada." She glanced at his page. "Which one's yours?"

"That's the problem. Mine says everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person. But when I try to say it in my own words, I just say the same words in a different order."

Amina laughed, then leaned closer. "Okay, here's a thing. My cousins live in Germany, and last summer my uncle showed me their constitution. It's called the Basic Law, from 1949, and Article 1, the very first article, starts with 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.' That's it. That's the first sentence of the whole thing. Before free speech, before anything."

Vincent stared at her. "Dignity comes first? Not rules, not government. Dignity."

"That's what he said. Canada's opens by saying what it is, like a definition. Germany's opens by saying what nobody is allowed to touch."

He tested the idea right there, the way he tested everything, out loud and sideways. "So if dignity is first, then everything after it has to fit underneath it. Even the stuff about who gets to delegate power to whom. Even a section about leisure." He frowned. "Wait, is there a section about leisure?"

"Mobility," Amina said. "You're spiralling."

"Spiritually." But something had clicked. He borrowed her pen, crossed out his notes, and wrote a single sentence at the bottom of the page.

When Ms. Park called his name in the chamber, with the coach from the community league and a bored city clerk watching from the back row, Vincent stood up and read the right word for word first, because that was the rule. Then he closed the paper.

"In my own words," he said. "Your dignity is off the table. It doesn't matter what you did, or what anyone thinks of you. It can't be violated, and it can't be traded away. It's like the floor everything else stands on." He paused. "Some countries say that on line one."

Ms. Park wrote something on her clipboard. "Where did you find that comparison?"

"Amina's cousins," Vincent said. "She shared."

Amina, three rows back, lifted her mobility rights paper and waved it like a flag.

The pool deck smelled like chlorine and nerves. Felix stood with eleven other kids at 7:40 in the morning, waiting for the coach to post the tryout order for the school swim team, and his stomach was doing slow flips.

"I'm not warming up," Dean said beside him. "I want to watch the first heat instead, see how fast the other guys actually are. Know what we're up against." Felix had planned to do the same thing, sit on the bench and study the competition. But something nagged at his conscience, a memory of last season's time trials, when he had climbed in cold and felt like his arms were made of rope for the first lap. The coach had told nobody anything. He'd just noticed that the kids who jogged the deck loop and did arm swings before racing always seemed to hit their pace in the first lap, not the third. Felix had a theory about that, something he could not see but could test: maybe it was heart rate and muscle temperature, that getting both up somehow made the muscles work better before a hard effort. That was the whole idea, and it was simple enough to try.

"You go watch," Felix said. "I'm going to jog and stretch first." Dean rolled his eyes and headed for the bench. Felix jogged two easy loops of the deck, then did moving stretches, arm circles and leg swings, until he could feel his pulse ticking quicker under his jaw and warmth spreading through his shoulders.

When his heat was called, he climbed onto the block feeling loose, almost buoyant, and when the whistle blew his arms caught the water on the very first stroke. He touched the wall and looked at the board, and there it was: a personal best, in the first race of the morning. Dean swam two heats later, and Felix watched him go out stiff, grinding through the opening lap while the field pulled away. Afterward Dean dragged himself out, breathing hard, shaking his arms out one at a time.

"That water was freezing," Dean said. "It's like my muscles wouldn't turn on."

"Ask Felix," Kianna said from the next lane, wringing out her cap. "He told me he jogged and stretched before his heat. Something about heart rate and muscle temperature."

Dean squinted at him. "So you're saying I swam slow because I skipped it? Paraphrase that for me in one sentence, because it sounds like you're saying I lost to a bench."

"I'm saying the bench beat you," Felix said, and pointed at the team list going up on the wall, where Dean's name sat one spot below the cut line.

Chloe spread her history notes across her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled like lemon polish and, faintly, like the mushrooms Grandpa was frying for lunch. "The Treaty of Versailles," she read out loud, "and how it helped lead to the Second World War." She glared at the sentence as if it might apologize and turn into something easier.

"Still stuck on that?" said Isabelle, who had come over supposedly to help, but who was currently balancing a spoon on her nose.

"Mr. Pham wants us to explain why, not just list dates," Chloe said. "And I don't get it. The treaty was in 1919, the war started twenty years later. How does one thing cause the other?"

Grandpa wandered in with a plate of fried mushrooms and a squint at the map she had propped against the sugar bowl. Chloe traced the western edge of Germany with her finger. Then she noticed something odd. A whole stretch of Germany's own land, right along the Rhine River next to France, was shaded on the map's legend as demilitarized. No German troops allowed there. That made no sense to her. It was like drawing a line through your own bedroom and saying nobody from your family could stand in it.

"Grandpa, why couldn't Germany put soldiers in its own land?"

He shrugged happily, because shrugging was one of his favorite activities. "You have a book there. Books know more than grandpas."

So she tested her idea. France had been invaded before and was afraid of it happening again, she thought. If a country wanted to invade France, it would have to march through that stretch along the river. Without troops there, that stretch became something like a wall. She flipped through the treaty book until she found the name: the Rhineland. It wasn't a wall of stone, it was a buffer zone, land left empty of soldiers on purpose.

"It's like the hedge!" Isabelle said suddenly, spoon finally falling off her nose.

"What hedge?"

"The one outside. Come on." Isabelle dragged her out the back door to the garden, where an invasive vine had been sneaking into the yard all summer. Between the vine and the roses stood Grandpa's thick hedge. "The vine wants to invade the roses, but the hedge is in the way. It's a buffer."

Chloe looked at the hedge, then at the vine snaking along the fence, then back at the house. Somewhere behind the kitchen window, fungus was probably already growing on Grandpa's forgotten half of a lemon. Things spread when nothing stops them. Then she ran inside and found the next part in the book herself: Germany later sent troops into the Rhineland anyway, and nobody stopped that either. The wall had been on paper only.

"Here's my whole explanation," she announced, standing on a kitchen chair because it felt more convincing. "France was scared of being invaded, so the treaty made the Rhineland, that strip of Germany along the Rhine next to France, a place with no German troops, a buffer zone. Then Germany broke that rule, and breaking it was like a test nobody stopped. So a man in a kitchen in 1936 looks at the map and sees he can go anywhere."

"That was the spoon's idea, actually," Isabelle said. "I want footnote credit."

"Fine. Footnote: the spoon."

Lucy sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with six library books fanned around her like a card trick gone wrong. Her essay assignment was due Monday: take a position, outline three supporting points, then draft. She had already written her thesis on an index card in purple marker: "Pigeons are a menace to cities and should be driven out." She tapped the card against her chin. Easy. Everyone hated pigeons. Three points would practically write themselves.

By page forty of the first book, she was frowning. The book claimed pigeons were astonishingly smart, could recognize human faces, and had once saved entire flocks of carrier messages during wars. The second book said cities would have a bizarre amount of dropped food litter without pigeons cleaning it up. "Traitors," Lucy told the books. "All of you."

She called Veronica, who showed up ten minutes later with popcorn and zero sympathy. "So your evidence says the opposite of your thesis," Veronica said, munching. "Bummer."

"I can't start over. I have the whole outline. Point one: droppings. Point two: crowds. Point three: they're basically rats with wings." Lucy held up the index card like a shield.

Veronica leaned over the third book. "It says here some pigeons went nearly to extinction because people hunted them. Passenger pigeons. Billions of them, gone." She looked up. "That's sad, not menacing."

Lucy stared at the card. Then she flipped it over, and on the blank side wrote in smaller, less confident purple: "Pigeons deserve a place in cities because they clean up litter, are highly intelligent, and have helped humans for centuries." She frowned at it. "But what do I even call this thing now, since my first one was wrong?"

"Working thesis," said Mr. Suryanto from the doorway, holding a plate of his wife's samosas because he firmly believed studying required snacks. He set it down between them. "That's what my professor called the first one, anyway. It works until the evidence points somewhere else." He shrugged and went back to his own kitchen.

Lucy and Veronica looked at each other. "So the first one wasn't wasted," Lucy said slowly, "it was just... working." She grabbed a fresh index card and started building her new outline. Point one: litter cleanup. She had three sources for that already.

"Menace to cities," Veronica read over her shoulder, laughing. "You really committed to that one."

"I had a whole paragraph planned about a pigeon that stole my sandwich in the plaza." Lucy snatched a samosa. "Fine. New plan. The pigeon keeps the sandwich, and I integrate it into point two as proof of their intelligence." She wrote the sentence down, underlined it twice, and propped the card where she could see it.

At the Japanese booth at the cultural festival, Ellie stood in front of a menu written in both English and Japanese, holding a crumpled practice sheet in her pocket. Maika had promised to teach her enough Japanese to order lunch, since Ellie's family was visiting Tokyo in the spring and she wanted to surprise her grandmother by ordering on her own. The plan was simple: three phrases, one order, one question about the price. Ivana had already ordered a plate of yakisoba by pointing at the menu, which felt like cheating to Ellie, though Ivana said it was efficient.

The booth had been set up like a tiny restaurant, with paper lanterns strung along the front and a man in an apron taking orders behind a counter. Maika leaned close and whispered the first phrase, and Ellie repeated it, then wrote it out phonetically on her sheet. When she tried the second one, the word for "how much," she kept slipping into the rhythm of English, and Maika laughed so hard the paper lanterns above them swayed.

"You have to let the sounds land soft," Maika said. "Like dropping a pebble in water, not throwing it."

Ellie tried again, slower this time. The man behind the counter looked up and nodded, so she stepped forward, heart tapping, and said the whole order in one careful line. The words came out smaller than she had practiced, but they came out. Then she asked the price question, and he answered with a number she almost missed. She counted out the bills exactly, added a little extra, and left the coins on the counter beside her tray, the way her family always did at restaurants back home.

She had taken three steps toward the tables when the man came around the counter and caught up with her. He held out the coins in his open palm and shook his head, polite but firm, as if she had dropped her keys. Ellie stared at the shiny coins, and a principle assembled itself in her mind: what looked like politeness at home looked like a mistake here. She remembered a travel show where a server ran a whole block to return change a family had left on the table, and suddenly that scene made sense. Tipping was not part of it at all.

"Keep it," she started to say, then stopped, because Maika was already translating something the man said, quick and gentle.

"He says thank you, but this is the exact price. Nothing extra is expected."

Ellie took the coins back and bowed a little, which made the man smile. Ivana, watching from a table with her yakisoba, raised her chopsticks in salute. Ellie sat down and turned the practice sheet over, writing a new note to transmit to her future self in Tokyo: pay the exact amount, and do not leave money on the table, because someone will always run after you to give it back.

"Next time I'm ordering dessert too," Ivana said. "In Japanese, if you teach me."

Ellie looked at the dessert case behind the counter and folded the coins into her pocket. "Mochi," she said. "I already know that word."

Aubrey pushed the coffee table against the wall so the living room had room for two actors and one imaginary dragon. Loukas flopped onto the couch with his script, which was useless, because tonight there was no script. Tomorrow was the drama camp showcase, and Mr. Rao had put them together as a pair for the improv section.

"Remember the rule," Aubrey said, retrieving two hairbrushes from the kitchen drawer to use as microphones. "It's called 'yes, and.' You accept what your partner gives you, and then you add something new."

"I know, I know." Loukas popped up, took a brush, and grinned. "Start."

Aubrey held her brush to her mouth. "Good evening, we're live at the world's largest pickle festival."

"Yes," said Loukas, nodding.

She waited. He kept nodding. The silence stretched until the imaginary crowd probably left. "And?" she finally said.

"And... yes?"

"That's the problem. You keep agreeing but you never add anything, so the scene just stalls, like a car with no gas." She tried again. "Good evening, we're live at the world's largest pickle festival, where a giant pickle has just come to life."

"Yes," said Loukas.

"Add something! Anything! The pickle is doing something."

"Yes... the pickle is standing there."

Aubrey groaned and dropped onto the couch cushion beside him. It was like playing catch with someone who caught the ball and then sat down with it. She stared at the ceiling and thought. Loukas was diligent, honestly. He'd memorized every line of the camp skit in one night. Maybe the problem wasn't effort. Maybe the problem was that he thought agreeing was the whole job, when agreeing was only half.

"Okay, new plan," she said. "Whatever I say, you say yes, and then you make it weirder. Weirder than my weird. Can you do weird?"

"Excuse me, I am a champion of weird."

"Prove it. Scene: we're two astronauts landing on Mars."

"Yes, and the Mars rover is our tour guide and it only speaks in knock-knock jokes," Loukas said immediately.

Aubrey blinked, then laughed so hard she snorted. "Yes, and the first joke is so bad it knocks over a rock, and the rock rolls downhill and reveals a door."

"Yes, and the door has perfect symmetry, two handles, two windows, and it opens from both sides at once."

"Yes, and behind it is a whole pickle festival, which means we never left Earth!"

They went back and forth for twenty minutes, building a Mars hotel run by a pickle with a clipboard, and the scene never once stalled. When Aubrey's mom leaned in from the kitchen to say it was almost time for Loukas to head home, they both looked up, startled, like they'd actually been on Mars.

"Same time tomorrow before the showcase?" Loukas asked, setting his hairbrush microphone down with great ceremony.

"Yes," said Aubrey, "and bring the dragon."

Rosalie sat down in the computer lab with the fundraiser notebook open beside the keyboard. Ms. Castillo had given her one job before Friday: turn the class bake sale records into a spreadsheet with a column total and a bar chart, so the principal could see what each table earned. Ameera had already typed the numbers, and now it was Rosalie's turn to make the sheet do the math.

She clicked the empty cell under the column of earnings and typed =SUM(B2:B9). Eight tables, eight numbers. The total appeared: forty-one dollars and fifty cents. Rosalie frowned. She assessed the column again, adding the figures in her head the slow way, table by table. When she got to fifty-five dollars, she stopped. The machine was short by thirteen dollars and fifty cents.

"Can't you just type the right number in?" said Maika, leaning over from the next computer. "The principal won't check."

Rosalie shook her head. "If the total is wrong, the chart is wrong, and then the whole thing is a lie." She looked at the cells one at a time. Seven of them sat snug against the right edge of their boxes, but the number for Table 4, thirteen fifty, huddled on the left side, exactly where words sat. She remembered Ameera pasting that one in from a text message because the Table 4 kids had sent their earnings by phone.

She deleted the cell, typed 13.50 fresh, and pressed Enter. The number jumped to the right edge, and the total at the bottom changed on its own to fifty-five dollars. So that was the rule, she thought, and she felt it click into place like a locker: SUM skipped anything that wasn't a real number, no warning, no red mark. A pasted figure could look like a number and still be nothing but text to the machine, quietly left out.

Then she built the chart. She selected the table names and the earnings, clicked the bar chart button, and the bars rose across the screen. Table 3's bar stood tallest, tall enough to look almost aggressive next to Table 5's stubby little block. She added a title, Class Bake Sale Income, and printed one copy for Ms. Castillo and one for the bulletin board outside the office.

At the door she ran into Ameera, who read the chart upside down and then right side up. "Table 4 did all right," Ameera said. "I thought they'd earned nothing."

"They did earn something," Rosalie said. "The sheet just didn't know it yet." She folded the extra copy and put it in her binder, next to the notebook with all the messy original numbers, the ones she wasn't ready to recycle. Ameera was already walking off down the hall with the good news, and the paper still smelled faintly warm from the printer.

Piper slapped the crumpled sign on Mr. Rowe's desk before the bell finished ringing. "The bookstore by the mall banned backpacks. That's a violation of my Charter rights. Section 8, unreasonable search."

Mr. Rowe picked up the sign and read it. "Assignment's due Friday, Piper. You have to explain a right in your own words. This is a start."

"Better than a start. It's real." She pointed at the small print: NO BACKPACKS. NO EXCEPTIONS. "They searched Loic's bag last Saturday. Made him open it right at the counter."

After class she found Loic and Terrence at the lockers and laid out her plan. "If the Charter protects us, we test it. We walk in with the backpacks and cite the section. If they back down, the rule doesn't restrict us anymore."

"Or we get banned from the only bookstore we can walk to," Terrence said.

Loic shrugged. "I'm in. I still want my money back anyway."

Saturday, Piper led them through the door with her backpack straps gripped tight. The same clerk stepped in front of the counter. "Read the sign."

"I did. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms says you can't search us without reason."

The clerk folded his arms. "Kid, we're not the government. The Charter applies to governments, not to us."

Piper froze. She had read the whole document twice for the assignment and never once thought about who it was aimed at. The clerk waited, arms still crossed, and she realized he wasn't guessing. "You're sure?"

"My sister's a lawyer. I've heard the speech a hundred times."

They bought nothing and walked out. Terrence kicked a pebble across the parking lot. "So we can't do anything?"

"There's still the assignment," Piper said slowly, pulling out her phone. She searched the Charter's text, scanning for the words that mattered. Governments. The word sat there in her notes from Monday, circled twice, and she had skipped right past it. "Okay. New idea. The sign isn't a Charter problem. But the city bus kicked me off last month for the same reason, and the bus is the government. That's my example."

"You're going to write about yourself?" Loic asked.

"I'm going to write about the difference." She was already typing notes. "Friday, Mr. Rowe's going to ask who did their project on a real event. Mine's going to be the only one with a twist."

Terrence squinted at her. "What twist?"

Piper held up the phone, showing a photo she'd taken of the bookstore's front window. Below the NO BACKPACKS sign sat a smaller plaque: PROPERTY OF THE CITY LIBRARY BOARD.

Loic leaned in. "Is a library board the government?"

Piper grinned and pocketed the phone. "Ask my essay."

Ethan's fingers hit the last chord of "The Little Peasant Dance" a full eight seconds before the recording ended. He pulled his hands off the community centre piano and stared at the clock on the wall. Mr. González had given every piano student a spot in the Friday recital, but at this rate Ethan would finish his piece while everyone else was still settling into their chairs. Why did he always rush? He didn't feel fast inside. The music felt slow to him, steady even, yet somehow the clock said otherwise.

"You did it again," said Mouhamed, who was sprawled on the bench beside him with his trumpet case open. "Giuliana timed you. Sixty-one seconds. She says the recording is one minute and ten."

"Maybe the recording is wrong," Ethan said, though he doubted it. Giuliana appeared from behind the upright piano in the corner, holding her phone like a piece of evidence.

"The recording is fine. You're impulsive. You play every loud part faster." She tapped her phone. "Watch. You cruised through the middle section where it gets loud."

Ethan played just the middle section while she timed him, then played it again while pretending it was quiet, like a whisper. The quiet version took longer. That was strange. The notes were exactly the same in both versions. Same fingers, same keys, same everything. Somehow the loudness itself was dragging him forward, like a dog pulling a leash. But how could you notice something happening inside your own hands? It was like trying to watch your own eyes blink.

Then he remembered the shelf in the supply room, where Mr. González kept old method books and a strange pyramid-shaped brass box with a sliding weight on a metal arm. Mr. González had called it a metronome once. Ethan fetched it, wound the key, and set the weight the way Mr. González had shown a younger student last month. Tick, tick, tick. The sound was stubborn and even, refusing to hurry no matter what.

"Play with that," Giuliana said. "We'll verify it. You against the machine."

Ethan started the piece, matching his notes to the ticks. Whenever he pulled ahead, the tick landed behind him like a reproach, and he eased back. When the loud middle section arrived, he felt the old tug, but now he had something outside himself to check against, something that couldn't be charmed into speeding up. He finished, breathing hard. Giuliana looked up from her phone. "One minute and nine seconds."

Mouhamed leaned over the brass box. "Who even invented this thing?"

"Mr. González said a guy named Maelzel," Ethan said. "Johann Nepomuk Maelzel. He patented it in 1815."

"Patented? Like an invention?"

"Like an invention." Ethan slid the weight a notch lower, and the ticking slowed to a patient walk. He wondered what it would feel like to master a slow tempo instead of just surviving it. He set his hands on the keys again.

"Count me in," Giuliana said, thumb hovering over the timer. "Ready? Go."

Jessica pushed the folded poster board down the hallway toward Room 12, where the sign-language club met on Thursdays. Fraser had asked her to make the poster because her lettering was the neatest in grade eight, and the club needed members or it would be cancelled. She had lettered WELCOME TO THE DEAF CLUB in big blue capitals, and now she stood in the doorway holding it up.

Fraser's face went strange, half pleased and half worried. "Almost," he said. "Can you change one thing?"

Jessica frowned at her own work. She had spent two evenings on the swan curves of the F's. "Which thing?"

"Deaf has to be capital D." Fraser's hands moved while he talked, because that was how he talked with his cousin, quick shapes like birds taking off. "Lowercase deaf is the hearing condition. Capital D is the community, the culture, the sign language, all of it. James Woodward proposed that in 1972."

"Who's James Woodward?"

"No idea. My cousin told me. He said everybody in the club would know, and some people feel strongly about it."

Jessica sat down at the craft table with her pencil and eraser. She had made an assumption, she realized, that the word was just a word, and she felt vulnerable holding up her mistake in front of the whole room. The laminator smelled like warm plastic, and someone's phone was playing music too quietly to name the song.

She erased the lowercase d and redrew it tall, matching her other capitals. Then she tested the idea on Francois, who was taping the doorway and pretending not to eavesdrop. "If I write Deaf with a capital, does that include you, even though you can hear?"

Francois considered this while smoothing a wrinkle out of the tape. "I think that's the point. I'm learning sign because my grandmother went deaf at forty, small d. But me coming here, that's the big D part."

Jessica looked at the poster again, and a doubt crept in. She turned to Fraser. "So it's not wrong to write deaf lowercase ever?"

"It depends what you mean," Fraser said. "My cousin uses both about himself."

The adviser, Mr. Wiśniewski, leaned over from the next table where he was fixing the popcorn machine, and Jessica braced for a lecture. He only shrugged and said, "Ask them yourself," and nodded toward the door, where three students she had never met were peering in at the poster.

The tallest one read it slowly, lips moving, then looked at Jessica. "Who made this?"

"I did," she said, holding it a little tighter. "Should I change it back?"

The student smiled, but did not answer right away.

The group chat lit up at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, which meant August had found something in his grandmother's photo box again. This time it was a birthday card his grandfather had sent her in 1994, signed in careful blue ink: "Szabó István." August posted a picture of it with the caption, "My grandpa signed his own name wrong?? On a CARD???" Cade replied with three crying-laughing faces and the words "one job," and then the two of them began composing a corrective reply to a man who had been dead since 2009.

Lillian typed "wait" three times before anyone stopped. She was staring at the signature, and something about it was snagging in her brain the way a sleeve catches on a nail. In her history class, Ms. Yilmaz had put a roster on the board for a unit on family trees, and half the names had looked backwards to Lillian too: Kim Ji-ho, Wang Mei, Tanaka Aiko. Ms. Yilmaz had called roll that day and said the second name first, every time, without stopping to explain. So Lillian went to the class site, pulled up the unit, and found the worksheet she'd half-ignored in September. There it was in the margin, in her own handwriting because Ms. Yilmaz made them copy the tricky bits: In Hungarian, the family name comes before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.

"It's not wrong," she posted. "Hungarian puts the family name first. Same as Chinese, Japanese and Korean names. Szabó is his last name." The chat went quiet for a full minute, which in group-chat time was roughly a geological era. Then August sent a single "??????" and Cade wrote, "so his name is István Szabó and he wrote it the Hungarian way? on purpose?" Lillian confirmed it, and August replied that he had spent nine years of his life calling his grandfather "Grandpa Szabó" at family dinners while apparently using the correct order entirely by accident.

The next message was a photo of another card, this one from 2001, signed "Kovács Erzsébet," which August had always assumed was some aunt he'd never met. "That's my grandma," he wrote. "She's alive. I'm texting her." Ten minutes later he reported back: she had replied with a paragraph about the village where she grew up, where a peasant farmer on her street had been the only person with a telephone, and where she had nurtured a habit of signing her name properly because her schoolteacher had rapped knuckles over anything less. She closed, August said, by hoping he wasn't becoming one of those people who found handwriting obsolete, since a typed name told you nothing about a person.

Cade asked whether this meant he'd been filing Japanese names backwards in his head all through elementary school, and Lillian said basically yes. August changed the group chat name to "Szabó István Memorial Correct Order Society" and pinned the photo of the card to the top. Then he posted one more picture: his grandmother's reply, ending with the line, "Tell your friends the phone is not always right, but grandmothers usually are."

The dinner reservation was for six o'clock sharp, and the movie started at eight, which left Maelie exactly one hour and forty minutes to eat, apologize for nothing, and figure out why Zakary's grandmother kept looking at her like she had spilled something.

She hadn't spilled anything. She had checked.

It was Zakary's birthday, and his whole family had taken over the big round table at the restaurant near the mall. When Maelie arrived, the grandmother had pressed a small red envelope into her hands, and Maelie, who had brought a wrapped sketchbook for Zakary, had stood there holding both like she couldn't do math. She'd said thank you twice, then a third time, which made the grandmother smile, at least.

The trouble started with the ribs. They were glazed and slippery, and Maelie needed both hands, so she planted her chopsticks upright in her rice bowl the way she would have parked a pencil in a cup, reached over, and grabbed the biggest piece.

The grandmother's smile dwindle. Zakary's mother stopped pouring tea mid-stream. Across the table, Zakary made a small strangled noise.

"Maelie," he said quietly. "Take them out of the rice."

"Why?" Maelie looked down. Her chopsticks stood straight up out of the white rice like two little poles. They weren't hurting anything. "They'll roll off if I lay them down."

"Just take them out. Please. I'll explain later."

"Explain now. We have a movie at eight and I am not eating this entire dinner in the dark."

Zakary leaned across the birthday cake that hadn't even been lit yet. "Standing up in rice, chopsticks look like incense for the dead," he said, wincing. "So nobody leaves them like that. Rest them on the bowl edge. Or the holder. Like this." He laid his own pair across the top of his bowl.

Maelie pulled hers out fast, and the grandmother exhaled and went back to her tea. Maelie set her chopsticks down carefully, then picked them up again, then set them down again, testing the angle like the whole table was wired with voltage and one wrong move would light her up.

"Okay," she said. "New theory. Everything I do at this table is being graded."

"Nobody's grading you," Zakary said. "You got the envelope right. You used both hands. That was good."

She thought back. Both hands, yes. She'd done that without knowing why, just copying his mother. So there were rules, and the rules had reasons, and the reasons weren't written anywhere she could read them. She decided to run a test before the cake came: she refilled the grandmother's teacup, with both hands, and waited.

The grandmother said something to Zakary's mother, and they both laughed, and the grandmother patted Maelie's wrist.

"What did she say?" Maelie whispered.

"She said you learn faster than Zakary did, and that he once stuck his chopsticks in the rice at his own birthday dinner."

"I did not," Zakary said. "I was seven. That's not evidence."

Maelie checked the clock above the kitchen door. Six forty-two. Cake, then presents, then the movie, and she still had two pieces of rib to finish. She picked up her chopsticks properly this time, snapped up the biggest one, and held it out toward Zakary.

"Happy birthday," she said. "You almost died at seven. That's the best gift I've heard all night."

Jackson's family reunion was supposed to mean the whole afternoon at the lake, and the first thing he heard when he got out of the car was his little cousin refusing to go near the water. "Sharks," the boy said, arms crossed on the dock. "I saw a video about a boy who got bitten."

"There aren't sharks in this lake," Jackson said.

"There could be." The boy sat down on the boards and announced that he would not swim, not even to cool off, and the adults were already starting a negotiation over popsicles to get him to at least put his feet in. Jackson gave up and went to find Sofia and Billy, who had come with their families to the same gathering.

"The shark video had millions of views," Billy said when Jackson told them. "It was all over everything this summer. That one kid." He scrolled through his phone and held it up. A boy in a hospital bed, holding up a bandaged arm, grinning at the camera.

"It's weird," Sofia said. "My mom showed me the same story, and now my little brother won't get in our pool. A pool. And nothing ever happened to anyone we actually know."

Jackson turned his popsicle stick over in his fingers. One video, one kid, and now two little boys wouldn't swim. He thought about his science unit, where Ms. Flores had made them compare a tested claim to a single report. A tested claim held up across lots of cases. A single report was just one person's experience, vivid as anything, and it told you almost nothing about how often a thing happened. One story could feel like proof even when it wasn't. "So the question isn't whether it happened," he said. "It's how many times it happened out of all the times it could have."

They needed numbers, so they asked for phones and counted. Billy found the count of shark bites on swimmers for the whole coast last year: a few dozen, in a country where tens of millions of people go in the ocean. Then they counted the crowd at the reunion itself, about forty people, and figured that if every single one of them swam in the ocean every summer for the rest of their lives, the odds that any of them would ever be bitten stayed vanishingly small. Sofia wrote the numbers on a paper plate with a marker.

Jackson brought the plate to the dock and sat down next to his cousin. "You know the video was real," he said. "But real and common aren't the same thing. Here's how many bites there were, and here's how many people swam. It's like being scared of vending machines because one guy got hurt by one." He tapped the plate. "You remember the shark kid because the video was everywhere. You don't remember the millions of boring swims, because nobody films those."

"There's a name for that," Sofia said, coming up behind them with Billy. "Tversky and Kahneman called it the availability heuristic. In 1973. You judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind."

The boy looked at the numbers on the plate for a while, then at the lake, flat and glittering with nothing under it but weeds and one lost flip-flop from last summer. "Sharks still scare me," he said.

"Fine. Be scared and swim anyway," Jackson said. "I'll hold your hand until it ceases to matter, and then we race."

The boy stood up, tested the water with one toe, and jumped in with a splash that soaked the paper plate, numbers and all.

The phone store smelled like new plastic, and Jacob held the box with both hands while the cashier rang it up. His mom had said the phone was his, and his alone, which meant the mistakes would be his alone too. Kye and Jax had come along, and they crowded around as Jacob peeled off the shrink wrap right there at the counter.

"First app," Kye said. "Get a flashlight."

Jacob searched for it and tapped install. A box popped up on the screen. The flashlight app wanted permission to use his camera, his microphone, and all his contacts. He stared at it.

"Why would a flashlight need my contacts?" Jax asked. "It's a light."

Jacob thought about it. A flashlight did one job, and that job did not involve calling anyone. He could not see why the app wanted those things, and he did not like not being able to see why. He imagined everyone in his contacts list, all his aunts and his teachers and Mr. Berg from next door, being handed over to some app for no reason. He tapped deny, deny, deny, and installed it anyway. The flashlight worked fine.

Later that week, he was still thinking about it. If an app had to ask before it could use the camera, microphone, or contacts, then somewhere in the phone there had to be a record of what he had said yes to. He went into settings and dug around until he found a list of every app and what it was allowed to do. There it was. He scrolled through and diagnosed the problem right away: a weather app he had installed on Tuesday had permission to use his microphone, and he had agreed without reading. He tapped the little switch next to microphone and turned it off. He checked the camera and contacts too, and switched those off wherever an app had them but did not seem to need them.

At school on Monday, Kye brought it up again. "You were so paranoid at the store," he said.

"It asked for my contacts," Jacob said. "A flashlight."

"So what did you do?"

"Denied it. And I can take it back later in settings, if I ever say yes by accident."

Jax pulled out his own phone, found his app list, and went quiet. His flashlight app had contacts, camera, and microphone all switched on. He turned them off one by one, and his ears went red, but nobody said anything about the humiliation of it, because Kye was too busy checking his own phone.

At home, Jacob's mom asked how the phone was going. He said it was fine, and that he was keeping the settings screen handy. Then he took the phone out, opened the flashlight, and shined it at the ceiling.

Cooper spread the newspaper clipping across the library table and read it aloud to Adelie and Leela. "'The new skate park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste.'" He tapped the page. "This guy says our park is a waste."

"My dad says people write letters like that when they don't skate," Adelie said, dropping her backpack onto a chair.

Cooper pulled out his debate notebook. He had signed up to argue at the next city council meeting, and Ms. Girma had told him the library kept the meeting minutes in the reference section. His argument needed to be solid, not just loud. "If I'm going to answer this letter, I have to know which parts of it I can actually refute."

"Refute how?" Leela asked, flipping the clipping toward herself.

"Like, prove wrong. But look." Cooper drew a line down the middle of a fresh page. On the left he wrote "two million dollars" and underlined it. "That's either true or it isn't. Somebody can look it up. The city budget would show it." On the right side he wrote "a waste" and stared at it. "But that part, I can't look that up anywhere. There's no budget line for waste."

Adelie leaned over the notebook. "So one sentence, but two different kinds of thing in it?"

"Right." Cooper stood and went to the reference shelf. The minutes from last spring were bound in blue folders, and he found the vote on the skate park without much trouble. There it was: the contractor's bid, two million dollars, approved six to one. He carried the folder back to the table. "The number checks out. So the letter writer got the cost right, and I can't refute that part no matter how much I want to."

Leela frowned at the clipping. "Then what do you argue?"

Cooper copied the bid number into his notebook, then the vote count, then the date the park opened. He wrote slowly, because he was thinking. "The 'a waste' part. That's just his opinion. It can't be checked. But the number of people who use the park, that can." He looked up. "If I count skaters on a Saturday, that's a checkable number. My whole Saturday, gone, but it's a real count."

"Then his 'waste' claim has to stand against actual numbers," Adelie said.

"Exactly. And here's the weird part." Cooper tapped the original sentence again. "One sentence can mix both. The cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion. Same sentence." He grinned and closed the folder. "Leela, you're good at counting. I'll need a tally sheet."

"Bring two pencils," she said. "And my board."

Vincent had been diligent about his watercolour portrait for exactly three days, and today the cheeks were going to ruin everything. He had mixed what he thought was a soft rose for the blush on his subject's face, but the wash had gone on dark as a strawberry, and it was drying fast.

"It looks like she ran a marathon," said Keenan, leaning over from the next easel in Ms. Lindqvist's art room. "In the desert."

"Thanks. Very helpful." Vincent stared at the paper. Ms. Lindqvist had drilled one rule into them all week: build the portrait light to dark, layer by layer, because watercolour was unforgiving. He'd assumed unforgiving meant permanent, which meant the portrait was finished before it started.

Inaaya appeared behind him with her damp brush in hand. "Hold on. Watch this." She touched a clean tissue to the too-dark cheek and pressed lightly, then again with a corner of the tissue. When she lifted it away, the blush was lighter, the edge softer, and the strawberry had turned into something closer to a real blush.

"Wait. You can extract the paint? After it's on?" Vincent grabbed his own brush, wet it, and dabbed it against his subject's other cheek, then pressed tissue to the spot. Paint came up into the tissue, leaving the paper paler. He laughed out loud, and the kid across the room looked over to see what was so exciting.

"It's not a miracle," Inaaya said. "Ms. Lindqvist mentioned it Monday. You were probably staring at your palette."

He had been staring at his palette, actually. He'd spent the whole week treating watercolour like a treaty he couldn't break, one wrong move and the deal was off, portrait over. Now he was renegotiating. He dabbed again along the jaw where the shadow had gone too heavy, testing how much pressure lifted how much colour, how far he could push it before the paper started to fuzz.

"We should sign something," Keenan said, holding up his own ruined background, a sky gone stormy grey when he'd wanted pale morning. "A formal treaty. You teach me the dabbing trick, I give you my last chocolate milk at lunch."

"Done," Vincent said, and shook on it, already wetting his brush for Keenan's sky.

The bus to Camp Wanasetta smelled like sunscreen and somebody's granola bars, and Livia sat with her duffel between her knees like a guard dog. She had wanted to come, that was the thing. She had begged for two weeks in a lake cabin while her friends stayed home, and now that the trees were sliding past the window, she wished she had begged a little less.

Her cabin had four girls, and by the second night Livia had an alliance with Layan, who could braid hair, and a wary truce with Colt, who could burp the alphabet. Their counselor was Ms. Dela Cruz, who ran the waterfront and laughed loud at her own jokes. On Wednesday they earned a campfire: hot dogs, burnt marshmallows, a song about a moose that Colt ruined on purpose. When the fire burned down to gray coals, the girls started walking back to the cabin, and Livia followed for three steps before something snagged in her mind. The night before, she had watched Ms. Dela Cruz stand over the fire ring long after everyone else left, stirring the ash with a stick like she was looking for something.

"Wait," Livia said. "I don't think it's out."

Layan squinted at the ring. "It looks out. There's not even smoke."

"Smoke isn't the part you can see that matters," Livia said, though she wasn't sure that made sense until she said it. She ran back to the ring, grabbed the water bucket, and poured. The ash hissed and a curl of steam rose, and underneath, deep in the pile, an orange eye blinked open. She stabbed at it with the stirring stick until the orange closed, poured water again, and the whole ring went dark and quiet.

Ms. Dela Cruz came through the trees with her flashlight swinging. "What did I tell you all this afternoon?" she said, half scolding, half smiling.

"You said it at lunch," Layan said. "Drown it, stir it, drown it again. Then feel for heat, because if a fire is too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave."

"Too hot to touch is too hot to leave," Livia repeated, and held her palm above the ash, then lower, then touching. Warm, but not burning. She kept her hand there longer than she needed to, feeling the small heat that had been hiding under all that innocent gray.

Ms. Dela Cruz let them stay up past lights-out as a reward, and they sat on the cabin steps while Colt named constellations she made up on the spot. Livia should have been happy, and she was, mostly. But lying in her bunk later, listening to Layan breathe, she thought about how she had spent the whole first day homesick, writing a letter she never mailed, and how the only reason she knew to check that fire was because she'd been too miserable to sleep and had watched from her bunk window. The thing that worked for her had come out of the thing that had been worst. Her mom would call that a lesson. Livia just called it strange, and pulled the sleeping bag up to her chin. Outside, somewhere, an owl called twice and went quiet.

At breakfast, Layan slid her the last pancake and said, "You check the fire tonight, okay?"

Alex had saved thirty-two dollars in a cracked envelope under his mattress, and by Saturday he meant to own a used copy of Iron Hollow, the game everyone at school argued about at lunch. The problem was the online marketplace. Three weeks ago, eleven used copies sat on the listings page at fifteen dollars each. Last night there were only two, and the cheapest one was twenty-six dollars.

"They can't just change the price," Alex said on the bus, holding his phone so Heidi could see the screen. "It's the same disc."

Heidi leaned in. "There's still two left, though. Maybe the price drops again if nobody buys them."

Alex stared at the little green number under each listing. It had never occurred to him that a price could move around like a living thing, pushed by something he couldn't see. He decided to run a test. He would check the page every morning and evening, write down the price and the number of copies, and see whether there was a rule underneath it all.

On Tuesday there were two copies at twenty-six dollars. On Wednesday evening, one copy at twenty-eight. On Thursday morning, still one copy, and a seller named Iron Hollow had dropped it to nineteen dollars. By Thursday night it was gone, sold, and a new listing appeared at fourteen dollars, along with four more used copies in the same genre, all cheap. Alex wrote the numbers in his notebook until his hand ached. When the copies were scarce, the price climbed. When a stack of them showed up, the price sank like a stone in a pond.

He showed the notebook to Reet at lunch. Reet frowned at the columns. "So when lots of people want the scarce ones, the sellers can charge more, and then everybody stops buying?"

"And when the price drops, people buy more again," Alex said. "Heidi calls it the law of demand. It works as long as nothing else changes, like a new sequel coming out."

Reet tapped the page. "You have eighteen dollars and the price is fourteen. That's your window."

That night Alex asked his dad for the laptop, and his pulse did a strange leap when he opened the marketplace. There were six copies now, six, and the cheapest was twelve dollars. He clicked it so fast the touchpad squeaked. He typed his shipping address, checked the box, and pressed Buy.

The confirmation banner glowed at the top of the screen. Alex sat back, and a grin spread across his face, wide and involuntary. From the kitchen his dad called, "Is everything all right in there?"

"Everything is great," Alex shouted. He photographed the screen with his phone to send to Heidi and Reet. "It's coming by Saturday."

Eva had promised the whole coding cabin that by Friday demo night her program would ask for a number and say whether it was prime, and right now it said that 9 was prime, which it was not. She sat at the long pine table with her laptop open, running the loop again and watching the wrong answer blink at her. Kash leaned over from the next seat, grinning. "Nine is prime now? You've discovered new math."

"Don't humiliate me before I've had breakfast," Eva said, but her ears went hot anyway. Hana pulled her chair around so she could see the screen.

The problem was the flag. Eva had set a variable called found to zero, and inside the loop she changed it when a divisor appeared, and after the loop she checked it, except the check kept happening too early, or the flag kept its old value from the run before, or something she couldn't see. That was the worst part. The loop did its work somewhere she couldn't look, and the mistake was hiding in there like a bird in a hedge.

"Birds," Hana said suddenly, pointing at the poster taped to the cabin wall, a map dotted with arrows. "Migratory routes. That one crosses the equator twice, look, it goes all the way down and back." Eva looked, mostly to rest her eyes, and thought about how the map showed where the birds went but not why they knew to go there. Her program was like that too. It showed the answer but not the reason underneath.

Then Mr. Chowdhury, the mentor who ran the cabin, came by with his coffee. He read her screen for a moment, took the marker, and wrote four lines on the little whiteboard beside the table. Her loop, but with the word else tucked under it, and her print statement moved inside that block. He tapped the marker once against the board. "Else," he said, and went to refill his coffee, because he never explained anything twice or even once if he could help it.

Eva stared at it. "A loop gets an else?" she said. Hana frowned. Kash shook his head slowly, which meant he didn't know either, which meant nobody at the table knew, which made Eva feel a little better and a lot more curious.

She traced it with her finger on the screen. The else sat under the for, the way an else sits under an if, and the print was inside it. "So if the loop breaks, the else gets skipped," she said, "and if it never breaks, if it checks every number and finds nothing, then the else runs." No divisor found, so the number is prime. She deleted the flag, typed the else, and hit run.

9: not prime. 7: prime. 11: prime. 25: not prime.

"Run it on a million," Kash said. Eva typed it in.

The assignment was Adam's idea, which meant it was his job to coordinate it: Yara would handle the interviews, Thalia would bring her grandmother's prayer book, and Adam would find a place to start. He chose the old cemetery behind St. Brigid's, where the stones went back over a hundred years and the caretaker, Mr. Campbell-Brown, let students in after school as long as they closed the gate.

"Grandma's stone is this way," Thalia said, leading them past a row of leaning markers. She stopped at a granite slab with a small crucifix carved at the top, a figure on the cross with her head bowed. Yara found her own family a few rows over, at a plain cross with nothing on it, just clean lines. Adam wrote both descriptions in his notebook and stood between the two graves, tapping his pencil.

"Okay, so here's my theory," he said. "The crucifixes mark the Catholic graves and the plain crosses mark the Protestant ones. If the symbols are different, maybe the teachings are different too. So, Thalia, what does your church say happens after you die?"

Thalia brushed lichen off the edge of her grandmother's stone while she thought. "We go to heaven, but first most people go to purgatory," she said. "It's a purification. Like being cleaned up before you go in."

Yara frowned at her. "My church never says that. We go straight to heaven if we're saved. Pastor Ruiz says purgatory isn't in the Bible at all." The two of them stared at each other, and Adam could almost see the surprise traveling between them, because they had sat three seats apart in homeroom since fifth grade and never once guessed their churches disagreed on something this big.

Mr. Campbell-Brown came around the corner with a spray bottle and a stiff brush, working on a marker crusted with green. "Careful where you stand," he said. "This cleaner's corrosive. It'll eat through your shoe laces faster than the moss." Adam stepped back and asked him about the symbols, and the caretaker nodded slowly. "Catholics put up the crucifix, mostly, and the others keep it plain. Been that way longer than me."

Adam flipped to a fresh page and drew two columns, one headed with a crucifix and one with a plain cross. Under the first he wrote purification first, then heaven, and under the second, straight to heaven, no middle state. Then he added a third line at the bottom, for the question he would ask in class on Monday: what else do the two churches see differently that nobody has told us about? Yara borrowed his pencil to underline it, and Thalia zipped her grandmother's prayer book back into her bag as the shadows of the stones stretched long across the grass.

Emile pushed the folding table across the gym floor until it screeched against the volleyball line, and Emilien dumped a shoebox of notecards beside him. "This is our case," Emilien said. "Unbeatable." Ms. Henry had taped a sign to the bleachers that read CLAIM, EVIDENCE, WARRANT, and under it, in smaller letters, if you can't say the warrant, you don't have a point. Emile picked up the first card. It said, in Emilien's sprawling handwriting, "Cousin Jules failed math because of video games."

"Where's the evidence?" Emile asked. Emilien tapped the card. "It's right there. It happened. I watched it happen." Emile thought back to September, when his mother had blamed a broken dishwasher on the new detergent, and his father had quietly run it twice more with the old detergent before saying a word. It had still been broken. One try had proved nothing either way, his father said later, over the last clean plates they owned. Emile hadn't understood why that mattered until now.

He flipped through the rest of the shoebox. Every card circled back to Cousin Jules. "Your whole case," he said slowly, "is one guy." Emilien frowned. "One guy with a dramatic story." From the free-throw line, Maurice called over that his uncle had eaten video games for breakfast, basically, and done calculus in his sleep. Emilien shouted back that Maurice's uncle didn't count because he was "a statistical monster," which was somehow the funniest thing anyone had said all week, and even Ms. Henry, shelving the pinnies, put a hand over her mouth.

Emile laid the cards out in rows, like a coach drawing a play. "Look. Claim: games hurt grades. Evidence: Jules. That's it. There's no warrant connecting one cousin to every student in the school." He picked up a fresh card. "We need to quantify it. Survey thirty kids, games and grades, count them." "Counting is boring," Emilien said. "Counting wins," Emile said. "Ms. Henry's whole system is about being systematic. Claim, evidence, warrant, every single point, no skipping." He glanced up at the sign on the bleachers. "And there's a word for your cousin thing. Anecdotal evidence." Emilien squinted. "Is that an insult?" "It's a category," Emile said. "The category of stories that prove nothing."

Emilien looked at his shoebox, then at Jules's card, then at the empty gym, where thirty desks' worth of students would show up for the debate on Friday. He groaned the groan of a boy about to do real work, and Maurice jogged over with a clipboard he had clearly stolen from the equipment room. "Survey?" Maurice said. "I'll do the hallway before lunch. That's my zone." Emile handed him a pencil. "Fifteen before, fifteen after," he said. "And Jules?" Emilien held up the card, studied it one last time, then clipped it to the bottom of the stack, face down. "Backup material," he said. "For the emotional finale."

The message landed at 4:32 on a Tuesday, right when Christopher was supposed to be meeting Joey and Kurt at the basketball courts behind the school. He pulled out his phone under the bleachers and saw it glowing at the top of the group chat: WHERE ARE YOU, in letters so big and black they seemed to jump off the screen. It was from Kurt. Below it, Joey had already replied, "why are you yelling? lol."

Christopher typed back "omw 5 min" and started jogging. On the way he scrolled up through the chat, because something felt off. Kurt never wrote in capitals. His usual messages were all lowercase, drifting and lazy, things like "maybe i'll come" and "idk might be tired." Today there were three caps messages in a row. WHERE ARE YOU. THEN FORGET IT. NOT WAITING HERE ALL DAY.

At the courts, Kurt was sitting on the far bench with his hood up, spinning a ball on one finger. He didn't look up when Christopher jogged through the gate. Joey was shooting free throws, and he mouthed "good luck" with a grin that said he was planning to enjoy this.

"Hey," Christopher said. "Got held up in science. Mr. Iyer kept us late because half the class turned in, like, one paragraph."

"Whatever," Kurt said, still spinning the ball.

Christopher sat down on the bench. He had a theory forming, and he tested it the way he tested things, carefully, out loud. "You wrote in all caps today. Joey thought you were yelling at us."

"I was not yelling," Kurt said, finally looking up. "It's just typing."

"Kind of yelling, though," Joey called from the foul line. The ball clanked off the rim. "Everybody reads caps that way. It's like shouting on a screen."

Kurt frowned at his phone like it had betrayed him. "Nobody answers my normal messages," he said. "I type 'anyone at the courts' and it just sits there for an hour. I type it big and you two show up in five minutes."

Christopher checked the chat history to be sure, scrolling back two weeks. He counted. Kurt's lowercase messages got answered, on average, maybe once in five, a rough ratio of one reply for every five sent. Then again, half of those had been sent at ten at night, when everyone else's phones were off, so quiet hours and being ignored often coincided. The caps messages had been sent at peak time, right after school. That was probably the whole difference. "It's not the size," Christopher said. "It's the timing. You text us at ten p.m. and expect us to answer. Nobody's awake. My phone is off and I'm lethargic by then anyway, half asleep on the couch."

"So I shouted for nothing," Kurt said.

"You shouted and it worked out badly," Joey said, jogging over. "Christopher showed up because you texted at the right time, and now we all think you're mad."

Kurt pulled his hood down. There was a silence that was almost funny, the three of them standing there while the truth sat in the middle of the court like a loose ball nobody wanted to pick up. "I wasn't mad," Kurt said. "I just wanted to play."

"Then next time type like a normal person," Christopher said, "with one or two question marks, and maybe wait longer than nine minutes before declaring an emergency."

"Nine minutes," Joey repeated, delighted. "It was nine minutes."

"Fine, fine." Kurt stood up, bounced the ball once, hard. "First to eleven. Losers explain group chat etiquette to Mr. Iyer."

"He already knows," Christopher said, taking position at the top of the key. "He's the only one who types in lowercase and still gets answers."

Romy had six minutes to figure out how the new student should be greeted, and her spreadsheet of welcome ideas had failed her completely. She sat in the empty computer lab, scrolling through a school database of international student records that Ms. Joshi had left open on the desktop. Faris, transferring from a school in New Zealand, was arriving today, and Romy, as head of the welcome committee, wanted the greeting to be right. Not an approximate guess, but right.

She had one clue. In the notes column of his file, a previous teacher had written a single strange line: "greets with hongi." Romy searched the word and found a photo of two people pressing their noses and foreheads together, eyes almost closed. She read that it was a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand, and that it meant the sharing of the breath of life. She read it twice, because it sounded made up, like something Kabir would invent for a bet.

She decided to test it. If she offered her hand and Faris expected a hongi, the moment would go stiff and wrong, and a whole year of awkward homeroom mornings would be thwarted before it began. So at the door of the gym, when Faris arrived with his aunt and a box of mangoes for the class, Romy leaned in and pressed her nose and forehead gently against his. For a second he was completely still. Then he smiled so wide that his aunt laughed, and Kabir, holding the banner behind them, nearly dropped it.

"You know the hongi," Faris said.

"It's for sharing the breath of life," Romy said. "Right?"

He nodded and handed her a mango, and she gave him the welcome folder she had decorated, because in her grandmother's house no guest ever arrived without a gift and no host ever let one leave without one. Faris turned the folder over in his hands like it was something rare. In return his aunt insisted Romy keep a mango, refusing three times before Romy understood that refusing back was part of the game.

At lunch, Faris sat with his elbows off the table, waiting until everyone was served before he ate, while Kabir tore his parantha with his fingers and reached across for the pickle. Romy watched them both and realized politeness was not one rule but a hundred different ones, and the only way to learn them was to lean in, nose first.

"Same time tomorrow?" Faris asked, lifting his mango.

"Same time tomorrow," Romy said, and pressed her palm flat on the table like a promise.

Victor had the folded paper in his back pocket all through school, and the moment he got home he spread it on the kitchen table like a treasure map. His prescription, the optometrist had called it, and next to two sets of numbers were the letters OD and OS. He'd assumed OD meant something ordinary until Winnie, peering over his shoulder on the bus, had gone quiet and said, "Sinister is right there. OS. That can't be good." Now Victor sat alone at the table, turning the paper toward the window light, trying to decide whether to be worried.

He texted Winnie, who lived two houses down, and she arrived within minutes with her bike helmet still on. "Did you look it up?" she asked.

"No. I want to figure it out first." He tapped the paper. "There's a trick my grandpa, a veteran, uses for puzzles. Read what's actually there, not what you're afraid of. The doctor measured my eyes one at a time, remember? She covered my left eye, then my right. So the two lines have to mean one eye each." He covered his own left eye with his palm and squinted at the clock across the kitchen. The numbers were a smear. Then he covered his right eye, and the clock sharpened a little, still fuzzy but readable. "My right eye is the worse one. Now I just need to know which line is the right eye."

"That's the scary line," Winnie said. "The one with more numbers."

Victor studied the paper. The OD line had the bigger numbers. If his right eye was worse, and OD held the bigger correction, then OD had to be his right eye, and OS his left. "It fits," he said slowly. "But I don't know why they'd call it that."

He called the optometrist's office. The receptionist put him on hold, and a second voice came on, an older woman who sounded like she'd answered this question a thousand times. "OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye, from the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister," she said. "It's on every prescription we write."

Winnie let out a breath. "So sinister just means left. I donated a whole afternoon to being scared of that."

"You were scared for both of us," Victor said, and she laughed. He thanked the woman and hung up, then carried the paper to the fridge and pinned it under the magnet shaped like a slice of pizza. In a week the actual glasses would arrive, and the clock on the wall, the one that had been a smear for months, would have crisp black hands and readable numbers.

"Come on," Winnie said, grabbing his sleeve. "Before your mom gets home, let's test your bad eye on the stop sign at the corner. I'll cover one at a time."

Addisson had signed up for drama camp expecting improv games, not debate, but on the first Tuesday Ms. Sharma announced a mock trial about whether the camp's ancient furnace should be replaced. "Building a case is acting too," she said. "You're performing an argument." Addison wanted the lead role, which meant she had to build a case with a claim, evidence, and a warrant for every point, and she had no idea what a warrant was.

Her team drew the side against replacement, which felt impossible. Everyone in the rehearsal hall had frozen in the same draft all week. Jaiveer wanted to open with a story about a little kid shivering in the hallway. "It'll make the judges cry," he said. "Crying wins."

Their opponents, led by Andrei, showed up with a clipboard. He rattled off numbers: repair logs, temperature readings, the cost of a new boiler against ten more years of patching. He didn't raise his voice once. When Jaiveer told his shivering story, one judge nodded, but the other two kept writing on their pads, and when the verdict came, the numbers team won. Addison stared at the score sheet and felt something shift in her head, like finding the mechanism inside a magic trick. The sad story had moved people, but it hadn't proved anything.

That night she couldn't hibernate like the camp rabbit in the nature hut display; she lay awake turning it over. In the camp library she found a battered copy of Aristotle's "Rhetoric" and read until her flashlight dimmed. The next morning she found Jaiveer at breakfast. "He said there are three ways to persuade," she told him. "Ethos, pathos, and logos. Pathos is the emotions, like your story. Logos is reasoning and evidence, like Andrei's clipboard. And ethos is whether the judges trust the speaker." Jaiveer set down his toast. "So we used one out of three."

"Exactly. We need all three." They spent a tedious afternoon rebuilding the case. Claim: the furnace should not be replaced this year. Evidence: the repair records and the budget numbers, checked twice. Warrant: if the records show the furnace has broken down only once in three years, and the camp needs that money for scholarships, then replacement can wait. Addison practiced her delivery until the other campers started calling her "the lawyer."

At the rematch, Andrei raised an eyebrow at her new clipboard but stuck to his old speech, smooth and confident. Addison gave the numbers first, then, at the end, one story, about a camper who might not come back next year without the scholarship fund. She watched the second judge put down her pen. When Ms. Sharma called the debate for Addison's team, Jaiveer grabbed her arm and lifted it like a referee. "The lawyer rests," he said, and the whole hall laughed.

Anna slid her presentation notes across the lab table so Alanna could see them. "The reward pathway," she said, tapping her diagram of the brain. "That's the part nicotine hijacks. It floods the pathway with dopamine, and the brain learns to want it again."

Mr. Malik had given them a week to prepare their health talk, and Anna had spent most of it drawing arrows on her poster. The arrows were the easy part. The hard part was the question he kept asking: not just what nicotine did, but why people couldn't simply stop.

"It's like being hungry," Alanna offered. "Sort of."

"Except you can postpone lunch," Anna said. "My cousin Marcus vapes, and he can't postpone anything. Last summer he got restless at my house every couple of hours and had to go outside. Every time. I used to think he just liked standing in the driveway."

She thought about that summer now, how she'd teased him about it, and how his jaw had tightened before he laughed. She hadn't understood what she was watching. Maybe she should have.

"Wait," Alanna said slowly. "Every couple of hours. Like clockwork?"

Anna pulled out her phone and found the note she'd made in August, back when she'd started counting out of curiosity. 10:15, driveway. 12:30, driveway. 2:40, driveway. "I looked it up this morning," she said. "The body clears about half the nicotine in roughly two hours. That's why the effect fades so fast and he'd get the urge for another dose. His brain wanted the pathway flooded again, and the level in his blood kept dropping."

"So his brain isn't broken," Alanna said. "It's just following a schedule he never asked for."

"Basically." Anna taped her diagram to the whiteboard, then stood back and frowned at it. The arrows went one direction only. She uncapped a marker and drew a loop: nicotine in, dopamine up, level falls, urge, nicotine in again. "We should present it like this. Not a straight line. A circle."

During fifth period, Payton wandered over to their table while they practiced. "You're going to tell everyone my brother's got a two-hour timer in his head?" she said. She didn't sound angry, exactly, but she didn't smile either.

"I'm not naming anyone," Anna said. "Just the science." She hesitated, because last summer she'd named Marcus to half the neighborhood as a joke. "I didn't get it back then. I do now."

Payton picked up the marker and added a small stick figure on the loop, right where the urge was. "Put him there," she said. "That's exactly what Ty looks like when he's waiting."

The bell above the door of his grandfather's study had a way of announcing Oliver before he could knock, and today it rang twice because his elbow caught it on the way in. He was carrying a notebook with a school assignment folded inside: compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. He had until Monday, and so far his page had one word on it, which was "heaven," and a doodle of a cloud.

"Grandpa, can I ask you something for my project?" He set the notebook on the desk between a jar of pens and a small brass lamp that his grandfather lit every morning. "You're Hindu, and Grandma was raised going to church. So you two believed really different things, right?"

His grandfather put down his newspaper. "Sit. Ask."

Oliver sat on the stiff wooden chair he had sat on since he was six, when his feet had not reached the floor. "Okay. So in church they say you go to heaven, and that's the best thing. And in Hinduism you get reborn. So is being reborn the good part? Like, the reward?"

His grandfather's eyebrows went up, and Oliver knew he had gotten something wrong, the same feeling as handing in a math test and watching the teacher pause at question four.

"Let me show you something." His grandfather opened a drawer and took out a photograph, luminous in the lamplight, of Oliver's great-grandmother standing in a doorway with her hands folded. "She was a veteran of many things, your great-grandmother. Hard years, good years. Suppose she is born again after this life. Then born again after that. And again. A wheel that keeps turning."

"Forever?"

"For a very long time. Now, is that what she would hope for, or escape from?"

Oliver looked at the photograph. The woman in it looked tired in a patient way, like someone who had carried a lot and set it down carefully. He turned his pencil over in his fingers, thinking. If heaven was the goal in Grandma's old church, then maybe Hinduism had a goal too, and maybe the goal was not more turns of the wheel. "So there's something past the wheel," he said slowly. "Getting off it."

His grandfather smiled, one of his small ones that Oliver had to earn. "It is called moksha," he said. "Liberation from the cycle of rebirth. It is the highest goal of human life."

Oliver wrote it down, spelling it twice under his breath to get it right. Then he read back what he had. "So both of them have a highest thing. Heaven for Grandma's church, moksha for yours. They're not the same, but they're both like, the top of the mountain." He paused. "Different paths up it?"

"That is your project, beta. I only answer questions."

Oliver grinned and flipped to a fresh page to make a chart. He would allocate one column to each faith, with rebirth and the stopping of rebirth on one side and heaven on the other, and he would need more room than Monday allowed. Footsteps came down the hall, and his grandmother appeared with a plate of sliced mango, setting it between the notebook and the lamp without a word, the way she always did when she knew he would be there awhile.

"Take two pieces," his grandfather said, pushing the plate toward him. "You have a mountain to draw."

Evelyn jammed her backpack into the seat beside her and pulled out the folded printout of the district swim standings. The bus rattled out of the school lot, and she smoothed the paper on her knee. There it was: Ridgeview relays, ranked first; her own team, ranked second. One spot. Two weeks until the final meet.

"You're staring again," said Louka, dropping into the seat across the aisle. She held up her phone, screen out. "Kylian's mom recorded the state finals from TV. Watch this race, the hundred-meter freestyle. It's insane."

Evelyn leaned over. Two swimmers hit the wall nearly together, and the clock on the screen split them: one finished in 47.31, the other in 47.32.

"A hundredth of a second," Louka breathed. "That's a blink. That's less than a blink." She replayed it three times, and Evelyn watched the silver medalist's face each time, like she was hoping the ending might change.

Evelyn sat back. Second place by a hundredth of a second. Her team was second in the district standings. She had been picturing her team as just barely behind Ridgeview, close enough to touch, because that was what second place felt like. But the rankings never said how far apart first and second actually were. The gap could be a hundredth of a second, or it could be a whole minute. She dug into her bag for a pencil. On the back of the printout she copied the times listed under the standings: Ridgeview's season-best relay, then her team's. She subtracted. Seven seconds. Seven whole seconds, not seven hundredths. She let that digest while the bus swayed around the corner by the bakery.

"That's not a blink," she said out loud.

"What?" Louka looked up.

"The rankings only show order. They don't show distance. We could be behind by a hundredth or by a minute, and the paper looks exactly the same." She tapped the standings. "I did the math. We're seven seconds back. I thought we were close. We're not close."

Louka's shoulders dropped, but then she lifted the phone again. "Okay, but watch this one. The same silver medalist, a different year." On the screen, the swimmer lost by a margin so wide the camera cut away before she touched the wall. "Second place again," Louka said quietly. "Same rank. Totally different race. I keep watching her because I want to figure out what she does after she loses. She wrote a memoir about it, did I tell you? My mom ordered it. The cover says she came back and won the next season."

Kylian shoved down the aisle and grabbed the pole, out of breath. "Coach posted the lineup. Evelyn, you're anchoring the relay." He grinned. "You. The last leg. Seven seconds is a lot, but the anchor swims against their anchor, and their anchor had a bad taper last year, and if you go out fast and hold, and Louka gains on the second leg, and we all drop half a second, that's two seconds right there, and relays are weird, anything can happen."

"Half a second each," Evelyn said, writing it down, the numbers suddenly durable and real on the page instead of a fog of worry. "Louka, second leg. That's you."

Louka closed the video and sat up straight. "Then I'm not just watching the silver medalist anymore. I'm going to swim like her next year, after she came back."

The bus hissed to a stop at the corner by the pool, and Kylian was already first through the doors, shouting, "Seven seconds! Let's go eat them!"

The trail dropped toward the river just as the sun cleared the ridge, and Elizabeth stopped so suddenly that Annabel bumped into her backpack. Below them the canyon walls rose in bands of color, red and cream and a thin stripe of black near the bottom, like a layer cake cut open by the river itself.

"We have to figure this out before Ms. Navarro's talk tonight," Elizabeth said, pulling out her notebook. Their assignment was to explain, at the campfire, how a river could carve a canyon over millions of years, and she had promised to have an answer that made sense.

Braelynn crouched at the edge and pointed at the highest stripe, a pale band near the rim. "I bet that top layer is the oldest. It's the biggest one, so it must have taken the longest to make."

Elizabeth wrote it down, then frowned at it. Something about the guess bothered her, though she couldn't say what. "Let's test it," she said. "Not the whole canyon. Something small."

Below the trail, a side stream trickled down a slope of sand and gravel left by earlier floods. Elizabeth found a flat tin plate from her cook kit and set it in the streambed where the water slowed. "If the river drops stuff when it slows down, then whatever lands first should end up underneath." Annabel poured a handful of dark gravel into the current upstream, and after some of it tumbled past, a few pebbles sank onto the plate. Then Braelynn poured white sand. It settled over the dark pebbles in a thin, even sheet.

Elizabeth tipped the plate out, studied the little pile, and felt her stomach jump. The white sand sat on top. The dark pebbles, which had arrived first, lay on the bottom.
