She ate dinner, texted Selma a grumpy message, and went to bed early, almost hoping to sleep the whole problem away.

At seven the next morning she was back in the band room, alone except for the hum of the radiator. She lifted the flute, breathed in, and played measure thirty-four. Every note landed clean, one after another, fast and exact, and the last one rang out like a small bell. She stared at the keys. She had not practiced even once since last night. She played it again to be sure, and again it worked.

At lunch she dragged Selma to the library computer and typed in sleep and finger practice. She read aloud, quiet and fast: "A night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve performance the next day without any extra practice." Selma leaned over her shoulder.

"So your hands kept working while you slept, and you got better for free," Selma said.

"That's what it looks like." Kaitlyn closed the search window and grinned. "So Friday, I'm going to practice the hard part, then sleep, then walk into rehearsal and nail it."

"Mr. Swampy is going to cherish that," said Selma. "He keeps telling everyone sleep fixes more than they think."

Kaitlyn picked up her flute case. "Then let's go tell him measure thirty-four is fixed."

Ryder crouched beside the trail map at the base of the ridge, tracing the dotted line with one finger while Kyan leaned over his shoulder. "Mr. Campbell said we each have to teach the group something on the way up," Kyan said. "You picked monsoons, right?" Ryder nodded, though his stomach had been uneasy since breakfast. Last month he had stood in front of his class with a poster about rain in South Asia, and it had gone badly. He had said the ocean pushes water at the land, Juno had asked how, and he had frozen. The whole class had laughed, and the memory still stung like a scraped knee. He did not want today to humiliate him the same way twice.

The three of them started up the switchbacks, Juno taking the lead with the water bottle everyone had forgotten to fill properly. "So teach us," she called back. "My cousin in India texted me yesterday. She said the rain arrives right when the heat is worst, and she wants to know why." Ryder opened his mouth, and the old wrong answer crowded in, the ocean pushing, and he shut it again. "Give me a minute," he said. "I want to get it right this time."

At the lookout they stopped. Below them the land stretched dry and brown to the west, but to the east, far off, the valley turned green where the river ran through it, the fields along it fertile and crammed with crops. Ryder stared at the two sides of the view and something clicked into place, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. Land and water, side by side, acting differently. He remembered his cousin's rice paddies in the photos she sent, standing in water, drinking sky.

"Okay," he said, pulling out his notebook. He pointed at the brown slope beneath them, baked in the afternoon sun, then at the green line of the valley. "In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean." He put his hand on a sun-hot rock, then imagined the river below, cooler even now. "So warm air rises over the land." He raised his palm and lifted it slowly. "And moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it." He swept his other hand inland like a slow wave.

"That's why the rain comes when the heat is worst," Juno said slowly, watching his hands. "The hottest time is when the moist air is pouring in." Kyan grinned. "And the rice needs all that water. That's why it matters so much there." Ryder felt the knot in his stomach loosen. Whether the class would laugh at him again next week, he still did not know, and he guessed he would find out either way.

They hiked on toward the ridge, and Juno handed him her phone with her cousin's last message glowing on the screen: "So explain it to me, then." Ryder began typing, one careful sentence at a time, while the trail climbed ahead of them into the pines.

The living room was so full that Brody had to sit on the arm of the couch, next to Lexie, who was wearing an elastic headband in team colours and had claimed the good spot hours before kickoff. On the screen, the pregame show flashed old highlights while the commentator talked about history. That was when the argument started.

"Brazil won the first World Cup," said Brody's uncle, absolutely certain. "Everybody knows that."

"No, it was England," said the coach, who had come over with a cooler of snacks. "They invented the game."

"England invented the game, sure," Lexie's grandfather said from the recliner, "but they didn't win the first one. I think it was Argentina."

Lexie groaned beside Brody. "Every time we watch a game, this happens. Last month they argued for a whole hour about the offside rule." She had a reason to care, too. She had appointed herself official scorekeeper for their living room predictions, and she kept a chart on the fridge. Whoever guessed right about the first World Cup question would get bragging rights for the rest of the season, and she wanted that to be her.

Brody didn't say anything at first. He was doing what he always did when the grown-ups started up: sorting through what he actually knew versus what he had merely heard. He remembered a page from a book he'd read in Mr. Côté's class last year, something about a small country that hosted a huge tournament. But a fuzzy memory wasn't evidence. If he was going to settle this, he needed to test it.

"I'll be right back," he said, and slipped out to the hall bookshelf where the soccer books lived. The book was there, its spine cracked from being opened so many times. He carried it back into the living room, where the argument had now expanded to include whether the first tournament had even had a final.

"Wait," Brody said. He set the book on the coffee table and turned the pages carefully. "It says here the first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930. And Uruguay won it. They beat Argentina four to two in the final."

The room went quiet except for the television. Lexie leaned over to see the page herself, because she was not the trusting kind. "Four to two," she confirmed. "It's right there."

"Well," said her grandfather, sitting up straighter in the recliner, "then I was half right. Argentina was in the final."

"Half right isn't right," the coach said, but he was grinning. "Kid, you just saved us from another hour of this."

Lexie got up and went to the fridge. She came back holding her prediction chart and a marker. "So nobody gets the point," she said, "since you all guessed wrong." Then she paused, marker hovering. "Except Brody didn't guess. He looked it up." She thought for a moment, then wrote his name in the point column anyway. "Research counts double in my system."

"That's not how your system worked yesterday," Brody said.

"It's how it works now," said Lexie, and she capped the marker with a click just as the referee's whistle pierced the room and everybody turned back to the screen.

Hudson sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open and a spreadsheet full of numbers that refused to mean anything. Three hundred and forty students had answered the survey about the museum field trip, rating it from one to five, and his job was to document the results for the school newspaper by Friday. He had a column of grades, a column of ratings, and no idea which grade had actually liked the trip.

He had tried sorting, which just rearranged the mess. Then his father, passing through with the mail, said, "You need a pivot table," the way he said things like "you need a pension plan," as if Hudson were thirty-five with a desk job. Hudson found the button anyway, dragged the grade column into Rows and the rating column into Values, and watched the spreadsheet count for him: forty-one sixth graders, fifty-three seventh graders, sixty-two eighth graders. Counting, though, only told him how many people answered, not what they thought. Sixty-two eighth graders could have all hated it.

He texted Cecelia, who had done the data project last semester. "How do you make ratings into one number per grade?" She sent back a screenshot with a tiny dropdown circled in red, the one that said "Count." He clicked it. The list offered Sum, Count, and Average. He chose Average, mostly because he was out of ideas, and the numbers changed: sixth grade 4.7, seventh grade 4.2, eighth grade 3.1. There it was. The sixth graders had loved the dinosaur hall, the eighth graders apparently had not, and one rating at a time had hidden the whole pattern until he switched the summary from Count to Average. He tested it, to be sure, by switching to Sum and back again, and the same means reappeared every time.

He remembered the assembly in September, when the principal had asked for feedback and then read out three random comments, one of them from an eighth grader who called the trip "fine." Everyone laughed, and nobody asked whether "fine" was the whole story. Maybe it hadn't been. Maybe the principal hadn't known about averages either. Hudson wasn't sure whether that made the man careless or just busy, and he left the question alone while he built a bar chart of the three means.

Mr. Sutherland knocked on the back door just as Hudson finished, holding a plate of biscuits because that was how their street worked. "Still fighting with that spreadsheet?" the old man asked. "My wife used to say those things were versatile. She ran a whole charity on one."

"Look at this," Hudson said, and turned the screen toward him. "Eighth grade gave the trip a 3.1."

The market smelled like apples and grilled corn, and Matthew stood behind Ms. Zhang's table with a crate of onions at his elbow. He was there because his mother had signed them both up for the Saturday cooking demo, and because Campbell had left a note in his locker that morning: "I might come by the market. If I'm not busy." Campbell was always busy lately, ever since Matthew had called his eating habits childish in front of half the cafeteria.

"Claw grip," Ms. Zhang said, curling her fingers so the knuckles jutted forward like a small pale wall. "The blade rides your knuckles. The onion is too tough to bite you." Matthew copied her, tucking his fingertips in, and brought the knife down through the onion in slow slices. His eyes burned, and he turned his head away. "The fumes feel toxic," he said, blinking hard. Ms. Zhang laughed. "Water in a bowl by the board helps. They drift toward it." There was a small pot of water already set out, and after he moved the bowl closer, the stinging eased.

"Raw pieces taste sharp," Ms. Zhang said, pushing a sliver toward him. He tried it and his whole mouth puckered. "Now watch what heat does." She melted butter in a wide pan, turned the flame to its lowest setting, and poured the onions in. "Slow," she said. "You can't quantify patience with a timer. You go by color." Matthew stirred every few minutes and kept a scrap sheet clear of the floor, because the hand-lettered sign at the stall said raw onion was toxic to dogs, and someone's terrier was sniffing under the table.

While the onions cooked, Campbell appeared at the end of the row, hands in his pockets, pretending to examine a basket of peppers. The note had said "if I'm not busy," but here he was, ten minutes after the market opened. Matthew decided not to say anything about it. "We're making sauce," he called instead. "You can stir if you want."

Campbell drifted over and picked up the wooden spoon. The onions in the pan had gone soft and golden, and the smell was completely different from the sharp raw one, sweet and brown like something baked. "That's the same onion?" Campbell asked, leaning in. "Taste it," Matthew said. Campbell shook his head. "I don't eat onions. You know that." He watched the steam valve on the lid of the pasta pot rattle, then looked back at the pan.

"Your loss," Matthew said, and lifted a golden strand out on the spoon, blew on it, and ate it himself. Campbell stared at the pan for a second, then took the spoon before Matthew could set it down and tried a piece. He chewed slowly. "Okay," he said. "Put some in my bowl. More than yours."

Emilie had been playing the borrowed violin for exactly six days, and it still sounded like a cat complaining. Worse, it had stopped matching the piano. On Monday, her open strings had matched Ms. Henry's notes. By Thursday, one of them had gone flat, and she couldn't tell which one or why.

In the band room after school, she tuned against the piano again. The A string was the culprit. When she played it with the piano key, the two sounds wobbled against each other, a slow, seasick pulse. She remembered something odd, though. When she loosened the tuning peg last Tuesday, just to see what it did, the note had slid downward as the string slackened. Tightening had pulled it back up. She had assumed she bumped something else. Now she wondered.

"If the string's tighter, does it vibrate faster?" she asked herself under her breath. "Faster vibration, higher pitch. Slower, lower." It was a guess, a pattern with exactly one example behind it, and she wanted to test it before she trusted it.

Ajay was in the corner assembling his trombone. He wanted the band's small "democracy," as Ms. Henry jokingly called the vote for section leader, to go his way next week, and he'd been practicing until the custodian kicked him out. He slid his chair over. "What are you doing?"

"Testing something." Emilie plucked the string, listened, then loosened the peg a tiny bit and plucked again. The note dropped, unmistakably. She tightened it back and the pitch rose. "So loosening makes it vibrate slower and sound lower. That's what happened all week. The peg's been slipping on its own, a little every day."

"That's why you've been getting flatter," Ajay said.

"Exactly. It wasn't me." She turned the peg slowly, plucking after each small adjustment, chasing the wobble between her string and the piano until the two sounds locked together and the pulse vanished. She did the same for the other strings, even though only one had drifted, checking each against the piano so nothing else crept down on her.

Ajay watched, then pointed at her peg. "Push it in a little when you turn. Mine did that last year."

She pressed the peg firmly into its hole as she gave it a final nudge. The note held steady, bright and matching the piano, and she played the scale Ms. Henry had assigned, all the way up, every note clean. Ajay lifted his trombone and played the same scale beside her.

Bennett set six bean plants on the kitchen table in a row, all in matching yogurt cups. The science fair was in five days, and his project claimed that fertilizer made plants grow faster. The problem was that all six plants had been fertilized since day one, and while they were tall and green, Matilda's question from yesterday kept bugging him. "Faster than what?" she had asked, tilting her head at his poster. He had said "than normal," and she had said "like what normal?" and he had said "just normal," which even he could tell was a terrible answer.

"You're staring at beans like they're going to confess," said his little sister, dropping her backpack on a chair.

"They might have to," Bennett said.

His mom's plant sat on the windowsill above the sink, a scraggly little bean in plain dirt that had never gotten a drop of fertilizer. Bennett looked at it, then at his six, and felt something click. His plants weren't proof of anything. If he'd never raised a bean without fertilizer, then even the scraggly windowsill plant couldn't save him, because it had different dirt, a different window, different watering. Everything about it was different, so any difference in height could come from any of those things, not just the fertilizer. What he needed was plants treated exactly like his six, same cups, same window, same water, except for the one thing being tested. He grabbed his notebook and wrote it down before the idea could escape.

He called Matilda. "I'm starting over," he said. "Eight new beans. Four get fertilizer, four don't. Everything else identical."

"Those are called a control group," Matilda said. "Lyla did one for her mold project. Four untouched, four gross."

"Four gross," Bennett repeated gravely. "That's basically a metaphor for my whole week."

Five days was tight but a bean in a wet paper towel could sprout in three, and Ms. Szabó had said late entries could show growth charts instead of finished plants. On Saturday morning, he lined up the new cups on the table, measured his windowsill plant for the hundredth time, and texted Matilda a photo of two identical sprouts, one labeled F and one labeled N. He titled it "The showdown is imminent." She replied with a bean emoji and the words "my money's on the plain one."

By Monday, all eight had poked up through the soil, and the plain ones were, annoyingly, slightly ahead. Bennett grinned anyway and wrote the numbers down. The data was doing exactly what data was supposed to do, which was refuse to agree with him yet. "Grow," he told the control group. "Or don't. Either way, I finally have something to measure."

Austin sat at Xander's kitchen table with his Spanish book open to a blank page. The assignment was due Monday: one paragraph about plans for next year, all in the future tense. Xander's grandmother had offered to check their work, and Xander, who had spoken Spanish since he was small, kept leaning over to peek at Austin's paper.

"You wrote 'yo jugo fútbol el año que viene,'" Xander said. "That's not future tense. That's like saying you already juice soccer."

Austin erased the sentence so hard the paper ripped a little. The problem was that he couldn't find the future anywhere. He flipped to the verb charts in the back of the book. In Spanish, the future was built right onto the verb itself, an ending you could see and hear. Then a question slid into his mind and wouldn't leave. He tried it out loud. "Wait. What's the future ending in English?"

Xander stopped chewing his granola bar. "What?"

"The ending. Like Spanish has one. What is it for English?"

Xander opened his mouth, closed it, and stared at the table. "There isn't one," he said slowly, like he didn't trust his own answer. His grandmother, stirring soup at the stove, laughed and said something in Spanish that made Xander's ears go red.

Austin grabbed a napkin and wrote three sentences: I will run. I am going to run. I run tomorrow. He looked for the ending on "run" in every one of them. Nothing changed on the verb. The future lived somewhere else entirely, in the words sitting in front of it. Will. Going to. That was the whole system. He tested it against the window, the fridge, Xander's dog snoring under the chair: the chair will break, the soup is going to boil. It held every time. The insight felt like finding a trapdoor in a floor he'd walked across his whole life.

"So English just borrows helper words," Xander said, reading over his shoulder. "Spanish incorporates the future right into the verb. That's actually kind of cool."

Austin started his paragraph over. He wrote about next year in careful Spanish, attaching the future endings where they belonged, and when he got stuck he checked the napkin. His plan was modest: he would join the Spanish club, he would learn to cook his grandmother's rice, he would visit the affluent neighborhood across town where his cousin lived, because his cousin had promised him a tour. When he finished, Xander's grandmother read the whole thing and nodded.

"Buen trabajo," she said, and set a bowl of soup in front of him. Austin picked up his spoon, then paused. "The soup will be amazing," he said, and grinned at Xander. "See? No ending. Just a helper."

The cafeteria had been turned into a restaurant called El Sol, with paper tablecloths and a chalkboard menu, and Ms. Farah-Ali stood at the door collecting imaginary reservations. Brayden's grade depended on ordering a full meal in Spanish and asking what it cost. That was the whole assignment. It sounded easy until he remembered he had exactly one week of restaurant vocabulary and a tendency to say the first word that came into his head.

He sat down across from Cleo, who was rehearsing under her breath like the menu might be confiscated. At the next table, Sirine was already playing server for another group, pad in hand, wearing the unimpressed expression of someone working a double shift.

"Quiero el taco," Brayden said when his turn came. Sirine wrote it down without looking up. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

"Seis dólares." Flat. Businesslike. She moved to the next table.

Brayden watched her take Cleo's order, and something bothered him. Sirine hadn't been rude exactly, but she hadn't smiled either, and he'd seen her smile at the table before his, twice. He ran the orders back through his head. The boy at the first table had said something longer, something with a soft sound at the front. Quisiera. Brayden had written it in his notes and then, in the margin, "???"

He had a theory. Maybe the word itself carried the attitude. He'd noticed in English that "I want" and "may I have" got different reactions from his mother, and his mother was one person, but here was a second data point. One server, two words, two faces. That wasn't proof. But it was testable.

He waited until Sirine looped back to take dessert orders. Cleo went first, said "quiero el flan," and got the same polite blankness. Then Brayden leaned forward and tried it.

"Quisiera el helado," he said. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

Sirine's pad stopped midair. She smiled, an actual smile, and said, "Tres dólares, y muy buena elección," which he understood well enough to feel his ears go warm.

"So that's the trick," Cleo whispered. "Quisiera."

"Means 'I would like,'" Brayden whispered back. "I want versus I would like. Watch." He raised his hand and called Sirine over one more time, purely for research. "Quisiera agua, por favor." Smile. Then, quietly, just to check, "quiero una servilleta." The smile thinned to a professional line. The pattern held. Two trials, same result, both directions.

After class, Ms. Farah-Ali stopped him at the door. "You ordered three times, Brayden."

"I wanted to preserve the data," he said. "Science." She looked at him for a moment, then wrote something in her grade book that was probably good.

Cleo caught up with him in the hall. "Tomorrow I'm trying it on the lunch lady."

"She doesn't speak Spanish."

"The attitude translates," Cleo said, and pushed through the doors toward the cafeteria.

Rebecca spread her outline across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with the salt shaker and a mug of cold cocoa. The prompt, printed at the top in her careful printing, read: Should our school switch to a four-day week? She had written her thesis at the bottom of the page: Our school should switch to a four-day week. Below it sat her three points: it saves money on buses, it cuts energy costs, and it lowers spending on electricity. The clock over the stove ticked while she read them over.

Mr. Hu had said the outline governed the whole essay; whatever she put in those three lines would decide every paragraph that came after. So she wanted to get them right before drafting a single word. She slid point one to the top and tapped the pencil against her teeth.

Her phone buzzed against the wood. It was Titus, whose class had done the same assignment last period. He had offered to trade reviews, so Rebecca photographed her outline and sent it, then pulled his toward her. His essay argued for keeping the school garden, and his points were that gardens teach science, that gardens need water to grow, and that gardens attract bees. She frowned at that and typed: your point two isn't a reason, it's just a fact.

His reply came fast. Yours is worse. Look at two and three.

She read them again. Cuts energy costs. Lowers spending on electricity. The cocoa had gone bitter at the bottom of the mug, and she took a sip anyway while she stared. Both of those said the school spends less money. The words were different, but the reason underneath was one reason wearing two shirts. She counted on her fingers: bus money, energy money. That was it. Two.

She tried a fix. If point three had to be truly different, she needed a reason that wasn't about money at all. She thought about Skyler, who took care of her little brothers every day and still made honor roll; a free day might help students like her, or it might strand them. Rebecca turned the pencil over and erased. New point three: a longer weekend gives students time for jobs and family. That was a different kind of reason, and the classroom suddenly felt like fertile ground in her mind, full of examples she could actually use: Skyler's schedule, the farm stand on Route 9 that hired eighth graders on Saturdays.

She texted Titus back: you were right, two of mine were the same reason in disguise. Do I get to fix yours? She wrote under his outline: if gardens need water, then your job is to prove the school can afford the watering, so merge that into point one. Then find a second real reason. He sent back a thumbs-up and a photo of his dog asleep on his homework.

Rebecca copied her outline onto a clean sheet, all three lines sitting level under the thesis like fence posts the same height. She read them aloud in the quiet kitchen, and the third one made her think of Skyler again, and of the empathy Mr. Hu kept asking them to show for readers who disagreed. Fine, she thought, she would answer the skeptics too. She sharpened the pencil with the little sharpener screwed to the wall and started her first draft, "Our school should switch to a four-day week, because it saves money on buses, lowers energy costs, and gives students time for work and family."

The art shack at Camp Windrow smelled of pine sap and pencil shavings, and Jonathan had claimed the stool by the window because it gave him a view of the dirt road that curved past the mess hall. He wanted his drawing to look like a real street, with depth that pulled you in, but his first attempt had come out flat as a pancake. Mylo leaned over his shoulder and squinted at it.

"Looks like the road is standing up," Mylo said. "Like a wall with lines on it."

"Thanks," Jonathan said, but he knew it was true. Ms. Johansson, the art instructor, had pinned a handout to the corkboard that morning showing a street scene with a single dot in the middle of the page and straight lines running out from it in every direction. At the bottom of the sheet, in her looping handwriting, was one instruction: "Draw your orthogonals first." She was outside now helping Avianna stretch a canvas, so there was nobody to ask.

"Orthogonals," Mylo read over his shoulder. "What are those, the lines?"

Jonathan studied the handout. The dot was labeled the vanishing point, and every line that touched it was some edge that ran away from the viewer: the two sides of the road, the curbs along it, the tops of the roofs on either side. Lines that went across the page, like the fronts of the buildings, never touched the dot at all. That was the pattern. He tested it by laying his ruler from the dot to the edge of his paper, then to another edge, then to a spot where a roofline would sit. They all angled back toward that one point like roads merging. "The lines that run back toward the vanishing point," he said slowly, "road edges, curbs, rooflines. Those are the orthogonals." He said the word out loud just to hear how it fit.

He started over on fresh paper, sketching the dot first, then sweeping his ruler four times to set the road edges and curbs, then adding the rooflines so they ran to the same point. The road immediately stopped being a wall and became a road, sliding away from him. Avianna came in with wet canvas on her arm and stopped mid-step.

"Oh," she said. "That one goes somewhere."

"It's an illusion," Jonathan said, grinning. "The paper's flat. My eyes don't think so, though."

Mylo sat down beside him with his own paper, which was sparse compared to Jonathan's, almost empty except for one careful dot. "Lend me your ruler," he said. "I want mine to go somewhere too."

Jonathan slid the ruler across the table, and Mylo's pencil whispered its first line toward the vanishing point.

Paisley spread the ballots across the ping-pong table in the games room at the community centre. There were thirty-three of them, one for each student who had voted yesterday in the mock election Mr. Walker had organized. The Green Team had won seventeen seats out of thirty-three on the classroom map, even though most of the ballots did not say Green.

"That's not fair," said Clarke, dropping into the chair across from her. "Green got almost every riding."

"Ridings are the whole problem," Paisley said. She sorted the ballots into piles by colour. Green had eleven. Blue had nine. Orange had eight. Purple had five. "Eleven out of thirty-three is a third of the vote. But look at the seat chart." She slid Mr. Walker's hand-drawn map across the table. Green had taken seventeen of the thirty-three ridings because its voters were spread out, just enough of them in each one to win it.

Ruben arrived with a laptop and set it down beside the ballots. "Mr. Walker said to look up a real one," he said. "Canada, 2015, federal election." He opened the results page and turned the screen toward them. Paisley leaned in and found the numbers. The Liberal Party had won 184 of 338 seats, a majority, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote.

"Thirty-nine and a half percent," she said slowly, "and they got more than half the seats. More than half." She wrote the two numbers side by side on the whiteboard by the vending machines. "So the same thing happened for real. A third of our voters gave Green more than half our seats, and under forty percent gave the Liberals a majority."

"That's the conventional way we vote, I guess," said Clarke. "Most places do it like that."

"So it's normal," said Ruben.

"Normal isn't the same as fair." Paisley did not want to resent the Green Team, exactly, since nobody had cheated, but she felt something sour sitting in her chest anyway, and she decided to test it. "Ruben, if we counted proportionally, what would Green actually get?"

Ruben divided on the laptop. "Eleven out of thirty-three votes is about a third, so eleven seats."

Paisley rewrote the seat chart on the whiteboard. Green dropped from seventeen to eleven, Blue rose from seven to nine, Orange from six to eight, and Purple from three to five. Nobody had a majority anymore. "Under the first way, Green runs everything on a third of the votes," she said. "Under the second way, they'd have to make a deal with someone."

"That's proportional representation," Ruben said, reading the heading on Mr. Walker's worksheet. "It's right there on the page."

Paisley stood back and looked at the two charts. "My inference is that the seat map hides the real votes," she said. "You can't see the piles just by looking at who won each riding. That's why it felt wrong before I counted."

Mr. Walker came in carrying a box of juice boxes and stopped at the whiteboard. "You found the 2015 numbers?"

"Liberals, 184 out of 338 seats, with about 39.5 percent of the votes," Paisley said. "A majority."

"Hm," said Mr. Walker, and set down the box. "So which system do you three want to argue for on Friday?"

Paisley capped her marker and pointed at the second chart. "This one. And I can prove it with thirty-three ballots."

The first thing Sarah learned about hosting a dinner party was that thirteen-year-old boys eat like seagulls. Her cousin had devoured four rolls before anyone else had finished buttering one, and now he was turning his attention to Inaaya, who had just admitted, very quietly, that she couldn't swim.

"Everyone can swim," her cousin said, mouth half full. "Even my dog can swim. What do you do at the pool, just stand there?"

Sarah's stomach did a small, turbulent flip. Across the table, Larissa caught her eye with a look that said, do something. Sarah put down her fork.

"Stop it," she said. "That's rude."

"Oh, I'm rude?" Her cousin straightened up like a lawyer who had just been handed a winning case. "I'm just asking a question. It's a free country." He turned back to Inaaya. "So do you wear floaties? Do you have little arm floaties?"

Inaaya stared hard at her plate. The plan had backfired. Sarah had challenged him head-on, and now he was twice as loud, because arguing had turned a small tease into a performance with an audience.

Mr. Li, their neighbor, had come over with a lemon cake, and Sarah suddenly remembered it sitting on the counter behind her. She had exactly one piece of information that her cousin wanted more than anything in the world. She took a breath and stood up.

"Grandma's cutting the cake," she announced, loud enough to reach every chair at the table. "The lemon one. Whoever gets the end piece gets the extra frosting."

Her cousin's head whipped around so fast his napkin slid off his lap. "The end piece? That's mine. I called it in the car."

"Nope," said Larissa, catching on instantly. "I called it first. I texted Sarah at four o'clock."

"You did not. That's not a real call!" Her cousin was already half out of his seat, and the swimming topic had gone completely out of his head, like a balloon let go outdoors. Inaaya looked up, and then, to Sarah's surprise, she laughed.

"He fell for the frosting," Inaaya said. "Like a cartoon villain."

Sarah slid into her chair, pleased and a little amazed. She had spent the whole week watching her aunt mediate arguments between her cousin and his little sister, and her aunt never said "stop it." She said things like "who wants to set the table?" or "should we check on the pie?" Every single time, the argument just dissolved, as though it needed an audience to keep breathing. Sarah had suspected there was a rule hiding in there, and tonight she had finally tested it. Distracting worked. You could interrupt teasing without ever challenging the teaser directly, which meant no argument, no "it's a free country," and no audience for the performance.

Mr. Li came in carrying the cake on a blue plate, and Sarah watched her cousin hover at his elbow like a seagull at a fishing dock.

"The end piece goes to whoever was kindest at dinner," Mr. Li said mildly.

"Aunt Sarah," her cousin said instantly. Then he paused, and something crossed his face, slow and grumpy, like weather coming in. He turned toward Inaaya. "Um. If you want, our pool opens in June. I could teach you the basics. I'm basically a fish."

"You're basically a seagull," said Larissa.

"A majestic seagull," her cousin said, holding out his plate. "I'll take the end piece now."

Sydney stood behind the market table with three onions in front of her and a promise she could not take back. She had told Briella she would bring homemade pasta sauce to the sleepover on Saturday, from scratch, no jars, and Briella had laughed in that way that made Sydney feel both embarrassed and stubborn at the same time.

"Tomatoes first," said Mr. Owusu, the farmer whose stall she was helping in exchange for vegetables. He handed her a knife and a bowl of tomatoes. Sydney pressed the blade down on one, pushing hard, and the knife skated off the slick skin and shot sideways across the table. She caught it before it clattered to the ground, her heart thudding.

"That knife's dull," Mr. Owusu said. He pulled another from his canvas roll, tested its edge on a scrap of paper, and handed it over. "Try this one."

Sydney held the new knife above the tomato, waiting for it to slip again. Instead it sank through the skin with almost no pressure at all. She looked at the first knife, then the second, turning the idea over. The dull one had needed her to shove it, and shoving was what made it slip. The sharp one did the work itself. She tested it twice more to be sure: hard push on the old knife, it skidded; light touch on the new one, it cut clean. It seemed backward, a sharp knife being the safer one, but there it was.

Mr. Owusu watched her stack tomato halves. "You figured that out yourself just now, didn't you," he said. It was not really a question.

"Last summer," Sydney said, keeping her eyes on the cutting board, "I cut my thumb trying to slice an apple at my grandma's. I blamed myself for being careless." She had not thought about that day in months, and now it arrived abruptly, complete with the sting and the bandage and her grandma's worried face. Maybe the knife had been dull all along. Maybe she had pushed hard because pushing was the only way to make it work. She did not say any of this out loud, because she was not sure yet, and some judgments she wanted to leave open a while longer.

"Same idea with the onion," Mr. Owusu said. "Curve your fingers under, knuckles forward, like a claw. The knife rides the claw, and the onion takes the sharp edge."

Sydney curled her fingers and set the blade against the onion's papery skin. A light touch, and it fell into even pieces, clean as anything. Domenic wandered over from the honey stall and watched her dice the second onion without a single slip.

"You're making that look easy," he said.

"Concept is simple," Sydney said, smiling at her own half-joke. "It's the knife that does the work." She swept the onion into the pot of tomatoes hissing on the camp stove, and the whole corner of the market began to smell like Saturday.

The Skate Park Committee was supposed to meet at four o'clock under the big oak at the edge of the playground, and Nicholas had the agenda folded in his back pocket. He had written it the night before: call to order, treasurer's report, vote on the spring budget, new business, adjourn. Only three people showed up on time: Nicholas, Ananya, and Joelle.

"Should we wait?" Joelle asked. She was bouncing a tennis ball against the bench.

"The agenda says the meeting starts at four," Nicholas said. "Let's do the treasurer's report first, since that's just reporting, and by the time we get to the vote the others will be here." Ananya read out the numbers from her notebook: the club had forty-two dollars and some approximate amount in coins she hadn't counted. Then she said, "Might as well vote on the budget now. It's us three, that's a majority of the executive anyway."

So they voted. Nicholas counted the hands, wrote "budget passed, 3 to 0" on the agenda, and moved on. Ten minutes later Mr. Mori came across the playground with four club members who had been helping him carry equipment, and one of them, a boy named only by his role as the club's secretary, stopped dead when he heard what they had done. "You voted with three people. Half the club wasn't even here. That doesn't count."

"It counts," Ananya said. "We followed the agenda."

The secretary pulled a folded page from his bag, which turned out to be a letter he had written to the club after last month's chaotic meeting, and read it aloud: "Dear Skate Park Committee. At our last meeting, four members voted to spend the treasury on a ramp while seven others stood around the swings unaware a vote was happening. I looked up meeting procedure, and here is what I found. A quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the group's decisions to count. Our bylaws say that number is five. Until five members are present, nothing the group votes on counts. Respectfully, the secretary."

Nicholas did the arithmetic. Seven members present now, which was more than five. He looked at his agenda, crossed out "budget passed, 3 to 0," and said, "We do the vote again, this time with everyone." Nobody argued, because the letter was right there in black and white.

They went through the budget item by item. Joelle wanted twenty dollars for a repair kit, Ananya argued for saving most of it, and after everyone who wanted to speak had spoken, Nicholas called the vote. It passed, five to two. He wrote the real number on the agenda while the sun pressed down and the back of his neck began to perspire, and he thought that running a meeting was less like being in charge and more like being a referee; the rules weren't his to bend. "Same time next week," he said, holding up the paper. "Bring the letter. I'm pinning it to the oak."

John slid his story across the library table to Henry. "Read it and tell me what's wrong with it. Sophie said it broke somewhere, but she wouldn't say where."

Henry read. The story was about two brothers lost in a jungle with a lush canopy overhead, arguing about which way the river ran. Henry's finger stopped halfway down the second page. "Okay, wait. Who's talking here? One of them says 'We should follow the water,' and then right after, it says 'The water goes east, you're walking us in circles.' Is that the same brother arguing with himself, or the other one?"

"It's the other one. Marcus. The older brother." John leaned over the page. Both lines sat in the same block, with a few sentences of description tucked between them.

"So the reader has to guess." Henry tapped the paper. "I guessed wrong the first time, and then the whole argument made no sense. I thought Caleb was losing his mind."

John took the story back and looked at it. In the books on his shelf at home, conversations never looked like this. He stood, found a copy of Hatchet in the stacks, and opened it to a scene where Brian talked to a pilot, then to himself. Every time the speaker changed, a new paragraph started. When Brian spoke twice in a row, both lines stayed together in one block. John flipped to three more books, and each one did the same thing. "New speaker, new paragraph," he said. "Every time."

"So what do I do?" Henry asked.

"You don't do anything. I fix it." John went back to his seat, took out a pen, and broke the argument apart. Caleb's line about the water became its own paragraph. Marcus's reply moved down below the description of the river fog. He read it again and could hear the two voices separating, one sharp and one tired.

Mr. Yip passed by on his way to the reference shelf and paused. "Is that the draft for Friday? May I offer a critique?"

"You can," John said, "but don't prescribe a fix. I think I found it myself." He handed over the pages anyway.

Mr. Yip read the argument scene, then the climax, where Marcus pulls Caleb back from the riverbank just as the ground gives way. He set the pages down. "The climax lands," he said. "And I always know exactly who is talking."

John took the story back and folded it into his binder. Henry was already reaching for the pen. "Okay, now read it to me out loud. I want to hear the part where the bank collapses."

Arthur sat cross-legged on the living room rug with three index cards, a chewed pencil, and Mahmoud sprawled on the couch above him, eating the last of the pretzels from a bowl that had started out full an hour ago.

"Okay, listen," Arthur said, and read off his first card. "Claim: all kids hate homework. Evidence: a survey in our class showed most people want less of it. Warrant: if people want less of something, they dislike it."

Mahmoud swallowed. "That's the most aggressive thing I've ever heard you say, and you knocked over Micheal's lunch tray in October."

"It's debate. You're supposed to sound sure."

"Fine. I'm the other side." Mahmoud licked salt off his thumb. "Micheal told me yesterday he actually likes his math homework because it calms him down. One kid. Your whole thing just fell apart."

Arthur stared at his card. The clock in the kitchen ticked, and somewhere upstairs a washing machine thumped like a slow heartbeat. He flipped the card over and wrote Micheal's name on the back, as if filing it as evidence against himself.

"So one counterexample kills it," he said slowly. "Then maybe I shouldn't say all." He tried another version, quieter this time. "Most kids hate homework."

"Better," Mahmoud said, "but you just told me your survey said most people want less homework. Wanting less isn't the same as hating. I'd want less rain but I don't hate rain."

Arthur pulled his knees up. He had thought the formula was simple: claim, evidence, warrant, three cards, done. Instead every strong word he picked seemed to have a trapdoor under it. He wrote usually, crossed it out, wrote it again. "Usually kids hate homework. Probably. Most of the time."

"There's a word for that, I think," Mahmoud said, peering over the arm of the couch. "My sister did debate. A qualifier. Usually, most, probably. Words like that."

Arthur wrote the word at the top of a fresh card and underlined it twice. "It's like armor that costs you something," he said. "The claim gets weaker but it gets way harder to knock down."

They drilled it three more times, Mahmoud hurling counterexamples like darts, Arthur adjusting word by word until his case held. When Mahmoud finally couldn't break the third card, he dropped the empty pretzel bowl on the rug and grinned.

Arthur gathered his cards and squared the edges. The case was solid now, careful and small, and he felt a strange pang about that, because the version in his head had been louder and bolder and completely wrong. He put a rubber band around the stack, then set Micheal's name card on top, where he'd see it first.

"Tomorrow," he said, "I'm going to thank Micheal for ruining my homework."

The automatic doors of the pharmacy sighed open, and Adam walked in with his hands still shaking a little. He had not slept at all last night. The science project was due this morning, and he had stayed up until sunrise gluing labels onto his model of the water cycle, and then the alarm had gone off before his eyes ever closed. On the bus, Kenneth had flicked Adam's ear as a joke, and Adam had grabbed Kenneth's wrist so hard that Nicholas had to say, "Whoa, calm down." Adam was here now to buy plasters for the cut on his thumb, which he had gotten from the project's wire frame, and he could not stop replaying the bus.

Mr. Papadopoulos was behind the counter, sorting boxes. "Late night?" he asked, glancing at Adam's face.

"How could you tell?"

"You have the look of every parent who comes in after a newborn." He slid the plasters across the counter. "Rough day too?"

Adam paid for them, then noticed a magazine rack by the window. One cover said YOUR BRAIN ON NO SLEEP in yellow letters. He picked it up while Mr. Papadopoulos helped the next customer, a woman with a cough. Inside, he found a short article. He read one line twice: In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala, a brain area that responds to threats. He whispered the strange word to himself. "Amygdala."

"Did you say something?" Mr. Papadopoulos asked.

"There's this part of the brain, the amygdala. It responds to threats. And in the study, people kept awake for a whole night reacted about 60 percent stronger to upsetting pictures." Adam looked up. "So Kenneth's joke this morning, maybe my brain thought it was a real threat. Because I'm exhausted."

Mr. Papadopoulos shrugged. "I sell plasters, not brains. But you look like you just solved a mystery."

It did feel like solving something, the way finding a hidden wire explains why a model tilts. The ear flick had been temporary, tiny, and his reaction had been huge. Maybe his brain's whole alarm network had been turned up loud by the sleepless night. Adam wondered: could he test this? He decided on a small experiment. Tonight he would do the opposite of last night, same bedtime three nights in a row, phone in the kitchen, and he would see whether small jokes felt small again.

Before leaving, he tried one more thing. He stood by the rack, put a hand on his stomach, and breathed in slowly through his nose for four counts, out for six, the way the magazine suggested. His shoulders dropped half an inch. The shaking in his hands did not vanish, but it did diminish, going quiet like a radio turned down.

At school the next morning, Kenneth flicked Adam's ear again. Adam turned, grinned, and flicked him right back.

The gymnasium smelled like hot glue and floor wax, and the air was so humid that Easton's display board curled slightly at the corners. He smoothed it flat and taped it down again, then stood back and stared at the word he had lettered across the top in blue marker: HYPOTHESIS. His project asked which brand of battery kept an LED burning longest, and his guess had been that the expensive brand would win. It had not. The cheap battery was still glowing on his table after nineteen hours, and the fancy one had died at midnight.

Kiaan leaned over from the next table, where his volcano oozed baking-soda foam onto a tray. "You look like your dog died."

"My hypothesis was wrong," Easton said. He said the word slowly, like a stone in his mouth. Last month he had nearly skipped writing one at all. Mr. Gagnon had circled the empty spot on his rough draft and written one word back: why? Easton had stayed up late that night making something up, just to fill the box, and he had envied Kiaan, whose volcano needed no guessing at all. Now the guess he had invented to please a teacher was the thing being proven wrong in public, under fluorescent lights, with judges walking the aisles.

Amina wandered over with her clipboard, judging sheet and all, because she had signed up as a student marshal for the extra credit. "What does that word even mean? Hypothesis?"

Easton opened his notebook to the page where he had looked it up for the board. "It comes from ancient Greek," he said. "It literally means putting or placing under."

Amina frowned. "Placing under? Under what?"

"That's what I asked. I thought I'd copied it wrong." He turned the notebook so she could see the printed page. "A hypothesis is something you place under your experiment. Like a foundation. You build the test on top of it." He had read that three times in his kitchen, the window open, a train horn far off, before it finally clicked.

"So yours was placed under and then crushed," Kiaan said, grinning.

"Basically." Easton looked at the little LED, still burning, stubborn and orange. Here was the part he kept turning over: if he had never written the guess, he would have run the same test and gotten the same result. But he would not have felt the result land anywhere. The wrongness needed something to be wrong about. He wasn't sure yet whether that made the guessing worth it or just painful, and he didn't try to settle it while the judges were circling.

Mr. Gagnon stopped at his table and read the whole board, top to bottom, including the part where Easton had written in red marker: My hypothesis was overturned. The cheap battery lasted longer. Then he tapped the still-glowing LED with one finger, like ringing a tiny doorbell.

"That one," Easton said, "still hasn't quit."

Lillian counted the broken toothpicks on the lab table and wrote down the number before she forgot it. The science fair was on Friday, and her bridge model still sagged in the middle like a tired hammock. Across the table, Teresa was supposed to be recording data, but she had filled the whole margin of the notebook with tiny spirals.

"Third trial," Lillian said, laying the last toothpick across the span. The bridge groaned and collapsed. Teresa didn't even look up.

That was the third time this week. Teresa, who last year had won the fair with a volcano she had rebuilt four times, now spent lunch in the library and flinched when the bell rang. Lillian wondered what had changed. It wasn't the project, because Teresa still knew every formula. It wasn't her family, because her little brother still waved at her through the gym window every Tuesday. Maybe it was something Lillian couldn't see at all, something running underneath like a wire inside the bridge.

On Thursday, Lillian tried a small test. She set a timer and simulated the fair, calling out like a judge would. "Contestant, explain your structure." Teresa's hands started shaking so hard she knocked over the glue bottle. She fled to the hallway, and Lillian found her sitting against the lockers with her knees pulled up.

"I'm not being dramatic over something trivial," Teresa said before Lillian could speak. "I keep telling myself it's just a bridge, it's just a crowd, but my heart pounds anyway. It's been like this since October. I couldn't even go to Angelica's party."

Lillian sat down beside her. "That's not trivial. That's a long time."

Teresa wiped her eyes. "My mom took me to a doctor last month. I told her everything, and she said it's an anxiety disorder. That's what it's called when the anxiety is really intense and it lasts a long time and it gets in the way of daily life." She picked at her sleeve. "Feeling anxious sometimes is normal. Everybody gets that. Mine just went past normal. The good part is it's treatable. I started seeing someone for it, and some days are already better."

"So it can get better," Lillian said slowly. It was like finding the actual weak joint in the bridge instead of guessing. "Then we build around it. Tomorrow I'll present our data, and you stand next to me and hold the notebook. If a judge asks you something, you can squeeze my elbow and I'll take it. Deal?"

"Deal," Teresa said, and almost smiled. "Also, your load is off center. That's why it keeps failing."

On Friday, Mr. Rossi paused at their table, nodded at the rebuilt span, and said it reminded him of his pension planning, "boring but sturdy, built to hold up for years." Teresa held the notebook steady through the whole presentation, and when the ribbons were handed out, theirs was red. Lillian felt the squeeze on her elbow, but this time Teresa was just pointing at the ribbon, saying, "Third place. We built that."

Hayden pushed through the pool doors on Tuesday feeling like a champion, which lasted exactly until he reached the stairs to the bleachers and his legs announced they were on strike. He gripped the railing and took the steps sideways, like a crab in swim trunks.

"You too?" Alma said from three steps up, lowering herself with both hands on the rail. "Yesterday after tryouts I felt amazing. I walked home. I had a snack. I ruled the world." She winced as she sat down. "Now I can barely fold myself into a chair."

Brodie arrived behind them, walking like a robot with low batteries. "Do not make me laugh," he said. "Laughing uses my stomach." He lowered himself onto the bench in one careful motion, then looked around the pool with narrowed eyes. "Something weird is going on. Everyone who swam hard Monday is hobbling today. The kids who didn't come Monday are fine. Is the pool cursed? Did someone put a hex in the deep end?"

Hayden had been wondering the same thing, sort of, minus the hex. He watched the other swimmers, counting. His sister had complained once after her first soccer practice of the season, but not that night. It hit her the day after, and worse the day after that. "I think it's not the pool," he said slowly. "I think it's timing. The soreness shows up late. Like a delayed package."

"A delayed package of pain," Alma said. "Worst mail ever."

At that moment a kid named Theo, who had felt so great Monday evening that he'd done a victory lap around the parking lot, attempted to climb the block for warm-up and made a noise like a startled goose. Mr. Pérez, the coach, just nodded as if he'd seen this exact thing every season for twenty years. "Anyone who says the word 'delayed' today gets out of treading-water drills," he called, and then pretended he hadn't said anything.

"Dude," Alma whispered, poking Hayden's arm, which he felt everywhere. "What's the word for when it hits later like this? My mom said it once. Delayed onset something."

"Delayed onset muscle soreness," said a girl from the next row, without looking up from stretching her calves. "It's usually worst 24 to 72 hours after a workout your body isn't used to." She flexed one foot and grimaced. "So tomorrow might be even worse than today. Plan accordingly." She said it like a weather report, then hobbled off toward the blocks, deeply buoyant despite everything, practically floating on her own smugness.

Hayden tested the idea in his head like a math problem. Monday was the hard, unfamiliar workout. Tuesday was one day later, and half the pool was walking like penguins. So Wednesday and Thursday, days two and three, could be the peak of the disaster. Factor in the fact that today's tryout would give their muscles new work to complain about, and Friday's final cut might happen right when everyone's legs were at their most dramatic. Which meant the swimmers who paced themselves, who migrated to the easier lanes and saved their arms, would look fresh exactly when it counted.

"Okay," he said, standing up in stages like a collapsing tent in reverse. "New plan. We go hard enough to make the team today, but we save the hero stuff. Our real competition is Thursday, when everyone else is noodle-legged."

Alma saluted, which hurt her shoulder, which made Brodie laugh, which hurt his stomach, which made Theo laugh from the blocks, which made him wobble, which made the whole pool go briefly, gloriously quiet.

"Steady," Mr. Pérez said, but he was smiling.

Hayden took the stairs down one careful crab-step at a time.

At his grandmother's backyard party, Owen sat at the wobbly card table with his cousin Jamie, scrolling through his phone while the grown-ups argued about the potato salad. Jamie had shown him a blog post claiming that a certain mushroom supplement could cure headaches in three days, because the writer's uncle had tried it and felt better. "See?" Jamie said. "Proof."

Owen wanted to believe it, because his mother got headaches all the time and he hated watching her lie down in the dark after work. But something bothered him. "One guy feeling better isn't really proof," he said. "Maybe his headache was going away anyway." Jamie rolled his eyes and stole a chip.

Across the yard, their neighbor Mr. Dang was grilling burgers, and Owen drifted over to him, since Mr. Dang worked at the university and always wore a T-shirt with a skeleton on it. "If someone writes something online," Owen asked, "how do you know if it's actually science?" Mr. Dang flipped a patty and squinted. "Depends where it's published. A blog is just one person typing. But before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors." He snapped his tongs. "It's called peer review." Then he went back to arguing with Owen's uncle about charcoal.

Owen had an idea. He walked back to the table and told Jamie they should look up the mushroom thing in an actual journal, not just the blog. They found the library's database on Owen's phone, and after some clumsy searching they found a real paper about the same supplement. The study had tested it on lots of people, not just one uncle, and the results showed it barely did anything for headaches. Owen felt a small, flat disappointment, but also something like satisfaction, the way a puzzle piece clicks even when the picture isn't what you hoped.

"So the blog guy just assumed it worked because of his uncle," Jamie said slowly, chewing the chip. Owen nodded. "And his motivation was probably selling the supplement. There was a link to buy it at the bottom." Jamie looked at his phone like it had tricked him personally.

Later, when everyone gathered around the picnic table for watermelon, Owen's mother asked what they'd been doing all afternoon. Before Owen could answer, Jamie said, "Owen proved that mushroom thing is fake." "We didn't prove anything," Owen said, cutting himself a slice. "The journal people checked it first. We just read it." His mother raised an eyebrow, and the aunts, in rare unanimous agreement, declared the watermelon excellent this year. Owen slid the biggest piece onto his mother's plate.

Dylan's backyard was too small for a real field, so he and Zaynab had marked out goals with laundry baskets at either end of the grass. It was the last week of July, and the air felt like a wet towel pressed against his face. He dribbled around Zaynab anyway, shot, and watched the ball skim the basket and roll into the hedge.

"Rematch Saturday," Zaynab said, flopping onto the porch steps. "But I'm dead. We only played twenty minutes."

Dylan sat down beside her, shirt soaked, though he'd barely sprinted. That was the strange part. Last August he remembered a practice in Texas at his cousin's house where the thermometer read higher, and he'd felt tired but fine afterward. Today felt worse than that, and cooler. He turned the idea over while a cicada droned somewhere in the maple.

At Saturday's game, the problem returned with company. Simona, who usually ran the whole field twice without stopping, kept her hands on her knees at halftime, her face flushed. Dylan's own head ached in a dull, steady way. The other team, their usual adversary from across town, looked just as wrecked, so at least it was even.

The next morning Dylan decided to invest an hour in figuring it out. He spread a damp dish towel over the porch rail in the thick morning air and a second damp towel on a chair inside the air-conditioned kitchen. He checked them every ten minutes. The indoor towel went stiff and dry first. The outdoor one stayed limp, cool to the touch but dripping long after. He didn't have a name for what he was watching, but he could see that something in the sticky air was slowing the towels down.

"You look like a scientist," Zaynab said, arriving for practice with a water bottle the size of a fire extinguisher.

"Watch this." He held up both towels. "The one inside dried in half the time. Same water, same kind of towel. The wet air outside is the difference." He rubbed his forearm, still damp from an hour ago. "Sweat's the same. It cools you when it dries off you. When the air's already full of water, it dries slow, so it barely cools you at all. That's why we die out there even when it's not the hottest day."

"So the Texas practice," Zaynab said slowly.

"Dry air. The sweat dried fast. It was hotter but it worked better." He was already changing his mind about the week's plan. No more full-field scrimmages in August humidity. Short drills, long shade breaks, cold water on the wrists. Maybe even practice in the evening, when the air sometimes thinned out.

From the fence, Mr. Aydın, who had been watering his tomatoes in a slow, indifferent drift that wet half of Dylan's lawn as well, called over, "You two should be drinking more of that."

"We figured that out," Dylan said. He tossed Zaynab the ball, backing toward the basket goal. "First one to three, then we sit in the shade like sensible people."

The cultural center smelled like cardamom and hot oil, and Dominic stood near the door holding his mother's coat because she had gone to find his aunt among the crowd. Outside, a procession was forming for Vaisakhi, and he could hear drums beating somewhere down the block, deep thumps he felt in his ribs.

Dominic wanted to know why this day mattered so much, but he did not want to ask and look like the only one who did not know. He had tried reading a poster in the lobby, but it just showed a schedule. So he made a plan: if he stood near the stage where families gathered, someone would probably tell the story out loud, and he could listen without asking.

He found a spot beside a family from his school, and next to them stood Khloe from his math class. A small girl tugged her uncle's sleeve and said, "Why is everyone so happy today?" The uncle crouched down. "Vaisakhi is the day, in 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," he said. Khloe caught Dominic's eye and whispered, "That's the community of initiated Sikhs, I think. My dad told me once."

Dominic tested his idea again at the craft table, where Ernest was attempting a paper flag with orange and blue. "Did you hear that story too?" Dominic asked. Ernest shook his head, so Dominic repeated the uncle's words, and Ernest nodded slowly. "So that's why the procession stops at certain corners," Ernest said. "They're retelling it, like stations." Dominic had not thought of that. He felt a small flush of pride that his listening had worked, and also a little embarrassed that he had been biased against asking in the first place, assuming everyone else had been born knowing things he had to hunt down.

They followed the procession out onto the street, where the drums got louder and the crowd spilled past the storefronts like a river pushing past its banks, a frontier of orange fabric moving down the block. Khloe walked with them, and the three of them stopped at each corner where the procession paused. Dominic noticed that people who knew the story explained it to people who did not, freely, without anyone having to disclose that they were confused.

At the last corner, the small girl from before ran up to Dominic and held out a piece of sweet she had been given, an extra one. "You were listening to my uncle too," she said. "He tells it the best." Dominic took the sweet and said, "He really does." The drums rolled again, and the whole street surged forward together.

The classroom smelled like whiteboard marker and nervous kid, and Wyatt was one of the nervous kids. Twelve spellers stood in a line at the front while Mr. Crowchild shuffled his index cards at the podium. Nylah leaned over from the next spot and whispered, "You look like you're about to be launched into space."

"I'm fine," Wyatt whispered back, which was a lie. He had studied every night for two weeks, and last night his dad had said, "Consider it income, all those words you're banking," which had made sense only because Wyatt was saving up for a new bike.

The first three rounds knocked out half the line. Saanvi got out on "raspberry," missing the silent p, and sat down at a desk in the front row with her arms crossed, watching like a hawk. Then it was just Wyatt, a kid from another class, and Nylah, who breezed through "picnic" like it was her own name.

"Chorus," said Mr. Crowchild. "Language of origin: Greek."

Wyatt opened his mouth and then closed it. The k sound. K? C? Something else? He assumed the k sound was always spelled with a k or a c, but wait. Greek. His brain flipped back to the study list, where "chorus" had sat next to "chaos," and he'd noticed both started with a ch that sounded like k. Both from Greek. So Greek words used ch for that sound, and this word was Greek, so it probably started with ch. He was guessing, but it was a guess with a shape to it.

"C-h-o-r-u-s. Chorus."

"Correct," said Mr. Crowchild, and Wyatt let out a breath that had been waiting in his chest since Tuesday.

Next round, Nylah got "chef." Mr. Crowchild said, "Language of origin: French." Nylah frowned, spelled it with a k, and sat down next to Saanvi with a groan. She pointed a finger at Wyatt. "Wait. You did the same sound in chorus with a ch. Why does yours work and mine doesn't?"

"It's the French," Wyatt said, still working it out as he said it. "The sh in 'chef' comes from French. The k sound in 'chorus' is spelled ch because it comes from Greek. French spells it sh, Greek spells it ch." Nylah stared at him, then laughed, which was better than the glare he'd been expecting.

"That's ridiculous. That's actually brilliant. I'm mad I didn't know that."

"One more word and we're done," said Mr. Crowchild, holding up the final card. His face was neutral, but his eyes had that glint teachers get when they know they've got a good one. Wyatt planted his feet and waited.

"Monarch," said Mr. Crowchild. "Language of origin: Greek."

Alexandre unfolded the card table in the gymnasium and set out twelve little cups, each one labeled in his neatest handwriting: lemon juice, soap water, vinegar, baking soda mix, cola, and seven more. His poster read THE INVISIBLE COLOR OF CHEMICALS, and beside it sat a stack of thin strips that looked like scraps of purple paper. The judge would come by at ten thirty, which gave him forty minutes to fix his problem: three of his samples were turning the strips the wrong color, and he had no idea why.

"You look like your project is fighting you," said Sehaj, leaning over from the next table, where a volcano oozed baking-soda foam onto a tray.

"It is." Alexandre held up two strips, one pink, one blue. "I tested the soap twice and got two different answers. If I can't trust the paper, I can't trust anything on my table."

Sehaj picked up a strip and turned it over. "Where did you even get these?"

"Ms. Girma lent me the pack from the science room." Alexandre stopped. Ms. Girma had also lent him a book about indicators, which he had shoved in his backpack and never opened. He dug it out now, and Isa, who had wandered over from her table about magnets, read the page he flipped to out loud. "Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark."

"Lichens?" Isa said. "Like that scratchy gray stuff on my grandma's garden wall? That's in this paper?"

Alexandre looked at the strip in his hand and felt the whole problem turn over in his mind. The paper wasn't some factory chemical with rules he couldn't see. It came from something growing on rocks and bark, and if it was a living dye, maybe it could go stale, or get damp, or be damaged by heat. He had kept the strips in his back pocket all morning while he carried his boxes. His own body heat and sweat could have ruined a few without leaving any mark he could see.

He laid out a test. From the borrowed pack he took six fresh strips he had never handled, using tweezers from the art kit Isa carried. He tested the soap again, twice, with fresh strips and with the pocket-warmed ones. The fresh strips both turned blue. The pocket ones gave him the scrambled answers. "It's not the soap," he said. "It's me. I cooked the strips."

"So the invisible thing wasn't the acid," Isa said slowly. "It was the damage you couldn't see either."

When Ms. Girma stopped at his table with her clipboard, he walked her through it, and he even advocated labeling every kit "keep strips cool and dry," since half the class would probably carry them in pockets too. She wrote something down and smiled. Alexandre won a red ribbon, third place, behind Isa's magnets and Sehaj's volcano.

After the fair, his mother picked him up early so they could stop by his grandfather's house. Waiting at the gate, Alexandre ran his thumb over the crusty gray growths on the garden wall and thought about how much of chemistry seemed to be like this: rules you couldn't watch working, causes you had to corner with a test, and the insight that the proportional effort of one careful morning of checking your tools was worth more than an afternoon of guessing. The wall was damp where a sprinkler had sprayed it. He peeled a tiny fleck of lichen loose, folded it into his notebook, and put the notebook in his front pocket, where he promised himself it would stay cool and dry.

At the ribbon ceremony, Sehaj had slipped Alexandre's own pocket-warmed strips into the cup labeled lemon juice, so Alexandre's display card, photographed by the local paper, showed vinegar turning blue and lemon juice turning pink under a heading that read, "Student masters the pH scale." The photographer looked at his camera, looked at the table, and said, "Kid, that's the best one I've seen all day."

Willow had wanted to sign up for the ropes course on the first day of camp, but by Thursday she still hadn't climbed higher than the second rung. Every time she looked up at the platform, her heart pounded so hard she could feel it in her ears, and she told the coach her harness felt loose even when it didn't.

At dinner in the mess hall, she pushed around the camp cuisine, which everyone agreed was not authentic anything, just noodles and mystery stew. Nathaniel sat down across from her with his tray. "You froze again today," he said. "Same as Tuesday."

"I despise that course," Willow said, though that wasn't quite true, and she knew it. What she despised was the shaky, breathless feeling that took her over at the bottom of the ladder. She tried to picture the last three attempts, looking for a pattern. On Tuesday her shoulders had been up near her ears. Wednesday, same thing. "Nathaniel, put your hand on your stomach and take a breath," she said suddenly.

He raised an eyebrow but did it. "Okay. Now what?"

"Watch your shoulders too." Willow put her own hand on her belly and breathed in. Her shoulders rose; her stomach stayed flat. His did the same. "We're breathing wrong," she said. "Mr. Lindqvist said one word to me after the swim test, belly breathing, but I didn't listen."

Mr. Lindqvist ran the waterfront, and that evening Willow found him coiling rope by the dock. "Is belly breathing where your stomach goes out instead of your shoulders going up?" she asked.

"That's the one," he said, and went back to his rope.

Willow and Nathaniel practiced on the bunk porch until lights-out. On the tenth try, her belly finally rose while her shoulders stayed still, and the breath felt longer, deeper, like it actually reached somewhere. She made herself do it slowly ten times in her sleeping bag, and for the first time all week she fell asleep before the crickets quit.

Friday morning she stood at the ladder again. Halfway up, her heart started hammering, and she felt her shoulders creeping toward her ears. She stopped, hung there, put one hand flat against her belly, and breathed in until her stomach pushed against her palm. Three breaths. Her shoulders dropped. She climbed the last four rungs and pulled herself onto the platform, where Nathaniel was already waiting.

"Figured it out," he said.

"Still figuring," Willow said, and looked down at the lake.

Emilia checked her reflection in the concession stand window for the third time since kickoff. Behind her, the whole crowd groaned as the away team scored, but she barely noticed, because Terrance was walking toward her with two hot chocolates and a nervous grin that matched her own.

"You made it," he said, handing her one. "I thought maybe you'd bail."

"Bail? I've been planning this since Tuesday." As soon as she said it, she regretted it. Too eager. But Terrance laughed, a real laugh, and then she felt something worse than regret: her whole face heating up like a stove left on.

She turned toward the field fast. "Great defense," she muttered, to nobody.

Brooklyn appeared beside her with a foam finger and no mercy. "Your face is the color of a stop sign."

"I know." Emilia kept her eyes on the game. She had read something months ago in a science magazine in Ms. Pham's classroom, and now she was trying to piece it back together. Blushing was blood, she remembered that much. Something about blood vessels widening, letting more blood flow near the skin. That was why faces turned red, and why, she reasoned, pressing something cold against her cheeks might shrink that flow back down. She tested the idea immediately, pressing the hot chocolate cup against her cheek even though it was warm and made everything worse.

"Smooth," Brooklyn said.

"Shut up. It was worth a try."

By the start of the fourth quarter, the score was tied and the crowd had gotten loud, everyone sensing the game climbing toward its climax. Emilia had stopped trying to hide every blush. When Terrance joked that her cheering had probably frightened the quarterback into fumbling, she laughed, went red again, and just let him see it.

"You do that a lot," he said, not unkindly.

"Blushing? Yeah. It means the blood vessels in my face are widening, letting more blood flow near the skin." She shrugged. "Apparently my face can't keep a secret."

Terrance turned red himself. "Huh. Mine too, then."

The clock wound down, and with eleven seconds left the home team kicked the winning field goal. The stands exploded, and Terrance, catching her hand in the chaos of everyone standing and screaming, held on even after the noise faded. The scoreboard lights blinked. Her cheeks burned, and this time she didn't turn away.

"Hot chocolate rematch next Friday?" he asked.

Isaac had four days to learn the trumpet solo for Friday's assembly, and one Saturday free. He spread his music on the bed, looked at the clock, and decided to do all two hours at once. He played the same sixteen measures until his lips buzzed, then played them again. By dinnertime he could get through the solo, mostly.

On Monday, in the music classroom, his lips had gone soft again. Mr. Chen set the metronome ticking and Isaac fumbled the same passage, the one with the tricky leap up to the high G. Mr. Chen just said, "Again." Isaac missed it again.

"You sounded fine Saturday," Isaac told Karl after class. Karl had heard him through his bedroom wall all weekend.

"Fine how?" Karl said. "You played it, like, forty times in a row."

Isaac thought about that on the walk home. Forty times in a row, and now it was gone. He thought about how he had learned his locker combination last fall. He hadn't drilled it for an hour. He'd tried it once each morning, and by Thursday his hand knew it without looking. Maybe the same total time worked differently if he split it up.

So he ran a test on himself. He still had two hours left before Friday, so he parceled it out: twenty minutes Monday night, twenty Tuesday, twenty Wednesday, twenty Thursday. Each night the passage started rough, then came back faster than the night before. By Thursday's session he hit the high G on the second try, then every try after that.

Loukas, who sat first trumpet, had his own problem. He'd been cramming his scales the night before every lesson and kept stumbling on the same ones. Isaac mentioned what he'd tried, keeping it short. Loukas shrugged, but on Wednesday he showed up at Isaac's desk. "I did fifteen minutes a night instead of one big block. Same total time, I checked. It's better. That's annoying, actually." Isaac just grinned and kept packing his bag.

Friday came, and the gym filled with the whole school plus parents who'd bought tickets, since ticket revenue paid for the new risers the band needed. Isaac stood in the second row. When his sixteen measures arrived, his fingers moved before he had to think, and the high G came out clean and bright, hanging in the air over the gym.

Afterward, Mr. Chen found him by the doors. "That was a significant improvement since Monday. What changed?"

Isaac held up his trumpet case. "Short practice. Lots of days in a row."

"Good," said Mr. Chen. "Same time Monday."

Loukas elbowed him. "Told you it was annoying."

Juliette had a talk to give on Monday about how a river carves a canyon, and she had exactly one idea: build a river in the kitchen sink. She layered sand, dirt from the flowerpot, and flour into a glass baking dish, pressing each layer flat. Flour on the bottom, sand in the middle, dirt on top. It looked like a sad dessert.

Zac arrived just as she turned on the faucet. "What are we supposed to be learning from this?" he asked, dragging a stool to the counter.

"Watch the water." She angled the dish so a thin stream cut across the layers. At first nothing happened, which was annoying. Then the stream found a low spot and began to chew into the top layer, carrying brown crumbs downstream in a muddy plume. Where the water slowed at the far end, the crumbs settled into a tiny fan. "There," she said. "The river digs where it's fast and drops stuff where it's slow. It's erosion and deposition at the same time."

Zac leaned in. "Okay, but if it keeps cutting, it gets down to the sand. Then the flour. Then what?"
